**Key terms.** a patch file is an e-mail; `From:`, `Date:` and `Subject:` become author, author date and subject; diffstat is ignored; committer is whoever runs `git am`; same patch ID, new commit ID; `base-commit`

**Common weak answer.** "A patch file is a diff, and `git am` recreates the same commit." Weak because it is an e-mail whose headers carry the author and the message, and the applied commit is a new object with another committer and another commit ID. Only the tree and the patch ID are equal.

**Follow-up.** The maintainer's branch has moved and the series no longer applies. What do you see, what do you run, and what could the contributor have done to make this cheaper?

**A strong reply covers.** `git am` stops and reports that the patch does not apply; `git am --show-current-patch=diff` shows it. Run `git am --abort`, then `git am -3` and resolve. The contributor's part is `--base` in `git format-patch`, so that the series states its base and is applied to it.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14D](../textbook/ch14d-frontier.md), section 14D.11 and 14D.12

#### Q76

**Question.** Explain geometric repacking with three packs of 500, 30 and 30 objects. What happens at the next run, and what is never rewritten?

**Model answer.** Geometric repacking keeps packs in a sequence in which each is at least twice as large as the next, counted in objects, by merging only the small ones. `git repack --geometric=2` computes a cut over the existing packs: the packs that break the progression are repacked into one, and as many of the larger packs as possible are left intact. With 500, 30 and 30, the two small packs break the rule, because 30 is not at least twice 30. At the next run those two are merged, together with the loose objects written since, into one pack of sixty objects plus the new ones; provided 500 is still at least twice that, the progression holds again and the pack of 500 is not rewritten. That is the purpose: the cost of a run is proportional to the new data and not to the repository, whereas `git gc` and `git repack -a` rewrite everything every time. Chapter 26, section 26.4 shows the same with packs of 507, 24 and 24 becoming 507 and 104.

**Key terms.** each pack at least twice the next; size counted in objects; only the small packs merge; cost proportional to new data; the large pack is left intact; `git repack --geometric=2`

**Common weak answer.** "It merges all packs into one, more efficiently." Weak because the purpose is the opposite: only the packs that break the progression are merged and the large pack is left alone, which is why several packs are the normal state of a healthy repository.

**Follow-up.** With packs of 507 and 24 objects the next run merges nothing and leaves a third pack behind. Why, and is a growing number of packs a problem to fix?

**A strong reply covers.** The cut is computed over the packs that exist; 507 and 24 are in progression, so nothing is merged and the new loose objects become a pack of their own. Several packs are normal and the multi-pack-index makes them cheap to read; hundreds of packs with no multi-pack-index mean maintenance has not run.

**Reference.** [Chapter 26](../textbook/ch26-performance.md), section 26.4


### Git internals: senior level

#### Q77

**Question.** We have six versions of a 16 MB file. What does the pack contain, which version is stored whole, and what happens when a byte in that version is damaged?

**Model answer.** If the six versions differ in a few lines, the pack holds one version whole, compressed with zlib, and five small deltas: lists of copy and insert instructions against a base object. In the demonstration of Chapter 3, section 3.7 the newest version is the whole one and the older versions form a chain of depth one to five, the opposite of what "Git stores diffs" suggests; the choice of base is a heuristic and may change at any repack. Every object still reads back complete, because IDs are computed from full content and packing changes none of them. Damage to a byte of the whole version therefore affects more than one object: the other versions are rebuilt from that base, so reading them fails as well, and `git verify-pack` names the offset. The fix is to restore the pack from a backup or another clone, or to recreate the base object from intact content and repack. If the file is a compressed archive or model weights, deltas gain nothing, because deltas need similar bytes.

**Key terms.** one base stored whole; delta chain; newest version whole in the demonstration; full content on every read; `git verify-pack`; restore from another clone or backup; base choice is a heuristic

**Common weak answer.** "Git stores the first version and a diff for each later commit, so only one version is affected." Weak because the demonstration shows the newest version whole and the older ones as deltas, a delta is between similar objects and not per commit, and damage to a base breaks every object whose chain passes through it.

**Follow-up.** Why does the size on disk of one version tell you little about which commit made the repository large, and how do you measure storage per object?

**A strong reply covers.** A delta is between two objects chosen for similarity, not the change a commit made, and the base is arbitrary and can change at a repack. `git cat-file --batch-check` with `%(objectsize)`, `%(objectsize:disk)` and `%(deltabase)` shows the logical size, the cost in the pack and the base of each object.

**Reference.** [Chapter 3](../textbook/ch03-git-internals.md), section 3.7 and 3.15

#### Q78

**Question.** `git fsck` says `dangling commit`. Walk me through what you check before you decide whether anything is at risk.

**Model answer.** Nothing is at risk yet, and the risky step would be a cleanup, so I change nothing first; `git fsck` itself only reads. Dangling means an unreachable object that no other unreachable object refers to: the tip of a lost line, so finding it finds everything behind it. I inspect the commit with `git cat-file -p` or `git log` on its ID, then check `git reflog` to see whether a reflog entry names it. Two cases are routine. A commit that only `FETCH_HEAD` names is reported, because that file is not a starting point for reachability. And since Git 2.53, `git fsck` skips reflog entries dated after the moment it starts, so a commit made with a wrong clock or a scripted `GIT_COMMITTER_DATE` looks dangling although the reflog lists it; `git gc` does not apply that rule and keeps the commit. If the commit matters, I give it a ref with `git branch rescue/<x> <id>`. What would put it at risk is `git gc --prune=now`, or the two-week grace period running out once no reflog entry holds it.

**Key terms.** unreachable versus dangling; starting points of `git fsck`; reflog entry; reflog entry dated in the future; grace period; `git branch rescue/<x> <id>`; do not prune

**Common weak answer.** "Dangling commits are garbage; run `git gc --prune=now` to clean up." Weak because dangling describes where `git fsck` started looking, not what will be deleted, and the proposed cleanup destroys the recovery material.

**Follow-up.** Git 2.55.0 reports a dangling commit and Apple's Git 2.50.1 on the same Mac reports nothing for the same repository. Explain the disagreement and say which source you trust.

**A strong reply covers.** The rule that skips reflog entries newer than the start of the run arrived in Git 2.53.0, so 2.55.0 applies it and Apple's 2.50.1 does not. The reflog is the authority: it still names the commit, and `git gc` ignores the rule, so nothing is deleted.

**Reference.** [Chapter 3](../textbook/ch03-git-internals.md), section 3.8 and 3.10

#### Q79

**Question.** Why can a corrupt object survive `git cat-file` and `git status` but not a clone over the network?

**Model answer.** Because Git does not recompute an object's ID on every read. Ordinary commands look the object up by its name and serve what the file contains. In Chapter 3, section 3.8 a loose object is overwritten with a valid zlib stream that has the same header and length but other content; `git cat-file -p` prints the altered content with exit status 0 and `git status` reports nothing. Two operations do recompute IDs. `git fsck` hashes what it finds, compares the result with the file name, and reports a mismatch and a missing blob. And Git's transport sends object content without IDs: the receiving side computes every ID itself, so an object cannot arrive under a name its content does not have, and the clone fails. The caveat is that `git clone` from a local path skips the transport and copies or hard-links the files, bad object included; `--no-local` forces the transport. That substitution was crafted. Random damage such as a flipped bit normally breaks the zlib stream and fails loudly on the first read.

**Key terms.** no recomputation on read; `git fsck` recomputes IDs; transport sends content without IDs; receiver computes every ID; local clone copies or hard-links; `--no-local`

**Common weak answer.** "Git verifies checksums whenever it reads an object, so corruption is always caught." Weak because the transcript shows a well-formed object with wrong content served as it is; only `git fsck` and a transfer through Git's transport recompute IDs, and a clone from a local path does not.

**Follow-up.** How do you repair that object without another clone, and why does Git not replace the bad file when you write the correct content?

**A strong reply covers.** Content alone determines the ID, so `git hash-object -w` on the intact file in the working tree recreates the object, and a clean `git fsck` proves it. Git will not rewrite an object it believes it has, so the bad file under `objects/` must be removed first.

**Reference.** [Chapter 3](../textbook/ch03-git-internals.md), section 3.8

#### Q80

**Question.** What is the difference between `ORIG_HEAD`, `FETCH_HEAD` and `refs/heads/main` as far as garbage collection is concerned?

**Model answer.** Only `refs/heads/main` protects anything. The starting points for reachability are the refs under `refs/`, `HEAD`, the reflogs and the index, and garbage collection keeps what those reach. `ORIG_HEAD` is a root ref: an ordinary ref stored outside `refs/`, which `git update-ref` can write and which has no reflog of its own. `FETCH_HEAD` is a pseudoref: a file with one line per fetched ref plus notes, which `git update-ref` refuses to write. Neither is a starting point. Chapter 3, section 3.10 fetches a teammate's branch by path so that it lands in `FETCH_HEAD` only; `git fsck` reports the commit as dangling, and `git gc --prune=now` deletes it, after which the name is still there and resolves to nothing. So a commit named only by `FETCH_HEAD`, a position saved only in `ORIG_HEAD`, or a tree in `AUTO_MERGE` is protected by nothing except the two-week grace period. The rule that follows: give anything you rely on a ref under `refs/` before you depend on it.

**Key terms.** starting points for reachability; root ref; pseudoref; not a starting point; grace period only; give it a ref

**Common weak answer.** "They are all refs, so whatever they point at is kept." Weak because only the refs under `refs/`, `HEAD`, the reflogs and the index are starting points; the transcript shows a commit named only by `FETCH_HEAD` deleted by a prune.

**Follow-up.** A reviewer fetches a colleague's branch by URL, intending to inspect it next week. What should the command have been, and what is the exposure if it was not?

**A strong reply covers.** `git fetch <url> <branch>:refs/heads/review/<name>`, or `git switch -c review/<name> FETCH_HEAD` straight afterwards, so that a ref under `refs/` names the commit. Otherwise only the grace period protects it, and the next fetch overwrites `FETCH_HEAD`, so even the name is lost.

**Reference.** [Chapter 3](../textbook/ch03-git-internals.md), section 3.10 and 3.8

#### Q81

**Question.** A release script reads `.git/refs/heads/main` and checks that the content is forty hexadecimal digits. It has worked for years and now fails in two repositories with two different errors. Explain both root causes at the storage level, and state the rule that prevents this class of failure.

**Model answer.** The script depends on two storage details that are not fixed. In the first repository the refs are stored with the reftable backend: created that way through `init.defaultRefFormat` or `git init --ref-format=reftable`, or converted in place with `git refs migrate --ref-format=reftable`. There is no file per branch, so reading the path fails. The same symptom appears with the files backend when the ref is packed. In the second repository the object format is SHA-256, so a valid commit ID is longer than forty hexadecimal digits and the length check rejects it. I would confirm both with `git rev-parse --show-object-format --show-ref-format`. Both repositories announce themselves: `repositoryformatversion` is 1 and an `[extensions]` section names the formats, which makes older Git versions refuse the repository instead of misreading it. The rule is to ask Git and never read the `.git` directory: `git rev-parse`, `git for-each-ref`, `git refs list`. Chapter 14D, section 14D.5 shows both failures from one unchanged script.

**Key terms.** reftable has no file per branch; packed refs; SHA-256 object IDs are longer; `extensions` and `repositoryformatversion`; ask Git, never read `.git`; `git rev-parse` and `git for-each-ref`

**Common weak answer.** "The repositories are corrupted, so clone them again." Weak because both are valid: one stores refs with reftable and the other uses SHA-256. A new clone keeps the object format of its source and takes its ref format from local settings, so the script fails again.

**Follow-up.** You repair the script with `git repo info`. What risk have you introduced into shared automation, and how do you contain it?

**A strong reply covers.** `git repo info` is marked EXPERIMENTAL (it arrived in Git 2.52), so its output and options may change between releases. In shared automation either pin the Git version or use `git rev-parse --show-object-format --show-ref-format`, which answers the same question.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14D](../textbook/ch14d-frontier.md), section 14D.5 and 14D.4 and 14D.12

#### Q82

**Question.** What does Git 2.55 run when a commit triggers automatic maintenance? How does that differ from `git gc`, and what does each delete?

**Model answer.** A command that writes objects ends by starting `git maintenance run --auto`, quiet and detached, and each task runs only if its threshold is met. Since Git 2.54 the default strategy is geometric, and `git gc` is not among the commands it starts. The trace in Chapter 26, section 26.3 shows six: `git pack-refs`, `git reflog expire`, a `git repack` that also writes a multi-pack-index, an incremental `git commit-graph write`, `git worktree prune` and `git rerere gc`. An ordinary geometric repack merges only small packs and does not look at reachability, so what this strategy deletes is reflog entries past their expiry; unreachable objects are dealt with only at an all-into-one repack. `git gc`, or the `gc` task, rewrites all packs into one, with a single commit-graph file and no multi-pack-index, puts unreachable objects into a cruft pack, and runs `git prune`, which deletes loose unreachable objects past the two-week grace period. `git gc` also does not take the lock the way `git maintenance run` does, so the manual recommends `git maintenance run --task=gc`.

**Key terms.** `git maintenance run --auto`; geometric strategy, default since 2.54; no `git gc`; reflog expiry; cruft pack at an all-into-one repack; `git prune` and the grace period; maintenance lock

**Common weak answer.** "Git runs `git gc --auto` after about 6,700 loose objects." Weak because that is the behavior before Git 2.54; the current default runs `git maintenance` with the geometric strategy, whose ordinary runs do not prune unreachable objects.

**Follow-up.** The manual page of Git 2.55 says in two places that only the `gc` task is enabled by default. How do you settle what really runs, and how do you ask whether a run would do anything?

**A strong reply covers.** The manual is inconsistent with itself, so a run decides: `GIT_TRACE=1` on a commit shows `git maintenance run --auto`, and a traced `git maintenance run` lists six commands with no `git gc`. `git maintenance is-needed --auto`, per task with `--task`, answers by exit status and needs Git 2.53.

**Reference.** [Chapter 26](../textbook/ch26-performance.md), section 26.3 and 26.19

#### Q83

**Question.** What is a cruft pack, and why can a repository under the default strategy hold unreachable objects for a long time?

**Model answer.** A cruft pack is a pack that holds only unreachable objects, with a companion `.mtimes` file recording when each object was last touched. It exists so that garbage can wait out its grace period, two weeks by `gc.pruneExpire`, without becoming thousands of loose files; the grace period itself exists because a running command may be about to reference such an object. Under the default geometric strategy an ordinary run does not look at reachability at all: it packs new loose objects and merges small packs, and a cruft pack is written only when the repack is all-into-one. In Chapter 26, section 26.5 ten unreachable objects sit inside the large pack; a default maintenance run packs three new objects and leaves the ten where they are, because that pack is not rewritten. The `gc` task separates them into a cruft pack, where they are still readable by ID, and `git gc --prune=now` then deletes them. So unreachable objects can outlive two weeks by a long time, which matters after a secret has been removed from history.

**Key terms.** only unreachable objects; `.mtimes` file; grace period; a geometric run ignores reachability; all-into-one repack; the `gc` task; `git fsck --unreachable`

**Common weak answer.** "Unreachable objects are deleted after two weeks." Weak because two weeks is the earliest moment and applies to a run that prunes; default geometric runs do not examine reachability, so the objects stay inside the large pack.

**Follow-up.** A repository is large although its history is small, and `git count-objects -v` shows no loose objects. How do you confirm that retained garbage is the cause?

**A strong reply covers.** Garbage no longer shows as loose files. Count it with `git fsck --unreachable | wc -l` and look for `.mtimes` files in `objects/pack`: the pack that has one is the cruft pack. Removing it is the deliberate purge of Chapter 21B, not routine maintenance.

**Reference.** [Chapter 26](../textbook/ch26-performance.md), section 26.5 and 26.3

#### Q84

**Question.** What two kinds of data does a commit-graph hold, and which commands does each help? What happens when the file is stale, and when it is damaged?

**Model answer.** First, the graph with generation numbers: for every commit its parents, root tree, date and a generation larger than that of every ancestor. A walk that asks whether one commit is an ancestor of another can stop at commits below the target's generation instead of walking to the root, which helps `git merge-base`, `git branch --contains`, `git tag --contains` and `git log --graph`. Second, optional changed-path Bloom filters: per commit, a probabilistic set of the paths that differ from its first parent, answering "definitely not" or "maybe". Only the "maybe" commits need a tree comparison, which helps `git log -- <path>` and `git blame`; in Chapter 26, section 26.6 the work falls from 94 comparisons to 13. A stale file is slower, not wrong: Git notices commits missing from it and reads those from the objects. A damaged file is another matter: Git does not verify its checksum on every read, and in Lab 16.4 a damaged file changed the answer of `git rev-list --count`. Diagnose with `git commit-graph verify` and `-c core.commitGraph=false`; then delete and rewrite the file.

**Key terms.** generation numbers; changed-path Bloom filters; "definitely not" or "maybe"; stale is slower, not wrong; `git commit-graph verify`; `core.commitGraph=false`; derived data

**Common weak answer.** "It is a cache of the log, and Git rebuilds it automatically if anything is off." Weak because it names neither kind of data, and a damaged file is not detected on every read: it can change answers until someone verifies or bypasses it.

**Follow-up.** Two clones of the same repository give different answers to the same history question. What is your first move, and why is it safe?

**A strong reply covers.** Bypass the derived data first: rerun the command with `-c core.commitGraph=false` and run `git commit-graph verify`. If the answers then agree, delete `objects/info/commit-graph` or `commit-graphs/` and write it again. That is safe because the file is derived data; it must never be copied between repositories by hand.

**Reference.** [Chapter 26](../textbook/ch26-performance.md), section 26.6, 26.16 and 26.17

#### Q85

**Question.** Why are bitmaps a server feature? What does the counter `pack-reused` tell you?

**Model answer.** A reachability bitmap stores, for selected commits, one bit per object in the pack saying whether that commit reaches it. Its use is the question a server answers for every clone and fetch: which objects does this client need, that is, everything reachable from the wanted commits minus everything reachable from what the client has. Without a bitmap that is a walk, commit by commit and tree by tree; with one it is a few bitwise operations, and stretches of the existing pack can be copied to the client verbatim. That is why `repack.writeBitmaps` defaults to true in bare repositories and false otherwise, and why `scalar` sets `pack.useBitmaps=false` on clients. In Chapter 26, section 26.8 the same `git gc` gives only the bare repository a `.bitmap` file. The counter `pack-reused`, reported by `git pack-objects` on the serving side under `GIT_TRACE2_PERF=1`, counts objects copied from the existing pack as one stretch with no per-object work: all 519 with the bitmap, none without it, when the objects were found by a walk and reused one at a time. Both clones were identical.

**Key terms.** one bit per object for selected commits; enumerating objects; bitwise operations instead of a walk; default in bare repositories; `repack.writeBitmaps`; `pack-reused`; identical result

**Common weak answer.** "Bitmaps compress the repository so clones are smaller." Weak because a bitmap changes nothing about what is sent: both clones in the transcript are identical, and the gain is in how the server finds and copies the objects.

**Follow-up.** You run a bare mirror for CI, and clones wait a long time before any transfer progress appears. What do you check on the mirror, and what will a bitmap not fix?

**A strong reply covers.** A long wait before any progress is the server enumerating objects, the phase a bitmap shortens: check that the bare mirror is repacked as a whole and has a `.bitmap` file. A bitmap does not shrink the pack; a long transfer is blob content, which partial clone addresses.

**Reference.** [Chapter 26](../textbook/ch26-performance.md), section 26.8 and 26.10


### Git internals: principal level

#### Q86

**Question.** When would you migrate a repository to reftable, what breaks if you do it carelessly, and what stays the same?

**Model answer.** I migrate where reftable solves a problem we have: branch names that differ only in case on the case-insensitive filesystems of macOS and Windows, tens of thousands of refs, or automation that updates many refs at once and needs that update to be atomic. In the `files` format, deleting a packed ref rewrites the whole `packed-refs` file and multi-ref updates are not atomic. The command is `git refs migrate --ref-format=reftable`, with `--dry-run` as its preview. Carelessness breaks three things. Anything that reads `.git/refs`, `packed-refs` or `logs/` by hand finds stubs or nothing. A tool built on an older Git library refuses the repository, because the format is declared by an extension with repository format version 1. And the migration cannot handle linked worktrees and must not run while anything else writes. What stays the same: every ref value, the reflogs, the objects, every plumbing answer, and the rule that a ref cannot be both a name and a prefix of names. The format is local, so a `files` clone still fetches from a reftable server.

**Key terms.** case-insensitive filesystems; atomic multi-ref updates; `git refs migrate`; linked worktrees block it; stop all writers; older tools refuse the extension; plumbing answers unchanged

**Common weak answer.** "Reftable is newer and faster, so migrate everything." Weak because it names no problem being solved, ignores tools that read ref files or cannot open a repository with the extension, and omits the limits on linked worktrees and concurrent writers.

**Follow-up.** After the migration, a monitoring script that tests for the file `ORIG_HEAD` or reads `.git/HEAD` misbehaves, while one that tests for the file `MERGE_HEAD` still works. Explain the difference.

**A strong reply covers.** In reftable, root refs such as `ORIG_HEAD` and `AUTO_MERGE` are records in the tables and `.git/HEAD` is a stub that names an invalid branch. `MERGE_HEAD` and `FETCH_HEAD` are pseudorefs and stay files in every format. Scripts should ask `git rev-parse --verify --quiet` or `git symbolic-ref HEAD`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 3](../textbook/ch03-git-internals.md), section 3.13

#### Q87

**Question.** Why do we keep our repositories in SHA-1 although Git supports SHA-256, and what would have to change for that to change?

**Model answer.** Because the two object formats cannot exchange objects and our hosting does not publicly accept the newer one. The first is a Git fact, the second a GitHub fact. In Git, SHA-256 repositories are a supported format since 2.42, chosen with `git init --object-format=sha256` and fixed for the life of the repository; there is no interoperability, so fetch and push between the formats fail in both directions, and there is no conversion. On GitHub there was no publicly available support for SHA-256 repositories on 1 October 2026; a private preview is reported by third parties, but no GitHub announcement confirms it, so the course marks it unverified. A repository that must live on GitHub therefore stays SHA-1. The risk is bounded: since Git 2.13 the default SHA-1 code is the collision-detecting variant, which recognises the patterns of the known attacks. What has to change is the ecosystem: Git 3.0 plans SHA-256 as the default for new repositories, conditional on libraries, applications and forges being ready, with no plan to deprecate SHA-1.

**Key terms.** no interoperability between formats; fixed at `git init`; no public GitHub support on 1 October 2026; collision-detecting SHA-1; the Git 3.0 plan is conditional; never assume forty digits

**Common weak answer.** "SHA-1 is broken, so we should convert now." Weak because there is no conversion and no exchange between the formats, GitHub does not publicly host SHA-256 repositories, and it ignores that Git's default SHA-1 code detects the known collision attacks.

**Follow-up.** Given that, what do you require of our internal tooling today so that a later change of object format does not break it?

**A strong reply covers.** No code may assume forty hexadecimal digits: ask `git rev-parse --show-object-format`, or accept 40 and 64, because the length is a property of the repository. Decide the format at `git init`, never edit `extensions.objectformat` afterwards, and treat a SHA-256 repository as an island.

**Reference.** [Chapter 3](../textbook/ch03-git-internals.md), section 3.14

#### Q88

**Question.** A laptop lost power during a commit, and Git now reports that the index file is corrupt. What did we lose, and what general rule decides which files under `.git` may be deleted and rebuilt in an incident and which must be restored from another copy?

**Model answer.** We lost at most the staging state. The index is derived data except for what was staged and never committed. I confirm the damage with `head -c 12 .git/index | xxd`, which no longer shows the `DIRC` signature, then delete the file and run `git reset`, which rebuilds it. History and the working tree are untouched; only what was staged has to be staged again. The general rule is primary versus derived. Derived data is rebuilt: the index, a pack's `.idx` with `git index-pack`, the commit-graph, the multi-pack-index. Primary data cannot be recreated by Git from anything else and is restored from another clone or a backup: loose objects and packs, refs and `packed-refs`, reflogs, `HEAD`, configuration and hooks. Deleting `MERGE_HEAD`, a ref file or anything under `objects/` by hand is damage, not repair. One qualification helps in practice: content determines the ID, so a lost object can be recreated from identical content found anywhere, with `git hash-object -w`.

**Key terms.** primary versus derived data; `rm .git/index && git reset`; only staged, uncommitted content needs a second look; `git index-pack`; restore objects and refs from another copy; reflogs and hooks are never cloned

**Common weak answer.** "The repository is corrupt; clone it again and copy the files over." Weak because history and the working tree are intact and one command rebuilds the index, while a fresh clone discards reflogs, hooks and local configuration, which are primary data and never cloned.

**Follow-up.** Which of the primary files does a clone or a push never carry, and what follows for how you back up a repository you cannot afford to lose?

**A strong reply covers.** Reflogs, hooks, `info/exclude` and local configuration are never cloned or pushed. A copy of `.git` taken while no Git process writes is the only backup that includes them; a backup through Git's transport instead has every object ID recomputed on the way. Use both, with a scheduled `git fsck`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 3](../textbook/ch03-git-internals.md), section 3.2, 3.12 and 3.15

#### Q89

**Question.** An engineer staged a file containing a credential, noticed it, unstaged the file and reports that it "never entered the repository". Explain to a non-specialist executive why that statement is wrong, how long the credential stays, and why routine maintenance cannot be relied on to remove it.

**Model answer.** The statement confuses what Git lists with what Git stores. `git add` writes the file's content into the object database as a blob at that moment; unstaging removes the index entry that pointed at it, not the blob. Chapter 3, section 3.8 shows it: after `git rm --cached` the status lists an untracked file, yet `git fsck` reports a dangling blob and `git cat-file -p` prints the token. Anyone with access to that directory, or to a container image, CI cache or backup that includes `.git`, can read it. How long it stays: an unreachable object is deleted two weeks after it became unreachable at the earliest, and only by a run that prunes. Since Git 2.54 automatic maintenance uses the geometric strategy, whose ordinary runs do not examine reachability, so the object can remain much longer. Had it been committed, reflog entries and every clone that has the commit would hold it as well. So the credential must be treated as readable, and removal is the deliberate purge procedure of Chapter 21B, not something to wait for.

**Key terms.** `git add` writes a blob; unstaging removes only the index entry; dangling blob; two weeks at the earliest; geometric runs do not examine reachability; deliberate purge

**Common weak answer.** "It was never committed, so it is not in Git." Weak because the blob is written at `git add`, stays readable by its ID after unstaging, and is removed only by a pruning run after the grace period, which default maintenance may postpone for a long time.

**Follow-up.** The purge will use a prune without a grace period. What are the preconditions before you allow that command on a repository, and what is the recovery if it removes too much?

**A strong reply covers.** Preview with `git fsck --unreachable` and `git prune -n`, work in a repository you have copied first, and make sure no other process writes to it. There is no recovery inside the repository, only another clone or a backup, which is why it is never routine maintenance.

**Reference.** [Chapter 3](../textbook/ch03-git-internals.md), section 3.8 and 3.16; [Chapter 26](../textbook/ch26-performance.md), section 26.5

#### Q90

**Question.** A repository's packs are several times larger than its content and history seem to explain, and nobody has committed large binaries recently. Which mechanisms in the object store can produce that, how do you tell them apart, and when is a full repack with non-default settings a defensible decision?

**Model answer.** Three mechanisms, and I measure before touching anything. First, old blob content: `git rev-list --objects --all` piped into `git cat-file --batch-check` and sorted by size lists the largest blobs in history with their paths. Committed archives, datasets or model weights gain nothing, because deltas need similar bytes, and files above `core.bigFileThreshold` are stored without any attempt. Second, retained garbage: `git fsck --unreachable | wc -l` and `.mtimes` files in `objects/pack` reveal unreachable objects that geometric maintenance has not pruned. Third, poor delta selection: `git pack-objects` picks candidates by a heuristic, sorting by type, size and name and comparing within a window of ten to a depth of fifty. Dropbox reported in 2026 that this heuristic paired translation files of different languages because of the directory layout, and that a server-side repack with a larger window and depth took its monorepo from 87 GB to 20 GB, by its own figures. Only that third finding justifies a non-default full repack, run once and benchmarked. The first points to Git LFS or partial clone, the second to a deliberate purge.

**Key terms.** measure the dimension first; largest blobs of the whole history; unreachable objects and `.mtimes` files; delta heuristic of type, size and name; window and depth; one benchmarked repack

**Common weak answer.** "The history is too big; rewrite it or start a fresh repository." Weak because it skips the measurement: the size may be content that does not delta, retained garbage or poor delta selection, each with its own evidence, and the chapter's example shrank through repacking, not through deleting history.

**Follow-up.** The consultant's nightly `git gc --aggressive` and Dropbox's repack both recompute deltas. Why do you reject the first and accept the second?

**A strong reply covers.** The nightly job recomputes every delta each night with no measured gain and without the maintenance lock; the manual calls it probably not worth it without benchmarks. Dropbox's was one measured repack for a diagnosed cause. `%(objectsize:disk)` and `%(deltabase)` from `git cat-file --batch-check` show how each object is stored.

**Reference.** [Chapter 3](../textbook/ch03-git-internals.md), section 3.7; [Chapter 26](../textbook/ch26-performance.md), section 26.5 and 26.15


## Area 3: Branching

Q91 to Q121. Branches and tags as refs, HEAD, upstream configuration, worktrees.


### Branching: foundational level

#### Q91

**Question.** What is a branch, what does creating one cost, and what does Git know about the branch it was created from?

**Model answer.** A branch is a ref under `refs/heads/` that names one commit and moves forward when you commit while it is the current branch. It contains no commits: "the commits on a branch" is not a stored list but the set reachable from the commit the branch names. Creating a branch writes one ref holding one commit ID, with its own reflog, and copies nothing; Chapter 2, section 2.8 shows the object list identical before and after `git branch`. That low cost follows from the design goal of supporting thousands of parallel lines of work. About the branch it was created from, Git knows nothing: it records no parent branch. Two branches that share history share reachable commits, and that is all, which is why merge and rebase must be told the other side. In the default files format the ref is a small file, but that is a storage detail and not a guarantee; `git rev-parse` and `git for-each-ref` work with every format.

**Key terms.** ref under `refs/heads/`; names one commit; reachable set; one ref written, nothing copied; no parent branch; `git for-each-ref`

**Common weak answer.** "A branch is a copy of the code taken from its parent branch." Weak because a branch is one ref to one commit, creating it copies nothing, and Git has no notion of a parent branch.

**Follow-up.** If Git records no parent branch, how does `git status` know what a branch is up to date with, and is that the same thing?

**A strong reply covers.** It is not the same thing. That line uses the upstream, a configured relation stored as the `branch.<name>.remote` and `branch.<name>.merge` settings in `.git/config`, which point at a remote-tracking branch. It says which ref to compare with, not where the branch was created from.

**Reference.** [Chapter 2](../textbook/ch02-mental-model.md), section 2.7, 2.8 and 2.11

#### Q92

**Question.** What is the difference between HEAD, a branch and a remote-tracking branch?

**Model answer.** All three are refs in your own repository; they differ in what they hold and in what moves them. A branch is a ref under `refs/heads/` that holds the ID of one commit, and a commit made on it moves it. HEAD says where you are. Normally it is a symbolic ref that holds the name of the current branch, not a commit, and in detached state it holds a commit ID directly; each worktree has its own HEAD. A remote-tracking branch such as `origin/main` is a ref under `refs/remotes/<remote>/` that records the last known position of a branch in another repository. Your commits never move it; `git fetch` updates it. An upstream is the pairing of a local branch with a remote-tracking branch through two configuration entries. `git for-each-ref` lists both namespaces and `git symbolic-ref HEAD` shows what HEAD names. So `main` on the server and `main` in a clone are two refs that share a name.

**Key terms.** all three are refs in the local repository; `refs/heads/`; symbolic ref naming the current branch; `refs/remotes/<remote>/`; last known position; moved by `git fetch`, not by commits

**Common weak answer.** "HEAD is the latest commit, a branch is your copy and `origin/main` is the branch on the server." Weak because HEAD usually names a branch, nothing is copied, and `origin/main` is a local ref that can be out of date.

**Follow-up.** `git status` says your branch is up to date with `origin/main`, and a colleague pushed ten minutes ago. Is Git wrong? What does the statement mean?

**A strong reply covers.** Git is not wrong. The comparison is between two refs in your repository and nothing in it talks to the server; `origin/main` is what your repository last heard. After `git fetch` it moves and status reports the branch as behind. "Up to date" describes your copy of the remote, never the remote.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.2 and 7.3 and 7.10

#### Q93

**Question.** What exactly is a branch? Define it in one sentence that mentions neither "copy" nor "line of development", and prove the definition with two commands.

**Model answer.** A branch is a ref: a name under `refs/heads/` that holds the ID of one commit, the tip, and the branch's history is whatever that commit reaches through its parents. The ref holds nothing but the ID. There is no list of the branch's commits, no record of where it started, no owner and no creation date. To prove it, run `git branch <name>` and then `git for-each-ref refs/heads`, which prints for every branch one commit ID, the object type and the full ref name. The new branch and the current one show the same ID, and creating it wrote no commit, no tree and no blob. `git rev-parse <name>` prints the same ID for one branch. I read refs with plumbing and not by path, because after `git pack-refs --all` the file under `.git/refs/heads/` is gone and in a reftable repository it never exists. `git log <name>` is a walk that starts at that ID and follows parent links.

**Key terms.** ref under `refs/heads/`; holds one commit ID; tip; history by reachability through parents; no list of commits and no start point; `git for-each-ref`

**Common weak answer.** "A branch is a copy of the project", or "the commits made since it branched off". Weak because nothing is copied and no set of commits is stored; the ref is one name and one ID, and everything else is computed by walking parents.

**Follow-up.** If a branch is only a name for one commit, how do you repair two unpushed commits that were made on local `main` and belong on a feature branch, and how much data is copied?

**A strong reply covers.** Nothing is copied; it takes two ref writes. `git switch -c <feature>` creates a branch at the current commit and attaches HEAD to it, carrying uncommitted edits along, and `git branch -f main origin/main` then moves `main` back, which is allowed once `main` is not checked out. Both reflogs record the moves.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.2

#### Q94

**Question.** Describe the objects and refs created by `git tag v1`, `git tag -a v1` and `git tag -s v1`. What does `v1^{}` resolve to in each case?

**Model answer.** `git tag v1` creates one ref, `refs/tags/v1`, that holds the commit ID directly, and no object. `git tag -a v1` creates one tag object and one ref that holds the ID of that tag object; the object has an `object` line naming the commit, a `type` line, the tag name repeated, a `tagger` line and the message. `git tag -s v1` creates the same pair with a signature block appended to the message by the external signing program; a signed tag is an annotated tag whose text ends in a signature. So there are three kinds and two mechanisms: a bare ref, or a ref plus an object. `v1^{}` follows tag objects until it reaches something that is not a tag, so in all three cases it resolves to the commit. For the lightweight tag that is what the ref already holds; for the other two, `git rev-parse v1` gives the tag object's ID instead. No reflog is written for tags unless `core.logAllRefUpdates` is `always`, and HEAD, the index and the working tree are not involved.

**Key terms.** ref under `refs/tags/`; tag object; `object`, `type`, `tag` and `tagger` lines; peeling; signature appended to the message; three kinds, two mechanisms

**Common weak answer.** "A lightweight tag points at a commit, and an annotated tag is the same thing with a message." Weak because it misses the mechanism: the annotated tag is a separate object with its own ID, which is what the ref holds, so `v1` and `v1^{}` differ, and a signed tag is that same object with a signature appended.

**Follow-up.** Someone runs `git tag -a v1-audited v1` where `v1` is already an annotated tag. What is created, what does Git say about it, and where does `^{}` end?

**A strong reply covers.** A nested tag: a new tag object whose `object` line names the first tag object and whose `type` is `tag`, plus a ref. Git 2.55 prints a hint that this is probably a mistake and suggests tagging the peeled object. `^{}` still follows both tag objects down to the commit.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14B](../textbook/ch14b-config-tags-signing.md), section 14B.8

#### Q95

**Question.** What exactly does `git worktree add` create on disk, in the new directory and in the repository?

**Model answer.** It creates two things and copies no objects. In the new directory it writes the checked-out files and a `.git` file, not a directory, whose one line points into the repository. In the repository it creates a private directory `.git/worktrees/<id>/`, where the ID is the directory name the worktree was created with. That directory holds what belongs to this worktree alone: its `HEAD`, its `index`, `logs/HEAD`, `ORIG_HEAD` and the other root refs, plus two small files. `gitdir` points back at the `.git` file of the working tree, which is how `git worktree list` and `git worktree prune` find out whether the working tree still exists, and `commondir` holds the relative path to the shared `.git`. With `-b`, or with only a path, a new branch ref is also created in the shared refs. The main worktree's files, index and HEAD are unchanged. Chapter 25, section 25.2 shows these files, and `git worktree list` prints one line per worktree with the main one first.

**Key terms.** `.git` file, not a directory; `.git/worktrees/<id>/`; its own HEAD and index; `gitdir` and `commondir`; no objects copied; shared refs and objects

**Common weak answer.** "It makes a second copy of the repository in another folder." Weak because no objects are copied: the new directory has a one-line `.git` file, and only HEAD, the index and a few other per-worktree files are new, inside the one repository.

**Follow-up.** The new directory is later moved with `mv`. Which pointer is now stale, what does `git worktree list` show, and does the worktree's ID change?

**A strong reply covers.** The `gitdir` file in the administrative entry still names the old location, so the listing marks the worktree `prunable`. `git worktree repair` with the new path rewrites the pointer. The ID stays the name the worktree was created with, which matters when you write `worktrees/<id>/HEAD`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 25](../textbook/ch25-worktrees.md), section 25.2 and 25.3

#### Q96

**Question.** Which parts of a repository are shared between worktrees and which are per worktree? How do you find out for a path you are unsure about?

**Model answer.** Per worktree are the working tree files, HEAD and therefore the current branch, the index, the HEAD reflog, the other root refs such as `ORIG_HEAD`, `MERGE_HEAD`, `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD` and `FETCH_HEAD`, and the state of an operation in progress such as `rebase-merge/`. Shared by all worktrees are the object database, every ref under `refs/` including branches, tags, remote-tracking branches and `refs/stash`, `packed-refs`, the reflogs of branches, `config` unless `extensions.worktreeConfig` is on, `hooks/`, `info/exclude` and the remotes. The manual's rule is that refs starting with `refs/` are shared, with three exceptions, `refs/bisect/*`, `refs/worktree/*` and `refs/rewritten/*`, and that root refs are per worktree. The manual also warns not to guess. Ask `git rev-parse --git-path` with the path: it prints a location under the private directory or under the common one, and `git rev-parse --git-dir` and `--git-common-dir` print those two directories. The visible consequences: a commit made in one worktree exists in the others at once, while staging is private.

**Key terms.** HEAD and the index are per worktree; refs under `refs/` are shared; `refs/stash` is shared; config and hooks are shared; `refs/bisect/*` exception; `git rev-parse --git-path`; `--git-common-dir`

**Common weak answer.** "Each worktree has its own branches and its own stash; only the objects are shared." Weak because every ref under `refs/` is shared, the stash included, and so are configuration and hooks; only HEAD, the index and in-progress state are private.

**Follow-up.** HEAD is per worktree. How do you name the HEAD of another worktree from where you are, and what is that useful for?

**A strong reply covers.** Prefix it: `main-worktree/HEAD` for the main worktree and `worktrees/<id>/HEAD` for a linked one, where the ID is the directory name under `.git/worktrees/`. From any worktree this lets you inspect a commit that only another worktree's detached HEAD holds.

**Reference.** [Chapter 25](../textbook/ch25-worktrees.md), section 25.3


### Branching: working engineer level

#### Q97

**Question.** What is in `.git/HEAD` in the three states: on a branch, detached, and on an unborn branch? How does each state change what `git commit` does?

**Model answer.** On a branch, the file holds a symbolic ref, the text `ref: refs/heads/<name>`. A commit then writes the new commit ID into that branch ref; the HEAD file keeps the same text, and HEAD follows only because it names the branch. Detached, the file holds a commit ID. A commit there writes the new ID into HEAD itself, no branch moves, and the commit is referenced only by HEAD, so it is reachable from no branch once you leave. On an unborn branch, in a new repository or after `git switch --orphan`, the file names a branch whose ref does not exist yet. `git rev-parse --verify HEAD` fails, `git branch` lists nothing and `git branch <new>` fails because there is no commit to point at. The first commit has no parent, and writing it creates the ref. An unborn branch that you leave without committing disappears, because no ref was ever written.

**Key terms.** symbolic ref `ref: refs/heads/<name>`; branch ref moves, HEAD file unchanged; detached HEAD holds a commit ID; referenced only by HEAD; unborn branch; first commit creates the ref

**Common weak answer.** "HEAD is the latest commit." Weak because HEAD normally contains a branch name, not a commit; that model cannot explain why a commit on a detached HEAD moves no branch or why a new repository has a HEAD and no branch.

**Follow-up.** You rewrite HEAD alone with `git symbolic-ref HEAD refs/heads/<other>`. What does `git status` report, and what does that tell you about what `git switch` does beyond changing HEAD?

**A strong reply covers.** Only one file changed, so the index and working tree still hold the old branch's content, and `git status` reports the difference between the commit HEAD now names and the index as staged changes, a staged deletion in the transcript. A switch is that ref change plus an update of index and working tree.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.3 and 7.7

#### Q98

**Question.** A colleague's two days of commits are "gone" after she checked out a tag and later switched back to `main`. Walk through the recovery and explain why it works.

**Model answer.** Nothing is gone. Checking out a tag detached HEAD: it held a commit ID instead of a branch name. Each commit she made advanced HEAD itself and no branch, so those commits were referenced only by HEAD. When she ran `git switch main`, HEAD moved away and no ref reached them any more; Git printed a warning that named the commits and the command that keeps them. The objects still exist, and the reflog of HEAD still records every position HEAD had. So I run `git reflog` in her clone, find the `commit:` lines above the last `checkout: moving from <id> to main` entry, take the ID of the newest one, and run `git branch <name> <id>`. `git log --oneline --graph --all` then shows the work again. It works because a commit never depended on a branch for its existence; a branch is only a name for it. The prevention is one rule: give a detached HEAD a branch before leaving it.

**Key terms.** detached HEAD; commits referenced only by HEAD; no ref reaches them; reflog of HEAD; `git branch <name> <id>`; objects still exist

**Common weak answer.** "The commits were deleted when she switched branches; restore from a backup." Weak because switching deletes nothing: the objects are in her repository and the HEAD reflog lists them. The answer also misses that the recovery must be done in her clone.

**Follow-up.** How long does she have before the recovery stops working, and what exactly would make the commits unrecoverable?

**A strong reply covers.** By default a reflog entry not reachable from the current tip expires after 30 days, and an object that no ref and no reflog entry refers to is pruned once it is more than two weeks old. After both, the commits are gone, so create the branch now.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.7 and 7.14

#### Q99

**Question.** What does `git switch -c fix origin/main` write to `.git`, including configuration?

**Model answer.** It writes a new ref, `refs/heads/fix`, holding the ID of the commit that `origin/main` names, and a reflog for that branch whose first line records how it was created. It rewrites HEAD to `ref: refs/heads/fix` and appends a `checkout: moving from ... to fix` line to the reflog of HEAD. Because the start point is a remote-tracking branch and `branch.autoSetupMerge` is true by default, it also writes the upstream as two configuration entries, `branch.fix.remote` and `branch.fix.merge`; the output line "set up to track" reports that. The index is updated to the start point, and so are the working tree files that differ between the old and the new tip, with a refusal if a local edit would be overwritten. It writes no commit, no tree and no blob, moves no other ref, and nothing changes on the remote. The manual calls `-c` the transactional equivalent of `git branch` followed by `git switch`.

**Key terms.** new ref under `refs/heads/`; branch reflog; HEAD rewritten; `branch.<name>.remote` and `branch.<name>.merge`; `branch.autoSetupMerge`; no objects written

**Common weak answer.** "It copies `origin/main` into a new branch." Weak because no objects are written; the command creates one ref, changes HEAD and, with a remote-tracking start point, adds two configuration entries that the candidate did not mention.

**Follow-up.** What is different when the start point is a local branch, and why does `-c` stop when `fix` already exists while `-C` does not?

**A strong reply covers.** A branch created from a local branch gets no upstream: `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref '@{upstream}'` fails. `-c` refuses to change an existing branch; `-C` resets it like `git branch -f`, and the branch reflog records the reset, so the old position is one entry away.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.6 and 7.10

#### Q100

**Question.** `git log main..feature` and `git diff main..feature`: how do the two dots differ in meaning? Which one do you want for a review?

**Model answer.** In `git log` and `git rev-list`, a range is a set of commits: `main..feature` is every commit reachable from `feature` and not from `main`, the work the feature has that `main` lacks. In `git diff`, the two dots select no set at all: `git diff main..feature` compares the two tips directly, the same as `git diff main feature`. If `main` has moved on since the branches diverged, that diff also shows `main`'s newer commits in reverse, as if the feature had removed them. For a review I want three dots, `git diff main...feature`, which compares the merge base of the two with `feature` and so shows what the feature changed. Three dots in `git log` mean something else again, the commits reachable from exactly one side. According to GitHub's documentation, a pull request page also calculates its changed files from a merge base, focusing on what the pull request introduced.

**Key terms.** range as a set of commits; `git diff A..B` compares two tips; three-dot diff starts at the merge base; `main`'s commits shown reversed; symmetric difference in `git log`; merge base

**Common weak answer.** "Both show what is on `feature` that is not on `main`." Weak because that holds only for `git log`; the two-dot diff mixes in everything `main` gained since the merge base, which misleads a reviewer.

**Follow-up.** How do you put a number on how far two branches have diverged, and why is "3 commits ahead" an incomplete statement?

**A strong reply covers.** `git rev-list --left-right --count main...feature` prints the commits only on each side in operand order, and `%(ahead-behind:main)` in `git for-each-ref` gives the pair for every branch. The counts are measured from the merge base against a named ref, so "ahead" means nothing until you say ahead of what.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.8

#### Q101

**Question.** Which commands for working with branches and refs are dangerous enough that you would want a preview, and what is the preview for each?

**Model answer.** Three carry the dangerous label in Chapter 7. `git branch -D`, and `git update-ref -d`, delete a ref and its reflog with no merge check; the preview is `git log --oneline main..<branch>`, which lists the commits about to lose their name. `git switch --discard-changes`, or `git checkout -f`, overwrites uncommitted changes in the index and working tree; the preview is `git status` and `git diff`. Writing a file under `.git/refs/` by hand skips validation, locking and the reflog; there is no preview, the answer is to use `git update-ref`. A second group needs caution. `git branch -d` checks merge status and `git branch --merged` previews it; `git fetch --prune` is previewed by `git remote prune origin --dry-run`; `git tag -d` and `git tag -f` leave only the ID in their output; and for `git branch -f`, `git branch -m` and `git switch -C`, I check `git branch -vv` or `git rev-parse <ref>` first, knowing the old value stays in the reflog.

**Key terms.** `git branch -D` deletes ref and reflog; `git log --oneline main..<branch>`; `git switch --discard-changes`; hand-written ref files; `git remote prune origin --dry-run`; old value stays in the reflog

**Common weak answer.** "Only `git branch -D` is dangerous, and the reflog always saves you." Weak because `-D` removes the branch's reflog, discarded uncommitted edits are in no reflog, and the answer names no preview for any command.

**Follow-up.** Which of those operations has no recovery at all, and why can neither the reflog nor `git fsck` help?

**A strong reply covers.** `git switch --discard-changes` on edits that were never staged. Content becomes an object only when it is added or committed, so there is nothing for a reflog or `git fsck` to find. A deleted ref, by contrast, leaves its commits in the object database.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.16 and 7.15

#### Q102

**Question.** `git describe` prints `v1.0.0-2-gc053f0d` on a laptop and fails in CI. Explain every part of the string and the failure.

**Model answer.** The string has three parts: the nearest annotated tag in the commit's history, the number of commits between that tag and the commit, here two, and the letter g, for git, followed by the commit's abbreviated ID. Lightweight tags are ignored unless `--tags` is given. The whole string is a valid revision, so it can be pasted into `git show`. In CI the checkout is shallow: one commit and no tags, which `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` and an empty `git tag` confirm. `git describe` needs a tagged ancestor and the commits between it and HEAD, so it has nothing to describe. Fetching only the tag is not enough, because the commits between the tag and the tip are still missing and Git cannot count them; `git fetch --unshallow` repairs it. The default is a GitHub Actions matter, not Git: `actions/checkout` fetches one commit and no tags unless `fetch-depth: 0` is set. Fetch full history and tags in jobs that compute a version, and make the release job fail when `git describe --exact-match` fails.

**Key terms.** nearest annotated tag; commit count since the tag; g plus abbreviated commit ID; shallow clone; tags and intermediate commits missing; `fetch-depth: 0`; `git describe --exact-match`

**Common weak answer.** "CI has a different Git version, so pin the version or hard-code the tag." Weak because the cause is repository state, not the version: a shallow checkout has no tags and no intermediate commits. The usual half-fix, fetching only the tag, still fails because the commits in between cannot be counted.

**Follow-up.** After a patch release was tagged on a release branch, `git describe main` still names the older tag. Is that a defect, and how do you answer "which release contains this fix"?

**A strong reply covers.** No. `git describe` only looks backward along history, and the patch tag is not an ancestor of `main`. A backported fix is a copy with a new commit ID, so `git tag --contains` on the original finds nothing; `git cherry -v release/1.2 main` compares patches, and the trailer written by `git cherry-pick -x` records the source.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14B](../textbook/ch14b-config-tags-signing.md), section 14B.12 and 14B.14

#### Q103

**Question.** Why does Git refuse to check out one branch in two worktrees? Describe what would go wrong, in terms of refs and indexes.

**Model answer.** A branch is one ref, and each worktree has its own index and files, which are assumed to correspond to the commit that ref names. If two worktrees had the same branch checked out, a commit in one would advance the shared ref, and the index and files of the other would stay at the old commit, because Git has no mechanism that updates another worktree's index when a ref moves. Chapter 25, section 25.4 builds the situation with `git worktree add --force`: the worktree nobody touched reports staged changes, and its staged diff is the inverse of the new commit, since `git status` compares HEAD, now the new commit, with an index that still describes the old tree. A `git commit` there would record the old tree on top of the new commit, a silent revert. The same rule makes Git refuse to delete or force-update a branch that another worktree uses. The repair is `git reset --hard` in the stale worktree when it has no work of its own; the prevention is `--detach` or a new branch.

**Key terms.** one ref, two indexes; the index is per worktree; staged diff is the inverse of the new commit; silent revert; `git worktree add --force`; `git reset --hard`; `--detach` or a new branch

**Common weak answer.** "Because the two directories would overwrite each other's files." Weak because the directories are separate; the problem is one shared ref moving under a second index that nobody updates, which turns the next commit there into a revert.

**Follow-up.** The stale worktree does contain real uncommitted work. What is the lowest-risk repair, and which two states make a branch count as checked out although `git worktree list` shows a detached HEAD?

**A strong reply covers.** Stash the work, run `git reset --hard`, then pop the stash, because committing first would revert the other commit. A branch that is in the middle of a rebase or a bisect in some worktree is in use by that worktree although the listing shows it as detached.

**Reference.** [Chapter 25](../textbook/ch25-worktrees.md), section 25.4

#### Q104

**Question.** `git branch -d` says a branch is used by a worktree at a path that does not exist. What happened, and what are the two commands that diagnose and fix it?

**Model answer.** Someone deleted the worktree's directory by hand, for example with `rm -rf`, instead of running `git worktree remove`. Git's record of a worktree is the administrative entry under `.git/worktrees/`, and that entry still exists with its HEAD naming the branch, so the branch still counts as checked out and the one-branch rule protects it from deletion. The diagnosis is `git worktree list`: the entry is shown as `prunable`, meaning its `gitdir` file points at a location that no longer exists. The fix is `git worktree prune`, previewed with `--dry-run --verbose`, which removes entries whose working tree is missing; after that `git branch -d` succeeds. Git would do this by itself in time: `git gc` prunes such entries with the `gc.worktreePruneExpire` default of three months, and the automatic maintenance of Git 2.54 and later includes a worktree-prune task. Until then the claim on the branch remains. The prevention is to remove worktrees with `git worktree remove`, never by deleting the directory.

**Key terms.** directory deleted by hand; stale entry under `.git/worktrees/`; `prunable`; `git worktree list`; `git worktree prune`; `--dry-run --verbose`; `git worktree remove`

**Common weak answer.** "Force the deletion with `git branch -D`." Weak because the forced form is refused for a branch that a worktree uses, and it does not address the cause, a stale administrative entry that still claims the branch.

**Follow-up.** Before you prune, what must you rule out, and what is lost together with the entry?

**A strong reply covers.** Rule out that the directory was moved and not deleted: a worktree moved with `mv` is also listed as `prunable`, and the right command is `git worktree repair` with the new path. Pruning deletes the entry's HEAD reflog, so commits made on a detached HEAD there are held by nothing.

**Reference.** [Chapter 25](../textbook/ch25-worktrees.md), section 25.6 and 25.8

#### Q105

**Question.** A teammate ran `git stash pop` and got changes they had never seen. The repository has four worktrees. Explain.

**Model answer.** The stash is not per worktree. Stash entries hang off the ref `refs/stash`, and every ref under `refs/` is shared by all worktrees, with only the bisect, worktree and rewritten namespaces excepted. The repository therefore has one stash list, and its newest entry may have been made in another directory, on another branch, by another person or agent. `git stash pop` applied that foreign entry to the teammate's working tree. The evidence is `git stash list`, whose entries name the branch they were made on, and `git rev-parse --git-path refs/stash`, which resolves into the common directory and not into the worktree's private one. The lower-risk habit is to inspect an entry with `git stash show -p` before applying it, and to apply it in the worktree it belongs to. The prevention in a repository with several worktrees is to commit work in progress to its branch instead of stashing, and to instruct automated agents to commit to their branch and never to stash.

**Key terms.** `refs/stash`; refs under `refs/` are shared; one stash list for the repository; `git stash list`; `git stash show -p`; commit to the branch instead of stashing

**Common weak answer.** "The stash belongs to the branch or the directory, so someone must have used their machine." Weak because there is one stash list per repository, recorded under a shared ref, and every worktree reads and pops from it.

**Follow-up.** Which other things that people expect to be private to a worktree are shared in the same way, and how do you make one of them per worktree?

**A strong reply covers.** Configuration and hooks: `git config set` without a scope writes `.git/config`, which every worktree reads, and a `pre-commit` hook runs for commits in all of them. Per-worktree configuration needs `extensions.worktreeConfig` set to true and then `git config set --worktree`, which writes `config.worktree` in the private directory.

**Reference.** [Chapter 25](../textbook/ch25-worktrees.md), section 25.7 and 25.3


### Branching: senior level

#### Q106

**Question.** Why does `git branch -d` refuse a branch that was squash-merged once its upstream is gone (or when it never had one), why does it delete the same branch with a warning while the remote-tracking ref still contains it, and how do you prove the branch is safe to delete?

**Model answer.** Because `-d` tests reachability, not content. It deletes a branch only when the tip is fully merged in its upstream, or in HEAD if no upstream is set, which means the tip commit must be reachable from there. A squash merge puts a new commit on `main` that has the branch's content and none of the branch's commits. The tip is therefore not reachable from `main`, `git branch --merged main` does not list the branch, and `git log --oneline main..<branch>` still lists its commits. Reachability cannot see that the work landed. Whether `-d` refuses then depends on the upstream: while the remote-tracking ref still exists and contains the tip, the branch counts as merged into its upstream and `-d` deletes it with a warning that it is not merged to HEAD; once that ref is pruned, or for a branch that never had an upstream, Git compares with HEAD and refuses. The proof is a merge computed without a working tree: `git merge-tree --write-tree main <branch>` prints the ID of the tree a merge would produce, and if that equals `git rev-parse 'main^{tree}'`, merging the branch would change nothing. Then `git branch -D` is appropriate. The prevention is to delete the branch in the same step as the squash merge.

**Key terms.** reachability, not content; tip not reachable after a squash; `git branch --merged`; `git merge-tree --write-tree`; equal tree IDs; `-D` after proof

**Common weak answer.** "Git is confused; use `-D`, it was merged." Weak because it offers no proof. `-D` skips the merge check and deletes the reflog, so the claim "it was merged" must be verified first, and `--merged` cannot verify a squash.

**Follow-up.** Git 2.56 adds `git branch --delete-merged`. Would you rely on it to clean up squash-merged branches?

**A strong reply covers.** No. Described from the 2.56 documentation and not run in the course: it deletes only branches whose tip is reachable from their configured upstream, so a squash-merged branch is silently skipped, and it skips a branch whose upstream ref no longer exists. Keep `[gone]` plus `git merge-tree` for those.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.13 and 7.5

#### Q107

**Question.** Explain the `git branch -d` rule in terms of the upstream. Give one case where `-d` deletes a branch that `main` does not contain, and one where it refuses a branch that `main` does contain.

**Model answer.** The rule is about the upstream, not about `main`: the branch must be fully merged in its upstream branch, or in HEAD if no upstream was set. First case: a fix branch has been pushed and is equal to its upstream remote-tracking branch, but nobody has merged it. With `main` checked out, `git branch -d` deletes it and prints a warning that it has been merged to the remote-tracking ref but not yet merged to HEAD. `main` does not contain those commits; the local name is gone and the commits are still named by the remote-tracking branch. Second case: a feature branch is merged into `main`, but it has one commit that its upstream lacks. `-d` refuses with "not fully merged" and a warning that it is not yet merged to its upstream even though it is merged to HEAD. Chapter 7, section 7.5 runs both. Read both messages before reaching for `-D`.

**Key terms.** fully merged in its upstream; HEAD only when no upstream is set; pushed but unmerged branch is deleted with a warning; merged but unpushed commit makes `-d` refuse; read the warning; not a statement about `main`

**Common weak answer.** "`-d` deletes a branch only if it has been merged into `main`." Weak because the test is against the branch's upstream; the answer cannot explain either of the two cases, and it leads people to trust `-d` as proof that work reached `main`.

**Follow-up.** Given that rule, can a plain `git branch -d` delete `main` itself? What decides it, and how do you recover?

**A strong reply covers.** Yes. Nothing is special about the name: if `main` is not checked out and its tip is reachable from its upstream, `-d` deletes it together with its reflog. Recreate it from `origin/main`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.5

#### Q108

**Question.** Does Git know which branch a branch was created from? What is the closest it can offer, and why is a pull request's base branch not the same thing?

**Model answer.** No. Nothing in a repository records it: the new ref holds only a commit ID, the commit has no field for a branch, and the configuration gains no entry. The single trace is the first line of the branch's reflog, "Created from" and a name, which exists in that one clone and is removed by `git branch -D` or reflog expiry. `git branch --contains` answers reachability, not origin. The closest Git offers is a guess: `%(is-base:<commit>)` in `git for-each-ref` marks the ref most likely used as the starting point, chosen by a first-parent heuristic, and the guess changes with the refs that exist; delete the intermediate branch and it names `main`. The textbook's advice is a hint for humans, never an input to automation. A pull request's base branch is different in kind: a person chooses it when the pull request is opened and GitHub stores it, not Git, so no clone carries it.

**Key terms.** no parent-branch concept; ref holds only an ID; local reflog line "Created from"; `%(is-base:...)` heuristic; reachability is not origin; pull request base stored by GitHub

**Common weak answer.** "Yes, Git tracks the parent branch; `git branch --contains` or the graph shows it." Weak because those show reachability. Commits never belong to a branch, and every comparison needs a base that you name.

**Follow-up.** Branch B was created from branch A. A is squash-merged into `main` and deleted. What happens to B's changes against `main`, and what is the repair?

**A strong reply covers.** B's range against `main` now also lists everything A did, because A's commits are not in `main` after a squash and the base that was implied no longer exists. `git rebase --onto`, covered in Chapter 9, moves B to its real base; Git takes the target as an argument because it cannot infer it.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.9

#### Q109

**Question.** Why does `git fetch` fail on every clone after someone pushes `feature/login`, and what is the one-command fix?

**Model answer.** Because every clone still holds a stale remote-tracking ref named `origin/feature`. At some point a plain branch called `feature` existed on the server and was fetched; it was later deleted there, and no clone was told. The server now has `feature/login`, so the fetch tries to create `refs/remotes/origin/feature/login` while `refs/remotes/origin/feature` exists, and a ref cannot be a name and the prefix of other names at the same time. Git reports "cannot lock ref" or "unable to update local ref". The diagnosis is `git branch -r` showing `origin/feature` next to the new name on the server. The one-command fix is `git fetch --prune`, or `git remote prune origin`, which deletes the stale ref so the fetch succeeds. For prevention, reserve top-level names such as `feature` and `fix` for namespaces, never create a plain branch with one of them, and set `fetch.prune=true` on a team that uses namespaces.

**Key terms.** stale remote-tracking ref; a ref cannot be both a name and a prefix; one ref hierarchy; `git fetch --prune`; reserve namespace names; `fetch.prune=true`

**Common weak answer.** "The server is broken or the new branch is corrupt; re-clone." Weak because the conflict is in each clone's own remote-tracking refs. A re-clone hides the cause, costs every developer time, and leaves the naming policy that produced it unchanged.

**Follow-up.** Is this a limitation of storing refs as files, and would another ref storage backend make the problem go away?

**A strong reply covers.** No. With loose files the cause is visible as a file where a directory is needed, but the transcripts show the same refusal with packed refs and in a reftable repository. Ref names form one hierarchy and the rule keeps every name unambiguous, so only a naming policy prevents it.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.12 and 7.14

#### Q110

**Question.** Why does `git tag -d` have no undo through the reflog, while `git branch -D` sometimes does?

**Model answer.** Because tags get no reflog by default. `core.logAllRefUpdates` creates reflogs for branches, remote-tracking branches, notes and HEAD, and not for tags; the directory `.git/logs/refs` has no `tags` entry. So `git tag -d` and `git tag -f` leave no trace except the "was" ID they print, and you must note that ID at once. A branch does have its own reflog, but `git branch -D` deletes it together with the ref, so the branch's reflog is not what saves you. What sometimes saves you is the reflog of HEAD: if the branch's commits were ever checked out in this clone, `git reflog` still lists them, and `git branch <name> <id>` recreates the branch. In both cases the commit object itself still exists after the deletion; what was lost is the name. Recovery is a matter of finding the ID before the object grace period ends.

**Key terms.** tags have no reflog by default; `core.logAllRefUpdates`; `-D` deletes the branch reflog; reflog of HEAD; "was" ID in the output; recreate with `git branch <name> <id>`

**Common weak answer.** "Branches are in the reflog and tags are not." Weak because the branch's own reflog is deleted with the branch; recovery depends on the HEAD reflog, which helps only if those commits were checked out here.

**Follow-up.** For which kind of branch is `git branch -D` as unrecoverable as a tag deletion, and what do you run before deleting?

**A strong reply covers.** A branch whose commits were never checked out in this clone: the HEAD reflog has no entry for them, so only the printed "was" ID and the object grace period remain. Preview with `git log --oneline main..<branch>` to see exactly which commits would lose their only name.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.11 and 7.5

#### Q111

**Question.** On macOS, `git branch` shows no current branch and `git log --decorate` says `(HEAD, main)`. What happened?

**Model answer.** Someone switched to the branch with the wrong letter case, for example `git switch MAIN`. The default macOS volume format does not distinguish the two spellings, and with the files backend a loose ref is a file, so the wrong-case name found the right file and the switch succeeded. HEAD, however, recorded what was typed: `cat .git/HEAD` shows `ref: refs/heads/MAIN`. `git branch` lists `main` without an asterisk because the name HEAD holds is not in the list, and `git status` says "On branch MAIN". A commit in this state moves the file that exists, `refs/heads/main`. That is why the decoration reads `(HEAD, main)` and not `(HEAD -> main)`: both name the same commit, but HEAD does not point at `main`. The repair is `git switch main`, and nothing was lost. The prevention is lowercase branch names, and checking the HEAD file whenever the listing shows no asterisk.

**Key terms.** case-insensitive file system; loose ref is a file; HEAD records the typed name; `(HEAD, main)` versus `(HEAD -> main)`; `cat .git/HEAD`; `git switch main`

**Common weak answer.** "HEAD is detached." Weak because HEAD is still a symbolic ref; it names a branch spelling that is not in the list. The candidate should read `.git/HEAD` instead of guessing from the missing asterisk.

**Follow-up.** Can that machine end up with both `main` and `Main` as branches? Under what condition, and what happens afterwards?

**A strong reply covers.** Yes. While the ref is a loose file, `git branch Main` is refused as existing; after `git pack-refs --all` the file system is out of the picture and `Main` is created as a second ref. On that volume the two collide again as soon as one is written back as a loose file.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.15

#### Q112

**Question.** A release script clones the repository with `git clone --branch <tag>`, commits a generated file and pushes. It worked when a developer ran it in a normal clone on `main`, and it fails in the pipeline. Explain the root cause and the rules you would set for scripts that run Git.

**Model answer.** The script assumes a current branch, and the pipeline's checkout has none.
