A clone made with `--branch` and a tag name has a HEAD that holds a commit ID and no local branch at all; `git branch -a` shows "(no branch)" and the remote-tracking refs, and `git status` says "Not currently on any branch". A commit made there advances HEAD itself and is referenced only by HEAD, so the generated file is committed onto nothing, and a `git push` with no refspec fails because there is no current branch. This is not an error state. Detached HEAD is the normal condition of a CI job, a deploy checkout and a submodule; according to GitHub's documentation, on GitHub Actions the default checkout for `pull_request` events is a merge commit in detached HEAD, which the course did not run. The rules: scripts take the commit from `git rev-parse HEAD`, name the branch explicitly when pushing, and are written and tested for a detached HEAD.

**Key terms.** detached HEAD is normal in automation; clone at a tag has no local branch; commit referenced only by HEAD; `git push` with no refspec; `git rev-parse HEAD`; explicit branch when pushing

**Common weak answer.** "The pipeline's clone is broken; add `git checkout main` at the top." Weak because it treats a normal state as a fault and would build whatever `main` is instead of the requested tag. The checkout is correct; the script's assumption of a current branch is the defect.

**Follow-up.** The script labels each build with the output of `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`. What does the label say in the pipeline, what do the other two ways of asking return, and what should the label be?

**A strong reply covers.** It prints the literal word HEAD. `git branch --show-current` prints nothing and `git symbolic-ref HEAD` fails with status 128, so a script must handle all three. Label the build with the full commit ID from `git rev-parse HEAD`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.7 and 7.14

#### Q113

**Question.** A release tag was force-moved yesterday. Who has which version of it today, how do you find out, and what is the lowest-risk repair?

**Model answer.** Every clone holds its own copy of a tag, and a fetch creates missing tags but never overwrites one you already have. So clones that fetched before the move still have the original, while the server and every clone or CI checkout made after the move have the new one, and a plain fetch does not even report the difference. To find out, compare the server's peeled value with the local one: `git ls-remote origin 'refs/tags/<tag>^{}'` against `git rev-parse '<tag>^{commit}'`; `git fetch --tags` also reports the clash as a rejected tag. The lowest-risk repair is to put the tag back at its published position with `git push --force origin <tag>` from a clone that still has the original tag object, and to release the new content under a new version. Clones that picked up the moved tag in between must be corrected by hand with `git fetch --tags --force`. Prevention is a server-side rule that makes release tags immutable, and deploying by commit ID or image digest, not by tag name alone.

**Key terms.** every clone holds its own copy; fetch never overwrites an existing tag; peeled value from `git ls-remote`; restore the published position; new version for new content; `git fetch --tags --force`; immutable release tags

**Common weak answer.** "Everyone gets the new tag on the next fetch, so tell people to pull." Weak because a fetch never updates an existing tag: old clones silently keep the old one and new clones get the new one, so two builds carry one name, and the answer has no way to detect which machine has which.

**Follow-up.** Suppose nobody still has the original ref: the person who moved it overwrote their own, and the others fetched with `--force`. Is the published tag recoverable, and from what?

**A strong reply covers.** Usually yes. `git tag -f` and `git fetch --tags --force` leave the old tag object in the object database, unreachable, until it is pruned; `git fsck` lists it as a dangling tag and `git tag <name> <old-id>` restores the ref. Tags have no reflog by default, so that object is the only trail.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14B](../textbook/ch14b-config-tags-signing.md), section 14B.11 and 14B.21

#### Q114

**Question.** A rebase has stopped at a conflict and an urgent fix is needed on `main`. Compare three options: abort the rebase, a second clone, a worktree.

**Model answer.** First, the usual moves are closed: `git switch main` is refused while rebasing, and `git stash` fails because it cannot write a tree from an index that has unmerged entries. Aborting the rebase works, and it throws away the conflict resolutions already done. A second clone works and leaves the rebase alone, but it costs a full copy of the object database and a second set of remotes to fetch and keep in sync; it is the right choice when you need isolation. A worktree is the lowest-risk option here: `git worktree add -b` with a hotfix branch name, a new path and `main` creates the branch at `main` and checks it out in another directory without copying objects. The rebase state lives in `.git/rebase-merge/`, which is per worktree, so nothing done next door disturbs it. You fix, test, commit and push from the second directory, then run `git worktree remove`. The hotfix branch is a shared ref: it survives the removal with its upstream configured, and the rebase is exactly where you left it.

**Key terms.** `git switch` refused while rebasing; `git stash` fails on unmerged entries; abort discards resolutions; second object database; `git worktree add -b`; `rebase-merge/` is per worktree; hotfix branch is a shared ref

**Common weak answer.** "Stash the changes and switch to `main`." Weak because both commands are refused in the middle of a conflicted rebase; the answer shows no knowledge of the rebase state or of where it is stored.

**Follow-up.** The tests will not start in the new hotfix directory although they run in the original one. Why, and how could you have known in advance?

**A strong reply covers.** Ignored files are in no commit, so the new worktree has no virtual environment, no `node_modules` and no `.env`. `git status --short --ignored` in the main worktree lists what the new one lacks, and each worktree needs a setup step of its own.

**Reference.** [Chapter 25](../textbook/ch25-worktrees.md), section 25.5 and 25.1

#### Q115

**Question.** Is a commit that exists only on the detached HEAD of a linked worktree safe from `git gc`? When does that stop being true?

**Model answer.** Yes, for as long as Git knows the worktree. `git gc` takes the HEAD of every worktree into account, so a commit reachable only from another worktree's detached HEAD is not unreachable. Chapter 25, section 25.7 shows it: a commit that is on no branch survives `git gc --prune=now` run from the main worktree, and `git cat-file -t` on `worktrees/<id>/HEAD` still reports a commit. The protection lasts exactly as long as the worktree's administrative entry under `.git/worktrees/`. After `git worktree remove` or `git worktree prune` the entry is gone, and the worktree's HEAD reflog went with it, so nothing holds the commit. Pruning can also happen without anyone asking: when the directory was deleted by hand, `git gc` and the automatic maintenance of Git 2.54 and later remove the stale entry in time. The prevention is to put the work on a branch before removing a detached worktree. The recovery, before the next pruning of objects, is `git fsck --lost-found` in the main worktree.

**Key terms.** gc considers the HEAD of every worktree; administrative entry; HEAD reflog deleted with the entry; `git worktree remove` or `prune`; create a branch first; `git fsck --lost-found`

**Common weak answer.** "The reflog keeps it for a while, as for any commit." Weak because the reflog in question is the worktree's own HEAD reflog, which is deleted with the worktree's entry, so the usual safety net disappears at the moment of removal.

**Follow-up.** `git worktree remove` refuses when the tree has modified or untracked files. Does that refusal protect these commits?

**A strong reply covers.** No. The refusal concerns files in the working tree, not whether the commits at HEAD are on a branch: a clean detached worktree is removed together with its HEAD reflog. Preview with `git -C <path> log --oneline -3` and create a branch before removing.

**Reference.** [Chapter 25](../textbook/ch25-worktrees.md), section 25.7 and 25.8

#### Q116

**Question.** After moving a project directory to another disk, every linked worktree reports "not a git repository". What broke, how do you repair it, and how could it have been avoided?

**Model answer.** The main worktree moved, and worktrees are linked with absolute paths by default. Each linked worktree has a `.git` file whose one line names its private directory inside the main repository's `.git/worktrees/`. After the move that path no longer exists, so Git run inside a linked worktree finds no repository; `cat .git` there shows the old path. The repair is `git worktree repair` run in the main worktree at its new location: it rewrites the `.git` file of every linked worktree it knows. If the linked worktrees moved as well, run it in the main worktree with their new paths as arguments, and repair before any prune. Avoidance has two forms. Decide the directory layout before adding worktrees. Or, since Git 2.48, create them with `git worktree add --relative-paths` or set `worktree.useRelativePaths`, which helps when the repository and its worktrees are moved or mounted together. The chapter recommends leaving the default otherwise, because relative links set a repository extension that older Git versions refuse to read.

**Key terms.** absolute paths by default; `.git` file of the linked worktree; `git worktree repair` in the main worktree; both pointers; `--relative-paths` since Git 2.48; repository extension; decide the layout first

**Common weak answer.** "The worktrees are corrupted; delete them and add them again." Weak because only a pointer file per worktree is stale; `git worktree repair` rewrites it, while deleting the directories destroys uncommitted work.

**Follow-up.** What can `git worktree move` not move, and how do you protect a worktree on a disk that is not always mounted from being cleaned up?

**A strong reply covers.** It cannot move the main worktree, nor a worktree that contains submodules. `git worktree lock`, with `--reason`, protects a worktree from `prune`, `move` and `remove`; the manual's stated purpose is a working tree on a removable disk or a network share that is not always mounted.

**Reference.** [Chapter 25](../textbook/ch25-worktrees.md), section 25.6 and 25.11

#### Q117

**Question.** When is a separate clone the better tool?

**Model answer.** When you need isolation, because worktrees do not provide it: they share refs, stashes, configuration and hooks, and one object database. A separate clone is the better tool for an untrusted experiment, for rehearsing a destructive history rewrite, and for work that needs a different set of remotes and credentials. It is also the safer choice for a superproject with submodules: the BUGS section of the manual calls multiple checkout still experimental, with incomplete submodule support, and does not recommend it for a superproject. A clone is an independent copy, which a linked worktree is not: deleting the directory of the main worktree deletes the repository and the history of every linked worktree, so linked worktrees are not backups. The price of a clone is a second object database and a second set of remotes to keep current, which is why cloning again for every parallel task is outdated as general advice. And for a two-minute look at another branch from a clean working tree, neither is needed: `git switch` is enough.

**Key terms.** isolation; shared refs, stashes, configuration and hooks; untrusted experiment; rehearsing a history rewrite; different remotes and credentials; superproject with submodules; linked worktrees are not backups

**Common weak answer.** "Never: a worktree is a clone that costs less disk." Weak because a worktree shares refs, stashes, configuration and hooks with the repository it belongs to and disappears with it, so it gives neither isolation nor a backup.

**Follow-up.** A team keeps a bare repository and adds every branch as a linked worktree beside it. Is that layout valid, and what do you check?

**A strong reply covers.** Yes: a bare repository can have linked worktrees and no main one. Check how `fetch` behaves, because a bare clone made with `git clone --bare` has no remote-tracking branches configured, and keep worktrees beside a repository, not inside another working tree, where `git clean -d` can see them.

**Reference.** [Chapter 25](../textbook/ch25-worktrees.md), section 25.9 and 25.11


### Branching: principal level

#### Q118

**Question.** There are 340 branches on the server. You are accountable for the cleanup. How do you decide which can be deleted without losing anything, and what policy keeps the number from growing back?

**Model answer.** I would not decide by age or by a single command, because Git offers three tests for a stale branch and each has a blind spot. Age, from `git for-each-ref --sort=committerdate` over the remote-tracking refs, says when a tip last changed, not whether its work landed. Reachability, from `git branch -r --no-merged origin/main`, misses every squash-merged branch: `main` then holds a new commit with the content and none of the branch's commits. A deleted upstream, shown as gone after `git fetch --prune`, is the most reliable signal only on a team that deletes server branches after merging, and it says nothing about work that was never pushed. So for each candidate I read `git log --oneline main..<branch>`; if the range is empty, or `git merge-tree --write-tree main <branch>` prints the tree of `main`, nothing is lost. The policy: delete the branch in the same step as the merge, prune regularly, and use namespaced lowercase names so rules and listings can match by pattern.

**Key terms.** three tests, each with a blind spot; age is not merge status; squash merge defeats reachability; gone upstream after `git fetch --prune`; `git merge-tree --write-tree`; delete at merge time

**Common weak answer.** "Delete everything older than six months, or everything `git branch --merged` lists." Weak because age says nothing about whether work landed, and `--merged` cannot see squash merges, so one rule deletes unfinished work and the other leaves most of the pile.

**Follow-up.** After the cleanup, someone argues that deleting a branch on the server was also the right way to get rid of a credential committed on it. What is your answer?

**A strong reply covers.** It is wrong. Deleting a branch removes a name. It does not delete the commits, and it does not remove them from the server, from colleagues' clones or from a pull request. A branch deletion is never a way to withdraw content.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.13 and 7.12

#### Q119

**Question.** A director asks for a report built from Git alone: for every branch, who created it, when, from which branch, and which commits belong to it. Which of these can Git answer, and what do you offer instead?

**Model answer.** Git stores none of the four. A branch is a ref that holds one commit ID: there is no owner, no creation date, no record of where it started and no list of its commits. What exists is weaker. `git for-each-ref`, sorted by `committerdate`, can print the date and author of the tip commit, which says when the branch last changed and who wrote that commit, not who created the branch. The first line of a branch's reflog records its creation, but a reflog exists in one clone only and is removed by `git branch -D` or by expiry. Commits do not belong to a branch; I can only list those reachable from the tip and not from a base I name, with `git log main..<branch>` or `%(ahead-behind:main)`. So I would offer a report of tip date, counts against a stated base and upstream state, and take "created from" from the pull request's base branch, which GitHub stores, not Git.

**Key terms.** ref holds one commit ID only; no owner, no creation date, no start point; tip commit date is not creation date; reflog is local to one clone; commits relative to a named base; pull request base is GitHub's record

**Common weak answer.** "Git tracks all of that; parse `git log` and the reflog." Weak because the tip's author is not the branch's creator, the reflog is local and perishable, and commits are reachable from a branch, not owned by it.

**Follow-up.** A colleague proposes filling the "created from" column with `%(is-base:...)` from `git for-each-ref`. Why do you refuse?

**A strong reply covers.** It is a guess from a first-parent heuristic, and it changes with the refs that exist: in section 7.9, deleting the intermediate branch made it name `main`. The textbook's recommendation is a hint for humans, never an input to automation.

**Reference.** [Chapter 7](../textbook/ch07-branches.md), section 7.2 and 7.9 and 7.13

#### Q120

**Question.** `receive.denyNonFastForwards` is set on our Git server. Are our tags safe? How would you prove your answer?

**Model answer.** No. In Git 2.55.0 the code behind `receive.denyNonFastForwards` and `receive.denyDeletes` applies them only to refs under `refs/heads/`; the manual's wording does not say so, which is why people assume tags are covered. I would prove it by experiment against a scratch bare repository, as Chapter 14B, section 14B.11 does: set both settings, push an annotated tag, move it locally with `git tag -f -a`, then run `git push --force origin <tag>` and `git push origin --delete <tag>`. Both are accepted. On a plain Git server the protection is a server-side `update` hook, which is called once per ref with the ref name, the old ID and the new ID; it rejects any change to a release tag whose old ID is not all zeros, so creating a tag is allowed and moving or deleting one is not. On GitHub, which is a different layer, the equivalent is a tag ruleset that restricts updates and deletions; tag protection rules were retired in August 2024 in favor of rulesets.

**Key terms.** applies to `refs/heads/` only; `receive.denyDeletes`; proof by experiment on a scratch server; server-side `update` hook; old ID all zeros means creation; GitHub tag ruleset

**Common weak answer.** "Yes: non-fast-forward updates are denied, and moving a tag is one." Weak because it reasons from the name of the setting. In Git 2.55.0 the setting is applied to branches only, and the answer offers no experiment that would have exposed that.

**Follow-up.** With a tag rule in place on your own server, what must a consumer of somebody else's tags still do, and why?

**A strong reply covers.** Treat a tag as a mutable name held by someone else: record the commit ID next to every tag you depend on, deploy by commit ID or image digest, and pin third-party GitHub Actions by full commit ID. The Phase 0 report records real attacks in which actions referenced by tag were repointed.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14B](../textbook/ch14b-config-tags-signing.md), section 14B.11

#### Q121

**Question.** Your team wants several AI coding agents to work in one repository at once. What do worktrees give you, and what do they not give you?

**Model answer.** Worktrees give each agent its own directory, HEAD and index on one shared object database, created with `git worktree add -b` and one branch per task. There is no second copy of history and nothing to fetch between them: a branch committed in one directory can be diffed, merged or cherry-picked from any other immediately, and the one-branch rule gives each agent exclusive ownership of its branch. What they do not give is isolation. Ignored files are in no commit, so every worktree needs its own setup of dependencies and environment files. Ports, caches and local databases are outside Git's view and collide as they would between two clones. Stashes, configuration and hooks are shared, so an agent that pops a stash may take another agent's; the rule for agents is to commit to their branch and never to stash. Integration is still a merge, and overlapping edits still conflict. Cleanup is `git worktree remove` and `git branch -d` per task. For untrusted work or separate credentials, use separate clones.

**Key terms.** one shared object database; one branch per agent; no isolation; ignored files do not come along; shared stash, config and hooks; commit, never stash; integration is still a merge; cleanup per task

**Common weak answer.** "Worktrees isolate the agents: four worktrees are four clones without the disk cost." Weak because they share refs, stashes, configuration and hooks, and Git manages no ports, caches or dependencies; the answer also omits integration and cleanup.

**Follow-up.** One agent needs a commit identity different from the others. What happens if it runs `git config set user.email` in its own worktree, and what is the supported way, with its compatibility cost?

**A strong reply covers.** It writes the shared `.git/config` and changes the identity in every worktree. The supported way is `extensions.worktreeConfig` set to true and then `git config set --worktree`; the manual notes that older Git versions refuse to work in a repository that has the extension set.

**Reference.** [Chapter 25](../textbook/ch25-worktrees.md), section 25.5, 25.7 and 25.9


## Area 4: Merge

Q122 to Q141. Merge bases, the three-way rule, conflicts and their stages, strategies, rerere, auditing a merge.


### Merge: foundational level

#### Q122

**Question.** Why can Git merge two files incorrectly from a human perspective?

**Model answer.** Because a merge is a computation on text, not on meaning. Git computes it from exactly three snapshots, ours, theirs and the merge base, and compares lines; its own FAQ says it does not consider the history or the individual commits on the branches at all. A clean merge therefore certifies one property: no two changed regions overlapped. It says nothing about whether the result builds, passes its tests or makes sense. Two changes that are textually far apart and logically incompatible merge without a word, for example a renamed function on one branch and a new caller of the old name on the other. The second consequence is that intermediate history is invisible: a change applied on both branches and reverted on one comes back, because the reverting side equals the base and counts as having done nothing. Git is correct by its rules in both cases. The human expectation of a meaning-aware merge is what fails, so the merged tree must be tested before it reaches `main`.

**Key terms.** three snapshots; text not meaning; overlap of changed lines; semantic conflict; history between base and tips ignored; test the merge result

**Common weak answer.** "Git has merge bugs in complicated cases." Weak because none of the documented failures needs a bug: each follows from merging snapshots of text. The answer also offers no control, since it treats the cause as bad luck.

**Follow-up.** Name two merge options that make a result clean and wrong, and say how you would detect such a merge afterwards.

**A strong reply covers.** `-X ours` silently drops their side of every conflicting hunk, and `-X ignore-space-change` discards their whitespace changes, so a formatting branch counts as merged while the tree equals the first parent. `git show --remerge-diff <merge>` exposes both, because it repeats the merge with default settings.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.1 and 8.15

#### Q123

**Question.** `git merge feature` printed "Fast-forward". What changed in `.git`, and what did not?

**Model answer.** A fast-forward happens when the current commit is an ancestor of the commit being merged, so there is nothing to combine. What changed: the file for the current branch ref, for example `refs/heads/main`, was rewritten with the new commit ID; `ORIG_HEAD` received the old one; the reflogs of HEAD and of the branch each gained one line that says the merge was a fast-forward; and the index was rewritten, with the working tree updated as by a branch switch. What did not change: the object database. No commit, tree or blob was created, which `git rev-list --count --all` proves before and after. HEAD is still the same symbolic ref to the branch. Nothing in the history records that the new commits were ever a separate branch; only the local reflog knows. One detail from the chapter: every `git merge` call rewrites `ORIG_HEAD`, even one that prints "Already up to date." or refuses, so it is an undo pointer only until the next attempt.

**Key terms.** ancestor condition; branch ref moves; no new objects; `ORIG_HEAD`; reflog entry; no merge commit; index and working tree updated

**Common weak answer.** "Git created a merge commit that joins the two branches." Weak because a fast-forward creates no object at all; it also misses that the only record is the local reflog and that `ORIG_HEAD` is overwritten by the next merge attempt.

**Follow-up.** What is the production risk of a fast-forward leaving no trace, and how do you recover from one and forbid the next?

**A strong reply covers.** If an unfinished branch is fast-forwarded into `main`, its work-in-progress commits look as if they were made on `main` and no merge commit exists to revert. Before pushing, return with `git reset --merge ORIG_HEAD` after checking it, or take the commit from the reflog. Forbid it with `--no-ff` or `merge.ff=false`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.3

#### Q124

**Question.** State the three-way rule for a single path as a table of base, ours and theirs. Which rows never read file content?

**Model answer.** For each path Git compares three blob IDs: base, ours and theirs. If all three are equal, nobody changed the path and it stays. If only ours differs from the base, ours is taken; if only theirs differs, theirs is taken. If both sides differ from the base in the identical way, the change is taken once, without a message. If all three differ, Git merges the content of the three files line by line. A path absent in base and ours and present in theirs is added; a path unchanged in ours and absent in theirs is deleted. A path changed on one side and deleted on the other is a modify/delete conflict, and a path absent in the base and added differently on both sides is an add/add conflict. Only the row with three different IDs runs a content merge. The rows where at least two versions are equal are settled by comparing IDs, because equal content has an equal blob ID. The `git read-tree` manual states the first rows in terms of stages 1, 2 and 3.

**Key terms.** base, ours, theirs; blob ID comparison; same change taken once; content merge only when all three differ; modify/delete; add/add; stages 1, 2, 3

**Common weak answer.** "Git replays the commits of one branch onto the other and stops where they clash." Weak because a merge reads three snapshots, not commits, and most paths are decided by comparing IDs without reading any file.

**Follow-up.** The rows mention three snapshots and nothing else. Which two consequences of that surprise people in production?

**A strong reply covers.** The commits between the base and each tip take no part. A change both sides made identically is taken once and silently, and a change one side made and later undid counts as that side doing nothing, so the other side's version wins without a conflict (section 8.15).

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.4


### Merge: working engineer level

#### Q125

**Question.** What happens during a three-way merge?

**Model answer.** When both branches have commits the other lacks, a fast-forward is impossible and Git performs a true merge from exactly three snapshots: the tree of the commit HEAD points to (ours), the tree of the commit named on the command line (theirs), and the tree of their merge base. For every path it compares the three blob IDs. A path changed on one side only is taken from that side, an identical change on both sides is taken once, and only a path that differs in all three goes to a line-level content merge, where hunks that do not touch are both applied. If everything resolves, Git writes the new blobs and trees and one commit with two parent lines, moves the current branch ref to it, sets `ORIG_HEAD` and adds reflog entries. If a region was changed differently by both sides, the merge stops: HEAD stays, `MERGE_HEAD` is set, the index holds stages 1, 2 and 3 for the conflicted path, and the working tree file gets marker blocks. The default strategy that does this is `ort`.

**Key terms.** three snapshots; merge base; per-path blob ID comparison; line-level content merge; two parents; `MERGE_HEAD` and stages on conflict; `ort`

**Common weak answer.** "Git compares the two branches and combines the differences." Weak because it omits the third input: without the merge base Git cannot tell a line one side added from a line the other side deleted. It also treats the merge as a replay of commits, which it is not.

**Follow-up.** The tree of the merge commit is a snapshot that neither author wrote. What follows for testing, and what does GitHub Actions do about it by default?

**A strong reply covers.** Both parents can be green while the merge is red, so CI has to run on the merge result. For a `pull_request` event GitHub Actions by default checks out a merge of the head into the current base, computed on GitHub's servers; this is described from GitHub's documentation, not run in the course.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.4 and 8.8

#### Q126

**Question.** Define "merge base". How can two commits have more than one, and what does the default strategy do then?

**Model answer.** The merge base of two commits is their best common ancestor: a common ancestor that has no better common ancestor, where one ancestor is better than another if the other is its ancestor. It is the third input of every merge. Nothing stores it; Git computes it from the parent lines of commit objects each time a command needs it. Two commits have more than one merge base in a criss-cross: each branch has merged the other, so two common ancestors exist and neither is an ancestor of the other. `git merge-base --all` prints all of them, and without `--all` it is unspecified which one you get. The default `ort` strategy then merges the merge bases with each other first and uses that merged tree, the virtual merge base, as the base. If that inner merge conflicts, its markers stay inside the base, visible as stage 1 with the labels "Temporary merge branch 1" and "2", and the outer merge conflicts so that a human decides.

**Key terms.** best common ancestor; computed from parent links; criss-cross; `git merge-base --all`; virtual merge base; `ort`; stage 1 with markers

**Common weak answer.** "The merge base is the commit where the branch was created." Weak because nothing records where a branch came from: the base is computed from ancestry, it moves forward whenever one branch merges the other, and there can be two of them.

**Follow-up.** Why does Git not pick one of the two merge bases and proceed, and how would you demonstrate the consequence of picking one?

**A strong reply covers.** Either base alone silently reapplies one side's earlier decision: section 8.5 runs `git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<commit>` with each candidate and gets two clean, opposite results. A base that matches neither tip returns the question to a human. Prevention: between long-lived branches, merge in one direction only.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.2 and 8.5

#### Q127

**Question.** Two branches changed different lines of one file and the merge still conflicted. Give the exact condition under which that happens.

**Model answer.** A content conflict occurs when both sides changed the same lines of a file, or lines with no unchanged line between them, and did not make the identical change. The merge works on hunks, which are runs of base lines that a side replaced, removed or inserted into. Two hunks with no unchanged line between them form one region, and that region was changed by both sides, so Git reports a conflict even though the edited lines differ. One unchanged line between the edits is enough to keep them apart. Section 8.7 proves it with `git merge-file -p` on three plain files: line 2 against line 3 conflicts, line 2 against line 4 merges. Git draws the boundary there because an unchanged line is the only evidence of independence that text offers. The fix is to take the changed line from each side. No prevention is needed, and reaching for `-X ours` is wrong because it would drop their line.

**Key terms.** adjacency; hunks; no unchanged line between; one region; `git merge-file -p`; line as the unit; take both lines

**Common weak answer.** "Git conflicts only when both people edit the same line." Weak because the test is adjacency of hunks, not identity of lines; the answer cannot explain a conflict between line 2 and line 3 and tends to end in `-X ours`.

**Follow-up.** Which kinds of files meet that condition far more often than others, and why?

**A strong reply covers.** Jupyter notebooks, which store outputs and an execution counter next to the code, so two people who only ran the notebook changed the same lines and a conflicted merge can leave invalid JSON. Also append-only files such as changelogs, migration lists and dependency lists: every branch inserts after the same last line.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.7

#### Q128

**Question.** During a conflict, what are index stages 1, 2 and 3? How do you read "their" version of a file without touching the working tree?

**Model answer.** While a merge is stopped, the index holds up to three entries for each conflicted path instead of the usual single stage 0 entry. Stage 1 is the version from the common ancestor, stage 2 the version from HEAD, called ours, and stage 3 the version from `MERGE_HEAD`, called theirs. Each is a whole file stored as a blob. Ours means the commit you were on when you ran `git merge` and theirs the commit you named; it has nothing to do with who wrote what. `git ls-files -u` lists the entries and is the ground truth when a merge tool and the command line seem to disagree. To read their version without touching the working tree, use the stage syntax: `git show :3:path`. The two most useful commands in a resolution are `git diff :1:path :2:path` and `git diff :1:path :3:path`, because they show what each side did to the base, including changes that merged cleanly outside the marker block. `git add` on the path replaces the three entries with one stage 0 entry.

**Key terms.** stage 1 base; stage 2 ours (HEAD); stage 3 theirs (`MERGE_HEAD`); `git ls-files -u`; `git show :3:path`; whole-file blobs; stage 0 after `git add`

**Common weak answer.** "Ours is my code and theirs is my colleague's code." Weak because the roles follow the checked-out commit and the commit named on the command line, not authorship, and the answer usually cannot name a command that reads a stage.

**Follow-up.** Which conflict types leave fewer than three stages, and what do `git checkout --theirs` and `git restore --theirs` do on a path that has no stage 3?

**A strong reply covers.** An add/add conflict has stages 2 and 3 only; a modify/delete conflict has stage 1 and the modifying side; a file location conflict has one stage. On a path deleted by them, `git checkout --theirs` refuses, while `git restore --theirs` succeeds silently and removes the file. Neither marks the path resolved.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.8 and 8.10

#### Q129

**Question.** What does rerere record, and when? Why does a resolution recorded in a merge also serve a rebase in the other direction?

**Model answer.** With `rerere.enabled` set, Git records in two moments. When a conflict appears, it normalizes the conflict in each file: the labels are stripped from the markers, the two sides are sorted, and the base part of `diff3` output is removed. It hashes the conflict hunks and uses the result, the conflict ID, as the name of a directory in `.git/rr-cache`, where it stores the normalized conflict as `preimage`. When you conclude, at the commit or at `git rebase --continue`, it stores the resolved file as `postimage`. When the same conflict text appears again, in any merge, rebase, cherry-pick or revert, Git merges the old conflict, the old resolution and the new conflict and, if that is clean, writes the result into the file in place of the markers. The record serves the other direction because its name depends on the two competing texts, not on branch names, on which side is ours, or on the path; sorting the sides makes the swap in a rebase irrelevant. Rerere writes the file only: the index stays unmerged unless `rerere.autoUpdate` is true.

**Key terms.** `rerere.enabled`; normalized conflict; `preimage` and `postimage`; `.git/rr-cache`; conflict ID from the text; sides sorted; index left unmerged

**Common weak answer.** "Rerere remembers which side I chose for a file." Weak because it records conflict text and the resolved text, keyed by an ID computed from the normalized conflict, not a side or a path; the weak version cannot explain reuse across a merge and a rebase, or why a changed conflict is a new conflict.

**Follow-up.** When rerere replays a resolution during a merge, what do the command output, the file and the index look like, and why does that matter?

**A strong reply covers.** The merge still reports CONFLICT, says the automatic merge failed and exits with status 1; one extra line says the path was resolved using a previous resolution. The file has no markers, `git status` shows `UU` and the index keeps three stages. That stop is the only review a replay gets.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14C](../textbook/ch14c-stash-rerere-attributes-hooks.md), section 14C.3


### Merge: senior level

#### Q130

**Question.** A conflict was resolved with `git checkout --theirs path`, and a teammate's unrelated fix in that file disappeared. Explain the mechanism and prove it from history.

**Model answer.** `git checkout --theirs path`, like `git restore --theirs path`, writes the whole stage 3 version of the file to the working tree. It does not take their side of the conflicted hunks only. A conflicted file is mostly finished: every non-conflicting change is already merged outside the marker block, and the whole-file shortcut throws that merged result away, so any change our side had made elsewhere in the file is gone once the path is staged. Git lost nothing; a person chose a whole file. The proof is `git show --remerge-diff <merge>`: Git repeats the merge into a temporary tree and diffs it against the recorded tree, so the dropped lines appear as a removal outside the marker block. `git log -p` shows no diff for a merge, and plain `git show` prints nothing here because the dense combined format omits hunks where the result equals one parent. `git log --full-history -- path` is the second diagnostic. The repair is a new commit that restores the lines and says why.

**Key terms.** whole-file replacement; stage 3; non-conflicting changes already merged; `git show --remerge-diff`; combined diff is blind; restore in a new commit

**Common weak answer.** "Git lost the change during the merge." Weak because the merge had already kept the fix; the whole-file shortcut discarded it, and the answer offers no command that shows a hand-made change inside a merge commit.

**Follow-up.** How would you have resolved that conflict so the unrelated fix survived, and which configuration makes the mistake harder to make?

**A strong reply covers.** Read both intents with the stage diffs and `git log --merge`, edit only the marked region, and confirm with `git diff AUTO_MERGE` that the resolution removed only markers and one candidate. The chapter recommends `merge.conflictStyle=zdiff3`, which shows the base inside the block so each intent is readable.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.10 and 8.16

#### Q131

**Question.** Compare `git merge -X ours`, `git merge -s ours` and `git merge --squash` in terms of content and ancestry.

**Model answer.** `-X ours` is an option of the default `ort` strategy. It runs a real three-way merge, their non-conflicting changes arrive, and only conflicting hunks are decided for our side, without a conflict being reported. The result is a merge commit with two parents: content and ancestry, minus their side of each clash. `-s ours` is a different strategy. It does not look at their tree at all, the tree of the merge commit is identical to the tree of its first parent, and yet the commit has two parents, so `git branch --merged` lists the branch. That is ancestry without content, defensible for declaring a branch obsolete. `--squash` computes the same result as a merge, stages it and writes no `MERGE_HEAD`; the commit you then make has one parent. That is content without ancestry, the exact opposite of `-s ours`: `git branch -d` refuses to delete the branch and the merge base does not move. There is no `-s theirs`.

**Key terms.** strategy option versus strategy; conflicting hunks only; tree equals first parent; ancestry without content; content without ancestry; one parent; merge base does not move

**Common weak answer.** "`-X ours` and `-s ours` both keep my version." Weak because one merges everything except the clashes and the other discards their whole tree while recording the branch as merged; the answer also ignores that a squash records no ancestry.

**Follow-up.** A branch was squash-merged, work continued on it, and the second squash conflicts on a line the first squash already delivered. Explain it and give the rule.

**A strong reply covers.** The squash commit has one parent, so the merge base is still the original fork: `main` changed the line through the squash and the branch changed it too. Resolve in favour of the newer text, then keep to one squash per branch and delete it; branches that live on need real merge commits.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.6 and 8.12

#### Q132

**Question.** What do `git show <merge>`, `git show --first-parent <merge>` and `git show --remerge-diff <merge>` each display? Which one audits a conflict resolution?

**Model answer.** A merge commit stores a tree and no diff, so each view is a computation. `git show <merge>` uses the dense combined format: it shows lines that differ from every parent and omits hunks where the result equals one parent, so it is blind to a resolution that took one side unchanged. `git show --first-parent <merge>` is an ordinary diff against the first parent: everything the merge brought to the mainline, without telling branch content from hand-made changes. `git show --remerge-diff <merge>` repeats the merge into a temporary tree, conflict markers included, and diffs that against the recorded tree. No output means the merge is exactly what Git computes on its own; removed marker lines with one candidate kept are a resolution; a change with no markers nearby came from neither branch. The remerge diff is the one that audits a resolution. For comparison, `git log -p` shows no diff at all for a merge commit. For a release, `git log --merges --remerge-diff --first-parent` over the range lists every hand-made change.

**Key terms.** dense combined diff; first-parent diff; remerge diff; temporary re-merge with markers; no output means mechanical; `git log -p` blind to merges

**Common weak answer.** "`git show` on the merge shows what the merge changed." Weak because the combined format hides any resolution that equals one parent, which is the common case when someone takes one side, and it cannot separate hand-made changes from branch content.

**Follow-up.** A merge was made with `-X ours` and looked clean when it was made. Does the audit show it, and what are the audit's limits?

**A strong reply covers.** Yes: the remerge diff repeats the merge with default settings, so a merge made with `-X ours` or `-s ours` appears as a diff. Limits: Git 2.36 or later, two-parent merges only, so octopus merges are skipped, and an output format the manual declares subject to change, so read it and do not parse it.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.16

#### Q133

**Question.** A change was made on two branches and reverted on one. After the merge it is back. Explain with the merge base.

**Model answer.** The merge sees three snapshots, not the commits between them. In the merge base the setting has its old value. On the branch that applied the change and then reverted it, the tip has the old value again, so that side is equal to the base. On the other branch the tip has the new value. That is the row "only theirs changed it" of the three-way rule, so the new value is taken, with no conflict and no message. The apply-then-revert pair cancels out and the merge never sees it; the revert was a decision recorded in history that the snapshot does not carry. The evidence is three commands: `git show` of the file at the merge base, at the first parent and at the second parent of the merge. The manual describes this behavior and admits that some people find it confusing. If the revert must win, say so in a tree the merge will see: revert the change on the other branch too before merging.

**Key terms.** three snapshots; reverting side equals base; "only theirs changed it"; intermediate commits ignored; no conflict, no message; revert on both branches

**Common weak answer.** "The merge ignored the revert commit by mistake" or "someone re-applied it during the merge." Weak because nobody acted and nothing was ignored by mistake: the reverting side is identical to the base, so by the rule it did nothing.

**Follow-up.** Would `git show --remerge-diff` on that merge commit flag the returned change? Justify the answer.

**A strong reply covers.** No. The remerge diff shows only where the recorded tree differs from a mechanical re-merge, and this result is the mechanical one, so it prints nothing. The audit that works is showing the path at the merge base and at both parents. This is a deduction from section 8.16, not a transcript.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.15 and 8.4

#### Q134

**Question.** You reverted a merge and later merged the repaired branch; part of the feature is missing. What happened, and what is the correct sequence?

**Model answer.** `git revert -m 1` on a merge creates a commit that undoes the difference between the merge and its first parent. It undoes content. It cannot undo ancestry: the merge commit is still in the history, the branch's original commits are still ancestors of `main`, and `git branch --merged` still lists the branch. When the repaired branch is merged again, the merge base is past those original commits, so the merge brings only the commits added since. The manual states the rule: reverting a merge declares that you will never want the tree changes it brought in, and later merges bring only changes from commits that are not ancestors of the reverted merge. So the repair commits arrive, the original work does not, and the merge is clean. The evidence is `git log main..branch`, which lists only the new commits. The correct sequence is to revert the revert on `main` first and then merge the repaired branch; Chapter 11 covers that repair.

**Key terms.** revert undoes content, not ancestry; original commits already ancestors; merge base past them; only new commits arrive; revert the revert; `git revert -m 1`

**Common weak answer.** "Merge the branch again and the feature comes back." Weak because the original commits are already reachable from `main`, so a new merge has nothing to bring from them; the answer misses that a revert is a new commit, not a removal of history.

**Follow-up.** Why does `git revert` refuse a merge commit until you pass `-m`, and what exactly does `-m 1` undo?

**A strong reply covers.** A merge commit has one diff per parent, so Git needs to be told which parent is the mainline. `-m 1` undoes the difference between the merge and its first parent, which is what the receiving branch gained. For an octopus merge the choice is among more than two parents.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.18 and 8.1

#### Q135

**Question.** How can a server with no working tree decide whether a pull request merges cleanly? What does stock Git offer for that?

**Model answer.** A merge needs three trees and somewhere to write the result; it does not need a working tree. Stock Git exposes this as `git merge-tree --write-tree A B`, which performs a real merge with the same strategy as `git merge`, using only the object database: no index, no working tree, no ref update. It prints the ID of the resulting tree and exits 0 for a clean merge and 1 for a conflict; on a conflict it also prints the stage entries and messages, and the tree it wrote contains the markers. It works in a bare repository, where `git merge` refuses to run. `--quiet` gives a yes or no answer, and `git commit-tree` with two `-p` options plus `git update-ref` turns a clean tree into a published merge commit. On the GitHub side, its publications say that it uses the merge-ort strategy both to test whether a pull request merges cleanly and to create the merge. They do not say which command it runs; the course describes this from those pages and did not run it.

**Key terms.** `git merge-tree --write-tree`; object database only; bare repository; exit status 0 or 1; `git commit-tree` and `git update-ref`; merge-ort on GitHub; described, not run

**Common weak answer.** "GitHub checks out the branch and runs `git merge` on the server." Weak because a bare repository has no working tree and `git merge` refuses to run there; it also asserts a GitHub implementation detail that GitHub's cited pages do not state.

**Follow-up.** What is documented about GitHub Actions when a pull request has a merge conflict, and what should a script use to decide between clean and conflict?

**A strong reply covers.** GitHub's documentation states that workflows will not run on `pull_request` activity if the pull request has a merge conflict. A script must decide by the exit status of `git merge-tree`, as the manual warns, not by whether the list of conflicted files is empty.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.17 and 8.22

#### Q136

**Question.** `git merge --abort` is supposed to return you to the state before the merge. An engineer ran it during a conflicted merge and lost an uncommitted edit that predated the merge. How did the safety net fail, can the edit be recovered, and what do you tell the team?

**Model answer.** The safety net failed because `git merge --abort` is `git reset --merge`: it resets every staged path, and it cannot tell a merge result from an edit that predates the merge and that you staged meanwhile. The merge was allowed to start because the edit sat, unstaged, in a path the merge did not touch; such work normally survives both the merge and an abort. During the resolution a reflex `git add -A` staged it together with the resolved files, and the abort then reset it. The manual warns that abort will in some cases be unable to reconstruct the original changes. Recovery is possible: before a true merge starts on a tree with local changes, Git 2.55 runs `git stash create` as a safety copy. No ref points to that commit, so `git fsck` lists it as a dangling commit, and it lasts only until unreachable objects are pruned. The release in which this behavior began was not determined. The rule for the team: commit or stash before merging, and stage paths by name during a resolution.

**Key terms.** `git reset --merge`; resets every staged path; edit staged during the merge; `git stash create` safety copy; dangling commit in `git fsck`; lasts until pruning; stage by name

**Common weak answer.** "Abort always restores exactly what you had; the edit must have been lost some other way." Weak because abort resets all staged paths without knowing their origin, and the answer does not know about the unreferenced safety commit, so it gives up on a recoverable edit.

**Follow-up.** A different engineer used `git merge --autostash`, saw the hint to run `git stash pop` after the conflict, and `git stash pop` reports no entries. Where is their work?

**A strong reply covers.** The autostash is a stash-shaped commit that `.git/MERGE_AUTOSTASH` points to, not an entry in the stash list. `git merge --continue` and `git merge --abort` apply it. It reaches the stash list only after `git merge --quit` or `git reset --merge`, per the manual, or when applying it conflicts, as seen in the sandbox.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.19 and 8.21

#### Q137

**Question.** A wrong value reached `main` through a replayed resolution. Give the diagnosis and the complete fix. Why is a new commit alone not enough?

**Model answer.** The diagnosis is in the output of the merge or rebase: a line saying the path was resolved using a previous resolution, or staged using one when `rerere.autoUpdate` is set. Rerere matches conflict text, not intent, and replays a wrong recorded resolution as faithfully as a right one; apart from the file content the output is identical to the correct case. Nobody typed the value: it came from the `postimage` in `.git/rr-cache`. The correction on a conflict has three steps: `git rerere forget <path>` deletes the recorded resolution, `git restore --merge <path>` rebuilds the conflict from the index, and a fresh resolution followed by `git add` and the commit records the new one. If the wrong merge is committed and not pushed, undo it first with `git reset --keep HEAD^`, merge again, then forget. Because here it is pushed, fix forward with a new commit and still forget. A new commit alone is not enough because the wrong record is still in the cache, and the next rebase that meets the same conflict text brings the mistake back.

**Key terms.** "using previous resolution"; text not intent; `postimage`; `git rerere forget`; `git restore --merge`; fix forward when pushed; record survives the commit

**Common weak answer.** "Revert the bad value and move on." Weak because it repairs the tree and leaves the cause: the recorded resolution replays at the next identical conflict. It also treats the event as a typing mistake when no one typed anything.

**Follow-up.** Which settings and habits would have prevented it, and what are rerere's limits as a mechanism shared by a team?

**A strong reply covers.** Leave `rerere.autoUpdate` off unless tests run before every `--continue`, and read every replayed file: the stop with `UU` is the only review a replay gets. As a shared mechanism rerere is limited: records are per clone, they expire, and two people can replay different resolutions of one conflict.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14C](../textbook/ch14c-stash-rerere-attributes-hooks.md), section 14C.3 and 14C.14

#### Q138

**Question.** A rebase with rerere enabled dies with `Unable to create MERGE_RR.lock`. Give the root cause, the recovery and the prevention.

**Model answer.** The root cause the chapter gives is a race between two correct features for one lock. Each commit of a rebase starts `git maintenance run --auto` in the background. Since Git 2.54 its default strategy includes the task `rerere-gc`, which runs whenever `rr-cache` has an entry and takes `MERGE_RR.lock` while it works. If the next step of the rebase stops on a conflict at that moment, rerere cannot create the lock and the command exits with status 128. Nothing is damaged. The rebase is stopped at that commit with conflict markers, but rerere has neither recorded the conflict nor replayed a resolution for it, which `git rerere status` printing nothing confirms; a resolution made now would not be recorded. The recovery is to run `git rerere` by hand, resolve, `git add`, and `git rebase --continue`. The prevention is `git config set maintenance.rerere-gc.auto 0` in repositories where you rebase with rerere, plus an occasional `git rerere gc` by hand. The mechanism is inferred, not documented, and should be stated that way.

**Key terms.** lock race; background `git maintenance run --auto`; `rerere-gc` task since Git 2.54; `MERGE_RR.lock`; nothing damaged; run `git rerere` by hand; `maintenance.rerere-gc.auto`

**Common weak answer.** "A stale lock file from a crashed Git; delete it and retry." Weak because the lock belongs to a live background task that removes it itself, and the answer misses the real damage: rerere never saw this conflict, so the resolution goes unrecorded unless `git rerere` is run.

**Follow-up.** How confident are you in that root cause, and what evidence does the course have for it?

**A strong reply covers.** It is marked unverified: observed on Git 2.55.0 on macOS only, described in no manual or release note the course read, and inferred from the maintenance configuration plus a measurement. In twenty rebases per configuration the default failed between 1 and 10 times across runs; with the task off, never. Git 2.56 was not tested.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14C](../textbook/ch14c-stash-rerere-attributes-hooks.md), section 14C.3 and 14C.17


### Merge: principal level

#### Q139

**Question.** Both branches were green, the merge had no conflict, and `main` is red. Why can Git not detect this, and which process controls can?

**Model answer.** Git cannot detect it because a merge without conflicts means only that no two text changes overlapped. In the chapter's case one branch renames a function and updates the caller it can see, and the other adds a new module that calls the old name. The sides changed disjoint paths, so by the three-way rule each path is taken from the side that changed it and no file-level merge runs: there was nothing for Git to compare. The dependency lives in the language's import system, not in the text of any one file, and Git has no parser, type checker or test runner. The proof is to run the check on each parent of the merge commit, where both pass, and to list the paths each side changed with a three-dot `git diff --name-only`. The controls are outside Git: CI on the merge result of the pull request, a rule that the branch is up to date with `main`, or a merge queue. The repair is a normal commit on top of the merge, or `git revert -m 1`.

**Key terms.** semantic conflict; disjoint paths; no file-level merge ran; text not meaning; test the merge result; up-to-date rule; merge queue

**Common weak answer.** "Someone must have resolved a conflict badly." Weak because there was no conflict and no resolution: both parents pass and no path was changed by both sides. It looks for a culprit where the cause is the absence of a test on the merged tree.

**Follow-up.** Describe the variant of this failure in which no check turns red at all.

**A strong reply covers.** One branch renames a configuration key and another adds code that reads the old key with a default. Nothing fails: an evaluation run uses the default, the scores shift, and the merge shows no conflict and no red check. The chapter calls this quiet variant worse than the loud one.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.15 and 8.19

#### Q140

**Question.** Design the integration rules for `main` and one long-lived release branch so that history stays auditable and every feature stays revertable. Which merge practices do you mandate, and which demonstrated failure does each one prevent?

**Model answer.** I would mandate five practices, each tied to a failure the chapter demonstrates. One: update a local `main` with `--ff-only`, so a surprise divergence stops you instead of creating an unplanned merge. Two: integrate feature branches into `main` with `--no-ff` merge commits; each feature is then one unit that `git revert -m 1` can undo, and `git log --first-parent main` is the list of integrations. Three: never fast-forward `main` to a branch that has merged `main`, because that flips the first-parent line. Four: between `main` and the release branch, merge in one direction only; merging both ways builds a criss-cross with two merge bases, and the reported symptom is the same conflict coming back. Five: squash only branches that are deleted afterwards, because a squash moves content without ancestry and the merge base never moves. Around these rules, CI runs on the merge result, anything beyond resolving the conflict goes into a normal commit or is named in the merge message, and each release is audited with `git log --merges --remerge-diff --first-parent` over its range.

**Key terms.** `--ff-only` for updating; `--no-ff` for integrating; first-parent history; one-directional merges; one squash per branch; CI on the merge result; remerge-diff audit

**Common weak answer.** "Use merge commits everywhere, or squash everything; it is a matter of taste." Weak because each option has a specific, demonstrated failure: repeated squashes re-conflict, two-way merges create criss-crosses, and a fast-forward of an integrated branch destroys the mainline view that revert and bisect depend on.

**Follow-up.** Explain the first-parent flip you mentioned: how it happens with two ordinary commands, and what breaks afterwards.

**A strong reply covers.** Someone merges `main` into a feature branch, then `main` is fast-forwarded to that branch. First parent means what was checked out, so the feature commit now sits on the mainline and the earlier `main` commit on the second-parent side. Nothing is lost, but `git log --first-parent`, `git bisect start --first-parent` and changelog generators walk through the feature branch.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.12, 8.13 and 8.5

#### Q141

**Question.** A team proposes three measures against recurring conflicts: rerere with `rerere.autoUpdate` for everyone, `merge=union` on the changelog, and a keep-ours merge driver for the lock file named in `.gitattributes`. Assess each as a team-wide mechanism, including for pull requests merged on GitHub, and say what you would require.

**Model answer.** None of the three is a team-wide control. Rerere records live in `.git/rr-cache`, which is not pushed, fetched or cloned, so each engineer has their own records, they expire, and two people can replay different resolutions of one conflict. Rerere matches conflict text, not intent, and `rerere.autoUpdate` removes the one pause in which a replay can be reviewed; I would allow rerere for people who rebase long branches and keep that setting off unless tests run before every `--continue`. `merge=union` is built in and needs the attribute alone. It suits an append-only changelog, though the manual warns that it tends to leave added lines in random order, and it breaks files with structure. The keep-ours driver is named in a versioned file and defined in local configuration: a clone without the definition falls back to the text merge without a message, and a clone with it silently drops the other side's dependency. I would require a CI check that the lock file matches the manifest. On GitHub's servers that driver configuration does not exist, so merge attributes are local aids.

**Key terms.** `rr-cache` is per clone; text not intent; `rerere.autoUpdate` removes the review; `union` for append-only files; driver defined in local configuration; silent fallback; CI check on the lock file

**Common weak answer.** "Commit the attributes and turn rerere on; the conflicts go away for the whole team." Weak because rerere records and driver definitions never leave a clone, GitHub's merge does not have them, and two of the three measures resolve conflicts by silently choosing content.

**Follow-up.** Where the keep-ours driver is defined the merge is clean. What is the more honest setting for a lock file, and what does the merge look like then?

**A strong reply covers.** `-merge` on the path: Git refuses to merge it by content, reports a conflict, leaves the current branch's version without markers and puts all three stages in the index. Keep one side, regenerate from the merged manifest and commit. Whether GitHub honors the built-in `union` driver is not stated in the pages the course read.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14C](../textbook/ch14c-stash-rerere-attributes-hooks.md), section 14C.3, 14C.7 and 14C.15


## Area 5: Rebase

Q142 to Q167. Rebase in all its forms, and cherry-pick: replayed commits, rewritten history, and when not to rewrite.


### Rebase: foundational level

#### Q142

**Question.** A rebase "moves" a branch onto `main`. Describe what happens to objects, refs and HEAD, step by step, and name what has not changed when the command returns.

**Model answer.** Nothing is moved: a rebase writes new commits and then moves one ref. Git first lists the commits reachable from the branch and not from `main`, leaving out merge commits and commits whose change is already upstream. It detaches HEAD at `main` and replays the listed commits oldest first. Each replay is a cherry-pick: a three-way merge whose base is the original commit's parent, with HEAD as ours and the original as theirs, committed with the original author, author date and message, and with me, now, as committer. Only at the end is the branch ref set to the last copy and HEAD attached to the branch again. `ORIG_HEAD` records the old tip; the HEAD reflog gets one entry per step and the branch reflog one entry for the whole rebase. Unchanged when the command returns: the original commits, still in the object database and reachable through `ORIG_HEAD` and `<branch>@{1}`; `main`; every other branch and tag; the remote and GitHub. Chapter 9, sections 9.2 and 9.4, show each step.

**Key terms.** new commits, not moved commits; HEAD detached during the run; each replay is a three-way merge; branch ref moved once, at the end; `ORIG_HEAD` and the reflogs; originals stay in the object database

**Common weak answer.** "Rebase moves my commits on top of main." Weak because nothing is moved: copies with new commit IDs are written, the originals stay reachable through `ORIG_HEAD`, the reflog and every other clone, and the answer says nothing about HEAD being detached or about when the branch ref changes.

**Follow-up.** You do the same rebase twice: once with `git rebase main`, once by hand with `git switch --detach main`, `git cherry-pick main..<branch>` and `git switch -C <branch>`. Are the resulting commit IDs equal, and what does the answer say about what a commit ID records?

**A strong reply covers.** The trees are identical commit for commit. The commit IDs are equal only if the committer dates are equal too, which section 9.3 shows with runs in the same lab minute. A commit ID is a function of tree, parents, author, committer, dates and message, and does not record which command made the commit.

**Reference.** [Chapter 9](../textbook/ch09-rebase.md), section 9.2 and 9.4

#### Q143

**Question.** Why does a rebase change commit hashes: why does every rebased commit have a new ID even when its diff is identical? Which fields of the commit object changed, and which did not?

**Model answer.** Because a commit ID is a hash of the commit object, and that object names its tree and its parent, both of which differ in the replayed commit. Chapter 9, section 9.3, compares an original with its copy using `git cat-file -p`: three of the five inputs changed: the parent, which is the point of the operation; the tree, because the new snapshot also contains what `main` added; and the committer line, which records who created this object and when. The author line and the message are identical. Even with the same parent and tree the committer date would move, which is why Git fast-forwards over commits that would come out identical instead of copying them. Because each commit names its parent by ID, a new ID for one commit forces a new ID for every commit after it: IDs change from the first rewritten commit onward and never before it. What stays constant is the patch ID, a hash of the diff with line numbers ignored, which `git patch-id --stable` shows to be equal for both.

**Key terms.** hash of the commit object; parent and tree differ; committer changes, author is kept; every descendant changes; patch ID unchanged; fast-forward over identical commits

**Common weak answer.** "The diff is the same, so only the timestamp makes the ID differ." Weak because a commit is a snapshot with a parent, not a diff: the parent and usually the tree differ, the committer date is only the third input, and the answer misses that every later commit must change as well.

**Follow-up.** An interactive rebase reworded the fifth of six commits and nothing else. Which commits kept their IDs and why, and what outside the repository may now hold a stale ID?

**A strong reply covers.** The first four kept their IDs because Git fast-forwards over unchanged instructions; the reworded commit and the one after it are new objects. Stale IDs can sit in review comments, CI statuses, deployment records and training-run metadata; tags do not follow, and a replayed commit is signed only if you sign it now.

**Reference.** [Chapter 9](../textbook/ch09-rebase.md), section 9.3 and 9.6

#### Q144

**Question.** Why does cherry-pick create a new commit?

**Model answer.** Because a commit object is never modified, and its ID is a function of its content: tree, parents, author, committer, dates and message. A cherry-pick does not move or reuse the picked commit. It recomputes the change that commit made, with a three-way merge whose base is the commit's parent, and records the result on the branch I am on. That result has a different tree, the target branch's files plus the change; a different parent, the tip I picked onto; and a different committer line, me at the time I ran the command. Only the author, the author date and the message are carried over. Different content gives a different ID, so it cannot be the same commit, and the original stays on its own branch. Git stores no link from the copy to the original either, which is why `git branch --contains` with the original's ID does not list the target branch, and why `-x` exists to write the link into the message. Chapter 10, sections 10.1 and 10.3, show both objects with `git cat-file -p`.

**Key terms.** commit objects are never modified; the ID is a function of content; different tree, parent and committer; author and message carried over; no stored link to the original; `-x`

**Common weak answer.** "Because Git copies the commit to the other branch." Weak because it restates the observation: it does not say that the tree and the parent necessarily differ, that the ID follows from the content, or that no link to the original is stored.

**Follow-up.** Is there a case in which `git cherry-pick` creates no new object, and what happens to a signature on the original commit?

**A strong reply covers.** With `--ff`, cherry-pick fast-forwards instead of copying when HEAD already is the parent of the picked commit. Otherwise the copy is a new object: it is not signed by the original author, it is signed by you if you sign, for example with `-S`, and otherwise not at all.

**Reference.** [Chapter 10](../textbook/ch10-cherry-pick.md), section 10.1, 10.3 and 10.4

#### Q145

**Question.** Name the base, "ours" and "theirs" of a cherry-pick. How does a revert differ?

**Model answer.** For `git cherry-pick C` the base is the parent of C, ours is HEAD, the branch I am on, and theirs is C. The merge therefore yields HEAD plus the change that C made, and whatever else exists on C's branch plays no part. `git revert C` is the same three-way merge with base and theirs exchanged: the base is C itself and theirs is the parent of C, so the change is applied backwards and the result is HEAD minus the change of C. Chapter 10, section 10.11, proves it with `git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base`: the predicted tree, the tree of the revert commit and the tree from before the backport are one and the same. A revert is a new commit like any other. It uses the same sequencer, with `REVERT_HEAD` in place of `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD` and the same four ways out, and it needs `-m` for a merge commit for the same reason. Unlike in a rebase, the sides are not swapped here: HEAD is my branch.

**Key terms.** base is the parent of the picked commit; ours is HEAD; theirs is the picked commit; revert exchanges base and theirs; same sequencer; `REVERT_HEAD`

**Common weak answer.** "Ours is the current branch, theirs is the other branch, and the base is their common ancestor." Weak because the base is the picked commit's parent, not the merge base, and theirs is one commit, not a branch; the candidate cannot derive the revert from the same table.

**Follow-up.** Why is the base of a cherry-pick not the merge base of the two branches, and what practical consequence does that have when the pick conflicts?

**A strong reply covers.** The operation carries one commit's change, so the base is that commit's parent. Stage 1 can therefore show a version of the file your branch never contained, and the correct resolution applies the difference between stage 1 and stage 3 to your own version.

**Reference.** [Chapter 10](../textbook/ch10-cherry-pick.md), section 10.2 and 10.11

#### Q146

**Question.** Which fields does the copy share with the original commit, and which not? What follows for `git branch --contains`?

**Model answer.** The copy shares the author, the author date and the message with the original, and nothing else. Its tree is different, because it is the target branch's files plus the change. Its parent is the tip of the branch I picked onto. Its committer line names whoever ran the cherry-pick, at the time it ran. `git cat-file -p` on both objects, as in Chapter 10, section 10.3, shows this, and shows as well that no field points from the copy to the original: the two commits are unrelated in the graph. `git branch --contains` follows ancestry. Asked for the original's commit ID, it lists only branches that have the original as an ancestor, so it reports `main` and not the release branch, although the release has the fix. The answer is correct about ancestry and misleading about the fix. To find the copy I search for the line that `-x` records, with `git log --all --grep`, or I compare patch IDs with `git cherry -v`, which finds exact copies only.

**Key terms.** author, author date and message are shared; tree, parent and committer differ; no field links copy to original; ancestry knows nothing about copies; the `-x` line; patch ID

**Common weak answer.** "It is the same commit on another branch, so `--contains` lists both branches." Weak because the copy is a different object with a different ID and no ancestry relation to the original, so an audit by commit ID reports a backported fix as missing.

**Follow-up.** A developer ran `git cherry-pick -n` and then committed. Which of the shared fields are different now, and how is the credit restored?

**A strong reply covers.** With `-n` no `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD` exists, so the commit has the developer as author, and a message given with `-m` replaces the original one. `git commit -C <original>` reuses the original's message and authorship; afterwards, `git commit --amend -C <original>` restores them.

**Reference.** [Chapter 10](../textbook/ch10-cherry-pick.md), section 10.3 and 10.9


### Rebase: working engineer level

#### Q147

**Question.** A rebase is stopped at a conflict. Where do the branch ref, HEAD, `ORIG_HEAD` and `REBASE_HEAD` point? What does that imply for `--abort`?

**Model answer.** The branch ref has not moved: it still points at the old tip, and `ORIG_HEAD` names that same commit. HEAD is detached and sits on the last copy made so far, which is built on the new base. `REBASE_HEAD` names the original commit that is being replayed right now and exists only while a rebase is stopped. So four names resolve to three commits, which `git rev-parse` shows in Chapter 9, section 9.4. The plan is in the state directory `.git/rebase-merge`, and `git status` reads it back: what was done, what remains, and the ways out. The implication is that nothing is lost while a rebase is in progress. `git rebase --abort` only has to attach HEAD to the branch again and restore the index and working tree from it; the copies made so far are then reachable from nothing except the reflog. The one cost of aborting is the conflict resolution work in progress, which is discarded.

**Key terms.** branch ref unchanged; HEAD detached on the last copy; `ORIG_HEAD` is the old tip; `REBASE_HEAD` is the commit being replayed; state directory `.git/rebase-merge`; abort discards only resolution work

**Common weak answer.** "The branch is half rebased, so aborting is risky." Weak because the branch ref is not touched until the to-do list is empty; the candidate confuses HEAD with the branch and cannot say why `--abort` is safe or what it discards.

**Follow-up.** A developer left the stopped rebase with `git rebase --quit` instead of aborting. What state is the repository in, where is an autostash, and how do you get back to the branch?

**A strong reply covers.** `--quit` removes the state directory and nothing else: the branch is untouched, HEAD stays detached on the half-built history, and the index still holds the conflict. An autostash moves to the stash list. Recover with `git reset --hard` if the index is unmerged, then `git switch <branch>`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 9](../textbook/ch09-rebase.md), section 9.4 and 9.11

#### Q148

**Question.** During a rebase, what do `--ours` and `--theirs` refer to, and why? Give one concrete way this loses work without any error message.

**Model answer.** During a rebase the sides are swapped relative to a merge. Ours, stage 2, is HEAD, and HEAD is the new base plus the copies made so far, so it is the side I am rebasing onto. Theirs, stage 3, is `REBASE_HEAD`, my own commit being replayed, and stage 1 is that commit's parent. The reason is mechanical: a rebase detaches HEAD at the upstream commit and merges my commits into it one at a time, and ours is a position, whatever HEAD is. The silent loss in Chapter 9, section 9.11: at a conflict I run `git restore --ours`, meaning my change, then `git add` and `git rebase --continue`. The index now equals HEAD, the replayed commit has become empty, the default `--empty=drop` drops it and the next instruction runs, with no message. The rebase reports success and my commit is not in the branch. `git range-diff main ORIG_HEAD HEAD` proves it: the commit appears with `<` and no partner. The fix is `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD`, rebase again, and take `--theirs` or edit by hand.

**Key terms.** the sides are swapped; stage 2 is HEAD, the new base plus copies; stage 3 is `REBASE_HEAD`, your commit; an empty commit is dropped without a message; `git range-diff`; read `git status` before `--continue`

**Common weak answer.** "Ours is my branch and theirs is main, as in a merge." Weak because that inversion is the cause of the loss: in a rebase ours is the side being rebased onto, and the candidate cannot explain why a dropped commit produces no error.
