**Follow-up.** The resolution was correct this time, but the developer ran `git commit --amend` before `git rebase --continue`. What does the history look like afterwards, and why?

**A strong reply covers.** At a conflict stop HEAD is the previous copy, so the amend folded the resolution into that earlier commit, which now changes an extra file, and the stopped commit, left with nothing, was dropped. After a conflict the sequence is `git add`, then `git rebase --continue`; `--amend` belongs to an `edit` stop.

**Reference.** [Chapter 9](../textbook/ch09-rebase.md), section 9.11 and 9.14

#### Q149

**Question.** The reviewer approved three commits; after your rebase there are still three with the same titles. How do you show what changed, and how does the reviewer do it without access to your clone?

**Model answer.** With `git range-diff`, which compares two versions of a series of commits: it pairs each old commit with its new counterpart by similarity of the patches, not by position or ID. I run `git range-diff main ORIG_HEAD HEAD`, or `git range-diff main <branch>@{1} <branch>` from the reflog. Between the two columns `=` means the same patch, `!` a changed patch, printed as a diff of the two diffs, `<` only in the old series and `>` only in the new one. In Chapter 9, section 9.14, a commit with an unchanged title turns out to set a constant to a value the reviewer never saw, which no list of titles can show. A plain `git diff ORIG_HEAD HEAD` compares two snapshots and on a real branch also contains everything that arrived from upstream. The reviewer needs nothing from my clone: after `git fetch`, the previous tip is in the reflog of their own remote-tracking branch, so `git range-diff origin/main origin/<branch>@{1} origin/<branch>` works there. When I force-push a branch under review I paste the output into the pull request.

**Key terms.** `git range-diff`; pairing by patch similarity; the `=`, `!`, `<` and `>` markers; diff of two diffs; reflog of the reviewer's remote-tracking branch; a snapshot diff includes upstream changes

**Common weak answer.** "Compare the two tips with git diff, or compare the commit titles." Weak because a tip-to-tip diff mixes in everything that arrived from upstream and titles hide a changed patch; it also gives the reviewer no method that works in their own clone.

**Follow-up.** On a clean rebase in which nothing was edited, `git range-diff` reports one commit as removed and one as added under the same subject. Has a commit been lost?

**A strong reply covers.** No. The pairing is a heuristic: a small patch whose context line changed underneath it is not paired, and raising `--creation-factor` shows the pair with the context line as its only difference. A lost commit has `<` and no partner. The output format may change, so do not parse it.

**Reference.** [Chapter 9](../textbook/ch09-rebase.md), section 9.14

#### Q150

**Question.** `ORIG_HEAD` does not point where you expected after a rebase. Why, and what do you use instead?

**Model answer.** `ORIG_HEAD` is one ref that several commands write; it is not a record that belongs to the rebase. It names the old tip directly after the rebase, but the next `git reset`, `git merge`, `git rebase` or `git am` rewrites it. The common case, in Chapter 9, section 9.6, is a reset inside the rebase itself: at an `edit` stop I run `git reset HEAD^` to split a commit, and that overwrites `ORIG_HEAD` with the tip from before that reset. Section 9.16 shows the other case, a reset run for another reason after a bad rebase that nobody noticed. The durable handle is the reflog of the branch. A finished rebase writes one entry there, so `<branch>@{1}` means this branch before its last rebase, and `git reflog show <branch>` lets me count further back. I first create a rescue branch at that entry and inspect it, and only then run `git reset --hard` to it, after checking `git status`, because that command destroys uncommitted changes to tracked files.

**Key terms.** `ORIG_HEAD` is rewritten by reset, merge, rebase and am; a reset inside an `edit` stop; reflog of the branch; `<branch>@{1}`; one reflog entry per rebase; rescue branch before the reset

**Common weak answer.** "ORIG_HEAD always holds the tip from before the rebase, so reset to it." Weak because any later reset, merge or rebase overwrites it, including a reset made during the rebase, and a hard reset to the wrong commit compounds the damage.

**Follow-up.** How long does that replacement handle last by default, and which two habits destroy or defeat a backup of the old tip?

**A strong reply covers.** By default a reflog entry whose commit is no longer reachable from the branch tip expires after 30 days, and the objects are pruned after a further two weeks. Deleting the branch deletes its reflog, and a backup branch pointing into the range is moved by `--update-refs`; a tag stays.

**Reference.** [Chapter 9](../textbook/ch09-rebase.md), section 9.6 and 9.16

#### Q151

**Question.** "Cherry-pick applies a patch." What is imprecise about that sentence, and when does the difference show?

**Model answer.** A cherry-pick does not apply a patch; it performs a three-way merge. The base is the parent of the picked commit, ours is HEAD and theirs is the picked commit, so Git combines what changed from the parent to the commit with what changed from the parent to my branch, working with three complete versions of each file. A patch carries a few lines of context and fails when they do not match. The difference shows as soon as the target branch has drifted near the change. In Chapter 10, section 10.2, the hunk's context includes a line that reads differently on the release branch: `git apply --check` on the output of `git format-patch` refuses the change, while `git cherry-pick` succeeds, keeps the release's own line and adds the fix. `git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<commit>^ HEAD <commit>` predicts the tree of the resulting commit exactly. The sentence also hides the second half of the operation: the result is recorded as a new commit with a new ID and no stored link to the original.

**Key terms.** three-way merge; base is the parent of the picked commit; three complete file versions, not context lines; `git apply --check` refuses; `git merge-tree` predicts the tree; a new commit with a new ID

**Common weak answer.** "It takes the diff of the commit and applies it to the current branch." Weak because that model predicts a failure whenever the context differs, cannot explain the three stages of a cherry-pick conflict, and omits that the result is a new commit with no link to the original.

**Follow-up.** If the three-way merge succeeds where a patch is refused, does a clean cherry-pick mean the backport is correct?

**A strong reply covers.** No. Applied cleanly says that the text merged, not that the code works there: a commit that uses something added by an earlier commit you did not pick applies and then breaks the build. Build and test on the target branch before publishing.

**Reference.** [Chapter 10](../textbook/ch10-cherry-pick.md), section 10.2

#### Q152

**Question.** A backport applied without conflict and broke the release build. Explain the mechanism and how you would have caught it.

**Model answer.** A cherry-pick carries one commit's change, the difference between that commit and its parent, and nothing else from the commit's branch. If the fix uses something that an earlier commit on `main` introduced, and that earlier commit was not picked, the text can still merge, and the code on the release branch then refers to something that does not exist there. Applied cleanly says that the text merged, not that the code works on that branch; Git has no notion of the dependency. To diagnose it, `git log -S'<name>' main` finds the commit that added the missing name. The fix is to remove the pick and then either pick the prerequisite as well or adapt the fix for the release line. I would have caught it by following the procedure of Chapter 10, section 10.9: after `git cherry-pick -x`, build and test on the release branch before publishing it. A backport also deserves review as new code, because it shows the original author's name on code that someone else merged, and possibly edited, on another branch.

**Key terms.** one commit's change only; a prerequisite commit was not picked; a clean text merge is not a working build; `git log -S`; build and test on the target branch; review a backport as new code

**Common weak answer.** "A clean cherry-pick means the change is compatible, so the build failure must be unrelated." Weak because the three-way merge compares text only; it cannot see that the fix depends on a commit that was not taken.

**Follow-up.** The broken pick has already been pushed to the shared release branch. How do you take it out, and how does that differ from the recovery for a pick that is still local?

**A strong reply covers.** With `git revert`, which adds a new commit that applies the change backwards. The chapter's safety table gives `git reset --hard` to the ID from the reflog as the recovery for a local pick, and `git revert` if it was already pushed.

**Reference.** [Chapter 10](../textbook/ch10-cherry-pick.md), section 10.9, 10.12 and 10.13

#### Q153

**Question.** Compare the state after a stopped cherry-pick of a range with the state after a stopped rebase. Where is HEAD, and what has happened to the branch?

**Model answer.** In a stopped rebase HEAD is detached on the last copy, the branch ref has not moved and still equals `ORIG_HEAD`, and the plan is in `.git/rebase-merge`. In a stopped cherry-pick of a range HEAD is not detached: it stays on the branch, and the branch has already advanced to the copy of every commit that succeeded. The commit that could not be applied is named by `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD`, the rest of the plan is in `.git/sequencer/`, whose `head` file records where HEAD was before the first pick, and `ORIG_HEAD` is not written. A pick of a single commit creates no sequencer directory at all. The ways out differ accordingly. `git cherry-pick --abort` returns the branch to the recorded starting point, so the picks that had succeeded are undone as well; `--quit` deletes only the bookkeeping and leaves a partly advanced branch with the conflict still in the index. The conflict sides differ too: in the cherry-pick ours is my branch, while in the rebase ours is the side I am rebasing onto.

**Key terms.** HEAD stays on the branch; the branch has already advanced; `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD`; `.git/sequencer/`; a rebase leaves the branch ref untouched; abort also undoes completed picks

**Common weak answer.** "It is the same as a rebase: the branch is untouched until you finish." Weak because a cherry-pick sequence commits directly onto the branch, so an interrupted one leaves it partly advanced, which is the case a script has to handle.

**Follow-up.** A release script cherry-picks a list of commits, and one of them conflicts in CI. What must the script do, and what must it never do?

**A strong reply covers.** Check the exit status and decide: `git cherry-pick --abort` returns the branch to a known state, because otherwise it is left partly advanced. Never a blind retry. `git status` names the commit the sequence is stuck on.

**Reference.** [Chapter 10](../textbook/ch10-cherry-pick.md), section 10.6; [Chapter 9](../textbook/ch09-rebase.md), section 9.4


### Rebase: senior level

#### Q154

**Question.** `git rebase main` on a feature branch conflicts in a file the branch never touched. Give two different root causes and the command that fixes each.

**Model answer.** Both causes show in one diagnosis: `git log --oneline main..HEAD` lists commits that are not mine. A rebase replays everything not reachable from `main`, and Git knows reachability only, not which commits I call mine. First cause: my branch is stacked on another branch that landed on `main` in another form, for example a squash that includes a review change. The lower commits are not ancestors of `main`, and their diffs differ from the squash, so neither the patch ID check nor the empty-result check removes them, and replaying them conflicts. The fix is `git rebase --abort`, then `git rebase --onto main <lower branch> <branch>`, which names the boundary. Second cause: the range contains a merge commit. A plain rebase leaves merge commits out and lays the other commits out in one line, so a resolution that existed only in the merge commit is not replayed and the conflict it resolved comes back at a single commit. There I abort and either run `git rebase --rebase-merges main`, redoing the resolution by hand, or integrate with `git merge main`.

**Key terms.** reachability, not branch ownership; `main..HEAD` lists foreign commits; lower branch landed as a squash; `--onto` names the boundary; merge commits are left out; `--rebase-merges`

**Common weak answer.** "Main changed that file, so resolve the conflict and continue." Weak because it resolves a conflict in commits that should not be replayed at all, never inspects `main..HEAD`, and will meet a conflict again at the next foreign commit.

**Follow-up.** After a squash merge of the lower branch, when does a plain `git rebase main` on the follow-up branch do the right thing without `--onto`, and how do you check before you run it?

**A strong reply covers.** Exactly when the squash equals the sum of your commits: each replay then comes out empty and is dropped under the default `--empty=drop`. Check with `git cherry -v main` first; for lines marked `+` that you believe are merged, expect an empty replay or a conflict.

**Reference.** [Chapter 9](../textbook/ch09-rebase.md), section 9.5, 9.10 and 9.12

#### Q155

**Question.** You force-pushed a rebased branch. A teammate now has every commit twice. Explain how that happened, how they repair it, and what you would have done differently.

**Model answer.** My rebase wrote copies with new commit IDs and my forced push replaced the server's branch with them, while the teammate's clone still held the originals with their own commit on top. After their fetch the two lines had diverged; they followed the status hint with `git pull --no-rebase`, and a merge keeps the commits of both sides. Git identifies a commit by its ID, so an original and its copy are different commits to it. The content is not duplicated, the history is. `git log --oneline --left-right --cherry-mark <old>...<new>` proves it by marking the pairs with `=`. The repair on their side is `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` to go back before the merge, then `git pull --rebase`, which uses the reflog of the remote-tracking branch to find the fork point and replays only their own commit; or explicitly, `git rebase --onto` with the old upstream tip as boundary. What I would do differently: before rebasing anything pushed, ask who has commits on top. If somebody does, agree first and send them the repair command, or merge instead.

**Key terms.** copies have new commit IDs; a merge keeps both sides; `--cherry-mark` pairs marked `=`; `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD`; fork point from the remote-tracking reflog; ask who has commits on top

**Common weak answer.** "Git duplicated the commits because of the force push; delete the branch and start over." Weak because the duplication came from the teammate's merge of two histories with different IDs, not from the push itself, and deleting the branch deletes its reflog, the most durable undo handle.

**Follow-up.** Why is the duplicated history more than cosmetic noise, in particular when the purpose of the rewrite was to remove a credential or a large file?

**A strong reply covers.** If the teammate pushes that merge, the commits the rewrite removed are back on the server, so one stale clone that merges and pushes undoes the cleanup. Every later reader of the history also meets each change twice.

**Reference.** [Chapter 9](../textbook/ch09-rebase.md), section 9.15 and 9.22

#### Q156

**Question.** Compare `--force`, `--force-with-lease`, and `--force-with-lease --force-if-includes`. Describe a sequence of events in which the second overwrites a colleague's commit and the third refuses.

**Model answer.** All three overwrite the server's ref; they differ in what must be true first. `git push --force` overwrites always. `git push --force-with-lease` overwrites only if the server's ref equals my remote-tracking branch: a compare-and-swap whose expected value I do not type. Adding `--force-if-includes` also requires that the tip of the remote-tracking branch is reachable from a reflog entry of my local branch, meaning my branch has contained it at some point. The sequence in Chapter 9, section 9.17: a colleague pushes a commit after my last fetch, and I rebase. The bare lease is rejected as stale, which is correct. Then something fetches for me: an editor, a status prompt, or habit. My remote-tracking branch now equals the server, the lease is satisfied, and `--dry-run` shows the push would replace a commit I have never looked at. With `--force-if-includes` the push is refused, because that commit is in no reflog entry of my branch. The fix is `git reset --hard origin/<branch>`, rebase again, and push with both checks. `push.useForceIfIncludes` adds the second check to every lease.

**Key terms.** compare-and-swap on the server ref; expected value read from the remote-tracking branch; a background fetch defeats the bare lease; reflog reachability check; `push.useForceIfIncludes`; explicit lease with an ID

**Common weak answer.** "Force-with-lease is the safe force push; it never overwrites other people's work." Weak because the lease compares against the remote-tracking branch, which any fetch updates, so after a background fetch it passes and overwrites a commit nobody on this machine has seen.

**Follow-up.** Is there a form of the lease that does not depend on your remote-tracking branch at all, and what does the Git manual say about the forms that do?

**A strong reply covers.** Yes: `--force-with-lease=<branch>:<expected ID>` states the commit you rebased from, so a background fetch cannot satisfy it. Per the chapter's version notes, the manual still calls the lease forms without an explicit value experimental; the chapter gives plain `--force` and the bare lease no appropriate use.

**Reference.** [Chapter 9](../textbook/ch09-rebase.md), section 9.17 and 9.24

#### Q157

**Question.** A colleague's pushed commit vanished from their own branch after `git pull --rebase`. Nobody ran a destructive command on their machine. Explain the mechanism and recover the commit.

**Model answer.** Someone else replaced the server's branch with a plain `git push --force`, after a rebase that did not include the colleague's commit. On the colleague's machine `git pull --rebase` then did what it is designed to do. It replays only the commits after the fork point, and the fork point is the newest commit of their branch that was once the tip of their remote-tracking branch. Because they had pushed the commit, that was the commit itself; nothing comes after it, so nothing was replayed and their branch was set to the new upstream. Git reads the situation as upstream having discarded the commit, the same logic that repairs a duplicated history. The evidence is `git reflog show origin/<branch>`, which holds the commit below the forced update, and `git merge-base --fork-point`. The commit is not lost: it is `<branch>@{1}` in the reflog of their local branch, so `git cherry-pick <branch>@{1}` followed by a normal push restores it. Prevention: no plain `--force` on a branch anyone else pushes to; the lease with `--force-if-includes` refuses in exactly this situation.

**Key terms.** plain `--force` replaced the server ref; fork point; reflog of the remote-tracking branch; upstream discarded the commit; `<branch>@{1}`; cherry-pick from the reflog

**Common weak answer.** "The pull has a bug, or the commit was garbage collected." Weak because the pull behaved as designed and the commit is still in the branch reflog; the answer never identifies the forced push from another machine as the cause, so it cannot prevent a repeat.

**Follow-up.** Could the server have told you what the branch pointed at before, and what does that imply for recovery if no clone has the commit any more?

**A strong reply covers.** In the chapter's demonstration, no: a bare repository keeps no reflog by default, so the server cannot say what the branch used to be. Recovery depends on a clone that still has the commits; GitHub's own instruments are summarised in Chapter 13, not in this chapter.

**Reference.** [Chapter 9](../textbook/ch09-rebase.md), section 9.13 and 9.17

#### Q158

**Question.** What do `--update-refs` and `--rebase-merges` each add to a plain rebase, and what does each still leave for you to do?

**Model answer.** A plain rebase moves one branch and lays the commits out in one line. `--update-refs` adds an `update-ref` line to the to-do list directly after each commit that another local branch points at, and sets those branches to the corresponding copies when the list is finished. It leaves three things to me. It does not move tags, remote-tracking branches, or a branch checked out in another worktree, so a stack can end up half moved. Undo is per branch: `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` restores only the branch I am on, and each other branch comes back from its own reflog. Publishing is per branch, each ref with its own lease. `--rebase-merges` rebuilds the branch structure with `label`, `reset` and `merge` instructions instead of leaving merge commits out. It leaves the content of the merges to me: each is a fresh merge, so conflict resolutions and manual amendments from the original merge commits have to be redone by hand, with rerere reducing that work, and it does not move the side branch's ref unless I add `--update-refs`.

**Key terms.** `update-ref` lines in the to-do list; stacked branches; tags and other worktrees are not moved; undo and publish per branch; `label`, `reset` and `merge` instructions; merge resolutions redone by hand

**Common weak answer.** "Update-refs rebases all my branches and rebase-merges preserves the merges exactly." Weak because only local branches that point into the range are moved, and a rebuilt merge is a fresh merge whose original conflict resolution is not carried over.

**Follow-up.** With `rebase.updateRefs` set to true, a developer made a backup with `git branch backup/x` before a risky rebase. Afterwards the backup equals the rebased tip. Explain, and name a backup that works.

**A strong reply covers.** A backup made with `git branch` is a branch that points into the rebased range, so `--update-refs` moved it along with the others. Mark the old tip with a tag, which stays behind, or write down the commit ID, or rely on the reflog of the branch.

**Reference.** [Chapter 9](../textbook/ch09-rebase.md), section 9.9 and 9.10

#### Q159

**Question.** A fix was backported with `-x`. Give three ways to establish that the release branch contains it, and say which of them can give a wrong answer and why.

**Model answer.** First, by commit ID: `git branch --contains <original>`. It follows ancestry, and the original is not an ancestor of the release branch, only its copy is, so it lists `main` alone. Here that is misleading. Second, by the recorded line: `git log --all --oneline --grep` for the text that `-x` appended, then `git branch --contains` on the commit found. That is a proof: a commit on the release branch states that it is a copy of the original, and the line survives adaptation of the change. Its weakness is procedural: the line is missing if `-x` was not used, if it was deleted in the editor, or if the pick was finished with `git commit -m`. Third, by patch ID: `git cherry -v release/1.4 main`, where `-` marks a commit that has an equivalent on the release. In Chapter 10, section 10.9, it prints `+` for the backported fix, which is wrong: a context line inside the hunk differs on the release, so the two diffs are not textually the same. Patch comparison finds exact copies only.

**Key terms.** ancestry does not know about copies; the line recorded by `-x`; `git log --grep`; `git cherry -v`; patch IDs match exact copies only; a differing context line is enough

**Common weak answer.** "Run `git branch --contains` with the fix's commit ID; if the release is not listed, the fix is not there." Weak because ancestry does not know about copies, so this reports a correct backport as missing, and trusting `git cherry` alone fails for any adapted backport.

**Follow-up.** After the release branch is merged back, your changelog generator counts the fix twice. Which query gives the real difference between the two lines, and what does it still miss?

**A strong reply covers.** `git log --left-right --cherry-pick release/1.4...main` leaves out the pairs with equal patch IDs; `--right-only` narrows it to what `main` has and the release lacks. It has the same limit: an adapted backport is invisible to patch comparison and is still listed.

**Reference.** [Chapter 10](../textbook/ch10-cherry-pick.md), section 10.9 and 10.10

#### Q160

**Question.** In a cherry-pick conflict, stage 1 shows a line that never existed on your branch. Where does it come from, and how do you use it to resolve correctly?

**Model answer.** Stage 1 is the base of the three-way merge, and for a cherry-pick the base is the parent of the picked commit, not the merge base of the two branches. That parent lives on the other line of development and already contains earlier changes made there, so it can be a version of the file that my branch never contained. Chapter 10, section 10.7, shows it with `git ls-files -u` and `git show :1:<path>`: the merge base still has the old endpoint, and stage 1 already has the new one. I use stage 1 as the reference for what the commit did. The change to carry over is the difference between stage 1 and stage 3, there one added argument. I apply that difference to my own version, stage 2, leave the rest of my line as it is, then run `git add` and `git cherry-pick --continue`. Taking theirs whole would also bring in the unrelated earlier change, smuggled in through a conflict resolution. Setting `merge.conflictStyle` to `diff3` or `zdiff3` puts the base into the conflict markers.

**Key terms.** stage 1 is the parent of the picked commit; not the merge base of the branches; carry the difference between stage 1 and stage 3; apply it to stage 2; taking theirs whole smuggles in unrelated changes; `diff3` or `zdiff3` markers

**Common weak answer.** "Stage 1 is the common ancestor, so something is corrupt; take theirs, because theirs is the fix." Weak because the base is the picked commit's parent by design, and taking theirs whole imports unrelated changes from the other line into the release.

**Follow-up.** After resolving, one developer finished with `git commit --no-edit` and another with `git commit -m`. What is wrong with each resulting commit, and what is right about both?

**A strong reply covers.** Both keep the original author, because `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD` still exists. `--no-edit` skips the cleanup, so the `# Conflicts:` comment lines become part of the message; `-m` replaces the prepared message, so the line that `-x` wrote is gone. Finish with `git cherry-pick --continue`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 10](../textbook/ch10-cherry-pick.md), section 10.7 and 10.12

#### Q161

**Question.** What does `git cherry-pick -m 1 <merge>` create, and why is it not equivalent to merging the branch?

**Model answer.** A merge commit has two parents, so "the difference between a commit and its parent" is ambiguous, and Git refuses the pick unless `-m` is given. `-m 1` takes the first parent as the base. The change relative to the first parent is everything the merged branch brought in, so the result is one new commit that carries the whole branch's content as a single change. That commit keeps the title of the merge and has a single parent. It is not a merge. Ancestry records nothing about the branch: for Git its commits are still unmerged on this line, `git branch --no-merged` still lists the branch, and a real merge later would add those commits to the history next to this copy. A merge commit is a promise that everything from its parents is included; a cherry-pick promises nothing about the commits around it. If I want everything a branch has, I merge it; if I want individual changes, I pick the commits of the branch, not the merge. Chapter 10, sections 10.4 and 10.13.

**Key terms.** two parents make the change ambiguous; first parent as the base; a single-parent commit titled like a merge; the branch is still unmerged in the graph; `git branch --no-merged`; a merge is a promise about its parents

**Common weak answer.** "It cherry-picks the merge, so the branch is now merged into the release." Weak because the result has one parent and records no ancestry: Git still considers the branch unmerged, and a later real merge adds the same commits next to the copy.

**Follow-up.** `git revert` needs the same option for a merge commit. Why, and where does the textbook treat the consequences?

**A strong reply covers.** A revert is the same three-way merge with base and theirs exchanged, so with two parents Git must be told which parent defines the change. Chapter 10, section 10.11, states this and refers to Chapter 11, sections 11.8 and 11.9, for what reverting a merge does to later merges.

**Reference.** [Chapter 10](../textbook/ch10-cherry-pick.md), section 10.4, 10.12 and 10.13


### Rebase: principal level

#### Q162

**Question.** When would you choose a merge over a rebase for the same integration, and when the reverse? Argue both sides for a team that bisects often.

**Model answer.** Both produce the same final content: Chapter 9, section 9.18, shows the two results with the same tree. Everything else differs. I merge when the branch is shared, because a merge only adds commits while a rebase needs a forced push and everybody's cooperation; when the branch conflicts with upstream at many commits, because a merge resolves once; and when I want a record of what was integrated and one revert with `-m 1` to undo it. I rebase a private branch to get one line of history. For a team that bisects, the argument for the rebase is fewer paths to walk. The argument against is that every replayed commit is a new snapshot that nobody has run, one per commit, whereas a merge keeps the trees that were built and tested and adds one new snapshot. Bisect finds a regression only if every commit builds, so for this team a rebase needs `--exec` with the test command, or a squash. The target branch can also decide: a GitHub rule that requires linear history blocks merge commits.

**Key terms.** same final tree; replayed commits are snapshots nobody ran; `--exec` per commit; shared branch means merge; one resolution versus one per commit; merge commit records and reverts the integration; linear history rule

**Common weak answer.** "Rebase gives a clean history and merge a messy one, so always rebase." Weak because it treats the choice as taste: it ignores whether the branch is shared, that replayed commits are untested snapshots that can break a bisect, and that a merge records the integration and can undo it as one unit.

**Follow-up.** You chose the rebase and CI is green on the branch tip. What exactly has been proved about the intermediate commits, and how do you close the gap?

**A strong reply covers.** Nothing: only the tip snapshot was run, and a check at the tip says the branch is broken, not which commit broke it. `git rebase --exec "<test command>" main` runs the check after every commit and stops at the first failure, where you amend and continue.

**Reference.** [Chapter 9](../textbook/ch09-rebase.md), section 9.6 and 9.18

#### Q163

**Question.** You own the policy for history rewriting across an engineering organization. Which controls do you place on GitHub, which in client configuration, review and CI, and which commonly proposed control do you refuse to rely on?

**Model answer.** I separate branches that others build on from branches one person owns. On GitHub I block force pushes on `main` and on release branches and leave topic branches open to their owners; as described in GitHub's documentation, a new ruleset has that rule enabled by default and classic branch protection disables force pushes by default. On clients I set `push.useForceIfIncludes`, so every lease carries the second check, I rule out plain `git push --force`, and I set `rebase.missingCommitsCheck` to `error`, so a deleted to-do line cannot drop a commit silently. In review, a force-push to a branch under review comes with `git range-diff` output in the pull request, and comments are answered with fixup commits that are folded once with `--autosquash` before the merge. A CI job that fails while a subject starts with `fixup!`, `squash!` or `amend!` keeps unfolded corrections out of `main`. What I refuse to rely on is Git hooks: `pre-rebase` can refuse a rebase and `--no-verify` skips it, and the manual calls which other hooks run during a rebase an accident of implementation.

**Key terms.** block force pushes on shared branches; `push.useForceIfIncludes`; `rebase.missingCommitsCheck`; range-diff in the pull request; CI check on fixup subjects; hooks are not a control; ask who has commits on top

**Common weak answer.** "Ban rebase and force push everywhere, or enforce the rule with a pre-rebase hook." Weak because rebasing a branch only you use is safe, a blanket ban removes the fixup-and-fold review workflow, and a hook that `--no-verify` skips enforces nothing.

**Follow-up.** Suppose one laptop does not carry your client settings. Which of your controls still hold, and what stays exposed?

**A strong reply covers.** The server-side ones hold: the GitHub rule on `main` and release branches, and the CI check. A topic branch that two people push to stays exposed to a plain force or to a bare lease after a background fetch, so the working rule remains: ask who has commits on top before rebasing.

**Reference.** [Chapter 9](../textbook/ch09-rebase.md), section 9.15, 9.17 and 9.22

#### Q164

**Question.** A model card and a training run's metadata record the commit ID of the code that produced a model. After the pull request was merged, that ID is on no branch. Explain to a non-specialist executive what happened and what you would change.

**Model answer.** Nothing was corrupted; a reference was taken too early. A commit ID is derived from the commit's content, and that content includes the ID of its parent. Any replay of a commit therefore writes a new commit with a new ID, and whatever stored the old ID now refers to a commit that is no longer on the branch. A rebase before the merge does that in Git. On GitHub, as described in its documentation, the Rebase and merge button always lands commits with new IDs and an updated committer, unsigned, and Squash and merge puts one new commit on the base branch, so the head branch's commits do not become its ancestors. A `-x` line that points at a private commit fails the same way once that branch is rebased. What I would change is the rule for when an ID may be recorded: commits whose IDs are recorded where they must stay valid, a released tag, a deployment record, a model card, are not rebased, and before any rebase the author asks what has recorded these IDs.

**Key terms.** the commit ID depends on content and parent; a replay writes new commits; Rebase and merge and Squash and merge land new commits; do not rebase commits whose IDs are recorded; tags do not follow a rebase; signatures are not carried over

**Common weak answer.** "Git lost the commit, or somebody deleted it." Weak because nothing was deleted: the ID was recorded from a branch that was replayed afterwards, and the answer offers no rule for when an ID is safe to record.

**Follow-up.** Someone proposes tagging the commit before the rebase so that the record survives. Does the tag follow the rebase, and does a signature carry over to the replayed commit?

**A strong reply covers.** A tag does not follow a rebase: it keeps pointing at the old commit, and the new history no longer contains that commit. Signatures are part of the commit object, so a replayed commit is a new object, signed only if you sign it now, with `-S` or `commit.gpgSign`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 9](../textbook/ch09-rebase.md), section 9.3 and 9.22; [Chapter 10](../textbook/ch10-cherry-pick.md), section 10.13

#### Q165

**Question.** Two long-lived branches exchange fixes by cherry-pick in both directions. What problems accumulate, and what would you change?

**Model answer.** Every exchanged fix exists under two commit IDs with no link in the graph, and three things degrade. First, "what does one branch have that the other lacks" stops being answerable from the graph: `git branch --contains` follows ancestry and misleads, and patch comparison with `git cherry` or `git log --cherry-pick` finds exact copies only, so every adapted pick looks missing. Second, anything that counts commits, such as a changelog generated from `git log`, double-counts the duplicates. Third, every later merge between the two branches has to reconcile them. Identical changes merge cleanly, but an adapted copy means the two sides changed the same lines differently, and the merge conflicts or, with unlucky context, combines them in a way nobody reviewed. What I would change: stop using cherry-pick as the routine way to keep the branches in step and make one direction the rule, either fixing on the oldest supported branch and merging upward, or fixing on `main` first and backporting. Where picks remain: `-x` always, tests on the target branch, and audits by the recorded line.

**Key terms.** duplicates with no link in the graph; adapted copies defeat patch comparison; double-counted commit lists; later merges must reconcile the copies; one direction as the rule; `-x` and audit by the recorded line

**Common weak answer.** "Nothing accumulates; Git recognises identical changes when the branches merge." Weak because only identical changes merge silently: adapted picks conflict or combine unreviewed, and the question of what each branch lacks can no longer be answered from the graph.

**Follow-up.** You make `-x` mandatory for every pick. Under which conditions does the recorded line itself stop being a reliable link?

**A strong reply covers.** When it points at a private commit: if the original lives only in one clone, or its branch is later rebased, the recorded ID refers to a commit nobody can find. The line also disappears if it is deleted in the editor or the pick is finished with `git commit -m`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 10](../textbook/ch10-cherry-pick.md), section 10.9, 10.10 and 10.13

#### Q166

**Question.** When do you fix on the oldest branch and merge upward, and when on `main` with a backport? Argue both.

**Model answer.** Two conventions are in use, and the mechanics are the same in both. The Git project commits a fix on the oldest supported branch that needs it and merges upward. The argument is structural: newer branches contain older ones, so ancestry answers whether a line has the fix, and cherry-picks, with the duplicates they leave, are the exception. Trunk-based practice fixes on the main line first and cherry-picks to the release branch. The argument there is about omission: a fix made on the release branch can be forgotten on `main` and come back as a regression. Its price is the one this chapter documents: the same change under two commit IDs, an audit that depends on the `-x` line because `git branch --contains` and patch comparison can both mislead, and a merge that must reconcile adapted copies if the lines ever meet again. My judgment is to choose by which failure costs the organization more, a fix lost on `main` or history that ancestry cannot audit, and then to hold to one direction instead of mixing both.

**Key terms.** fix on the oldest supported branch and merge upward; newer branches contain older ones; fix on `main` first, then backport; a forgotten fix returns as a regression; duplicates and the `-x` audit; one direction, not both

**Common weak answer.** "Always fix on main and cherry-pick; merging release branches upward is outdated." Weak because it names one convention only and cannot state what merging upward buys, ancestry that answers the audit question, or what backporting costs, duplicates.

**Follow-up.** Under the backport convention, what do you record for an ML service whose release line is the version a customer's evaluation was signed off against?

**A strong reply covers.** A backport changes the line that was signed off, so record it where the sign-off lives. The `-x` line gives the auditor the original commit, and the original commit leads to the review and the tests. The backport itself is built and tested on the release branch.

**Reference.** [Chapter 10](../textbook/ch10-cherry-pick.md), section 10.9 and 10.13

#### Q167

**Question.** Design an unattended job that backports a list of approved fixes from `main` to a release branch. What must it do at each step, how does it fail safely, and what can it not prove?

**Model answer.** The job switches to the release branch and cherry-picks the listed commits with `-x` and `--empty=drop`. `-x` writes the only link between copy and original that travels with the history, and the later audit depends on it. Without `--empty=drop` a fix that is already present stops the job; with it, the fix is left out with a notice. The job must check the exit status. A sequence commits directly onto the branch, so a conflict leaves the branch partly advanced with `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD` set. The safe reaction is `git cherry-pick --abort`, which returns the branch, the index and the working tree to the state before the first pick, plus a report of the commit that `git status` names. It never retries blindly. After a clean run it builds and tests on the release branch, then opens a pull request against that branch. What the pick cannot prove is that the code works there: applied cleanly says the text merged, and a fix that depends on an unpicked commit applies and fails. A person reviews the backport as new code.

**Key terms.** `-x` as the audit link; `--empty=drop` for unattended runs; check the exit status; `--abort` returns to a known state; never a blind retry; a clean pick is not a tested build; review as new code

**Common weak answer.** "Loop over the commits with cherry-pick and push if there is no conflict." Weak because it ignores the partly advanced branch after a failed sequence, stops on a fix that is already present, records no link for the audit, and treats a clean text merge as a tested release.

**Follow-up.** Six months later an auditor asks which of the approved fixes are on the release branch. Which query do you trust, and which two would you not trust on their own?

**A strong reply covers.** Trust a search for the recorded `-x` lines with `git log --grep`, because that line survives adaptation. Do not trust `git branch --contains` with the original IDs, which follows ancestry only, or `git cherry` alone, which marks an adapted copy, or one whose context differs, as missing.

**Reference.** [Chapter 10](../textbook/ch10-cherry-pick.md), section 10.6, 10.8 and 10.9


## Area 6: Undo

Q168 to Q184. Reset, revert, restore and stash: choosing the undo that destroys least.


### Undo: foundational level

#### Q168

**Question.** Why does `git reset --hard` not necessarily delete commits permanently?

**Model answer.** Because a reset moves a ref and deletes no object. `git reset --hard <commit>` makes the current branch name another commit and rewrites the index and the tracked files to match; the commits that left the branch are still in the object database. They also still have names: the reset writes the previous tip to `ORIG_HEAD` and appends an entry to the reflog of HEAD and to the reflog of the branch, and Git never deletes an object that a reflog entry names. Chapter 13, section 13.2 shows that even `git gc --prune=now` leaves such a commit in place. So `git reflog` shows the old tip, and `git branch <name> <id>` or `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` brings it back. By default the reflog entry for a commit the branch no longer reaches is kept for 30 days. What a hard reset does destroy for good is uncommitted work that was never staged, since no object was ever written for it.

**Key terms.** a ref moves, no object is deleted; reflog entry; `ORIG_HEAD`; reachability; 30 days; never-staged work is the real loss

**Common weak answer.** "The commits are deleted, but Git keeps a backup for a while." Weak because nothing is deleted or copied: the branch ref was moved, and the same commit objects stay reachable from the reflog.

**Follow-up.** Under which conditions does a commit that was reset away become permanently unrecoverable?

**A strong reply covers.** When the last reflog entry that names it is gone, through expiry or `git reflog expire`, a collection has then deleted the unreachable object, and no other clone, server, bundle or backup holds a copy.

**Reference.** [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.4 and 11.5; [Chapter 13](../textbook/ch13-recovery.md), section 13.2

#### Q169

**Question.** What is the difference between revert and reset?

**Model answer.** `git reset <commit>` moves the current branch ref to another commit, and its mode decides whether the index and the working tree are rewritten too; the commits after the target leave the branch, so it rewrites history. `git revert <commit>` adds one new commit whose change is the opposite of what the named commit changed; nothing is removed and the branch only moves forward. Three consequences follow. Reset is for private history, because a teammate's clone still names the commits you removed, while revert is the correction for shared history and reaches everyone as a normal update. Reset takes the whole branch back to a point, while revert reverses one commit anywhere in history and leaves later commits in place. And a revert is a three-way merge against the current files, so it can conflict, whereas a reset merges nothing: `--hard` overwrites uncommitted changes to tracked files, and `--keep` refuses instead. Neither deletes an object: commits dropped by a reset stay in the reflog.

**Key terms.** moves the branch ref; adds an inverse commit; private versus shared history; one commit versus a point in history; can conflict; no force push needed

**Common weak answer.** "Both undo a commit; revert is the safe one." Weak because it gives no mechanism: reset moves a ref and drops commits from the branch, revert adds a commit, and that difference decides which is allowed on shared history.

**Follow-up.** How do you decide, with evidence, which of the two is allowed for a given commit?

**A strong reply covers.** Run `git fetch`, then `git branch -r --contains <commit>` and `git log --oneline @{u}..`. If a remote-tracking branch contains the commit, it is shared and gets a revert; if it appears only among the commits the upstream lacks, it is private and may be reset.

**Reference.** [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.2, 11.4 and 11.8

#### Q170

**Question.** A colleague asks for "the undo command". Name the five commands that Git offers for undoing work, and say which of working tree, index, branch ref and history each one writes.

**Model answer.** Git has no single undo; it has five commands, each defined by the places it writes to. `git restore` copies a stored version of the named paths into the working tree, into the index with `--staged`, or into both, and moves no ref. `git reset` moves the current branch ref, and its mode decides whether the index and the working tree are rewritten to match. `git revert` adds one commit that applies the inverse change, so the branch advances and history only grows. `git clean` deletes untracked files from the working tree and touches nothing else. `git stash push` records the index and the working tree as commits that only `refs/stash` reaches and then resets both to HEAD, without moving the branch. Before choosing, I ask whether the history is private or shared: reset rewrites, so it is for private history, while revert is safe on a branch other people have.

**Key terms.** restore; reset; revert; clean; stash; the four places; private versus shared history

**Common weak answer.** "Use `git reset --hard`, it undoes anything." Weak because it treats one destructive command as a general undo, ignores which of the four places is written, and ignores whether the history is shared.

**Follow-up.** Which of those five leave no record in Git from which the previous state could be restored, and why?

**A strong reply covers.** `git restore` into the working tree and `git clean`. A restore creates no object, moves no ref and writes no reflog entry, and an untracked file was never an object, so content that was never staged or committed cannot come back through Git.

**Reference.** [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.1, 11.2 and 11.12

#### Q171

**Question.** HEAD, the index and the working tree hold three different versions of one file. What does each hold after `git reset --soft HEAD~1`, after `--mixed` and after `--hard`, and what does `git status -s` print?

**Model answer.** All three modes move the current branch to the parent commit and write the previous commit ID to `ORIG_HEAD`; they differ in how far the change spreads. After `--soft`, HEAD holds the parent's version, the index still holds the staged version and the working tree still holds the edited version, so `git status -s` still prints `MM`, now measured against the older commit. After `--mixed`, the default, the index is rewritten to match the new HEAD and the file on disk is untouched, so the status prints ` M`, one unstaged modification. After `--hard`, HEAD, the index and the working tree all hold the parent's version and the status is empty; the staged version and the unstaged edit are gone from every place you can name. In no mode is an object deleted: the commit that left the branch stays in the object database and in both reflogs. Chapter 11, section 11.4 shows the three runs side by side.

**Key terms.** branch ref moves; `ORIG_HEAD` written; index rewritten by mixed; working tree rewritten by hard; `MM` status; no object deleted

**Common weak answer.** "Soft keeps the changes, hard deletes the commits." Weak because it does not say what the index holds in each mode, and it is wrong about deletion: every mode moves a ref and removes no object.

**Follow-up.** After the soft reset, what would `git commit` record, and where is the commit that left the branch?

**A strong reply covers.** A commit made then would record the staged version directly on top of the parent commit. The commit that left the branch is still an object, named by `ORIG_HEAD` and by the reflog entries of HEAD and of the branch.

**Reference.** [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.4

#### Q172

**Question.** Where is the stash list stored, and what exactly does `git stash drop 'stash@{1}'` write?

**Model answer.** The stash list is not a structure of its own. It is one ref and its reflog: `refs/stash` holds the object ID of the newest entry, and `.git/logs/refs/stash` has one line per entry, oldest first, in the ordinary reflog format. `git stash list` prints the message column of that file, which is not necessarily the subject of the commit, and `stash@{1}` is reflog syntax on that single ref. `git stash drop 'stash@{1}'` therefore writes very little: it deletes that entry's line from the log and rewrites the next line so that it follows the entry before it; when the newest entry is dropped, `refs/stash` moves or is deleted. It deletes no object. The dropped commit still exists, unreachable now, until unreachable objects are pruned, two weeks by default. `drop` prints the ID of the dropped commit, and `git stash store` with that ID puts the entry back while the objects exist. That is why the chapter labels `drop` and `clear` dangerous and still recoverable for a while.

**Key terms.** `refs/stash`; reflog of one ref; one log line per entry; drop deletes a log line; objects stay unreachable; pruning after two weeks by default; `git stash store`

**Common weak answer.** "Stashes are kept in a stash area, and drop deletes the stash." Weak because there is no separate area: drop edits one reflog and deletes no object, which is the fact that makes recovery possible and also the reason the stash is not durable storage.

**Follow-up.** Given that storage, is the stash an acceptable place to keep a week of work, and how do stashes get to another machine?

**A strong reply covers.** No: an entry is reachable only through one line of one reflog, and `drop` and `clear` delete such lines. Nothing fetches or pushes `refs/stash`. Since Git 2.51, `git stash export --to-ref` writes the entries as a chain of ordinary commits that can be pushed like a branch, and `git stash import` rebuilds them.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14C](../textbook/ch14c-stash-rerere-attributes-hooks.md), section 14C.2 and 14C.15


### Undo: working engineer level

#### Q173

**Question.** An engineer ran `git reset --hard HEAD~3` in a dirty tree. What can you recover, with which commands and for how long, and what is gone? Why is that part gone?

**Model answer.** The deciding question for each piece of work is whether Git ever stored it as an object. The three commits were stored, the reset moved a ref and deleted nothing, and the reflog recorded the move, so `git reflog` shows the old tip and `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`, or `ORIG_HEAD` as the very next command, brings them back. By default a reflog entry for a commit its branch no longer reaches is kept for 30 days. Staged changes were written as blobs by `git add`; the reset removed the index entries that referred to them, so `git fsck --lost-found` lists them as dangling blobs and `git cat-file -p` prints their content, until garbage collection removes unreachable objects older than two weeks. Edits that were never staged are gone, because no object was ever written and `--hard` overwrote the only copy. Untracked files survive, except one at a path the target commit tracks. Prevention is to commit or stash first, or to use `git reset --keep`.

**Key terms.** stored as an object; reflog; dangling blob; `git fsck --lost-found`; never staged; 30 days and two weeks; `git reset --keep`

**Common weak answer.** "Everything is gone, a hard reset is permanent", or the opposite, "the reflog has all of it." Weak because the reflog lists commits only: staged content needs `git fsck`, and never-staged edits were never objects.

**Follow-up.** Ten files were staged before the reset. What does recovering them look like in practice, and what information about them is lost for good?

**A strong reply covers.** `git fsck --lost-found` yields ten anonymous blobs, copied under `.git/lost-found/other`, and I identify them by reading their content. The file names are lost, because a blob stores content only and the name lived in the index entry.

**Reference.** [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.5

#### Q174

**Question.** What is `ORIG_HEAD`, which commands write it, and why is the reflog the more reliable tool?

**Model answer.** `ORIG_HEAD` is one file in `.git` that holds one commit ID: where HEAD was before the last command that moved it in a drastic way. The manual lists `git am`, `git merge`, `git rebase` and `git reset`; `git pull` writes it too because it runs a merge or a rebase, and so does `git stash push`, which ends with an internal reset. `git commit`, `git commit --amend`, `git switch`, `git cherry-pick` and `git revert` do not write it. It is one slot, not a history: the next writer overwrites it, a command that does not write it leaves a stale value from an earlier operation, possibly on another branch, and it has no reflog of its own. The reflog keeps the whole sequence, one entry per movement with the command that caused it, for HEAD and for each branch. So I use `ORIG_HEAD` only as the very next command after a reset, merge or rebase, check it with `git log -1 ORIG_HEAD`, and in every other case reset to a reflog entry.

**Key terms.** one slot; drastic commands; `git stash push` writes it; stale value; branch reflog; very next command

**Common weak answer.** "`ORIG_HEAD` is the previous commit, so resetting to it undoes the last command." Weak because it means the position before the last reset, merge, rebase or am, not before the last command, and cherry-pick, revert and amend never write it.

**Follow-up.** Give a concrete sequence in which `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD`, run after a merge, fails to undo the merge.

**A strong reply covers.** Merge, then `git stash push`: the stash ends with a reset to HEAD, which rewrites `ORIG_HEAD` to the merge commit itself, so the reset leaves the merge in place. The reflog entry below the merge line names the commit to reset to.

**Reference.** [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.4; [Chapter 13](../textbook/ch13-recovery.md), section 13.5

#### Q175

**Question.** When do you choose `git reset --keep` over `--hard`? What does `--merge` do to staged changes, and why was it designed that way?

**Model answer.** I choose `--keep` whenever I want to drop commits, because on a clean tree it does the same as `--hard`, and on a dirty tree it either carries my uncommitted changes across or stops and says why. It moves the branch and updates the files that differ between HEAD and the target, leaves local changes in all other files alone, and resets the index, so a staged change comes out unstaged. `--merge` keeps unstaged changes and discards staged ones, from the index and from the file. It was designed for backing out of a merge, where whatever is staged is merge output and should go; its proper uses are `git reset --merge ORIG_HEAD` right after a completed merge, which keeps unrelated edits, and `git reset --merge` without a commit to clear a conflicted index. Because it destroys staged work, I preview with `git diff --cached`. `--hard` discards staged and unstaged changes alike and overwrites an untracked file at a path the target commit tracks, without a message.

**Key terms.** carries local changes across; refuses on overlap; index is reset; staged changes discarded; merge output; `git diff --cached`

**Common weak answer.** "`--keep` and `--merge` are both the safe reset." Weak because `--merge` throws staged changes away, and the answer does not explain that it exists for backing out of a merge.

**Follow-up.** In which cases does `git reset --keep` refuse to run, and what state does a refusal leave behind?

**A strong reply covers.** It refuses when a file that must be rewritten has a local change, staged or unstaged, and when an untracked file sits at a path the target commit tracks. On refusal nothing moves: the branch, the index and the files are as before.

**Reference.** [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.6

#### Q176

**Question.** Compare `git clean -fdx` with `git reset --hard`: which files does each destroy, and for which of them does Git still hold an object?

**Model answer.** They destroy different sets of files. `git reset --hard` rewrites the index and every tracked file to match the target commit, so it destroys uncommitted changes to tracked files and leaves untracked files alone, with one exception: an untracked file at a path the target commit tracks is overwritten. `git clean` with force, `-d` and `-x` deletes untracked files and directories and ignored files as well, which can include `.env` files, datasets and checkpoints; tracked edits are not its business, and it skips nested repositories. For objects: after the reset, commits are still reachable through the reflog, and content that was staged survives as dangling blobs that `git fsck --lost-found` finds, while never-staged edits have no object. After the clean Git holds nothing, because an untracked file was never an object, so no reflog, no `git fsck` and no stash can reverse it. `git hash-object --stdin` followed by `git cat-file -t` proves the absence, as Chapter 11, section 11.10 shows.

**Key terms.** tracked versus untracked; ignored files; never an object; dangling blob; reflog; dry run with `-n`

**Common weak answer.** "Both are recoverable from the reflog." Weak because the reflog records ref movements only: it leads to commits, not to staged blobs, and nothing in Git ever held an untracked or ignored file.

**Follow-up.** How do you preview each command, and what do you run instead when you are not sure the files are disposable?

**A strong reply covers.** For clean, the same options with `-n` in place of `-f`, read line by line. For the reset, `git status -s`, `git diff HEAD --stat` and `git log --oneline <commit>..HEAD`. When unsure, `git stash push -u` clears tracked changes and untracked files, though not ignored ones, and keeps them as objects.

**Reference.** [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.5 and 11.10

#### Q177

**Question.** What is inside a stash entry and where is it stored? What happens when `git stash pop` conflicts? Give three reasons not to use the stash for long-term storage.

**Model answer.** A stash entry is a commit whose tree is the state of the tracked files; its first parent is the commit that was HEAD, its second parent records the index, and with `-u` a third parent holds the untracked files. `refs/stash` points at the newest entry, and older entries live only in the reflog of that ref. `git stash pop` is apply followed by drop, and the drop happens only if the apply succeeded: on a conflict the file gets conflict markers, the index gets unmerged entries, and the entry is kept. I then resolve, clear the conflict state with `git add` or `git restore --staged`, and drop the entry myself, or back out with `git reset --merge` and use `git stash branch`, which applies the entry on the commit it was made on, where it cannot conflict. Against long-term storage: a stash lives in one repository and no push sends it; one command drops it; and entries rot, because the further the branch moves on, the likelier the pop conflicts.

**Key terms.** commit with two or three parents; `refs/stash` and its reflog; entry kept on conflict; `git stash branch`; never pushed; one command drops it

**Common weak answer.** "A stash is a saved diff, and pop puts it back." Weak because an entry is a set of commits tied to a base commit, applying it is a merge that can conflict, and the answer misses that a conflicted pop keeps the entry.

**Follow-up.** A stash entry was dropped by mistake an hour ago. How do you get it back, with and without the terminal scrollback?

**A strong reply covers.** With the commit ID that the drop printed, `git stash store -m "<message>" <id>` puts the entry back. Without it, the stash manual's recipe lists candidates from `git fsck --unreachable`. Both work only while the objects exist.

**Reference.** [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.11 and 11.15

#### Q178

**Question.** Draw the commits of a stash entry made with `git stash push -u`. Which tree holds the staged change, which the unstaged one, and what does `git stash show -p` compare?

**Model answer.** A stash entry made with `-u` is three new commits on top of the commit you were on. W is the stash commit itself: its tree records the tracked files as they were on disk, and it is a merge commit with three parents. Its first parent is H, the commit that was HEAD. Its second parent is I, a child of H whose tree records the index as it was. Its third parent is U, a commit with no parent whose tree holds only the untracked files; it exists only with `-u` or `-a`. `refs/stash` points at the newest W. The staged change is the difference between H and I, so the tree of I holds it, addressed as `stash@{0}^2`. The unstaged change is the difference between I and W, so the tree of W holds it. `git stash show -p` compares H with W, which is why staged and unstaged work appear as one change; `git stash show --only-untracked` reads the third parent. No tree mixes the three kinds of work, so they can be taken apart again.

**Key terms.** W, I and U commits; three parents; second parent records the index; third parent has no parent; `refs/stash`; `stash@{0}^2`; H against W

**Common weak answer.** "A stash is a saved patch of my changes." Weak because an entry is ordinary commits in the object database held by one ref, with the index recorded in its own commit; the patch picture cannot explain why staging can be restored or why a dropped entry can be found again.

**Follow-up.** How does Git itself build a stash entry without putting it on the stash list, and where does the course show Git doing that on its own?

**A strong reply covers.** `git stash create` writes the commits and prints the ID of W; no ref is written and no file is touched. `git stash store` puts such a commit on the list. The autostash of `git rebase --autostash` is one, never listed, and `git merge` on a tree with local changes runs `git stash create` as a safety copy.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14C](../textbook/ch14c-stash-rerere-attributes-hooks.md), section 14C.2; [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.19

#### Q179

**Question.** An engineer lost their staging after `git stash pop`. Why does the information still exist, and which single command restores it?

**Model answer.** Nothing was lost, because of the shape of a stash entry. The stash commit records the tracked files, and its second parent is a separate commit whose tree records the index as it was at the time of the stash. A plain `git stash pop` merges the stash commit into the files with the original HEAD commit as the base and ignores the second parent; only `--index` also reads it. So the careful staging comes back as unstaged changes. `pop` then drops the entry, but dropping removes a reflog line and no object, and `pop` printed the ID of the dropped commit. The single command that restores the staging is `git restore --staged --source='<id>^2' -- .`, which fills the index from the tree of that second parent. The prevention is `git stash pop --index` whenever the staging mattered. The objects stay until unreachable objects are pruned, two weeks by default, so the repair should not wait.

**Key terms.** second parent holds the index; `pop` without `--index`; dropped commit ID printed; unreachable but present; `git restore --staged --source`; `git stash pop --index`

**Common weak answer.** "The staging is gone; stage the hunks again by hand." Weak because the index was saved as its own commit and one command restores it; the answer also misses that plain `pop` and `apply` never read that commit.

**Follow-up.** The engineer closed the terminal, so the ID that `pop` printed is gone. How do you find the commit, and how long do you have?

**A strong reply covers.** The dropped entry is an unreachable commit, so `git fsck --unreachable` finds it, as in the recipe of Lab 8.6; `git stash store` with that ID puts it back on the list, or its second parent can be read directly. The window is until unreachable objects are pruned, two weeks by default.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14C](../textbook/ch14c-stash-rerere-attributes-hooks.md), section 14C.2 and 14C.14


### Undo: senior level

#### Q180

**Question.** Describe `git revert` as a three-way merge: what are base, ours and theirs? Use the answer to explain why reverting an old commit can conflict.

**Model answer.** A revert is a three-way merge with unusual inputs: the base is the commit being reverted, ours is HEAD, and theirs is the parent of the reverted commit. The difference from base to theirs is the inverse of the original change, and Git applies it to the files as they are now and records the result as an ordinary new commit on top of HEAD. It conflicts when a later commit changed the same lines: ours then differs from the base in the same place where theirs does, and Git cannot know which value is right today. The evidence is in the index during the conflict: `git ls-files -s` shows stage 1 as the file in the reverted commit, stage 2 as HEAD's version and stage 3 as the file in that commit's parent, and `REVERT_HEAD` names the commit being reverted. I resolve the file, `git add` it and run `git revert --continue`, or back out with `git revert --abort`. Reverting early, before other commits build on the bad one, is the prevention.

**Key terms.** base is the reverted commit; ours is HEAD; theirs is the parent; three index stages; `REVERT_HEAD`; computed against current files

**Common weak answer.** "Revert undoes the commit, like stepping back in time." Weak because a revert reverses one commit against the files as they are now, not everything since, and the answer cannot explain a conflict.

**Follow-up.** A revert of a range of commits stopped with a conflict at its second step. What state is the repository in, and what does each of the four ways out do?

**A strong reply covers.** The first revert is already committed, the index holds unmerged entries and `.git/sequencer/` holds the remaining steps. `--continue` commits and proceeds, `--skip` drops this step, `--abort` returns the branch to the recorded start so earlier reverts leave it, and `--quit` forgets the sequence but keeps the reverts and the conflict.

**Reference.** [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.8

#### Q181

**Question.** A bad commit is on `main` and the team has pulled it. Compare "revert and push" with "reset and force-push": what does each do to the server, to the teammates' clones and to CI?

**Model answer.** Revert and push adds one commit that applies the inverse change. On the server `main` only moves forward, so the push needs no force and takes the same route as any other commit, a pull request if `main` requires one, so CI sees an ordinary new commit, and every teammate's next pull brings it in as a normal update. Reset and force-push moves the branch backwards. A teammate's clone still holds a ref that names the removed commits, so the next teammate who pushes from such a clone puts them straight back or merges them with the replacements; the hard reset also destroys the engineer's own uncommitted work, and the force push destroys commits that others pushed in the meantime. CI records that quote the old commit IDs stay valid when history is only added to. On GitHub, not Git, a new ruleset blocks force pushes by default and classic branch protection disables them by default, so on a protected `main` the revert is normally the only route. The reason is mechanical, not etiquette.

**Key terms.** adds a commit; non-fast-forward; teammates' refs keep the old commits; removed commits come back; block force pushes; private versus shared history

**Common weak answer.** "Reset and force-push is cleaner because the bad commit disappears from history." Weak because the commit stays in every clone that pulled it and returns with the next push, and the force push can destroy other people's commits on the server.

**Follow-up.** An engineer has already reset or amended locally, and the plain push was rejected as a non-fast-forward. What is the lowest-risk way back?

**A strong reply covers.** Save any new work, run `git reset --hard @{u}` to return to what the server has, then `git revert` the bad commit and push normally. Prevention is `git fetch` and `git branch -r --contains <commit>` before any rewrite.

**Reference.** [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.2, 11.8 and 11.15

#### Q182

**Question.** You reverted a merge with `-m 1` last week. Today the fixed branch was merged again and the feature is incomplete. Explain the mechanism with the merge base and give two correct procedures. What would `-m 2` have undone, and why does a squash merge not show the problem?

**Model answer.** Reverting a merge undoes its content and leaves the merge in the commit graph. The merge commit is still an ancestor of `main`, and through its second parent so are the branch's old commits, so the merge base of `main` and the branch is the old branch tip. A merge combines what each side changed since the merge base: the branch contributes only the commits after that tip, while on `main` the revert is a change that deletes the feature, nothing opposes it, and it stays. The merge succeeds without conflict or warning; `git merge-base` and `git log --oneline main..<branch>` prove the cause. The two procedures are to revert the revert and then merge, or to recreate the branch as new commits with `git rebase --no-ff` from its starting commit and merge that. `-m 2` computes the inverse relative to the second parent, so it would have removed what `main` itself contributed, not the feature. A squash merge has no second parent, so the merge base stays where the branch started.

**Key terms.** merge stays in the graph; merge base is the old branch tip; revert the revert; `git rebase --no-ff`; mainline parent; squash has no second parent

**Common weak answer.** "The revert removed the merge, so merging again brings everything back." Weak because a revert changes content and never the graph: the old branch commits remain ancestors of `main`, and Git merges only what is new since the merge base.

**Follow-up.** Suppose the feature branch was rebuilt as new commits instead of being fixed by adding one. Which way out is now wrong, and why does a plain `git rebase main` not rebuild the branch?

**A strong reply covers.** Reverting the revert is now wrong: it conflicts with the rebuilt commits wherever they differ from the old ones, so merge the rebuilt branch directly. A plain rebase replays only what `main` lacks, one commit, on top of the revert; `git rebase --no-ff` from the starting commit recreates all of them.

**Reference.** [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.9

#### Q183

**Question.** A faulty change was applied to both `main` and a release branch. It was reverted on the release branch only, the release branch was later merged into `main`, and the fault is still live on `main`. Nobody saw a conflict. Explain the mechanism.

**Model answer.** A revert does not win a merge. A merge compares each side with the merge base and takes a change that only one side made. On the release branch the change and its revert cancel out, so relative to the merge base that side shows no net change in those lines. On `main` the same lines did change since the merge base. Git sees that one side changed the lines and the other did not, takes the change, and reports no conflict, because nothing disagrees. Merge works from content and the graph, not from the intention behind a revert commit. The Git FAQ has an entry on this case, Chapter 8 demonstrates it, and Chapter 11, section 11.15 states the working rule: after a revert on a release branch, check `main` separately. The mechanism is the same one that makes a reverted merge stay reverted when the branch is merged again: a change on one side that nothing opposes survives.

**Key terms.** merge base; no net change on one side; Git takes the one-sided change; no conflict; check each branch separately; revert on every branch that has the change

**Common weak answer.** "The merge should have carried the revert over, so Git lost it." Weak because the merge worked as defined: it compares both sides with the merge base, and a change followed by its revert is no change.

**Follow-up.** How do you correct `main` now, and what do you add to the release procedure so that this cannot recur?

**A strong reply covers.** `main` gets its own `git revert` of the faulty commit, pushed like any other commit. The procedure then requires that a revert on one branch is followed by an explicit check, and where needed a separate revert, on every branch that carries the same change.

**Reference.** [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.15 and 11.9


### Undo: principal level

#### Q184

**Question.** A faulty feature was merged into a protected, shared `main` with a merge commit and is deployed. You can revert the whole merge, revert the single faulty commit, or fix forward. How do you choose, and what must the runbook say so that the choice does not cause a second incident?

**Model answer.** On shared history every option must add commits, so I choose by what each costs later. Reverting the whole merge with `git revert -m 1` removes the content and leaves the merge in the commit graph: a later merge of the same branch brings only its new commits, and for `git bisect` the revert, and later the revert of the revert, is one large commit that undoes many small ones. Git's how-to therefore advises finding and reverting the single faulty commit, or fixing forward, and reverting a whole merge only when the merge as such was the mistake. The runbook says three things. The revert message must explain why and contain the re-merge procedure: revert the revert and then merge if the branch was fixed by adding commits, or merge the rebuilt branch directly if it was recreated. The same plan goes into the ticket. And every other branch that carries the same change, such as a release branch, is checked separately, because a revert on one branch does not win a later merge.

**Key terms.** add commits only; merge stays in the graph; re-merge procedure in the revert message; bisect cost; revert the single faulty commit; a revert does not win a merge

**Common weak answer.** "Always revert the merge, it is the safe option." Weak because it ignores the re-merge problem and the bisect cost and writes no procedure down, so the second incident arrives when the fixed branch is merged again.

**Follow-up.** An engineer asks for a one-time exception to force-push `main` because a credential was committed. Do you grant it, and why?

**A strong reply covers.** No. No undo command removes a secret: a revert leaves it in history in plain sight, and a reset or an amend leaves it in the reflog and, once pushed, on the server and in every clone and fork. The remedy is to rotate the secret.

**Reference.** [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.9, 11.13 and 11.15


## Area 7: Recovery

Q185 to Q200. The reflog, unreachable objects, `git fsck`, and the limits of every safety net.


### Recovery: foundational level

#### Q185

**Question.** How does the reflog help?

**Model answer.** A reflog is a local, append-only list of the values a ref has had, with the time, the person and the command behind each change, and every old value is a name that any command accepts. It helps in two ways. It keeps objects alive: a commit named by a reflog entry is reachable, so no collection deletes it, even after a reset, an amend or a rebase took it off its branch. And it tells me where to go back to: `git reflog` shows every movement of HEAD in order, `git reflog show <branch>` shows where one branch was before each operation, and I take the entry below the bad one. Selectors such as `HEAD@{1}` or `main@{yesterday}` address entries, and `git log -g` with `--grep-reflog` searches a long log. The reflog has no undo command; it gives old positions and I decide what to do, normally `git branch rescue/<what> <id>` first and then a cherry-pick, a merge or `git reset --keep`.
