Owning `/.github/` also covers `.github/workflows/`, and a workflow file decides what runs with the repository's token and secrets, so a change to it is a change to deployment and security posture. Without that line, anyone with write access can change the reviewers and the automation in one pull request. Three conditions make the protection real. The line must come last in the file, so that no later pattern such as `*.yaml` takes the workflow files away under last match wins. The code-owner option must be required by a rule on the default branch; otherwise the owner is only requested. And the owning team must hold explicit write access, or its line is skipped without an error. I would own it by a team, not by one person, and treat removal of that line as a dangerous change: restore it, then audit what merged in between.

**Key terms.** owner for `/.github/`; the line must come last; rule on the default branch; explicit write access; workflows run with secrets; bypass actors

**Common weak answer.** "Add a CODEOWNERS entry for the workflows folder." Weak because an entry alone only requests a review; if a later pattern overrides it, no rule requires it, or the team lacks explicit write access, the change merges unseen.

**Follow-up.** With all three conditions met, name the ways a workflow change can still merge without the approval you intended.

**A strong reply covers.** The person who merges is a bypass actor of the rule, or the change arrives through an indirect merge: both go around every review requirement. Also, an approval from any one owner suffices, so one member of the owning team is the whole control.

**Reference.** [Chapter 19](../textbook/ch19-codeowners.md), section 19.8 and 19.13

#### Q261

**Question.** When would you use the required reviewers rule instead of, or together with, CODEOWNERS?

**Model answer.** Together, in most cases. CODEOWNERS stays the ownership map: it lives in the repository, is reviewed like code, is visible to contributors in the tree, accepts users and emails as well as teams, and requests reviews even when nothing is required. Its limit is what it can express: several owners on a line means any one suffices, and it cannot say both teams, two members of one team, or a negated pattern. The required reviewers rule, generally available since 17 February 2026, lives in a ruleset that administrators edit: up to 15 teams, each with its own approval count from 0 to 10 for chosen file patterns, where zero adds the team for visibility, and an organization ruleset can cover many repositories. So I add the rule where a count or several teams are needed, or where one policy must hold across repositories. GitHub itself says the rule augments CODEOWNERS files and does not replace them. These facts are described from GitHub's documentation and changelog, not from a run.

**Key terms.** augments, does not replace; approval count per team; up to 15 teams; teams only; organization ruleset; any one owner suffices; reviewed like code versus edited by administrators

**Common weak answer.** "The new rule replaces CODEOWNERS, so migrate everything to it." Weak because GitHub positions it as an addition: it cannot name individuals, is not visible in the tree, and is changed by administrators outside code review.

**Follow-up.** What makes you cautious about depending on that rule today, and where can it not be used at all?

**A strong reply covers.** The textbook records an unresolved point: the documentation page and the REST schema describe this rule's pattern syntax differently, so test before you depend on it. It accepts teams only, each with write permission or higher, and is not available on user-owned repositories, which have no teams.

**Reference.** [Chapter 19](../textbook/ch19-codeowners.md), section 19.10 and 19.9


## Area 10: Pull requests

Q262 to Q278. What a pull request is, what it displays, reviews, the three merge methods, and their effect on history.


### Pull requests: foundational level

#### Q262

**Question.** What exactly does GitHub create when a pull request is opened? Which parts are Git data, and in which repository do they live?

**Model answer.** Opening a pull request moves no branch. GitHub creates a pull request object in its own database: the number, title, description, labels, reviewers, reviews, comments and review threads, none of which is in any clone. It also writes a little Git data into the base repository: a read-only ref `refs/pull/<number>/head` that names the head commit and, when the merge is clean, a test merge commit under `refs/pull/<number>/merge` whose parents are the latest base commit and the head commit. That test merge is on neither branch. Checks and commit statuses are GitHub data attached to commit IDs, and the Commits and Files changed tabs are computed from three commits, the tip of the base, the tip of the head and their merge base, and stored nowhere in Git. A normal clone never sees the pull refs, because the default refspec fetches `refs/heads/*` only; `git ls-remote origin` lists them and `git fetch origin pull/1/head:pr-1` takes one. Section 17.2 reproduces the Git part on a bare repository; the GitHub side is described from the documentation.

**Key terms.** GitHub object, not Git; refs/pull/N/head; test merge commit; base repository; read-only ref; default refspec; three commits

**Common weak answer.** "GitHub copies my branch and creates a merge branch on main." Weak because no branch is created or moved; it names no ref, does not say the Git data lives in the base repository, and does not separate the GitHub object (reviews, comments, checks) from Git data.

**Follow-up.** The head branch is deleted after the pull request closes. What still exists, where does it live, and what does that mean for a pull request that came from a fork?

**A strong reply covers.** `refs/pull/<number>/head` still names the commits in the base repository, so `git fetch origin pull/N/head` retrieves them; nobody can rewrite or delete that ref with Git. For a fork, opening the pull request stored the head commit in the upstream repository, on none of its branches.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.2


### Pull requests: working engineer level

#### Q263

**Question.** Why can a pull request show unexpected commits?

**Model answer.** Because the page is a computation, not a record of what you intended. A pull request stores two names, a base and a head, and GitHub's Commits tab is the output of `git log base..head`: every commit reachable from the head and not from the base. Unexpected commits therefore appear when the head contains commits that the base does not reach, or when the base is not the branch the work started from. GitHub documents five causes of a misleading page: the head branch was reused after a squash merge, so the merge base never moved; the base is wrong or was changed; the base branch moved, so the pull request page and a compare page can calculate from different merge bases; history was rewritten or force-pushed; and the diff is truncated or hidden, which removes files from view. Section 17.12 reproduces the first two in plain Git. Before opening, run `git fetch`, `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD` and `git diff --stat origin/main...HEAD`; a commit you did not write will be seen by the reviewer too.

**Key terms.** base and head names; git log base..head; reachable from head, not from base; merge base; squash then reuse; wrong base; check the range before opening

**Common weak answer.** "Someone else pushed to my branch" or "GitHub is out of date." Weak because the list is computed from reachability: the candidate has to explain the range and the merge base, and usually the extra commits are in the head because of the base chosen or a squash.

**Follow-up.** Somebody force-pushes the base branch itself. What do the open pull requests against it show afterwards, and what prevents it?

**A strong reply covers.** Every open pull request against that base lists the removed commits, and review comments on rewritten commits become outdated; GitHub's documentation says force pushing can corrupt pull requests. Prevention is a rule that blocks force pushes on shared branches (Chapter 18); `git push --force` to a shared base is labelled dangerous in section 17.21.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.12, 17.3 and 17.2

#### Q264

**Question.** Why does a pull request show a three-dot diff and not a two-dot diff? Construct a case in which they differ.

**Model answer.** GitHub's documentation states that pull requests show a three-dot diff, and gives the reason: the comparison uses the merge base, so it shows what the pull request introduces. For `git diff`, `base...head` means from the merge base of the two to the head, while `base..head` compares the two tips. To make them differ, create a branch from `main`, change two files on it, and let one commit land on `main` that raises a threshold in `config/routing.yaml` from 0.6 to 0.7. `git diff --stat origin/main...feature` shows your two files. `git diff --stat origin/main..feature` shows three, and the third appears reversed, as if your branch lowered the threshold, although the branch never touched that file: every change that landed on `main` after you branched shows up as its own reversal. That is what `git diff main` shows locally and the usual source of "GitHub shows something different from my terminal". The three-dot diff equals a two-dot diff whose left side is the output of `git merge-base`. Section 17.3 shows all three runs.

**Key terms.** three-dot diff; merge base; two tips; reversed change; what the pull request introduces; git merge-base

**Common weak answer.** "Three dots and two dots are the same thing; GitHub shows the difference between the two branches." Weak because a two-dot diff compares the tips and reports the base's newer commits as reversals; the candidate cannot explain why the terminal and the page disagree.

**Follow-up.** Is the three-dot diff what will change on `main` when the pull request merges? If not, which object answers that question?

**A strong reply covers.** No. It is what the head changed since the merge base, and it differs from the effect on `main` exactly when both sides changed the same thing. The test merge commit answers that question. Merging the base into the head makes the two diffs agree, and adds a merge commit to the commit list.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.3

#### Q265

**Question.** After "Squash and merge", `git branch -d` refuses to delete the local branch. Explain the refusal from the definition of "merged", and show how to verify that deleting is safe.

**Model answer.** `git branch -d` deletes only when the branch is merged into its upstream, or into HEAD when it has no upstream, and "merged" means reachable. A squash merge on GitHub writes one new commit with one parent and the same content; it records no parent link to the branch, so the branch tip is not an ancestor of `main`. After `git pull --ff-only --prune` the upstream is gone, Git compares with HEAD, finds commits that are not reachable, and refuses with "not fully merged". The root cause is that squash and rebase merges transfer content without ancestry, and Git cannot know that another commit carries the same changes. To verify, ask whether merging the branch would change `main` at all: `git merge-tree --write-tree main <branch>` must print the same tree ID as `git rev-parse main^{tree}`. `git cherry -v main <branch>` marks every commit with a minus sign after a rebase merge, but with a plus sign after a squash, so the tree comparison is the test that works for both. Then delete with `git branch -D`.

**Key terms.** merged means reachable; content without ancestry; upstream gone, compared with HEAD; git merge-tree --write-tree; tree comparison; git cherry; git branch -D

**Common weak answer.** "Git is confused; use `git branch -D`." Weak because it does not explain that -d protects the only ref to unreachable commits, and it skips the verification that the base already contains the content.

**Follow-up.** In which situation does `git branch -d` delete the branch after a squash merge anyway, and what exactly does `git branch -D` destroy?

**A strong reply covers.** While the remote-tracking branch still exists, `-d` deletes with a warning, because the branch is merged into its upstream (Lab 22.1). `git branch -D` deletes the ref and its reflog; the commits stay in the object database and, if the branch was ever checked out, in the reflog of HEAD. Recovery is `git branch <name> <id>`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.9

#### Q266

**Question.** Your fork's `main` cannot be fast-forwarded to upstream. What happened, how do you keep the stray work, and why is `gh repo sync --force` the wrong first move?

**Model answer.** Somebody committed on the fork's default branch, so the fork's `main` and `upstream/main` have diverged and a fast-forward is impossible. I confirm it with `git fetch upstream` and `git rev-list --left-right --count upstream/main...origin/main`: the left number is commits only upstream has, the right number commits only the fork has, and a non-zero right number is the stray work. To keep it, I move those commits to a branch first, which Lab 21.1 practises; only after they are held by another ref is it safe to bring the fork's `main` back to upstream, and the stray work then goes through a pull request from its own branch. `gh repo sync` fast-forwards, and with `--force` it hard-resets the fork's branch, which discards those commits; the chapter labels it dangerous, with recovery only by pushing the old commits back from a clone that still has them. Prevention is the chapter's three rules: never commit on the fork's default branch, branch from `upstream/main` after a fetch, and use one branch per pull request, deleted after the merge.

**Key terms.** commits on the fork's default branch; diverged; rev-list --left-right --count; move to a branch first; hard reset by --force; never commit on the fork's main

**Common weak answer.** "Run `gh repo sync --force`, it fixes the fork." Weak because that hard-resets the fork's branch and discards the commits that caused the divergence; nothing was counted or saved first.

**Follow-up.** For the next fix in the same clone, which commit do you start the branch from, and how do you make sure its upstream branch is in the fork and not in the shared repository?

**A strong reply covers.** After `git fetch upstream`, run `git switch -c fix/empty-subject --no-track upstream/main`: the branch starts from current upstream, not the fork's stale `main`, and `--no-track` keeps it from adopting `upstream/main` as its upstream branch. `git push -u origin fix/empty-subject` then sets the fork's branch as upstream.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.15, 17.19 and 17.21

#### Q267

**Question.** A contributor leaked a key in a pull request and deleted the branch. Is the commit gone?

**Model answer.** No. When the pull request was opened, GitHub wrote `refs/pull/<number>/head` in the base repository, and that ref outlives the head branch. In the chapter's imitation the branch is deleted on the server and a teammate still retrieves the commit with `git fetch origin pull/1/head`. GitHub documents the principle: after a pull request is opened it stores all of the changes remotely, and the commits are available in the repository even before the pull request is merged. The namespace is read-only; a push to it is rejected as an update to a hidden ref, so nobody can rewrite or delete these refs with Git. If the pull request came from a fork, the commit was stored in the upstream repository as well, and a fork and its upstream share the same Git data. Deleting the branch therefore removes nothing. The lowest-risk response is to treat the key as compromised and rotate it; Chapter 21B covers the repository side. The general rule from section 17.20: anything pushed to a pull request is published.

**Key terms.** refs/pull/N/head outlives the branch; read-only namespace; stored in the base repository; fork shares Git data; rotate the credential; published

**Common weak answer.** "Yes, the branch is deleted, so Git will garbage-collect the commit." Weak because a ref written by GitHub in the base repository still names the commit and cannot be deleted with Git; the answer also omits rotating the key.

**Follow-up.** The contributor replies that a fresh clone does not contain the commit, so nobody can have it. How do you show that this is wrong?

**A strong reply covers.** A clone fetches `refs/heads/*` only, which is why a normal clone lacks the commit, but the server still advertises the ref: `git ls-remote origin` lists `refs/pull/N/head`, and `git fetch origin pull/N/head:pr-N` or `gh pr checkout N` brings the commit into any clone.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.2 and 17.20


### Pull requests: senior level

#### Q268

**Question.** A pull request for a one-line change lists forty commits. Give three causes and the command that distinguishes them.

**Model answer.** The Commits tab is `git log base..head`, so forty commits means forty commits reachable from the head and not from the base. Three causes from GitHub's documented list: first, the head branch was reused after a squash merge, so the merge base is still the old fork point and the already squashed commits are listed again; second, the pull request targets the wrong base, for example a branch created from `main` and opened against `release/1.0`, so it carries every commit `main` has and the release branch lacks; third, history was rewritten or force-pushed, which leaves old and new copies of commits, or removed commits when the base itself was forced. I distinguish them after `git fetch` with `git log --oneline <base>..<head>` and `git merge-base <base> <head>`: my own earlier commits above an old fork point mean squash reuse; other people's commits, and a small `git rev-list --count` against another candidate base, mean wrong base. The repair is `gh pr edit --base` when the base is wrong, or `git rebase --onto` when the branch started in the wrong place.

**Key terms.** git log base..head; merge base; squash then reuse; wrong base; force-pushed history; git rev-list --count; git rebase --onto

**Common weak answer.** "GitHub has a display bug; refresh the page or close and reopen the pull request." Weak because the page is a computation over three commits. The answer must name the range, the causes and the diagnostic command, and must not treat the list as wrong.

**Follow-up.** You establish that the base is correct and the branch was started from the wrong place. Why does a plain `git rebase` onto the correct base not repair the pull request, and what does?

**A strong reply covers.** A plain `git rebase origin/release/1.0` replays every commit not on the release branch, including the ones that belong to `main`, and changes only the commit IDs. `git rebase --onto origin/release/1.0 origin/main fix/empty-subject` replays only the commits not on `origin/main`; then `git push --force-with-lease`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.12 and 17.3

#### Q269

**Question.** CI passed on the pull request and failed on `main` right after the merge. Which commit did CI test, and what closes that gap?

**Model answer.** CI tested the test merge commit, not your head and not what landed. For a `pull_request` event the GitHub Actions documentation says `actions/checkout` checks out the merge branch, `refs/pull/N/merge`: your commits merged with `main` as `main` was when that test merge was made. It is a stored commit, so it can be stale. Since 19 February 2026 GitHub regenerates it only when changes are pushed to the pull request branch, when the merge base changes, or when the current test merge is older than 12 hours; before that it was also regenerated on a page view. In the bare-repository imitation of section 17.2, after one more commit lands on `main`, `git merge-base --is-ancestor main refs/pull/1/merge` fails. So two pull requests can each be green against an older `main` and break it together. What closes the gap is a check on the merged result against the current base: "strict" required status checks, or a merge queue that tests the exact commit that becomes the new tip. The immediate repair is to fix forward or revert.

**Key terms.** test merge commit; refs/pull/N/merge; stale merge ref; 12 hours; strict required checks; merge queue; merged result

**Common weak answer.** "CI tested my branch, so something on main must be flaky." Weak because the default checkout for a pull request event is the test merge with an older base; the answer misses the stored, possibly stale merge commit and names no control that closes the gap.

**Follow-up.** An evaluation job posts a metric on every pull request. Which commit ID must it record, and why should a deployment never be gated on `refs/pull/N/merge`?

**A strong reply covers.** Record `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` next to the metric: the default checkout is the test merge, a commit in nobody's clone, so the number cannot otherwise be reproduced. The merge ref can be stale and the REST guide warns it becomes outdated without warning; gate on a check that ran on the commit that landed.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.2 and 17.11

#### Q270

**Question.** A reviewer approved, the author pushed another commit, and the pull request merged. Which two settings address this, and what does each cost?

**Model answer.** An approval is attached to the diff as it was when the reviewer approved. Without either setting, the sequence approve, push one more commit, merge lands a commit nobody reviewed; GitHub's documentation calls that a hijacked pull request. The first setting, dismiss stale approvals: GitHub records the state of the diff at approval, and if the diff changes the approving review is dismissed as stale and someone must approve again. Its cost is a re-review after every update, including a click on "Update branch", a rebase, or a related pull request merging into the target branch, so the diff can change without anyone touching your branch. The second, require approval of the most recent reviewable push: an approval must come from someone other than the last person to push. Stale reviews are then not dismissed, so earlier approvals can stand on a diff that has since changed; GitHub says dismissing stale reviews is safer. From the terminal, `gh pr merge --match-head-commit` merges only if the head is the commit you name.

**Key terms.** approval attached to a diff; dismiss stale approvals; most recent reviewable push; hijacked pull request; re-review cost; --match-head-commit

**Common weak answer.** "Require one approval; that covers it." Weak because an approval count does not bind the approval to the final diff. The answer must name both settings and say that the second leaves old approvals standing while the first costs a re-review after every update.

**Follow-up.** A maintainer creates the merge commit for the approved pull request in a local clone and pushes it straight to the protected branch. With either setting enabled, what happens and why?

**A strong reply covers.** GitHub notes that the push fails unless the contents of the merge exactly match the merge GitHub generated for the pull request: the server compares the pushed merge with its own test merge. A hand-made merge whose content differs from what GitHub computed for the pull request is therefore refused.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.5 and 17.16

#### Q271

**Question.** What does a merge queue test that a `pull_request` workflow does not? Why can a required check stay unreported forever on a queue?

**Model answer.** A `pull_request` workflow tests the test merge of one pull request with the base as it was when that merge was made. A merge queue groups the pull request into a `merge_group` with the latest version of the base branch and the changes of the pull requests ahead of it, on a temporary branch whose name begins with `gh-readonly-queue/{base_branch}`, and runs the required checks on that commit, the exact commit that becomes the new tip of the base. That commit is none of the pull request heads, and no `pull_request` run ever saw it. If a group fails its checks or conflicts, the pull request is removed from the queue and the entries behind it are rebuilt as new commits that must be tested again. Checks on queue branches are triggered by their own event: the GitHub Actions workflow must list `merge_group` next to `pull_request`. Without it the required status check is never reported for the queue commit and the merge fails. Section 17.11 imitates the queue in plain Git; the GitHub behavior is described from the documentation.

**Key terms.** merge_group event; gh-readonly-queue prefix; exact commit that lands; changes ahead in the queue; required check not reported; rebuilt entries

**Common weak answer.** "The queue runs the same CI again in order." Weak because it misses that the tested commit is a new commit containing the latest base and the entries ahead, and that a workflow without the `merge_group` trigger never reports the required check.

**Follow-up.** When would you advise against a merge queue, and who can use one at all?

**A strong reply covers.** A queue adds a CI run per group and latency per merge; for a few merges a day, "strict" required checks cost less. Queues are available in public repositories owned by an organization, or private repositories of organizations on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, so not under a personal account. The queue also fixes the merge method.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.11

#### Q272

**Question.** A pull request is shown as merged, yet nobody merged it and it had no approval. How is that possible?

**Model answer.** It is an indirect merge. GitHub marks a pull request as merged whenever its head commits become reachable from its base branch, by whatever route: the same commits merged through another pull request, or pushed directly to the default branch. The documentation states that this happens even if the branch protection rules on that pull request were not satisfied. A typical route: the upper of two dependent branches contains the lower one, a maintainer merges the upper pull request with a merge commit, and the lower head becomes an ancestor of `main`. The proof, as in section 17.13, is `git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/<lower-branch> main` exiting with status 0 and `git log --oneline main..origin/<lower-branch>` printing nothing. The mechanism: reviews and checks are properties of a pull request, reachability is a property of commits, and a rule that requires an approval is satisfied by the pull request that was actually merged. For an audit, answer from the pull request that carried the commits onto the base, and do not merge branches that contain unreviewed pull requests.

**Key terms.** indirect merge; reachable from the base; reviews belong to the pull request; reachability belongs to commits; merge-base --is-ancestor; rules not satisfied

**Common weak answer.** "An administrator must have force-merged it." Weak because no bypass is needed: reachability alone marks the pull request merged, and the candidate has not said which pull request actually carried the commits.

**Follow-up.** Besides this route, which other ways does a change reach a protected branch without the reviews the rules describe, and why does that matter before you speak to an auditor?

**A strong reply covers.** Section 17.20 names three: indirect merges, `gh pr merge --admin`, which merges a pull request that does not meet requirements, and bypass lists. Know all three before telling an auditor that every change was reviewed, and answer "who approved this commit" from the pull request that carried it onto the base.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.13 and 17.19

#### Q273

**Question.** A pull request was merged and its head branch was not deleted. The author adds one commit to the same branch and opens a second pull request. Describe what the second pull request shows under each of the three merge methods, and why.

**Model answer.** It depends on whether the first merge recorded ancestry. After "Create a merge commit" the old commits are ancestors of `main`, so `base..head` lists only the new commit and reuse is safe. After "Squash and merge" `main` gained one commit with a single parent and no link to the branch, so the merge base is still the original fork point. The second pull request lists the old commits again together with the new one, its three-dot diff shows the old changes again, and in the chapter's run the test merge fails with an add/add conflict in a file that only the author ever edited. After "Rebase and merge" the situation is the same, because `main` holds new copies under new commit IDs, with one difference: a plain `git rebase` skips the old commits. The root cause is content merged without ancestry: the merge base comes from parent links only. I prove it with `git merge-base origin/main <branch>` and `git log --oneline origin/main..<branch>`. Prevention is automatic deletion of head branches and a new branch from `main` for every pull request.

**Key terms.** content without ancestry; merge base unchanged; old commits listed again; add/add conflict; parent links only; delete head branches on merge

**Common weak answer.** "The second pull request shows only the new commit, because the old work is already in main." Weak because that holds only after a merge commit; after squash or rebase the content is in `main` and the commits are not, so the range and the three-way merge still see them.

**Follow-up.** In the squash case, why is a plain `git rebase origin/main` not the repair, and what is?

**A strong reply covers.** A plain rebase replays all four commits: in the chapter's run Git drops the first as already upstream and the second conflicts, because the squash already contains the third commit's fix of the same line. `git rebase --onto origin/main <last squashed commit>` moves only the new commit; then `git push --force-with-lease`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.12 and 17.9

#### Q274

**Question.** A pull request conflicts with `main`. One engineer proposes merging `main` into the branch, another proposes rebasing the branch onto `main`. Compare the two repairs and say what should decide between them.

**Model answer.** Both are legitimate. A conflicting pull request is the ordinary three-way conflict, detected on the server where nobody can resolve it, so the resolution has to arrive as new commits on the head branch. Merging the base into the head keeps the existing commit IDs, pushes as a fast-forward so nobody's clone of the branch is disturbed, and records the resolution in a merge commit that `git show --remerge-diff` can display; the commit list grows by one merge commit. Rebasing replaces the commits, needs `git push --force-with-lease`, folds the resolution into the rewritten commits so that no commit records that a conflict happened, and keeps the commit list clean. The chapter shows that both give reviewers the identical three-dot diff, and both change the diff, so both trigger stale-approval dismissal. What decides is the merge method. Under squash the shape of the branch disappears at merge time and the final history on `main` is identical, so the cheaper merge is enough. Under the merge-commit and rebase methods the shape lands on `main`, which is a reason to rebase.

**Key terms.** resolution arrives on the head branch; fast-forward push versus forced push; commit IDs kept or replaced; identical three-dot diff; stale-approval dismissal; merge method decides

**Common weak answer.** "Always rebase, merge commits make the history dirty." Weak because under a squash merge the final history on `main` is identical either way, and the rebase costs a forced push and rewritten commit IDs for no gain.

**Follow-up.** Somebody clicks "Update branch" or resolves the conflict in the web editor instead. What changed, where, and what must the author do before the next local commit?

**A strong reply covers.** GitHub merged the base branch into the head branch on its side; `gh pr update-branch` does the same by default and rebases with `--rebase`. The head branch on GitHub moved and the local branch did not, so pull before continuing. The web editor handles only simple competing line changes.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.7


### Pull requests: principal level

#### Q275

**Question.** Compare the three merge methods for a team that requires signed commits on `main` and must show an auditor that the reviewed commit is the deployed commit.

**Model answer.** Only "Create a merge commit" satisfies both requirements literally. It adds the feature commits to the base under their original commit IDs with their own signatures, plus one merge commit that GitHub signs, so `git merge-base --is-ancestor` on the reviewed head succeeds against `main`; under the signed-commit rule it works if every commit on the head branch is signed and verified. "Squash and merge" writes one new commit, committed and signed by GitHub, so none of the reviewed commit IDs is on `main`; and unsigned commits on the head branch still block the merge, because GitHub checks the commits introduced by the test merge. "Rebase and merge" always creates new commit IDs and adds them without signature verification, because GitHub has no access to the committer's private signing keys, so it cannot satisfy the rule; the documented workaround is to rebase and merge locally, then push. I would allow only the merge-commit method on that branch and state its costs: `git bisect start --first-parent`, and reverts that need `-m 1` with the re-merge trap.

**Key terms.** original commit IDs preserved; merge commit signed by GitHub; rebase and merge unsigned; head commits must be signed; ancestry test; reviewed equals deployed

**Common weak answer.** "Squash, because GitHub signs it and the history is clean." Weak because the reviewed commit IDs are then absent from `main`, so the audit requirement fails; it also omits that unsigned head commits still block a squash and that rebase and merge lands commits without signature verification.

**Follow-up.** The team still insists on squash for a clean history. What evidence can you give the auditor, and what does the chapter leave unverified about a squash commit?

**A strong reply covers.** The squash commit message links the pull request, as the default `(#1)` title does, and the reviewed commits remain under `refs/pull/N/head`, on no branch. Who is recorded as author of a squash commit, and whether other contributors become co-author trailers, is marked unverified in section 17.8.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.8 and 17.9; [Chapter 18](../textbook/ch18-branch-protection.md), section 18.10

#### Q276

**Question.** You are asked to pick one merge method for a 40-person ML platform team. What do you ask before answering?

**Model answer.** No method is best, and the tree of `main` is identical under all three, so I ask what the history must prove later. Must the reviewed commit IDs be the deployed ones, for an audit? Only the merge commit keeps them. Does a rule require signed commits on the target? Rebase and merge lands commits without signature verification. Does the team curate every commit so that each passes on its own? If not, the merge-commit and rebase methods put intermediate commits on `main` that CI never tested, and `git bisect` can stop on one; `--first-parent` helps only with merge commits. How will you revert: one ordinary revert for a squash, `-m 1` with the re-merge trap for a merge commit, one revert per commit for a rebased series. Are pull requests small and short-lived, with head branches deleted on merge, or are long-lived branches merged repeatedly? Reusing a branch is safe only after a merge commit. Is linear history required, which excludes merge commits? Is a merge queue in use, which fixes the method? The choice follows from those answers.

**Key terms.** what history must prove; reviewed commit IDs; signed commits; untested intermediate commits; revert cost; branch reuse; linear history

**Common weak answer.** "Squash, everyone uses it" or "merge commits, because they keep everything." Weak because it answers without asking about audit, signatures, bisect granularity, revert and branch lifetime, the factors that decide which cost the team can carry.

**Follow-up.** The answers are: small short-lived pull requests, no commit hygiene inside branches, no audit requirement on commit IDs. Which method do you pick, and which two practices must accompany it?

**A strong reply covers.** Squash: the unit of history becomes the pull request, bisect lands on a pull request and a revert is one command. The squash commit message must link the pull request, as the default `(#1)` title does, and head branches must be deleted on merge (`gh repo edit --delete-branch-on-merge`), with new work started from `main`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.9 and 17.8

#### Q277

**Question.** The bottom pull request of a two-layer stack is squash-merged and its branch is deleted. What state is the upper pull request in, what does GitHub do by itself, and would you let a release process depend on stacked pull requests?

**Model answer.** The upper layer is in the squash-then-reuse situation, because it was built on commits that never reached `main`. Without the stack feature GitHub only retargets: when a merged head branch is deleted, pull requests based on it switch to the merged pull request's base. Against `main` the upper pull request then lists both layers, and in the chapter's run its test merge fails with an add/add conflict. The transplant is yours: `git rebase --onto origin/main <old lower branch> <upper branch>` replays only the upper layer, followed by `git push --force-with-lease`. GitHub's stacked pull requests feature, in public preview since 30 July 2026, is documented to rebase the remaining branches automatically so the next pull request targets the default base; `gh stack` is not part of `gh` 2.88.1 and none of its commands were run for the course. I would not make a release process depend on a preview. A stack also multiplies force pushes and re-approvals, and a problem in the bottom layer delays every layer above. Layers that are not dependent should be independent pull requests.

**Key terms.** built on commits that never reached main; retarget only; git rebase --onto; add/add conflict; public preview; force pushes and re-approvals

**Common weak answer.** "GitHub retargets the upper pull request to main, so it is fine." Weak because retargeting changes the base name and not the ancestry: the squashed commits are listed again and conflict until the upper layer is transplanted.

**Follow-up.** While both layers are still open, a review fix is committed to the lower branch. What breaks, how do you prove it, and how do you repair it?

**A strong reply covers.** The stack is no longer linear: `git merge-base --is-ancestor <lower> <upper>` exits with status 1, because the upper branch still sits on the old tip. Rebase the upper layer onto the new tip with `git rebase <lower> <upper>` and push it with `--force-with-lease`; `git rebase --update-refs` moves a whole chain in one run.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.14, 17.12 and 17.20

#### Q278

**Question.** A team wants auto-merge enabled on the branch that deploys to production. What is auto-merge mechanically, what does it wait for, and what must be decided before you allow it?

**Model answer.** Auto-merge is a GitHub feature, not Git: a stored instruction on a pull request to merge with a given method as soon as every requirement is met. It must first be enabled for the repository, and the option is shown only on pull requests that cannot be merged immediately, that is, when a rule has an unmet requirement. The central point is that it waits for required things only. In a repository with no required checks and no required reviews there is nothing to wait for, and a red check that no rule names blocks nothing. Its one documented safety property: it is disabled if someone without write permission pushes new changes to the head branch or switches the base branch. A commit pushed by someone with write permission after the approval is not stopped by auto-merge; whether it merges unreviewed is decided by the stale-approval settings. So I decide those settings and the required checks before allowing it on a branch that deploys. Availability: public repositories on GitHub Free, public and private on paid plans.

**Key terms.** stored instruction; required things only; unmet requirement; disabled on push without write permission; stale-approval settings; repository setting

**Common weak answer.** "Auto-merge merges when CI is green and the pull request is approved." Weak because it waits only for what rules require; with no required checks or reviews it waits for nothing, and it does not stop a late commit from someone with write permission.

**Follow-up.** How does `gh pr merge` behave on a branch that has a merge queue, and what happened to the `@dependabot merge` comment command?

**A strong reply covers.** On such a branch `gh pr merge` adds the pull request to the queue when the checks have passed and otherwise enables auto-merge; the queue fixes the merge method and `--admin` bypasses the queue. `@dependabot merge` was removed on 27 January 2026; the current mechanism is auto-merge.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.10 and 17.5


## Area 11: GitHub Actions

Q279 to Q305. Workflows, events, runners, caching, artifacts, delivery and the debugging of failed runs.


### GitHub Actions: foundational level

#### Q279

**Question.** Explain the difference between `run: echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"` and passing the title through `env`. When is each evaluated, and by what?

**Model answer.** In the first form the expression is part of the script text. GitHub Actions evaluates `${{ ... }}` on the runner, per step, before the shell starts, and replaces it with its value, so the pull request title becomes text of the script that the shell then parses. The shell never sees the expression, only the result, and an untrusted title can therefore become shell commands. In the second form the expression sits in the step's `env` mapping, for example under the name `TITLE`, and the script says `echo "$TITLE"`. GitHub Actions still evaluates the expression before the step, but the value is handed to the process as an environment variable, and the shell expands that variable at run time as data. Chapter 20A, section 20A.5 calls the difference between those two a security boundary. The course workflows use the `env` form for every value, including values an attacker does not control, so that the habit is uniform. The attack itself is the subject of Chapter 21A.

**Key terms.** expression substituted before the shell starts; script text versus data; env mapping; shell expansion at run time; security boundary; untrusted input

**Common weak answer.** "They are equivalent; the `env` form is only tidier." Weak because it misses that the expression is substituted into the script text before the shell starts, so the first form lets the title be parsed as shell code.

**Follow-up.** You want to gate a step on whether a secret is set and write `if: secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN != ''`. Why does that not work, and what does timing have to do with it?

**A strong reply covers.** The `secrets` context is not available in `if`, at job or step level. Map the secret into `env` and test `env.NAME != ''` in a step-level `if`. A job-level `if` cannot read `env` either, because it is decided before a runner exists.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20A](../textbook/ch20a-actions-fundamentals.md), section 20A.5

#### Q280

**Question.** How do you pass a value from a step to a later step, and from a job to a later job? What cannot be passed this way, and what do you use for it?

**Model answer.** Within a job, a step that has an `id` appends `name=value` to the file whose path is in `GITHUB_OUTPUT`, and a later step reads `steps.<id>.outputs.name`. Appending `NAME=value` to the `GITHUB_ENV` file gives later steps an environment variable instead. This is needed because every `run` step is a new shell process, so an `export` or a `cd` does not survive the step. Across jobs, the step output must be re-exported as a job output under `jobs.<id>.outputs`, and the later job, which lists the first in `needs`, reads `needs.<id>.outputs.name`. Job outputs are strings, limited to 1 MB per job and 50 MB per run, and an output that looks like a secret is dropped with a message. Files cannot travel this way, because each job starts on a fresh machine. Build outputs go as an artifact, uploaded and downloaded by name; dependencies that can be recreated go in a cache, which may be absent. Always append with `>>` and quote `"$GITHUB_OUTPUT"`.

**Key terms.** GITHUB_OUTPUT; step id; job outputs; needs context; new process per step; fresh machine per job; artifact for files

**Common weak answer.** "Export an environment variable in the first step." Weak because every `run` step is a new process and every job a new machine, so the export reaches nothing; it also omits that files need an artifact.

**Follow-up.** A later step reads a step output and gets an empty string, with no error anywhere. What are the candidate causes?

**A strong reply covers.** A missing `id` on the writing step; a typo in the reference, since a property that does not exist evaluates to an empty string without an error; `>` instead of `>>`, which discards earlier lines; or a read from another job without a declared job output. Print outputs in the step that writes them.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20A](../textbook/ch20a-actions-fundamentals.md), section 20A.2, 20A.7 and 20A.12

#### Q281

**Question.** What is the difference between a cache and an artifact in purpose, scope, lifetime and trust? Which one may a release job consume?

**Model answer.** A cache is an optimization for files that are reused between runs and can be recreated, typically dependencies. An artifact is a set of files a job produced that must be passed to another job or kept after the run. Scope: a run can restore caches created on its own branch or the default branch, a pull request run also from its base branch, never from a sibling branch; an artifact is stored with its run and is downloadable by later jobs of that run. Lifetime: cache entries not accessed for 7 days are removed and a repository gets 10 GB without charge; artifacts are kept 90 days by default. Trust: cache contents are not signed, and anyone who can open a pull request can read caches of the base branch, while `actions/download-artifact` version 8 fails on a digest mismatch. A release job consumes the artifact, so that the files that were tested are the files that are deployed. A cache may be absent or stale and must never be the source of something you ship.

**Key terms.** recreatable versus produced; branch scope; 7 days eviction; 90 days retention; unsigned cache; digest mismatch; tested files are deployed files

**Common weak answer.** "Both store files between jobs; the cache is faster." Weak because it ignores that a cache may be absent, is scoped by branch, is unsigned and readable from pull requests, so it cannot be the source of a release.

**Follow-up.** A dependency was upgraded in the lock file, but CI keeps installing the old version. Explain the cache mechanism and the fix.

**A strong reply covers.** Caches are immutable per key and restore keys match by prefix, so a key that is not derived from the lock file, or a broad restore key, restores a stale entry. Put `hashFiles` of the lock file in the key and install with `uv sync --locked`; a manual key prefix invalidates everything at once.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20A](../textbook/ch20a-actions-fundamentals.md), section 20A.11 and 20A.12


### GitHub Actions: working engineer level

#### Q282

**Question.** A pull request's CI fails and the author says "it passes on my machine, same commit". What do you check first, and why can both be right?

**Model answer.** I check which commit the job checked out before reading any test output: the first lines of the checkout step's log, or the event, ref and commit that `gh run view` prints, compared with `git rev-parse HEAD` on the laptop. On a `pull_request` event GitHub Actions sets `GITHUB_REF` to `refs/pull/N/merge` and `GITHUB_SHA` to GitHub's test merge commit, and `actions/checkout` checks out that commit with a detached HEAD. That commit merges the pull request head into the current base, so it contains changes from `main` that the author's branch does not have, and it does not exist in the author's clone. Both results are correct because they tested different commits, which Chapter 20A, section 20A.8 demonstrates. To reproduce, run `git fetch origin`, switch to a detached copy of the branch and run `git merge origin/main`. The fix is to update the branch and repair the interaction. The prevention is a step that prints the checked-out commit in every workflow, and reading it first.

**Key terms.** refs/pull/N/merge; test merge commit; detached HEAD; GITHUB_SHA and GITHUB_REF; different commits tested; merge origin/main to reproduce

**Common weak answer.** "CI is flaky, re-run it." Weak because a re-run reuses the original commit and ref, so it fails the same way, and the answer never asks which commit was tested.

**Follow-up.** The commit ID in the CI log does not exist in your clone. How do you prove that your local reproduction is the same code that CI tested?

**A strong reply covers.** The merge commit ID differs, so compare trees: after merging `origin/main` into a detached copy of the branch, `git rev-parse HEAD^{tree}` equals the tree ID of the runner's HEAD in the section 20A.8 transcript. Equal tree IDs mean identical content, and the failure then reproduces locally.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20A](../textbook/ch20a-actions-fundamentals.md), section 20A.8 and 20A.16

#### Q283

**Question.** What does `actions/checkout` put on the runner by default? Name three tools or commands that give wrong results there, and say whether each fails or lies.

**Model answer.** By default `actions/checkout`, at the version the course pins, fetches one commit for the ref of the event, with `fetch-depth: 1` and `fetch-tags: false`. The runner has a complete snapshot of the files but no tags and no history, LFS pointers are not replaced by content and submodule directories are empty. Git records the commit in `.git/shallow` and treats it as parentless. First, `git describe --tags` fails with "No names found", which is the honest outcome. Second, `git describe --tags --always` lies: it exits with status zero and prints the abbreviated commit ID, which a build then stamps as the version. Third, `git log -- path` lies: it names the only commit as the last change to every file, because a parentless commit appears to add everything. Changed-file detection, blame-based analysis and changelog generators inherit the same confident wrong answers. The fix is `fetch-depth: 0` in the job that asks history a question, as Chapter 20A, section 20A.8 shows.

**Key terms.** fetch-depth 1; fetch-tags false; .git/shallow; grafted commit; git describe --always; wrong answers not errors; fetch-depth 0 per job

**Common weak answer.** "It clones the repository." Weak because it assumes a full clone with history and tags; the default is one commit without tags, and the dangerous cases are the commands that return a wrong answer instead of an error.

**Follow-up.** Someone sets `fetch-tags: true` and keeps the depth at one. Does `git describe` work now, and why?

**A strong reply covers.** No. The tag refs arrive, but `git describe` walks parent links from HEAD to find a tagged ancestor and the walk ends at the graft, so the error changes to "No tags can describe". Tags need the history between them and HEAD: `fetch-depth: 0`, or `git fetch --unshallow --tags` as a repair.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20A](../textbook/ch20a-actions-fundamentals.md), section 20A.8

#### Q284

**Question.** A job is green although `pytest | tee report.txt` had failing tests. Give the exact shell command line the runner used, and two ways to fix it.

**Model answer.** With no `shell` key on a Linux or macOS runner, GitHub Actions writes the `run` text to a temporary script file and executes `bash -e {0}`, where the placeholder is that file. The `-e` flag stops the script at the first failing command, but it does not look inside a pipeline: the status of a pipeline is the status of its last command unless `pipefail` is set. Here `tee` succeeded, so the step, the job and the run are green although pytest failed. Chapter 20A, section 20A.7 reproduces this locally with a failing command piped into `tee`. Fix one is `shell: bash` on the step, which changes the template to `bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail {0}`. Fix two is `defaults.run.shell: bash` once for the workflow, as workflow 3 does, so every `run` step gets `pipefail`. The lesson for a reviewer: a green job proves only that the last command of every pipeline succeeded, unless the shell was declared.

**Key terms.** bash -e {0}; pipefail; status of the last command; shell: bash; defaults.run.shell; bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail

**Common weak answer.** "The runner uses bash, and bash stops on errors." Weak because `-e` does not look inside a pipeline; without the exact template the candidate cannot say why `tee` decided the status.

**Follow-up.** The same step is moved into a job that runs in a `container`. What is the default shell there, and what does that do to your reasoning?

**A strong reply covers.** Inside a job container on Linux the default is `sh`, not `bash`, so the step no longer runs under the template you reasoned about. The remedy the chapters give for every shell difference is the same: state the shell, per step or through `defaults.run.shell`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20A](../textbook/ch20a-actions-fundamentals.md), section 20A.7 and 20A.16

#### Q285

**Question.** A matrix has `os` with two values, `python` with three, one `exclude` and one `include`. How do you count the jobs, and how do you make one of them allowed to fail?

**Model answer.** Start with the Cartesian product of the listed values: two operating systems times three Python versions is six combinations. `exclude` removes combinations, and a partial match is enough, so an exclusion that names one operating system and one version leaves five. `include` is processed after `exclude`: an entry is added to every existing combination it can extend without overwriting an original matrix value, and if it would overwrite one, it becomes a new combination of its own. In workflow 10 the entry for Ubuntu with Python 3.14 would overwrite `python`, so it is a sixth job. To let one job fail, give the matrix a variable such as `experimental` with the value false, set it to true in the `include` entry, and write `continue-on-error: ${{ matrix.experimental }}` on the job. Quote every version, because an unquoted `3.10` is the number 3.1. A run may generate at most 256 matrix jobs, and `fail-fast` defaults to true, which cancels the other matrix jobs when one fails.

**Key terms.** Cartesian product; exclude partial match; include after exclude; overwrite makes a new combination; continue-on-error from matrix; quoted versions; fail-fast

**Common weak answer.** "Multiply the lists and add one for the include." Weak because `include` adds a job only when it would overwrite an original matrix value; otherwise it extends existing combinations, and the answer says nothing about `continue-on-error`.

**Follow-up.** Which check do you make required for that matrix, and what is uncertain about the effect of the allowed-to-fail job on it?

**A strong reply covers.** Require one final job with a fixed name that runs with `if: ${{ always() }}`, needs the matrix job and fails unless `needs.test.result` is `success`. The chapter marks as unverified how that result aggregates a failure under `continue-on-error`; it expects `success` and has a lab observe it. Matrix check names are unverified too.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20A](../textbook/ch20a-actions-fundamentals.md), section 20A.10 and 20A.13

#### Q286

**Question.** Three merges land on `main` within five minutes and the deploy workflow uses `concurrency: production`. Which runs deploy, and why?

**Model answer.** With the default behavior of a concurrency group, the first and the third run deploy, and the second is cancelled without deploying. A concurrency group is a name under which GitHub Actions lets at most one run execute at a time. A run that is queued while another run of the group is in progress becomes pending, and any run already pending in that group is cancelled. So the first run is in progress, the second waits, and when the third is queued it replaces the second. Because `cancel-in-progress` is not set to true, the first run is not interrupted, which is what a deployment needs. This assumes the first deployment is still running when the others arrive, and the documentation states that ordering is not guaranteed. The result is usually acceptable, because the third run's commit contains the second merge. It is wrong when every run must happen, for example a database migration per commit: then use `queue: max`, available since 7 May 2026, which keeps up to 100 pending runs, or make the deployment cumulative.

**Key terms.** concurrency group; one in progress and one pending; pending run is cancelled; cancel-in-progress; queue: max; cumulative deployment

**Common weak answer.** "They run one after another, in order." Weak because by default only one run may wait per group; the pending run is cancelled when a newer one is queued, and ordering is not guaranteed.

**Follow-up.** Someone tries to recover the lost middle deployment by adding `queue: max` together with `cancel-in-progress: true`. What happens, and what is wrong with each setting on a deployment?

**A strong reply covers.** Combining `queue: max` with `cancel-in-progress: true` is a validation error. On its own, `cancel-in-progress: true` can stop a deployment half-way and leave a state nobody designed, and `queue: max` is recommended only where every run must execute.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20B](../textbook/ch20b-actions-delivery-debugging.md), section 20B.5 and 20B.16

#### Q287

**Question.** `git describe` works on every laptop and fails in the job. Explain the state of the runner's repository and give the minimal fix.

**Model answer.** The runner's repository is a shallow clone without tags. `actions/checkout` defaults to `fetch-depth: 1` and `fetch-tags: false`, so the job has one commit, listed in `.git/shallow` and shown as grafted in the log decoration, and nothing under `refs/tags`. `git describe` needs a tag that is reachable from HEAD through parent links; with no tags it exits with status 128 and the message "No names found". You confirm the state with `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`, `git tag --list` and `git rev-list --count HEAD`. The default exists because one commit is all most jobs need and it is fast on a large repository. The minimal fix is `fetch-depth: 0` on the checkout step of the one job that derives the version. The prevention is to derive versions in one job and never to silence the error with `--always` or a fallback version string, because that ships a wrong version, as Chapter 20B, section 20B.12 states.

**Key terms.** shallow clone; .git/shallow; no tags; reachable through parent links; fetch-depth: 0; never --always in a release build

**Common weak answer.** "The runner has a different Git version", or "add `--always`". Weak because the cause is a one-commit clone without tags, and `--always` replaces an honest failure with a wrong version.

**Follow-up.** Why not add `fetch-depth: 0` to every checkout so that nobody meets this again?

**A strong reply covers.** On a repository with a long history it turns a one-second fetch into a full clone for every job. Decide per job whether it asks history a question, and give full history only to that job.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20B](../textbook/ch20b-actions-delivery-debugging.md), section 20B.12; [Chapter 20A](../textbook/ch20a-actions-fundamentals.md), section 20A.8

#### Q288

**Question.** What exactly does `gh run rerun` re-run, and why is that dangerous for a deploy workflow?

**Model answer.** A re-run is not a new run. It is a new attempt of the same workflow run, which uses the same `GITHUB_SHA` and `GITHUB_REF` as the original event and the privileges of the actor who triggered the original; it is possible for 30 days and at most 50 times. With `--failed` it re-runs the failed jobs, and with `--job` one job. Nothing changes in Git, locally or on the remote. On GitHub there are new checks on the original commit and, for a deploy workflow, a new deployment of that commit. That is the danger: re-running last week's deploy run deploys last week's commit over today's, a rollback nobody announced. Before re-running, read the run's commit with `gh run view RUN_ID --json headSha` and ask Git whether it is behind what is deployed: `git merge-base --is-ancestor` against `main` exiting with status zero means the deployment would go backwards. Use a re-run to retry a flaky step of the latest run, and a fresh run for everything else.

**Key terms.** new attempt of the same run; original commit and ref; original actor's privileges; 30 days and 50 re-runs; deploys an old commit; git merge-base --is-ancestor

**Common weak answer.** "It runs the workflow again on the latest code." Weak because a re-run is a new attempt at the original commit and ref, which on a deploy workflow moves production backwards.

**Follow-up.** How do you make the pipeline itself refuse that backwards deployment, instead of relying on people to check?

**A strong reply covers.** Put a `git merge-base --is-ancestor` guard in the deploy script, which Chapter 20B, section 20B.16 gives as the prevention: refuse when the commit to deploy is an ancestor of what is already deployed. That test needs history, so the default one-commit checkout is not enough for the deploy job.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20B](../textbook/ch20b-actions-delivery-debugging.md), section 20B.14, 20B.16 and 20B.17

#### Q289

**Question.** Your CI bill rose after a repository became private and one job started timing out. What changed?

**Model answer.** Two documented things changed with the visibility, and neither is in the code. First, billing: standard GitHub-hosted runners are free in public repositories, while a private repository draws on included minutes, 2,000 per month on Free and 3,000 on Pro and Team, with list prices per minute and each job rounded up to a whole minute. Second, hardware: standard Linux and Windows runners have 4 CPUs and 16 GB of memory in public repositories and 2 CPUs and 8 GB in private ones. A suite that fitted before now runs slower, consumes more minutes, and can run out of memory or reach its `timeout-minutes`. So I ask for the visibility of the repository first, and for the runner label second. The remedies are to split the job or to pay for a larger runner, which is always billed. The cost levers follow from the rules: cancel superseded runs with a concurrency group, prefer one job with several steps because each job rounds up, keep macOS for what needs macOS, and shorten artifact retention.

**Key terms.** public versus private; included minutes; 4 CPUs and 16 GB versus 2 CPUs and 8 GB; each job rounded up to a minute; larger runners always billed; concurrency to cancel superseded runs

**Common weak answer.** "GitHub raised its prices." Weak because list prices were cut on 1 January 2026; what changed is that a private repository is billed and gets smaller standard runners.

**Follow-up.** Finance asks for the Windows and macOS multipliers so that it can forecast how fast the included minutes are consumed. What do you answer?

**A strong reply covers.** That the chapter marks it unverified: no 2026 page the research could fetch states how Windows and macOS minutes consume included minutes, and the multipliers of 2 and 10 come from older material. Do not quote a multiplier; use the list prices in force since 1 January 2026 and read actual usage in the billing settings.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20B](../textbook/ch20b-actions-delivery-debugging.md), section 20B.8 and 20B.10

#### Q290

**Question.** In which order do you investigate a failed run, and why is the log not first?

**Model answer.** I go from "did the right thing start at all" to "what did it say", because an answer early in the list makes everything after it irrelevant. Chapter 20B, section 20B.11 gives twelve questions in order: which workflow file, from which commit, defined the run; which event triggered it and which ref and commit the job checked out; what the token could do; which runner image and size; whether an environment was referenced and its rules passed; whether the same dependency versions were installed; whether the secrets were present; which commit of each action ran; only then the log of the failed step, with `gh run view --log-failed`; then artifacts, cache and concurrency. The log is ninth because the message of a failed step describes a symptom: a withheld secret is an empty string and appears as an authentication error, and a test failure may belong to a commit you did not write. The first two steps remove the most confusion: compare the commit ID from `gh run view` with `git rev-parse HEAD` locally.

**Key terms.** workflow then event then permissions; which commit was checked out; runner and environment; secrets as empty strings; log is ninth; gh run view --log-failed; compare with git rev-parse HEAD

**Common weak answer.** "Open the red step and read the error." Weak because the message describes a symptom; without knowing the commit, the event, the token and the secrets, the engineer debugs the wrong thing.

**Follow-up.** Give one concrete case in which reading the log first costs an hour that the second step of your order would have saved.

**A strong reply covers.** The case in Chapter 20A, section 20A.8: a pull request adds a metric and CI fails in an unrelated data-loader test. The author debugs the loader for an hour, while the checkout log showed `refs/pull/N/merge`: a loader change had been merged into the base twenty minutes earlier, and the job tested the merge.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20B](../textbook/ch20b-actions-delivery-debugging.md), section 20B.11

#### Q291

**Question.** What can a local emulator tell you about a deployment workflow, and what can it not?

**Model answer.** A local emulator such as `act` runs workflows in Docker containers on your machine, so a green local run is evidence about the shell logic of your steps and scripts, and about nothing else. Its own documentation lists what it does not implement: `concurrency`, job `permissions`, `environment`, OIDC, `timeout-minutes`, `continue-on-error`, step summaries and a complete `github` context. Those are the substance of a deployment workflow: the gate in front of the job, what the token may do, the group that keeps two deployments from overlapping, and the runner image. A linter is limited in the same direction. `actionlint` checks workflow syntax, expression types and embedded shell, which proves that a file is well formed; it cannot know that the history is shallow or that a secret is withheld, and the chapter notes that all six broken lab workflows pass the course's own parse check. So I treat a green local run as evidence about the scripts, never about the deployment, and I keep the procedure in repository scripts so that part can be tested locally.

**Key terms.** act runs steps in Docker; not implemented: environment, permissions, concurrency, OIDC; shell logic only; actionlint proves well-formedness; evidence about scripts not deployment

**Common weak answer.** "If it passes in `act`, it will pass on GitHub." Weak because the emulator does not implement environments, job permissions, concurrency or OIDC, which are the substance of a deployment workflow.

**Follow-up.** Given those limits, how do you test an environment gate before the first real production deployment?

**A strong reply covers.** On GitHub itself: create the environment before the workflow that uses it, keep its configuration in a reviewed script, read the rules back with `gh api`, and test the gate with a harmless run. Chapter 20B, section 20B.4 gives exactly that as the prevention.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20B](../textbook/ch20b-actions-delivery-debugging.md), section 20B.15


### GitHub Actions: senior level

#### Q292

**Question.** For each of `push`, `pull_request`, `schedule` and `workflow_dispatch`: which commit does the run refer to, and from which commit is the workflow file read?

**Model answer.** These are GitHub Actions facts, tabulated from the events reference in Chapter 20A, section 20A.4. For `push`, the run refers to the tip commit pushed to the ref, and the workflow file is read from that commit, which is why a branch can change its own CI. For `pull_request`, `GITHUB_SHA` is the test merge commit and `GITHUB_REF` is `refs/pull/N/merge`; the file is again read from the commit the event refers to. For `schedule`, the run refers to the last commit on the default branch and uses the file on the default branch, whatever happened elsewhere. For `workflow_dispatch`, the run refers to the last commit on the branch or tag the person chose, the workflow file is read from that chosen ref (`gh workflow run --ref` names the ref "which contains the version of the workflow file you'd like to run"), and the run can be started only if the workflow file also exists on the default branch (Chapter 20B, section 20B.11). In an investigation I confirm with the event, branch and commit fields of `gh run view` before reasoning further.

**Key terms.** tip commit pushed; refs/pull/N/merge; default branch for schedule; chosen ref for workflow_dispatch; file must exist on the default branch; three families of events

**Common weak answer.** "The workflow always runs on the commit you pushed, using the file from that branch." Weak because that is true only for `push`; a pull request run is about the test merge commit and a scheduled run is about the default branch.

**Follow-up.** A `pull_request` workflow is edited on a feature branch to remove a test. Does the edited file run for that pull request, and what does that imply for governance?

**A strong reply covers.** Yes. For `push` and `pull_request` the definition comes from the commit the event refers to, so anyone who can push a branch can change what those workflows do on it. Protect `.github/workflows/` with CODEOWNERS and a ruleset, as Chapter 20A, section 20A.17 advises.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20A](../textbook/ch20a-actions-fundamentals.md), section 20A.2 and 20A.4; [Chapter 20B](../textbook/ch20b-actions-delivery-debugging.md), section 20B.11

#### Q293

**Question.** A required check stays "expected" forever on documentation-only pull requests. Explain the mechanism and design a fix that keeps the path filter's saving.

**Model answer.** The workflow has a `paths` filter, and for a pull request GitHub evaluates it on the three-dot diff between the base and the head. A documentation-only change matches nothing, so the workflow never starts, no run exists and no check is created. A ruleset that requires that check waits for a result that will not come, because a workflow that never starts reports nothing, whereas a job skipped by its `if` reports success. You can predict the filter with `git diff --name-only main...branch`. The design that keeps the saving, which Chapter 20B, section 20B.13 labels an inference from the documented rules: remove the filter from the workflow, start it always, decide inside which jobs run with `if`, and require one aggregate job that runs with `if: ${{ !cancelled() }}`, lists the others in `needs`, and fails when any needed result is failure or cancelled. The expensive jobs are skipped, the aggregate check always reports, and the ruleset names one check.

**Key terms.** paths filter; three-dot diff; workflow never starts reports nothing; skipped job reports success; aggregate job; !cancelled(); needs results

**Common weak answer.** "Skipped checks count as passed, so this is a GitHub bug." Weak because it confuses a job skipped by `if`, which reports success, with a workflow that never started, which reports nothing.

**Follow-up.** Why must the aggregate job carry a status function and inspect the `needs` results explicitly, instead of only listing the other jobs in `needs`?

**A strong reply covers.** A job whose needed job failed is skipped, and a skipped job counts as passing, so a plain `needs` aggregate would let a failing pull request merge. The status function makes it run; the explicit test of `needs.*.result` makes it fail. The expressions page recommends `!cancelled()` over `always()`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20A](../textbook/ch20a-actions-fundamentals.md), section 20A.4, 20A.9 and 20A.16

#### Q294

**Question.** Why would you pin `actions/checkout` in a workflow by a 40-character commit ID, and what does the Node 24 change of September 2026 mean for a file that says `@v4`?

**Model answer.** A tag such as `v4` is a movable name, like a branch, so a workflow that says `@v4` runs whatever commit that tag names on the day of the run, with the job's token. A full commit ID names one fixed version of the action's code; the course pins every action that way and keeps the version as a comment, and Chapter 21A gives the full security argument. On the runtime: since 23 September 2026 Node 24 is the only JavaScript action runtime on github.com runners. An older major that declares `node20` in its `action.yml` is not rejected; according to the runner's source it is executed on Node 24, a configuration its authors did not test. So a file that says `@v4` may keep working, but on an untested runtime, and without later behavior changes: version 6 moved the persisted credential under `$RUNNER_TEMP`, and version 7 refuses fork pull request checkouts under `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run`. The rule is the Node 24 majors, pinned by commit ID.

**Key terms.** tag is a movable name; full commit ID; Node 24 only since 23 September 2026; node20 actions run untested on Node 24; current majors; version as a comment

**Common weak answer.** "Pinning is for reproducibility, and `@v4` stopped working when Node 20 was removed." Weak because the point is that a tag can move under a job that holds a token, and older majors are not rejected: they run on Node 24, untested.

**Follow-up.** With every action pinned, what else still moves under a workflow without any commit to the repository, and how do you take control of it?

**A strong reply covers.** The runner image. A `-latest` label is a moving name and a migration rolls out over weeks: `ubuntu-latest` moves from 24.04 to 26.04 between 19 October and 19 November 2026, and images are rebuilt weekly. Use a fixed label such as `ubuntu-24.04`, install tools with setup actions at stated versions, and put retirement dates in the calendar.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20A](../textbook/ch20a-actions-fundamentals.md), section 20A.13, 20A.14 and 20A.19

#### Q295

**Question.** A teammate proposes `if: always()` on the deploy job "so it is not skipped". What happens, and what do you propose?

**Model answer.** An `if` without a status function behaves as if `success() &&` stood in front of it, and a job whose needed job failed or was skipped is itself skipped. That skip is the protection. `always()` replaces the implicit `success()` and is true even when the run was cancelled, so the deploy job would run after failed tests, after a failed build that produced no artifact, and after someone cancelled the run to stop it. Chapter 20A, section 20A.17 says `if: always()` hides failures by design, and the expressions page advises against it for anything that could fail critically. My proposal: keep the default on the deploy job and find out why it was skipped; since 29 January 2026 the log of a skipped job shows the original `if` expression and its expanded values. If a status function is needed at all, use `!cancelled()` and test the needed jobs' results explicitly, as the aggregate jobs in both chapters do, with a comment that says why.

**Key terms.** implicit success(); always() true on cancellation; skip is the protection; !cancelled(); test needs results explicitly; hides failures by design

**Common weak answer.** "It makes the deploy more reliable because it always runs." Weak because the skip after a failed dependency is the protection; `always()` deploys after failed tests and even after a cancellation.

**Follow-up.** The deploy job is skipped because an upstream job failed, yet the pull request still shows as mergeable. How can that be, and what closes it?

**A strong reply covers.** A skipped job counts as passing, so a required check on a job that was skipped because a needed job failed may not block the merge. Require one aggregate job that runs with `!cancelled()` and exits non-zero when any `needs.*.result` is failure or cancelled.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20A](../textbook/ch20a-actions-fundamentals.md), section 20A.9 and 20A.17; [Chapter 20B](../textbook/ch20b-actions-delivery-debugging.md), section 20B.14

#### Q296

**Question.** You inherit a repository with twelve workflow files. In what order do you read one of them to predict when it runs, where, with what code, and with what permissions?

**Model answer.** I read it as those four questions in that order, because each answer constrains the next. First `on`: which events and filters start a run, since the event fixes which commit and ref the run is about and which copy of the file is used. `push` and `pull_request` read the file from the event's commit, `schedule` from the default branch, and a `paths` or `branches` filter can mean that no run exists at all. Second, each job's `runs-on`, any `container`, and the shell including `defaults.run`, because a fixed label, a moving label and an undeclared shell behave differently. Third, the checkout step: its `ref`, `fetch-depth` and `persist-credentials` decide which code and how much history are on disk, and the pins decide which action code runs. Fourth, `permissions` at the top and per job: when any permission is named, every unnamed one is none, and a job-level block replaces the workflow-level one. Last, `needs`, `if`, `concurrency` and `environment`, which decide whether and when each job starts.

**Key terms.** on and filters; which copy of the workflow file; runs-on and shell; checkout ref and fetch-depth; permissions unnamed are none; needs, if, concurrency, environment
