**Question.** In the TanStack incident no credential was stolen from storage. Walk through how a fork pull request led to a publish, and name the control that would have broken each link.

**Model answer.** As Chapter 21A, section 21A.18 summarizes the project's post-mortem of 11 May 2026, four documented behaviors chained. A `pull_request_target` workflow built fork code, so outsider code ran in the default branch's context, and that trigger bypassed the first-time-contributor gate; building under `pull_request` breaks this link. The fork's code poisoned the shared cache: read-only `permissions` did not stop it, because cache writes use a runner-internal token, and since 26 June 2026 low-trust triggers get read-only access to the default branch's cache. The release job restored that cache; `cache-mode: none` on a job that holds a publishing identity breaks this link. Malware then read the job's OIDC token from runner memory, and 84 malicious versions of 42 packages were published through the project's own trusted-publisher identity; `id-token: write` on one job only, bound to an environment with protection rules, with no untrusted code or cache in that job, is the control there. No npm token was stolen.

**Key terms.** `pull_request_target` built fork code; cache poisoning; runner-internal token for cache writes; release job restored the cache; OIDC token read from runner memory; `cache-mode: none`; trusted-publisher identity

**Common weak answer.** "An attacker stole the publishing token through a malicious pull request." Weak because nothing was stolen from storage: it misses the shared cache as the bridge between the low-privilege workflow and the release job, and that read-only `permissions` and OIDC did not prevent it.

**Follow-up.** The team says: "We had `permissions: contents: read` and we publish through OIDC, so we followed best practice." Which two assumptions in that sentence did the incident disprove?

**A strong reply covers.** That read-only `permissions` bounds what a job can change: cache writes use a runner-internal token. And that OIDC makes publishing safe: the post-mortem says trusted-publisher binding has no per-publish review, so any code path in the workflow can mint a publish-capable token.

**Reference.** [Chapter 21A](../textbook/ch21a-actions-security.md), section 21A.18, 21A.11 and 21A.10

#### Q333

**Question.** How would you give an LLM review agent access to pull requests from outside contributors?

**Model answer.** I would write the agent's job as if the pull request author had written it, because through the prompt they partly did. An agent reads attacker-controlled text and holds credentials, and for an agent, text is instruction: no `env:` technique separates data from code inside a prompt. So the job gets `permissions` as for untrusted code, with no write token unless required, the agent gets a dedicated low-privilege, spend-capped key, and it does not run automatically on untrusted contributions. The chapter labels that recommendation as an inference from its research report, not as GitHub guidance. It rests on two findings: an automated account ran a week-long campaign in February and March 2026 that combined `pull_request_target` abuse, branch-name and filename injection, and prompt injection against an AI reviewer; and researchers reported in April 2026 that coding agents run as GitHub Actions could be steered by pull request titles, issue bodies or comments into revealing CI secrets, which the chapter knows only from secondary reporting.

**Key terms.** text is instruction; prompt injection; dedicated low-privilege spend-capped key; no write token unless required; no automatic run on untrusted contributions; permissions as if the author wrote the job

**Common weak answer.** "Give it a read-only token and sanitize the prompt." Weak because nothing separates data from instruction inside a prompt, and the answer ignores the model key the agent holds and whether it runs automatically on outsiders' text.

**Follow-up.** The agent has to post its review as a comment, which needs a write scope. How do you provide that without letting text in the pull request steer a job that holds it?

**A strong reply covers.** Apply the documented privilege separation: the agent runs unprivileged and uploads its review as an artifact; a privileged `workflow_run` workflow posts it, treating the text as data and never executing or interpolating it. The chapter teaches that split for builds; applying it to an agent is my extension.

**Reference.** [Chapter 21A](../textbook/ch21a-actions-security.md), section 21A.17

#### Q334

**Question.** You may enable one organization-level control today. Which one, and why?

**Model answer.** The chapter prescribes no single choice, so the answer is a judgment that must name what the control breaks and what it leaves open. I would set the organization's workflow permissions default to read-only. It changes the token of every workflow that has no `permissions` key in every repository at once, including repositories created before 2 February 2023 that may still carry the permissive setting, and a restrictive organization default disables the permissive option below it. A legacy read-write default token is one of the three causes in the Nx post-mortem, where one injectable line plus a write token reached a publish credential. The runner-up is requiring actions to be pinned to a full-length commit ID, which answers the tj-actions pattern but makes every unpinned workflow fail, GitHub's own actions included. What my choice leaves open: it removes no secret from a job on a privileged trigger, and a workflow can still declare broader `permissions` itself. Policies do not replace code-owner review of `.github/workflows/`.

**Key terms.** workflow permissions default read-only; legacy read-write token; restrictive organization default; require full commit pinning; what the control leaves open; code-owner review of workflows

**Common weak answer.** Listing every available policy, or naming one without saying which recurring attack pattern it breaks and what it does not cover. Weak because the question tests prioritization and knowledge of each control's limit.

**Follow-up.** Six months later, how do you know that control is still doing its job, and what does it not see?

**A strong reply covers.** The default covers only workflows without a `permissions` key. So run a workflow scanner as a required check (CodeQL for workflows reports missing permissions, zizmor has `excessive-permissions`, Scorecard has Token-Permissions) and require code-owner review of `.github/workflows/` through a ruleset. A scanner does not know which job holds the credential that matters.

**Reference.** [Chapter 21A](../textbook/ch21a-actions-security.md), section 21A.8, 21A.3 and 21A.14

#### Q335

**Question.** A day after a history rewrite the secret is back on `main` and nobody force-pushed. Reconstruct what happened from the commit graph, and describe the fix for the server and for the clone.

**Model answer.** A stale clone merged the old history into the new one and pushed it as a fast-forward. The tip of `main` is a merge commit whose parents are the rewritten tip and a commit that descends from the old history, and `git log --merges -1` finds it. A colleague who cloned before the rewrite ran `git pull`. The fetch reported forced updates, the pull merged the new `origin/main` into a local branch that still descended from the old commits, and the push went from the clean tip to that merge, so no force was needed and no rule against force pushes objected. To Git these are two lines of work that someone chose to merge, as Chapter 21B, section 21B.18 demonstrates. On the server, force-push the clean refs again. In the clone, delete the tags and refetch, replay only the colleague's own commits with `git rebase --onto origin/main` from the old upstream tip, expire the reflogs and prune, then confirm that `git cat-file -t` on the first changed commit fails; or delete the clone and re-clone.

**Key terms.** stale clone; merge commit joining old and new history; fast-forward push needs no force; `git log --merges -1`; `git rebase --onto`; freeze and re-clone; server-side check

**Common weak answer.** "Someone must have force-pushed the old branch, or GitHub restored it." Weak because the push was an ordinary fast-forward of a merge commit, which no force-push rule blocks; the cause is a clone that still held the old commits and was allowed to push.

**Follow-up.** You told the colleague to "rebase onto the new main" and they ran `git rebase origin/main` after a fetch. What happened, and why did `git pull --rebase` behave differently when it was the clone's first contact with the rewrite?

**A strong reply covers.** After a plain fetch, `git rebase origin/main` treats every old commit missing from the new history as theirs and tries to replay it, the commit that added the secret included; the chapter's run stopped on a conflict. `git pull --rebase` as first contact still knew the previous `origin/main`, so it replayed only the local commit.

**Reference.** [Chapter 21B](../textbook/ch21b-repository-security-incident-response.md), section 21B.18

#### Q336

**Question.** When is a history rewrite the wrong response to a leaked secret? What does it cost?

**Model answer.** It is wrong whenever revocation already ends the risk, and it is always wrong before containment. For a credential that is revoked and whose provider logs show no use, the correct action is to record the decision and stop; GitHub's own guidance calls removal from history time-consuming and often unnecessary once the credential is revoked. It is also wrong on a public repository in the belief that it un-publishes anything, wrong in a working clone because the tool prunes reflogs and stashes, and wrong when each colleague runs the same command, since identical commands can produce different commit IDs. The cost: a freeze; a new ID for the first affected commit and every descendant, so recorded commit IDs go stale and review comments on open pull requests detach; removed signatures; force-push and tag rules switched off and back on; a re-clone or cleanup for every collaborator; and no recall of copies in forks, clones and cached views. A rewrite is warranted when data stays harmful after rotation or cannot be rotated, such as personal data or customer records.

**Key terms.** revoke first; rewrite only where warranted; every descendant gets a new commit ID; signatures removed; freeze and re-clone; cannot recall existing copies; record the decision

**Common weak answer.** "Always rewrite, to be thorough." Weak because it confuses cleaning the repository with ending the risk, ignores the cost to every clone, recorded commit ID and signature, and a rewrite cannot recall copies that already exist.

**Follow-up.** You do decide to rewrite. Which artifact of the rewrite belongs in the incident record, and why does an ML team in particular need it?

**A strong reply covers.** git-filter-repo's `commit-map`, which records the old and new ID of every commit. Experiment records, model cards and deployment manifests that stored an old commit ID now point at a commit that no longer exists on the remote; the map lets those IDs be translated.

**Reference.** [Chapter 21B](../textbook/ch21b-repository-security-incident-response.md), section 21B.14, 21B.16 and 21B.22

#### Q337

**Question.** Attacker code is found to have run in one of your CI jobs. The team rotates the one token that appeared in the attacker's output and closes the ticket. Why is that response incomplete, and how do you scope and sequence the rotation?

**Model answer.** It is incomplete because the unit of compromise is the runtime, not the token that happened to be seen. Once attacker code runs in a CI job or on a laptop, the scope is every credential that runtime could read. In GitHub Actions that means every secret the job received, the job token, and any OIDC token the job could request, because the technique that recurs in the chapters' case studies is reading the runner's memory, which log masking does not see. The rotation also has to be done together. The Trivy and LiteLLM case gives its root cause as incomplete, non-atomic credential rotation after a first incident, followed weeks later by a malicious release and force-pushed tags, and the Internet Archive was breached a second time through tokens it had not rotated. So I list every credential reachable from the affected runtime and rotate them at their issuers as one action. Then I look for what a write token leaves behind: unknown workflow files, self-hosted runners and repositories. Dependent services get the new credentials afterwards.

**Key terms.** scope is the runtime; every credential the job could read; rotate together; runner memory; partial rotation; unknown workflows and runners; Trivy and Internet Archive

**Common weak answer.** "Rotate the token that leaked and add it to the scanner." Weak because the visible token is only the one that was printed; partial, non-atomic rotation is the root cause the chapters give for the second compromise in the Trivy case and for the Internet Archive's second breach.

**Follow-up.** How do you make that rotation list shorter before the next incident?

**A strong reply covers.** Limit what each runtime holds: each secret referenced in one step of one job behind an environment, OIDC credentials valid for a single job in place of stored keys, read-only `permissions`, and fine-grained or App tokens with expiry in place of classic tokens.

**Reference.** [Chapter 21B](../textbook/ch21b-repository-security-incident-response.md), section 21B.22 and 21B.14; [Chapter 21A](../textbook/ch21a-actions-security.md), section 21A.18

#### Q338

**Question.** Your organization's plan for leaked keys is: "GitHub secret scanning notifies the provider, and the provider revokes the key." As the engineer responsible, explain where that plan fails and what you would put in its place.

**Model answer.** The plan treats detection as if it were revocation, and it assumes coverage that GitHub does not promise. In the supported-pattern data the chapter read on 1 October 2026, provider notification, push-protection blocking and validity checking are three independent columns: for some AI providers a key is blocked at push but the provider is not notified, and a Google API key is notified but not blocked. Notification concerns public leaks and does not guarantee revocation: GitHub revokes its own tokens and Anthropic documents automatic deactivation, but an xAI key flagged on 2 March 2025 stayed valid until 30 April 2025, and that alert had gone only to an individual. A private repository without Secret Protection has no push-time check at all, and GitGuardian found internal repositories about six times more likely than public ones to contain a hardcoded secret. In its place I would put a playbook in which we revoke at the issuer ourselves, alerts that reach a team, repository push protection with delegated bypass, scanning in CI over the full history, and short-lived credentials through OIDC.

**Key terms.** detection is not revocation; notification, blocking and validity are independent; public leaks only; alert in one inbox; private repositories need Secret Protection; revoke at the issuer; leak playbook

**Common weak answer.** "GitHub partners with the providers, so leaked keys are revoked automatically." Weak because notification is not revocation, coverage differs by provider and applies to public leaks, and the chapter's xAI case shows a flagged key valid for about two months.

**Follow-up.** In the chapter's case studies, who usually discovered the leak, and what does that imply for monitoring and for how reports reach you?

**A strong reply covers.** Outsiders, in nearly every case, and the worst outcomes involved single credentials with estate-wide read access. To know first, an organization needs its own monitoring of public GitHub, employees' and contractors' personal accounts included, and a reachable disclosure contact such as `SECURITY.md` with private vulnerability reporting.

**Reference.** [Chapter 21B](../textbook/ch21b-repository-security-incident-response.md), section 21B.12, 21B.15 and 21B.20


## Area 13: Open source

Q339 to Q353. Forks, upstream remotes, contribution etiquette, maintainers' tools, branching models and releases.


### Open source: foundational level

#### Q339

**Question.** Describe the three repositories of the fork workflow and the remotes in your clone. After `git switch -c fix/x upstream/main` followed by `git push -u origin fix/x`, what does `git status` compare your branch with, and where does the pull request live?

**Model answer.** Three repositories are involved, each with its own refs. The project is the remote named `upstream`, which I only fetch from to learn where its `main` is. My fork is `origin`, a server-side copy I own, which I fetch from and push to in order to publish branches. My clone is where the work happens. I start a branch from `upstream/main`, not from my fork's copy, so it is based on the project's current state. The surprising part is the upstream branch setting: `git switch -c` from `upstream/main` records `upstream/main` as the upstream branch, and `git push -u origin` then replaces it with the remote-tracking branch of the fork. After that `git status` compares me with my fork, not with the project, so I compare explicitly with `git log --oneline upstream/main..HEAD`. The pull request is a GitHub object in the upstream repository, with a `refs/pull/N/head` ref there; it does not exist in my repository at all.

**Key terms.** upstream remote is fetch only; origin is the fork; branch from `upstream/main`; `push -u` rewrites the upstream branch; `git log upstream/main..HEAD`; pull request is a GitHub object

**Common weak answer.** "Origin is the project and I push my branch to it." Weak because it collapses the triangle into one remote, does not say which ref the branch is based on, and misses that after `git push -u` the status line reports divergence from the fork and says nothing about the project.

**Follow-up.** Nothing updates your fork's `main` for you. How do you bring it up to date with plain Git, and what does the guard you use protect you from?

**A strong reply covers.** `git fetch upstream`, `git switch main`, `git merge --ff-only upstream/main`, `git push origin main`. If I committed on `main` by mistake, `--ff-only` stops instead of creating a merge commit that exists only in my fork and that every later pull request would carry.

**Reference.** [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.2 and 27.3


### Open source: working engineer level

#### Q340

**Question.** A colleague says the DORA research proves trunk-based development is best. What does it show, how was it measured, and what would you say instead?

**Model answer.** It does not prove that. DORA's capability page reports, from research conducted in 2016 and 2017, that higher delivery performance is associated with three or fewer active branches, merging to the trunk at least daily, and no code freezes or integration phases, and a companion capability says that working in small batches predicts performance. The evidence is survey-based, so it measures what respondents report about their own practice, not observed repositories, and it is correlational, so the right words are "is associated with", not "causes". It is also expressed in branch lifetime, number of active branches and batch size, and says nothing about Git Flow or GitHub Flow by name: a GitHub Flow team with one-day branches satisfies it and a nominally trunk-based team with week-long branches does not. What I would say to a CTO is that teams reporting short-lived branches and small batches also report better delivery, and that the variable we can act on is how long our branches live and how large our changes are, whatever we call the model.

**Key terms.** association not causation; survey-based; 2016 and 2017 research; branch lifetime and batch size; three or fewer active branches; no named workflow is ranked

**Common weak answer.** "DORA showed elite teams use trunk-based development, so we should switch." Weak because it turns a survey correlation into a causal ranking of named workflows, which the research does not contain.

**Follow-up.** If the name of the workflow tells you nothing, what would you measure in our own repository, and can you tell me how large the improvement will be?

**A strong reply covers.** Branch lifetime, number of active branches, merge frequency and change size. I cannot give a number: the course marks any specific effect size as unverified, its notes contain none, and the later reports were not read for it.

**Reference.** [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.13

#### Q341

**Question.** Under GitHub Flow, a customer asks for a release that contains only a security fix. What do you tell them, and what would you have needed to have in place?

**Model answer.** I tell them the truth about the model: under GitHub Flow `main` is what we ship, so the next tag on `main` contains everything merged since the previous tag. Section 27.9 shows it: the patch tag there contained the fix and an unrelated batch endpoint, and `git log --oneline --no-merges v1.4.0..v1.4.1` lists exactly what a customer would receive. For someone who pinned a version and expects the third number to mean bug fixes only, that breaks what the version number promised. What we needed is a line for the old version to stand on: a release branch, which can be created after the fact with `git switch -c release/1.4 v1.4.0`, the fix committed on `main` first and copied down with `git cherry-pick -x`, and the patch tag placed on the release branch. To make that routine we also need a CI pipeline for the release branch, a rule on the branch pattern, a written fix direction, and feature flags so unfinished work on `main` never blocks an urgent release.

**Key terms.** everything merged since the previous tag ships; `git log vA..vB`; release branch created at the old tag; `git cherry-pick -x`; patch release contains only the fix; CI per release line

**Common weak answer.** "We tag `main` after merging the fix, so the release is the fix." Weak because the tag names a commit whose history includes every other merge since the last release, and the answer never checks the range between the two tags.

**Follow-up.** You cut the fix-only release from a new release branch. How do you later prove the same fix is on `main` when the two commits have different IDs?

**A strong reply covers.** `git log --oneline --cherry-pick --right-only --no-merges main...release/1.4` must be empty; it compares patch IDs, not commit IDs. If the port needed conflict resolution the patch differs and the commit is listed, and the line added by `-x` is the evidence.

**Reference.** [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.9 and 27.14

#### Q342

**Question.** After a squash merge, `git branch --merged` does not list your branch. Why, and how do you establish that its work is on `main`?

**Model answer.** Because "merged" in Git means "reachable from", and a squash merge keeps the content while discarding the ancestry. `git branch --merged` and `git merge-base --is-ancestor` both test reachability. The squash created one new commit on the base branch with a single parent and no link to my commits, so my branch tip is not an ancestor of `main`. Git cannot record that several commits were folded into one without a second parent, since a commit's parents are part of its ID, and a second parent is exactly what a squash omits. The merge method is chosen on GitHub; the consequence is in Git. To establish that the work is there I test content, not ancestry: `git diff --stat main <branch>` printing nothing means `main` has everything the branch has, as section 27.3 shows, and when `main` has moved further I use a `git merge-tree` comparison against the tree of `main`. The prevention is to delete the branch on the fork and locally right after the merge and never reuse it.

**Key terms.** merged means reachable; squash creates a single-parent commit; ancestry discarded and content kept; `git merge-base --is-ancestor` exits 1; empty `git diff main <branch>`; delete the branch after merge

**Common weak answer.** "The merge has not synced yet; pull and it will show as merged." Weak because no fetch can create ancestry that the squash commit does not have; the answer does not know that Git's notion of merged is reachability.

**Follow-up.** In the course's run, `git branch -d` deleted that branch with only a warning although it was not merged into `main`. Why did Git not refuse?

**A strong reply covers.** The manual says `-d` requires the branch to be fully merged in its upstream branch, or in HEAD if no upstream was set. The upstream was the remote-tracking branch on the fork, which has every commit. A branch never pushed with `-u` would be refused.

**Reference.** [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.3 and 27.19

#### Q343

**Question.** Give the mechanism behind three of your team's practices: why small commits, why no force push on shared branches, why inspect before merging.

**Model answer.** Small commits, because a commit is the unit of `git revert`, `git cherry-pick`, `git bisect` and review; a commit that does three things can only be undone, ported or blamed as three things. Section 27.15 shows a load-test limit that reached production being reverted alone, with the feature intact, because it was a commit of its own. No force push on shared branches, because a forced push sets the server's ref to a commit that does not descend from the old one: everyone who fetched the old commits now has a history that diverges from the server, and the next careless merge brings the removed commits back. A rule on the server turns "we agreed not to" into "the server refuses". Inspect before merging, because a merge brings every commit reachable from the other side, not only the ones I had in mind. Three read-only commands answer it: `git log --oneline main..<branch>` for the commits, `git diff --stat main...<branch>` for the change since the merge base, and `git merge-tree --write-tree` for whether it merges cleanly.

**Key terms.** commit as unit of revert, cherry-pick and bisect; forced push diverges every clone; removed commits return on the next merge; merge brings everything reachable; `git log A..B`; `git merge-tree --write-tree`

**Common weak answer.** "Small commits are cleaner, force pushing is dangerous, and you should always look first." Weak because it restates the rules as taste; none of the three is tied to what a commit, a ref or a merge actually is, so the practice will be dropped under pressure.

**Follow-up.** Your team squash-merges every pull request. What does that do to the small-commits argument, and what practice follows?

**A strong reply covers.** The unit of undo becomes the pull request: in section 27.15 reverting the squashed commit removed the fallback feature together with the mistake. The conclusion is not "never squash" but to keep pull requests as small as the commits you would have wanted.

**Reference.** [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.15 and 27.16

#### Q344

**Question.** Your fork's `main` is two commits ahead of and forty behind upstream. How did that happen, and how do you repair it without losing the two commits?

**Model answer.** The forty behind is normal: nothing updates a fork's `main` for you while the project moves. The two ahead means someone committed or merged on the fork's `main`, which should only ever be an exact copy of the project's `main`. I confirm it with `git fetch upstream` and `git rev-list --left-right --count upstream/main...origin/main`, which prints forty on the left and two on the right; a second number above zero is what makes a fast-forward impossible. The repair follows the chapter's order: first move the stray commits to a branch, so they stay reachable, by creating a branch at the current `main` and pushing it to the fork. Then reset the fork's `main` to upstream: locally `git reset --keep upstream/main`, then `git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes` to my own fork, after previewing what the server holds. The two commits then become a normal feature branch that I rebase onto `upstream/main` and offer as a pull request. Prevention is never committing on the fork's `main` and always updating it with `git merge --ff-only upstream/main`.

**Key terms.** fork's `main` is a copy; `git rev-list --left-right --count`; move stray commits to a branch first; reset `main` to `upstream/main`; `--ff-only` as the guard; never commit on the fork's `main`

**Common weak answer.** "Run `git pull upstream main` and push." Weak because that creates a merge commit that exists only in the fork and that every later pull request will carry, which makes the divergence permanent instead of repairing it.

**Follow-up.** A teammate suggests `gh repo sync --force` as the one-line repair. What does it destroy, and how do you preview it?

**A strong reply covers.** It hard-resets the fork's branch to its parent, so commits made only there become unreachable on the fork. Preview with the `rev-list --left-right --count` command: a second number above zero means work would be dropped. Recovery is pushing the commits back from a clone that has them.

**Reference.** [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.3 and 27.19


### Open source: senior level

#### Q345

**Question.** A patch release went out without a fix that the previous patch release contained. Walk through how you find the cause from the repository alone, and what you add to the release process afterwards.

**Model answer.** The likely cause is that the fix was committed on the release branch only and the newer release was cut from `main`. Nothing in Git propagates a commit between branches; carrying it is a human step that nobody took. I prove it in three steps. First I compare the file at the two tags with `git show <tag>:<path>` to confirm the newer tag has the old line. Then `git branch --contains` on the fix commit shows it is reachable from the release branch only. Finally one of two checks, depending on our convention: `git merge-base --is-ancestor release/1.4 main` exits 1, or `git log --oneline --cherry-pick --right-only --no-merges main...release/1.4` lists the unported fix, as section 27.10 demonstrates. The fix is to port the commit to `main` with `git cherry-pick -x`, or merge the release branch upward if that is our convention, and ship a new patch version. Prevention is making that check a release gate in CI, because it is one command with a testable result.

**Key terms.** fix reachable from the release branch only; branches are independent refs; `git branch --contains`; `git log --cherry-pick --right-only main...release/x`; port then release a new patch; release gate

**Common weak answer.** "Git lost the fix in a bad merge." Weak because no merge happened at all: the commit was never carried to `main`, and the answer offers no command that shows where the fix is reachable from and no gate that would catch the next case.

**Follow-up.** Someone proposes moving the new release's tag to a corrected commit so customers get the fix under the same version. Why do you refuse?

**A strong reply covers.** Clones do not replace a tag they already have unless forced, so half the users would keep the old meaning; a moved tag is worse than a wrong tag. Release a new patch version. On GitHub, with immutable releases enabled, the tag name cannot be reused anyway.

**Reference.** [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.10 and 27.19

#### Q346

**Question.** State the two conventions for the direction of a fix. For each, give the invariant you can test and one way the test can mislead you.

**Model answer.** The conventions are opposites. Merge upward: commit the fix on the oldest supported branch that needs it, then merge that branch into the newer ones, as the Git project's own workflow document prescribes. The fix is one commit with one commit ID, and the invariant is that the release branch is an ancestor of `main`, tested by the exit status of `git merge-base --is-ancestor release/1.4 main`. That test misleads when an upward merge was resolved by discarding the release branch's side: ancestry holds while the fix is absent, and `git log --remerge-diff` shows what the resolver changed. Fix on `main` first and cherry-pick down: there are two commits, the ancestry test fails by design, and the invariant is that `git log --cherry-pick --right-only --no-merges main...release/1.4` is empty, which compares patch IDs. That test misleads when the port needed conflict resolution, because the diffs then differ and the commit is reported as missing although a human ported it; the line written by `git cherry-pick -x` is then the evidence.

**Key terms.** merge upward; fix on `main` first and cherry-pick down; ancestry invariant; patch ID comparison; `--remerge-diff`; `-x` trailer line as evidence; conflict resolution changes the patch ID

**Common weak answer.** "You always fix on `main` and cherry-pick; merging a release branch back is wrong." Weak because both conventions are legitimate, the answer names no testable invariant, and it does not know that either check can report the wrong result.

**Follow-up.** For a trunk-based team with late-cut release branches, which direction do you choose, and what does a forgotten step cost under each convention?

**A strong reply covers.** Pick down. A forgotten pick is not dangerous: the old release lacks a fix it never had. Under merge upward, a forgotten merge leaves `main` without the fix, and the upward merge also brings version bumps and release-only changes that must be neutralized.

**Reference.** [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.10

#### Q347

**Question.** What does a merge queue guarantee that "require branches to be up to date" does not, and what does it cost?

**Model answer.** Both address the same failure: two pull requests each pass their checks against an older `main` and break `main` together. Requiring branches to be up to date closes that hole and opens a race, because every merge makes every other pull request stale and its author must update and rerun. A merge queue, which is a GitHub feature, runs the required checks on temporary branches that contain the base plus the queued changes, in order, and merges what passes, so what was tested is what lands and nobody races. The costs: the checks run on the `merge_group` event, so a required check that does not listen for it never reports and the queue stalls; the merge method is fixed by the queue instead of chosen per pull request; and the throughput gain is real only at volume. The published numbers, about 2,500 pull requests a month from more than 500 engineers and an average wait down 33 percent, describe GitHub itself. A team merging five pull requests a day gets the correctness guarantee and little else.

**Key terms.** checks on the merged result; temporary branches with base plus queued changes; race from staleness; `merge_group` event; merge method fixed by the queue; benefit depends on volume

**Common weak answer.** "A merge queue makes merging faster." Weak because speed is a side effect at large volume; the answer misses the correctness guarantee, the race it removes and the workflow trigger it requires.

**Follow-up.** The queue is enabled, pull requests enter it and nothing ever merges. What is your first hypothesis and how do you fix it?

**A strong reply covers.** A required check does not run on `merge_group`, so it never reports and the queue waits indefinitely. Add that trigger to the workflow that produces the required check; Chapter 17, section 17.11 covers the mechanism.

**Reference.** [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.12 and 27.20

#### Q348

**Question.** You maintain an open-source project and receive a 3,000-line pull request from a stranger. What do you do, and what in your repository should have prevented it?

**Model answer.** A maintainer's scarce resource is attention, and a change this size from someone I do not yet know cannot be evaluated as one unit. I neither merge it on trust nor leave it silent. I thank the contributor, ask for an issue that states the goal so we can decide whether it fits the roadmap, and ask for the work to be split into pull requests of one logical change each, with a statement of what was tested. Before any workflow runs I read the diff, because in a public repository the default is that a first-time contributor needs a maintainer's approval before workflows run, and I look hardest at anything under `.github/workflows/`, lock files and the `Dockerfile`. What should have prevented it is the contract GitHub shows contributors: a `CONTRIBUTING` file that says "issue first for anything large", names the target branch, the test command and the merge method, plus issue and pull request templates. `CODEOWNERS` routes the review, and required checks keep `main` releasable; the fork workflow is what keeps untrusted contributors from pushing directly.

**Key terms.** maintainer attention; issue first for large changes; one logical change per pull request; `CONTRIBUTING` and templates; approval before workflows run for first-time contributors; workflow and lock file changes get a second reader

**Common weak answer.** "Review it carefully over a few evenings, or close it." Weak because both spend or waste the wrong resource, neither asks for the change to be split, and nothing is said about the contribution guide or about running a stranger's code in CI.

**Follow-up.** The contributor's checks are red because the evaluation job needs an API key. What do you tell them, and which repair do you refuse to make?

**A strong reply covers.** A red check that needs a secret is not their bug: workflows on pull requests from forks run without the project's secrets. A maintainer runs the privileged part after review. I refuse to switch to `pull_request_target` and check out the fork's code.

**Reference.** [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.4 and 27.17

#### Q349

**Question.** You rebased your pull request branch onto the new `upstream/main`, and the plain push to your fork was rejected. Meanwhile a maintainer had used "allow edits by maintainers" to push a small fix to that branch. What would a forced push do, how do you check before pushing, and how could you have updated the branch without this risk?

**Model answer.** The rejection is information, not an obstacle. The rebase replaced my commits with new ones that have a new parent and new commit IDs, so the fork's branch is no longer an ancestor of mine and Git refuses a non-fast-forward. A forced push sets the fork's branch to a commit that does not descend from the old tip, and it destroys any commit on that server branch that is not in my clone, which here is the maintainer's fix. Before pushing I run `git fetch origin` and then `git log HEAD..origin/<branch>`, which lists what would be dropped. If I must force, I use `git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes`: the lease succeeds only if the branch is where my clone last saw it, and the second option only if I integrated what I last saw. The lower-risk route after review starts is to merge `upstream/main` into the branch: no commit ID changes and a plain push is a fast-forward. Recovery is pushing the old tip back from any clone that has it.

**Key terms.** non-fast-forward rejection; rebase creates new commit IDs; maintainer's commit on the fork branch; `git log HEAD..origin/<branch>`; `--force-with-lease --force-if-includes`; merge instead of rebase after review starts

**Common weak answer.** "The push was rejected, so I force it; it is my own branch." Weak because the branch is not only mine once maintainers may push to it, the rejection is read as an obstacle instead of evidence, and no preview of what the server holds is made.

**Follow-up.** Once review has started, what does updating by rebase cost the reviewer, and what does updating by merge cost you?

**A strong reply covers.** After a rebase, review comments may lose their anchor and the reviewer needs `git range-diff` to see what changed; conflicts are resolved once per replayed commit. A merge keeps commit IDs and comments but leaves "merge upstream" commits in the branch. The project's contribution guide decides.

**Reference.** [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.3 and 27.4

#### Q350

**Question.** A new engineering manager wants to standardize on Git Flow for your continuously deployed hosted service because it is "the industry standard". What does Git Flow prescribe, what does its own author say about it, and what do you propose instead?

**Model answer.** Git Flow, published by Vincent Driessen on 5 January 2010, keeps two long-lived branches: `main` for released code and `develop` for integration. Feature branches start from and merge into `develop` with `--no-ff`; a release branch is cut from `develop`, receives only stabilization commits, and is merged into `main`, tagged, and merged back; a hotfix branch is cut from `main` and merged into both. On 5 March 2020 the author added a note which, as the course summarizes it, says the model was conceived for explicitly versioned software with several versions supported in the wild, that a team doing continuous delivery of a web application should adopt a simpler workflow such as GitHub Flow, and that no model is a cure-all. For our service it would add a second long-lived branch and two merges per release, while the tags already record what was released; the chapter's Git Flow history has six merge commits for three features, one release and one hotfix. I propose one long-lived branch with short branches, and a release branch only when a second live version exists.

**Key terms.** `main` and `develop`; release and hotfix branches merged twice; the author's 2020 note; explicitly versioned software with several supported versions; choose by context not by name; release branch without `develop`

**Common weak answer.** "Git Flow is the proven standard, so it is the safe default." Weak because the model's own author restricts it to versioned software with several supported versions, and the answer cannot say what the second long-lived branch buys a service with one live version.

**Follow-up.** In the chapter's demonstration, what did the Git Flow history get right that GitHub Flow with tags on `main` did not, and do you need `develop` to get it?

**A strong reply covers.** The patch release contained the fix and nothing else, because `main` receives only releases and hotfixes, and `git log --first-parent main` reads as a release log. A release branch gives the same result without `develop`, as strategy B in section 27.9 shows.

**Reference.** [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.7 and 27.14


### Open source: principal level

#### Q351

**Question.** Your company ships one hosted version today and will support two on-premises versions next year. What changes in your branching model, and on which day do you change it?

**Model answer.** Two questions decide a branching model: how many versions are live at once, and how often we release. Today the answer is one live version deployed continuously, so one long-lived branch is enough, with releases as tags on `main`. Each supported on-premises version needs a line that can receive fixes, so I add one `release/x.y` branch per supported version, tag patch releases there, write down the fix direction (fix on `main` first, then `git cherry-pick -x` down), make the port check a release gate, give every supported line its own CI pipeline and put a ruleset on the `release/**` pattern. I do not add Git Flow's `develop`; the release branch is the part that does the work. The day to change is the day the second live version exists, not earlier, because `git switch -c release/1.4 v1.4.0` creates the missing line at the tag after the fact. A branch is a ref, so the change is cheap in Git and expensive in habits, pipelines and rulesets.

**Key terms.** number of live versions; release frequency; `release/x.y` per supported version; fix on `main` first then cherry-pick down; port check as release gate; branch created at the tag after the fact; CI per supported line

**Common weak answer.** "We should move to Git Flow now so we are ready." Weak because it adopts a model by name, adds a second long-lived branch a hosted service does not need, and misses that a release branch can be created at an existing tag on the day it is needed.

**Follow-up.** Until that day you release patch versions as tags on `main`. What exactly does a customer receive when moving from 1.4.0 to 1.4.1, and what keeps an urgent release from being blocked?

**A strong reply covers.** Everything merged to `main` since the previous tag: `git log --oneline --no-merges v1.4.0..v1.4.1` in section 27.9 lists the fix and the batch endpoint. Unfinished work must sit behind feature flags so that `main` can be released at any commit.

**Reference.** [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.9 and 27.14

#### Q352

**Question.** In one repository a first fix was committed on `main` and cherry-picked to `release/1.4`. A second fix, on the neighbouring line of the same function, was committed on the release branch, and someone then merged `release/1.4` into `main`. The merge stopped with a conflict on a line that `main` never changed. Explain the conflict to an engineering director and state the policy you would set.

**Model answer.** The repository mixed the two fix directions, and the conflict is the bill. The upward merge brought everything on the release branch, including the picked copy of the first fix. Relative to the merge base, `main` changed one line, and the release branch changed that same line identically plus its neighbour, so the two changes overlap. Git dropped the identical line from the conflict and left the neighbouring line for a human, although `main` never touched it. Section 27.10 reproduces this. The larger cost is that such a repository satisfies neither safety check: the release branch is not kept as an ancestor of `main`, and it is not kept free of unported patches either, so no single command can tell us whether a release will regress. My immediate action is `git merge --abort`, then port the second fix in the direction we have chosen. The policy is one direction per repository, written down, and no routine cherry-picking between two long-lived branches, because two histories maintained that way cannot be reconciled by any check.

**Key terms.** mixed fix directions; upward merge brings everything on the branch; overlapping changes relative to the merge base; neither invariant holds; `git merge --abort`; one written direction

**Common weak answer.** "It is a normal conflict; resolve it and move on." Weak because it treats the symptom, does not explain why Git asked about a line `main` never changed, and leaves the repository in a state where neither release check means anything.

**Follow-up.** How do you turn the chosen fix direction from a habit into something the organization enforces?

**A strong reply covers.** Make the check a release gate in CI: the exit status of `git merge-base --is-ancestor release/x main`, or an empty `git log --cherry-pick --right-only main...release/x`. Put a ruleset on the `release/**` pattern and write the direction in `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.10 and 27.20

#### Q353

**Question.** Design the branching and governance model for a regulated company that runs a continuously deployed hosted product and also sells an on-premises edition whose customers stay a version behind. What do you write down, and what do you tell an auditor who asks which branching model you follow?

**Model answer.** The company sits in three rows of the context table at once, so I write down refs, rules and fix direction, not a model's name. Refs: `main` as the single integration branch with short-lived branches and feature flags for unfinished work, plus one `release/x.y` branch per supported on-premises version, because each supported version needs a line to receive fixes. Rules, enforced on GitHub by rulesets on `main` and on the `release/**` pattern: changes arrive through pull requests with required checks and required review by someone other than the author, and releases are signed tags. Fix direction: fix on `main` first, `git cherry-pick -x` down, with the port check as a release gate and CI for every supported line. To the auditor I say that compliance comes from enforced, logged rules, not from the name of the model: the audit asks who approved what and what exactly shipped, and the answers are the rule history, with bypasses made visible through Rule Insights, and a tag that names one commit.

**Key terms.** refs, rules and fix direction; `release/x.y` per supported version; rulesets on `main` and `release/**`; review by someone other than the author; signed release tags; bypasses visible; compliance from enforced logged rules

**Common weak answer.** "We follow Git Flow, which is audit-friendly because it has release branches." Weak because a model's name enforces nothing; it says neither who may move which ref nor how a bypass is seen, and it does not state the direction in which a fix travels.

**Follow-up.** Which parts of that design rest only on the team's agreement, and how does each one fail without anyone noticing?

**A strong reply covers.** Branch names mean nothing to Git, so a release branch named outside the pattern escapes the ruleset. The fix direction is a human step unless a gate checks it. "Request changes" and `CODEOWNERS` do not block a merge unless a ruleset says so.

**Reference.** [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.14 and 27.5


## Area 14: AI/ML workflows

Q354 to Q376. Notebooks, data and model versioning, Git LFS, reproducibility and CI for ML projects.


### AI/ML workflows: foundational level

#### Q354

**Question.** Why does deleting a large file in a new commit not make a rejected push succeed?

**Model answer.** Deleting the file adds a commit; it removes nothing. Git keeps every version of every file, so the large blob is still reachable from the earlier commits, and those commits are part of the push. GitHub blocks files larger than 100 MiB, and according to its documentation the block applies to any commit in the push that contains such a blob, not only to the latest tree. I would prove it with `git rev-list --objects <remote>/<branch>..<branch>` piped into `git cat-file --batch-check`, which still lists the blob with its full size. Running `git lfs track` and committing again does not help either, because tracking applies from the next `git add` and converts nothing in history. While the commits are unpushed, the lowest-risk fix is `git lfs migrate import` in its default scope, which rewrites only the unpushed commits of the current branch so that the blobs become pointers. Prevention is `git lfs migrate info` before the first push of a new binary type.

**Key terms.** blob still reachable from earlier commits; any commit in the push; 100 MiB block (GitHub); history rewrite; `git lfs migrate import`; default scope is unpushed commits

**Common weak answer.** "Delete it, commit, and push again", or "add it to `.gitignore` and track it with LFS". Weak because both only change the newest tree: the blob stays in an earlier commit that is still being pushed, and tracking does not convert files already in history.

**Follow-up.** Suppose the commits that contain the large blob are already on the remote and other people have fetched them. What does the fix become, and what undoes it afterwards?

**A strong reply covers.** It becomes a planned rewrite of published history, not a command: everyone stops pushing, one person rewrites and pushes with `--force-with-lease`, everyone else re-clones or resets. An old clone that pushes again brings the blobs back.

**Reference.** [Chapter 22](../textbook/ch22-git-lfs.md), section 22.2, 22.9 and 22.11

#### Q355

**Question.** What does Git store for an LFS-tracked path, what does LFS store, and where is each on your machine and on the remote?

**Model answer.** For an LFS-tracked path Git stores a pointer blob: a small UTF-8 text file with the keys `version`, `oid` and `size`, where the oid is the SHA-256 of the real content and the size is its length in bytes. In the chapter's example the pointer is 132 bytes. It is an ordinary blob in the Git object database, so it is hashed, committed and transferred by `git push` and `git fetch` like any other file. LFS stores the real content in a file named by its own SHA-256 under `.git/lfs/objects`. That file is not a Git object: `git cat-file`, `git fsck`, `git gc` and `git push` know nothing about it. The remote has the same two stores: the Git repository holds the pointer blob, and an LFS store beside it holds one full file per version. On GitHub the second store is a separate storage service with its own quota. The working tree holds the real content, written there by the smudge filter.

**Key terms.** pointer blob; `version`, `oid`, `size`; SHA-256 of the content; `.git/lfs/objects`; not a Git object; two stores on the remote; clean and smudge

**Common weak answer.** "Git stores a link to the file and LFS stores it in the cloud." Weak because it does not say that the pointer is an ordinary blob carrying the SHA-256 and the size of the content, that a local LFS store exists, or that Git's own commands never see the LFS objects.

**Follow-up.** How do you tell whether a working tree file currently holds the real content or the pointer, and why can `git status` be clean in both cases?

**A strong reply covers.** `git lfs ls-files` marks a path with `*` when the working tree file holds the content and with `-` when it holds a pointer. `git status` is clean in both cases because the clean filter recognises a pointer and passes it through unchanged, so the file matches the index.

**Reference.** [Chapter 22](../textbook/ch22-git-lfs.md), section 22.3 and 22.6

#### Q356

**Question.** Why does cloning a repository not install its clean filters and hooks? What would be possible for an attacker if it did?

**Model answer.** Because both are defined in a clone's own configuration, and Git never copies configuration from the source of a clone. A clean filter has two halves. The `.gitattributes` file names a driver for a path pattern; it is a tracked file, so it travels. The command behind the name is `filter.<name>.clean` in `.git/config`, which does not travel. Hooks are the same: they are not installed by cloning, and a shared hooks directory takes effect only after `core.hooksPath` is set in that clone. The reason is security, not oversight: a filter command runs on `git add` and a hook runs on `git commit`, so if a clone installed them, cloning a repository would let its author run commands on your machine. The nbstripout README states this limitation as deliberate. The consequence is shown in section 28.4: a fresh clone had the attribute, had no driver, and committed a notebook with all its outputs, and nothing warned the author. A committed attribute that names an unconfigured driver is a silent no-op.

**Key terms.** configuration is not cloned; attribute travels and driver does not; `.git/config`; `core.hooksPath`; arbitrary command execution on clone; silent no-op in a fresh clone

**Common weak answer.** "They are installed; `.gitattributes` and the hooks directory are in the repository." Weak because it confuses the tracked file that names a driver with the local configuration that defines it, and it misses the security reason entirely.

**Follow-up.** Since the configuration cannot travel, where does the control live, and what is the standing of a setup script that configures every new clone?

**A strong reply covers.** In a required CI check that runs the same checks on a fresh checkout, for example the filter's verify mode over every tracked notebook. A setup script is worth having and is a convenience, not a control, because nothing forces a clone to run it.

**Reference.** [Chapter 28](../textbook/ch28-ai-ml-workflows.md), section 28.4 and 28.10

#### Q357

**Question.** Which files in an ML repository are generated and must be committed anyway, and what is the test that separates them from generated files that must not be?

**Model answer.** The clear case is the lock file. A dependency range is resolved to exact versions at install time, so two installs a month apart differ; the lock file records one resolution. It is generated by a tool, and it is still committed, because it is an input to every later build. The test the chapter gives is whether the file can be regenerated identically from what is in Git. Build outputs, caches, run directories, tracker stores and notebook outputs pass that test or are products of a run, so they stay out. A lock file fails it, since the package index changes between resolutions. The same reasoning covers the small pointer and metafiles written by a data-versioning tool: a tool writes them, and they are committed because they are the only record of which data version a commit used. In a Java service the Gradle wrapper JAR is also expected to be committed according to Gradle's documentation, and the chapter flags it as a review blind spot because a reviewer cannot read it in a diff.

**Key terms.** lock file; input to every later build; regenerated identically from what is in Git; package index changes; pointer files; outputs stay out

**Common weak answer.** "Generated files never belong in Git." Weak because it applies a slogan instead of the test; a build without a committed lock file resolves different versions on different days.

**Follow-up.** Committing the lock file is not enough on its own. How does CI honor it, and what is the equivalent rule for the container image?

**A strong reply covers.** Install with `uv sync --locked`, which per the uv documentation fails instead of updating a lock file that is out of date. Pin the base image by digest, because a tag is a mutable reference like a branch, and let Dependabot update the pin.

**Reference.** [Chapter 28](../textbook/ch28-ai-ml-workflows.md), section 28.8 and 28.13

#### Q358

**Question.** Why is `merge=binary` a sensible attribute for a pointer file?

**Model answer.** Because a pointer is only meaningful as a whole, and Git's default merge works line by line. A pointer file is a few lines of text that record a checksum and a size for one version of a data file. If two branches each record a new data version, a line-based merge treats the checksum line and the size line as independent pieces of text, and a result whose checksum came from one side and whose size came from the other names nothing: no object in the store matches it. The `merge=binary` attribute, set in the tracked `.gitattributes` file, tells Git never to combine two pointers line by line, so the outcome of a merge is one side's pointer or the other's, chosen by a person who knows which data version is wanted. The chapter pairs it with `text eol=lf` on the same pattern, so the pointer is also never altered by line-ending conversion. The same reasoning is why weights and data travel as checksums at all: they cannot be reviewed or merged as text.

**Key terms.** pointer is atomic; line-based merge; checksum from one side and size from the other; names nothing in the store; `.gitattributes`; choose one whole version

**Common weak answer.** "Because pointer files are binary." Weak because they are small text files; the point is that a textual merge of two valid pointers can produce an invalid one, and the answer does not say what that invalid result would be.

**Follow-up.** Two branches each recorded a new version of the data set and you resolved the conflict in the pointer. How do you know the data in your working tree is the version the pointer names?

**A strong reply covers.** Git cannot tell me, because the data file is ignored. I run the pointer tool's verify, and its checkout to restore the bytes the pointer names, after confirming no unrecorded edits would be overwritten. The store must still hold that object.

**Reference.** [Chapter 28](../textbook/ch28-ai-ml-workflows.md), section 28.9


### AI/ML workflows: working engineer level

#### Q359

**Question.** Which two Git mechanisms does LFS use, and which parts of the setup travel with a clone?

**Model answer.** Git LFS is a separate program that plugs into Git through a clean and smudge filter selected by `.gitattributes`, and through hooks. The clean filter runs on `git add` and replaces the content by a pointer; the smudge filter runs on checkout and writes the real content back. `git lfs install` writes the filter definition into configuration, normally the global one and with `--local` the repository's own, including `filter.lfs.required=true`, and it installs four hooks: `pre-push`, `post-checkout`, `post-commit` and `post-merge`. The `pre-push` hook uploads the LFS objects of the commits about to be pushed, before Git sends the commits; the other three exist for file locking. Only `.gitattributes` travels with the repository, which is why it must be committed. The filter definition is local configuration and the hooks are local files, so a clone gets neither. On a machine where `git lfs install` was never run, the attribute names a filter that is not defined, an undefined filter is a no-op, and the working tree receives pointers.

**Key terms.** clean and smudge filter; `.gitattributes` travels; hooks are local; `pre-push` uploads; `filter.lfs.required=true`; undefined filter is a no-op

**Common weak answer.** "LFS is built into Git, so cloning the repository sets it up." Weak because LFS is a separate program, and of its three parts only `.gitattributes` is versioned; configuration and hooks have to be provisioned on every machine.

**Follow-up.** The upload of LFS objects lives in a hook. Name two ordinary actions that bypass it, and describe the state that results on the remote.

**A strong reply covers.** `git push --no-verify` skips the hook, and a `core.hooksPath` that points to a directory without the LFS hook never runs it. Either way the pointer is published without its object, and a teammate's checkout fails with a smudge error because the filter is required.

**Reference.** [Chapter 22](../textbook/ch22-git-lfs.md), section 22.3, 22.4 and 22.5

#### Q360

**Question.** A CI job fails because a model file is 132 bytes. Give the root cause, two diagnostics, and the fix for GitHub Actions.

**Model answer.** The job is reading an LFS pointer, not the model. On the runner no LFS filter was applied: `.gitattributes` names a filter called `lfs`, that filter is not defined there, and an undefined filter is a no-op. From Git's point of view nothing is wrong, so the clone succeeds, `git status` is clean, and the file is three lines of text starting with the word `version`. The first diagnostic is `head -c 200` on the file, which shows the pointer text. The second is `git lfs ls-files`, where a `-` marks a path whose working tree file is still a pointer; `git config get filter.lfs.smudge` printing nothing confirms the missing filter. On the GitHub Actions layer, `actions/checkout` downloads LFS files only when its `lfs` input is `true`, and the default is `false`, so the fix is to set that input. The textbook describes this from the action's definition and did not run it. The cost is that each download counts as LFS bandwidth for the repository owner.

**Key terms.** LFS pointer; undefined filter is a no-op; `head -c 200`; `git lfs ls-files` shows `-`; `lfs: true` on `actions/checkout`; bandwidth billed to the owner

**Common weak answer.** "The file was corrupted in the upload, so re-push the model." Weak because the repository is correct: the 132 bytes are the pointer that Git stores by design, and the defect is a missing filter on the consuming machine.

**Follow-up.** The checkout step already downloads LFS files and the job still sees pointers. Which other causes produce exactly this symptom?

**A strong reply covers.** `GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1` or `git lfs install --skip-smudge` makes the smudge filter pass pointers through. On GitHub, per its billing documentation, an exhausted LFS quota with no payment method on file makes clones retrieve only pointer files, which looks exactly like a machine without the client.

**Reference.** [Chapter 22](../textbook/ch22-git-lfs.md), section 22.7 and 22.12

#### Q361

**Question.** Explain what a clean filter marked `required` does differently from one that is not, and why that matters for a filter that strips notebook outputs.

**Model answer.** A filter is optional by default. The Git manual says that a missing driver definition, or a driver that exits with an error, is not an error and makes the filter a pass-through. Section 28.4 runs both cases with a filter command that does not exist. Without `required`, `git add` prints three error lines, exits with status 0 and stages the notebook with all three of its outputs. With `filter.<name>.required` set to true, `git add` fails with status 128 and nothing is staged. For a filter whose whole purpose is to keep outputs, and the data and credentials printed in them, out of history, a silent pass-through is the worst possible failure, because the commit looks normal. That is why nbstripout declares its filter required. The limit matters as much: `required` lives in the same local configuration as the driver, so a fresh clone that has neither gets no failure at all. The setting protects a configured clone whose tool broke; it does not protect an unconfigured clone, and only a CI check does that.

**Key terms.** optional filter is a pass-through; exit status 0 with outputs staged; `required` makes `git add` fail with status 128; silent failure; setting lives in local configuration; does not help an unconfigured clone

**Common weak answer.** "Required means the filter always runs for everyone." Weak because the setting is per clone and absent from a fresh clone, and the answer does not say what an optional filter does when its program is missing.

**Follow-up.** A developer hits "clean filter failed" on `git add` and unsets `required` to get unblocked. What do you tell them?

**A strong reply covers.** Install the tool or fix the path in that clone's configuration. Unsetting `required` converts a hard failure into a silent pass-through that stages the outputs, and the CI verify check will reject the commit anyway.

**Reference.** [Chapter 28](../textbook/ch28-ai-ml-workflows.md), section 28.4 and 28.16

#### Q362

**Question.** Your team "uses nbstripout", and a notebook with outputs is on `main`. How did it get there, and what do you change?

**Model answer.** "Uses nbstripout" describes some clones, not the repository. The committing clone had no filter: the attribute that names the driver is a tracked file and travelled with the clone, while the driver definition lives in each clone's configuration and did not. In that clone `git config get filter.<name>.clean` exits with status 1. Nothing stripped the notebook and nothing warned the author, and `required` could not help because it is part of the same missing configuration. A commit made through the web interface or another client has the same effect. What I change, in order: if an output printed a credential, rotate it first. Then strip the file in a configured clone with `git add --renormalize .` and commit. Then make the control one that travels: the verify mode of the tool, `nbstripout --verify` according to its documentation, which the course did not run, as a required check on a fresh checkout of every pull request. A setup step in the README and a required filter remain as conveniences that keep people from tripping the check.

**Key terms.** filter is per clone; attribute travels and driver does not; `git config get` exits 1; rotate if a secret was printed; `git add --renormalize .`; verify as a required CI check

**Common weak answer.** "Somebody bypassed the tool; remind the team to install it." Weak because nobody bypassed anything: an unconfigured clone is the default state, and a reminder is not a control.

**Follow-up.** You strip the notebook and commit the result to `main`. Is the output gone?

**A strong reply covers.** No. The new commit adds a snapshot; the earlier commit still holds the blob with outputs in every clone and fork. A printed key must be rotated, and removing the blob from history is a coordinated rewrite with `git filter-repo`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 28](../textbook/ch28-ai-ml-workflows.md), section 28.4 and 28.16

#### Q363

**Question.** `.gitignore` lists `*.ckpt`, and `git status` shows `model.ckpt` as modified. Explain, fix it, and say what your fix did not fix.

**Model answer.** The checkpoint was committed before the rule existed, and ignore patterns never affect files that are already tracked. The manual defines ignore files as specifying intentionally untracked files; the index decides what is tracked, not `.gitignore`. The evidence is in section 28.9: `git check-ignore -v` on the path exits 1, while the same command with `--no-index` shows the pattern does match the path. Retraining therefore shows as a change. The fix is `git rm --cached model.ckpt` followed by a commit, which removes the path from the index and leaves the file on disk; afterwards `git status --short --ignored` lists it as ignored. What it did not fix: history is unchanged, the blob is still reachable, and every clone still downloads it. A colleague who pulls that commit also has the file deleted from their working tree. Removing the blob from history is a rewrite with `git filter-repo`, with everything that implies for a shared repository, or you accept it and use a partial clone. If the file were a secret, rotation would come first.

**Key terms.** ignore rules do not apply to tracked files; the index decides what is tracked; `git check-ignore -v --no-index`; `git rm --cached`; blob still in history; deletion for colleagues who pull

**Common weak answer.** "Git has cached the old ignore file; clear the cache and it will be ignored." Weak because nothing is stale: the file is tracked, and the answer does not notice that untracking leaves the blob in every clone.

**Follow-up.** After your fix the checkpoint is ignored. Name two ways it can become tracked again, and what backs up the ignore rule.

**A strong reply covers.** `git add -f` defeats every ignore rule, and a weight file in a path no pattern covers is added by `git add .`. An ignore file prevents accidents and is not a security control; back it with a size and weight-file check in CI and a push ruleset on file size.

**Reference.** [Chapter 28](../textbook/ch28-ai-ml-workflows.md), section 28.9 and 28.17

#### Q364

**Question.** What does a local pre-commit hook guarantee? Name three ways a commit reaches the server without passing it, and the control for each.

**Model answer.** As a control it guarantees nothing; it gives the author feedback in seconds, in a clone where it is installed and not skipped. Three ways around it. First, it was never installed: hooks are not installed by cloning, and in section 28.10 a fresh clone with no `core.hooksPath` committed and pushed a 900 kB dump without anyone skipping anything. Second, `git commit --no-verify`, a documented option with honest uses. Third, a commit made through the web interface, the API or an agent's own Git client. A setup script reduces the first, but the control for all three is the same: run the identical checks in CI as a required check, enforced by a ruleset with restricted bypass, so the author cannot switch it off. One refinement by layer: a CI check sees a secret only after it has been pushed, so the credential must still be rotated. For secrets and oversized files the control is at push time on GitHub, with push protection or a push ruleset, which stops the bytes before they are stored.

**Key terms.** fast feedback and not a control; hooks are not cloned; `--no-verify`; web interface, API or agent client; required CI check with restricted bypass; push protection at push time

**Common weak answer.** "The hook blocks bad commits, so they cannot reach `main`." Weak because a hook that is not installed does not run, and a control the controlled person can switch off is not a control.

**Follow-up.** Why does the CI script check the range of commits a branch adds as well as the final tree?

**A strong reply covers.** A file committed and removed again within the branch is still in history, so the range check examines every file version the branch adds, and the tree check the snapshot to be merged. Both read blobs from Git, and the job needs `fetch-depth: 0`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 28](../textbook/ch28-ai-ml-workflows.md), section 28.10

#### Q365

**Question.** A colleague deleted a leaked provider key in a follow-up commit and considers the incident closed. What is still true, and what is the first action?

**Model answer.** Everything that made it an incident is still true. A commit that deletes a secret adds a new snapshot and leaves the old one in history: the key is in the earlier commit, in every clone and in every fork, and on GitHub the old commits stay reachable by commit ID. Most important, the key still works. The first action is therefore not a Git action: revoke or rotate the key at the provider. The order after that is to find out what the key could reach and whether it was used, and only then to clean up the repository, which means a coordinated history rewrite if we decide the blob must go; the full procedure is in the chapter on repository security. I would also say plainly that `git rm --cached .env` followed by a commit is not a response to a leak. For prevention the layer matters: a CI scan finds the secret after it was pushed, so only a push-time control on GitHub, such as push protection, keeps the bytes from arriving at all.

**Key terms.** deletion adds a snapshot; key remains in history, clones and forks; key is still valid; rotate or revoke first; assess what the key could reach; clean up last; push protection

**Common weak answer.** "It is fixed because the file no longer contains the key." Weak because the current snapshot is not the history, and the answer leaves a valid credential in every clone.

**Follow-up.** Why do you treat a leaked LLM provider key as more than a billing risk, and what do you arrange in advance to limit the damage?

**A strong reply covers.** What a key exposes depends on the provider and its scope; the course's example is a key that reached at least 60 private and fine-tuned models and was still valid two months after the first alert. Use a dedicated evaluation key with a spend cap, separate from production.

**Reference.** [Chapter 28](../textbook/ch28-ai-ml-workflows.md), section 28.14 and 28.10


### AI/ML workflows: senior level

#### Q366

**Question.** `git status` shows a tracked binary as modified immediately after a fresh checkout. Explain the mechanism and the two possible histories that lead to it.

**Model answer.** The commit holds the raw content on a path that `.gitattributes` assigns to LFS. With the filter installed, Git runs the clean filter on the working tree file before comparing it with the index; the filter produces a pointer, the index holds the raw blob, and the two differ, so the file is reported as modified although nobody edited it. Two histories lead there. In the first, the file was committed before the pattern was tracked: `git lfs track` only edits `.gitattributes` and applies from the next `git add`. In the second, a commit was made on a machine without the filter, such as a CI job or a fresh laptop, where `git add` stored the working tree bytes as they were; teammates then see a warning on pull that a file should have been a pointer but was not. The evidence is `git lfs fsck --pointers`, which exits non-zero and names the path, and `git cat-file -s HEAD:<path>` showing the full size. The fix is `git add --renormalize <path>` and a commit.

**Key terms.** clean filter yields a pointer; raw blob in the index; tracked after it was added; commit made without the filter; `git lfs fsck --pointers`; `git add --renormalize`

**Common weak answer.** "It is a line-ending or file-mode problem, run `git restore` on the file." Weak because restoring writes the same raw bytes again and the clean filter turns them into a pointer again; the mismatch is between the committed blob and the attributes.

**Follow-up.** Why does the prevention belong in CI or on the server and not in a local hook, and when is `git add --renormalize` not a sufficient fix?

**A strong reply covers.** The failing machine is by definition one where the local setup is missing, so only a CI job running `git lfs fsck --pointers` catches it. Renormalizing adds a commit and leaves the raw blob in history; for a file a host would reject, use `git lfs migrate import` on the unpushed commits.

**Reference.** [Chapter 22](../textbook/ch22-git-lfs.md), section 22.10 and 22.12

#### Q367

**Question.** A teammate gets "Smudge error ... remote missing object". What happened, who can fix it, and with which command? Why does a plain `git lfs push` not do it?

**Model answer.** A pointer was published without the object it refers to. The pointer blob is in the remote's Git history, but the content exists only in the author's `.git/lfs/objects`. That happens when the upload was skipped with `git push --no-verify`, when an upload was interrupted, or when the hooks directory has no LFS hook. Because the filter is marked required, the failing smudge fails the checkout, so the file is absent and not silently wrong. I would confirm it by comparing the `oid` shown by `git cat-file -p HEAD:<path>` with the contents of the remote's object store. Only someone who still has the object can fix it, with `git lfs push --all <remote> <branch>`, after which the teammate runs `git lfs pull`. A plain `git lfs push origin main` uploads nothing, because the client skips objects of commits that the remote-tracking branch already contains; it assumes those objects were uploaded with the commits. The `--all` option sends every object the branch references.

**Key terms.** pointer published without its object; `--no-verify` skips the pre-push hook; filter is required; `git lfs push --all`; remote-tracking branch already contains the commit; `oid` comparison

**Common weak answer.** "The teammate's LFS installation is broken; reinstall and run `git lfs pull` again." Weak because the teammate's client is working correctly: the object is not on the remote, and no action on the receiving side can produce it.

**Follow-up.** Nobody on the team still has the object. What is the state of the repository, what is the repair, and which habits prevent a repeat?
