**A strong reply covers.** The pointer is permanently dangling, and the only repair is a new commit with a file that exists. Prevention: never use `--no-verify` in LFS repositories, keep the LFS `pre-push` hook when adopting a hook manager, and run `git lfs prune` with `--verify-remote`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 22](../textbook/ch22-git-lfs.md), section 22.10 and 22.5

#### Q368

**Question.** What does `git lfs migrate import` do to commit IDs, to the working tree, and to the size of `.git`? What is the default scope, and what does `--everything` add?

**Model answer.** It is a history rewrite. In every commit in scope it replaces matching blobs by pointers and adds the `.gitattributes` line, so each rewritten commit and all of its descendants get new commit IDs, with the old messages, authors and dates; commits outside the scope keep their IDs. It leaves the working tree file as a pointer even with the filter installed, and `git lfs checkout` restores the content. The `.git` directory does not get smaller: the old commits are still in the reflog, so the old blobs stay until the reflog entries expire and a garbage collection runs, and the bytes are now also in `.git/lfs/objects`, once per version. The default scope is the current branch and only commits that are on no remote, which is the safe one; naming more branches adds their unpushed commits. `--everything` means every commit reachable from every local and remote ref, including commits already published. I would run `git lfs migrate info` with the same scope options first and read the commit count.

**Key terms.** history rewrite; new commit IDs for descendants; working tree left as pointers; `git lfs checkout`; reflog keeps the old blobs; default scope is unpushed commits of the current branch; `--everything` includes published commits

**Common weak answer.** "It moves the big files to LFS and shrinks the repository." Weak because it omits that commit IDs change, that the working tree is left with pointers, that `.git` does not shrink until the reflog expires, and that scope decides whether published history is rewritten.

**Follow-up.** After an import with `--everything`, `main` is reported as both ahead of and behind `origin/main`, and nothing has been pushed. Explain the state and recover from it.

**A strong reply covers.** The pushed root commit came into scope and received the `.gitattributes` line, so it and every descendant have new IDs and the two histories share no commit. Return each branch to its previous position from its reflog, then migrate again with the branches named.

**Reference.** [Chapter 22](../textbook/ch22-git-lfs.md), section 22.9 and 22.14

#### Q369

**Question.** How does `git lfs prune` decide what it may delete, and in which case does Git's reflog not protect you?

**Model answer.** `git lfs prune` deletes local LFS objects that meet three conditions together: the current checkout does not need them, they are not recent, and they have been pushed. Recent is defined by settings such as `lfs.fetchrecentrefsdays`, 7 days, plus `lfs.pruneoffsetdays`, 3 days, measured against the real clock. It refuses to delete what exists only on your machine: in the chapter's run two pushed versions were deleted and two unpushed ones stayed, including one that was not checked out. `--dry-run --verbose` previews, and `--verify-remote` asks the remote whether it really has each object before the local copy goes. A pruned object comes back with `git lfs fetch` as long as the remote has it. The exception is in the command's help text: the reflog is not considered, only commits, so LFS objects referenced only by orphaned commits are always deleted. After a reset or an amend, `git reflog` still shows the abandoned commit, but its model bytes may be gone. `git gc` never touches the LFS store.

**Key terms.** not needed by the checkout; not recent; already pushed; `--verify-remote`; reflog is not considered; orphaned commits

**Common weak answer.** "Prune removes old versions, and anything removed by mistake can be recovered through the reflog." Weak because the reflog recovers the commit and its pointer only; an object referenced solely by an orphaned commit is deleted and may exist nowhere else.

**Follow-up.** Design a disk-space cleanup for training machines that takes that exception into account.

**A strong reply covers.** Preview with `git lfs prune --dry-run --verbose`, then prune with `--verify-remote`. Before that, push any model version that matters, because objects referenced only by commits abandoned through a reset or an amend are deleted regardless of the reflog.

**Reference.** [Chapter 22](../textbook/ch22-git-lfs.md), section 22.8 and 22.13

#### Q370

**Question.** A run in the tracker names a commit. You check it out and get a different metric. List every cause you can think of, in the order you would test them, and the evidence for each.

**Model answer.** The commit is intact; what I doubt is that the commit alone identifies what ran. First, a dirty working tree: `git rev-parse HEAD` names the last commit and says nothing about modified tracked files, and classic tracking records only that commit, so two code states can share one commit ID. Evidence is a dirty flag, a diff hash or a saved patch in the run record. Second, untracked files: a new module on the import path changes behavior and is not in `git diff HEAD`. Third, the data: an ignored file edited in place, which Git never reports; I compare the checksum the run recorded with the pointer file and run the pointer tool's verify. Fourth, dependencies: an install from version ranges instead of the committed lock file, shown by the lock file hash. Fifth, the environment: an image tag that moved, where a digest would not. Sixth, the resolved configuration, including overrides. Seventh, the model: an alias or hub branch that moved. Last, for LLM evaluations, non-determinism, which is why results are compared with a tolerance.

**Key terms.** commit does not identify what ran; dirty working tree; untracked files; data checksum against the pointer; lock file and image digest; resolved configuration; mutable model reference

**Common weak answer.** "Someone must have rewritten history, or the tracker is wrong." Weak because the commit is intact and the tracker recorded what it was asked to; the answer ignores everything that determines a result and is not in a commit.

**Follow-up.** The run record says the tree was dirty and a patch was saved with it. How do you reproduce the number, and what do you say if no patch was saved?

**A strong reply covers.** Check out the recorded commit, test the patch with `git apply --check`, apply it, confirm that `git diff HEAD --binary` has the recorded SHA-256, restore the recorded data version and rerun. Without the patch the result cannot be reproduced: say so and rerun from a commit.

**Reference.** [Chapter 28](../textbook/ch28-ai-ml-workflows.md), section 28.7 and 28.8

#### Q371

**Question.** Compare Git LFS, DVC and a pointer file you maintain yourself. What is identical in all three, and what differs?

**Model answer.** The pattern is identical: hash the file, store the bytes outside Git under that hash, commit a small pointer that records the hash and size, and keep the real file out of Git's view. Git then versions the pointer, so log, diff, branches and pull requests work on it, and in all three the store is a dependency: a pointer whose object is gone identifies the data exactly and cannot produce it. They differ in how pointer and file are swapped and in constraints. Git LFS swaps them inside a required filter, so checkout is one step, and a clone without the LFS client silently gets pointers; on GitHub a file is capped at 2 to 5 GB by plan, billing is metered, each version is stored whole and objects are hard to delete. DVC, described from its documentation and not run in the course, writes a `.dvc` metafile, adds the data path to `.gitignore` and needs two steps: Git moves the metafile, then `dvc checkout` moves the bytes. A hand-maintained pointer has the same two steps.

**Key terms.** content-addressed store; pointer with hash and size; Git versions the pointer; filter swap versus two-step checkout; the store is a dependency; clone has pointers and not data

**Common weak answer.** "LFS stores big files in Git and DVC is for machine learning." Weak because neither puts the bytes in Git; the answer misses the shared mechanism and therefore the shared risk, which is the store.

**Follow-up.** What is the central weakness of the variants that ignore the real file, and where do you close it?

**A strong reply covers.** The pointer and the file can disagree and Git will not say so: an ignored file edited in place leaves `git status` silent. Only the tool's verify reports it, so the evaluation must refuse data that does not match its pointer and record the checksum it read.

**Reference.** [Chapter 28](../textbook/ch28-ai-ml-workflows.md), section 28.6 and 28.17


### AI/ML workflows: principal level

#### Q372

**Question.** Your LFS bill grows although nobody adds models. Name three mechanisms that can cause it.

**Model answer.** This is GitHub's accounting, taken from its billing documentation and not reproducible in a lab. First, every pushed version is stored in full: a one-byte change to a 500 MB file uses another 500 MB, so retraining or regenerating an existing model grows storage without any new file appearing. Second, downloads use bandwidth and uploads do not, and downloads by GitHub Actions count, so a CI matrix that pulls the same model in every job multiplies bandwidth. Third, usage always counts against the repository owner, and pushes to forks count against the parent repository's quotas, so contributors and forks spend the owner's allowance. Fourth, nothing is freed by deleting: objects removed from history still exist on the remote storage and keep counting. Billing is metered beyond an included monthly quota, 10 GiB each of storage and bandwidth on Free and Pro and 250 GiB each on Team and Enterprise Cloud; the prepaid data packs were removed. The textbook gives no per-GiB prices because it could not verify them.

**Key terms.** every version stored in full; bandwidth for downloads; Actions downloads count; owner pays for forks; objects are not freed; metered billing, no data packs

**Common weak answer.** "Someone must be pushing large files; find them and buy another data pack." Weak because storage grows with versions of existing files, CI downloads consume bandwidth with no push at all, and data packs no longer exist.

**Follow-up.** You rewrite history so that the models are no longer in LFS. Does the storage figure on GitHub go down, and what does that imply for policy?

**A strong reply covers.** No. Per GitHub's documentation the objects stay on remote storage and keep counting until the repository is deleted and recreated or Support removes them. The policy consequence is to decide what belongs in LFS before it is pushed, and to keep deletable data elsewhere.

**Reference.** [Chapter 22](../textbook/ch22-git-lfs.md), section 22.11 and 22.15

#### Q373

**Question.** When is LFS the wrong tool for model weights, and what would you use?

**Model answer.** LFS fits a modest number of mid-sized binaries that change rarely and must be versioned together with the code, such as reference checkpoints for tests. It is the wrong tool in five situations. Files above the plan's per-file cap on GitHub, 2 GB on Free and Pro, 4 GB on Team and 5 GB on Enterprise Cloud, are refused; use object storage or a model registry and keep the URI and a checksum in Git. Weights that change with every run are stored whole and billed per version, and nothing is ever freed; use DVC, which keeps small metafiles in Git and the data in a remote you control, or a model registry with the Git commit recorded beside each model version. Data that must be deletable needs storage with retention and deletion controls. Models published for others make consumers install the client and make your bandwidth pay for their downloads; use the Hugging Face Hub with a pinned `revision`, or GitHub Releases. Where contributors or CI may lack the client, use a download step with a checksum.

**Key terms.** changes rarely, versioned with the code; per-file cap by plan; every version stored whole and billed; DVC or a model registry; URI and checksum in Git; deletable data; pinned `revision`

**Common weak answer.** "LFS is the standard way to put models in Git, so use it for all weights." Weak because it ignores the per-file cap, per-version storage that is never freed, the owner paying for consumers' bandwidth, and silent pointer files on machines without the client.

**Follow-up.** When the weights move out of the repository, what remains in Git, and what does that record let you do?

**A strong reply covers.** A small text record: the URI and a checksum, or DVC's metafiles, with the Git commit recorded beside each model version in the registry. That ties a commit of the code to one exact model without Git carrying the bytes.

**Reference.** [Chapter 22](../textbook/ch22-git-lfs.md), section 22.13 and 22.11

#### Q374

**Question.** An open-source LLM project wants evaluations on pull requests from forks. Describe the collision, the dangerous workaround, and two designs you would defend.

**Model answer.** The collision is between two defaults. An LLM evaluation needs a provider API key, and GitHub Actions does not pass secrets to workflows triggered by `pull_request` from a fork, so the job fails on exactly the contributions the project most wants to evaluate. The dangerous workaround is switching the trigger to `pull_request_target`, which runs with the base repository's secrets, and then checking out the contributor's code: that executes untrusted code with your keys and your token, and a changed test file can print the key. The course's research report identifies this pattern behind several compromises, some in ML projects. The first design I would defend: run only cheap, secret-free checks on `pull_request`, including evaluation against a stub or recorded responses, and let a maintainer trigger the paid evaluation after reading the diff. The second: evaluate after merge on `main` and alert or revert on regression. In both, the evaluation job gets its own provider key with a spend cap, separate from production, so a leak is a bill with a ceiling.

**Key terms.** secrets withheld from fork pull requests; `pull_request_target` with checkout of fork code; untrusted code with secrets; secret-free checks on `pull_request`; maintainer-triggered evaluation; evaluate after merge; spend-capped key

**Common weak answer.** "Use `pull_request_target` so the secrets are available." Weak because it is the dangerous workaround itself: the contributor's code then runs with the base repository's secrets and token.

**Follow-up.** In the design where a trusted workflow reads the pull request's prompts as data, what counts as executing something from the pull request?

**A strong reply covers.** Test files, `conftest.py`, package scripts and anything a prompt template can make the harness import. The design is safe only if nothing from the pull request is executed; otherwise it is the dangerous workaround again.

**Reference.** [Chapter 28](../textbook/ch28-ai-ml-workflows.md), section 28.11

#### Q375

**Question.** An agent opens forty pull requests a day in your repository. Which of your existing controls still work, which do not, and what do you add?

**Model answer.** An agent is a contributor with a different Git client, unusual speed and no memory of our conventions, so the controls that still work are the ones that do not depend on the contributor: required checks, rulesets, push protection and required review enforced on the server. What stops working: local hooks, because an agent may use its own client or the API; conventions that live in people's heads; and review at human pace, which becomes the bottleneck or stops being real. What I add, following the course's inference from its research: every hook that matters also runs as a required check; pull requests stay small; a human approval that an automated approval cannot replace, enforced by a ruleset; no automatic agent runs on untrusted contributions and no write token unless required; a dedicated low-privilege, spend-capped key; conventions in a committed instruction file, with checks that enforce them anyway. Finally attribution, by a `Co-authored-by` trailer, a bot account or a signature, so that "which changes did an agent write" is a `git log` query.

**Key terms.** controls independent of the contributor; local hooks do not run; required checks and rulesets; human approval enforced by ruleset; prompt injection; least-privilege spend-capped key; attribution of agent commits

**Common weak answer.** "The agent follows our hooks and style guide like any developer." Weak because hooks are per clone and the agent may not use that clone, and it treats review capacity as unlimited.

**Follow-up.** How does text in an issue or a pull request title turn into a leaked CI secret, and how solid is the evidence that this happens?

**A strong reply covers.** The agent reads the text as instructions while holding credentials, so whoever steers it can read what it can. The course cites a February and March 2026 campaign, and April 2026 research on agents run as GitHub Actions that it verified only through one secondary article.

**Reference.** [Chapter 28](../textbook/ch28-ai-ml-workflows.md), section 28.15 and 28.10

#### Q376

**Question.** Design the record your evaluation harness writes so that a metric shown to the board can be reproduced a year later. What goes into it, which kinds of identifier do you forbid, and what do you not trust your experiment tracker to capture for you?

**Model answer.** The principle is that a commit alone does not identify what ran, so the record holds one immutable identifier for everything that determines the result. For code: the full commit ID, a dirty flag, the list of changed and untracked files, and a SHA-256 of `git diff HEAD --binary`, with the patch saved as an artifact. For data: the checksum of the bytes actually read, which must equal the committed pointer. For dependencies, the hash of the committed lock file; for the environment, the image digest; for the model, a registry version number or a full-length hub commit ID; and the resolved configuration itself. I forbid mutable references: branch names, HEAD, version ranges, image tags, "latest" and registry aliases. The policy is to refuse a tracked run from a tree that is dirty or has untracked files, or else to log status and diff. I do not trust the tracker: as the course describes it, classic MLflow tracking records the commit and not uncommitted changes, and Weights and Biases has code saving disabled by default, so I verify capture.

**Key terms.** commit plus dirty flag plus diff hash; untracked files; data checksum; lock file hash and image digest; resolved configuration; immutable identifiers not mutable references; verify tracker capture

**Common weak answer.** "We log the Git commit with every run, so it is reproducible." Weak because two different code states can share one commit ID, and data, dependencies, environment, model and configuration are not in the commit unless a reference to them is.

**Follow-up.** A year later the record is complete and the number still cannot be reproduced. Which dependencies outside the Git repository do you examine?

**A strong reply covers.** The data and model stores: a lifecycle rule that expired the object leaves a pointer that identifies the data and cannot produce it, because pointers are not backups. For an LLM evaluation also the provider: results are non-deterministic and are compared with a tolerance.

**Reference.** [Chapter 28](../textbook/ch28-ai-ml-workflows.md), section 28.7 and 28.8


## Area 15: Production incidents

Q377 to Q393. Running an incident: stabilise, preserve, diagnose, recover, verify, communicate, prevent.


### Production incidents: foundational level

#### Q377

**Question.** What are the four parts of an incident summary for a CTO, and what must never be claimed in the third?

**Model answer.** The four parts, in order, are what happened, the root cause, what was done and how it was verified, and prevention. What happened gives the impact first, in business terms, with times in a stated time zone and no names. The root cause is one sentence that names the mechanism and the layer: a Git default, a GitHub rule that was missing, a GitHub Actions default. The third part gives the recovery in one sentence and the check that proves it, and states what is not yet verified. Prevention names a control, its owner and its date; a control, not a promise to be careful. What must never be claimed in the third part is that something was verified when the check was not run. The summary for the rewritten production branch in section 30.15 says so openly: clones on CI caches were not yet verified. The form exists because a CTO decides three things from it: whether customers or outsiders are affected, whether anything is still at risk, and whether to spend on prevention.

**Key terms.** what happened; root cause with its layer; what was done and verified; prevention with owner and date; not yet verified; no names; impact first

**Common weak answer.** "A timeline of the commands we ran and who ran them." Weak because commands do not help a CTO decide anything, names turn it into blame, and it leaves out the layer, the proof of recovery and the control.

**Follow-up.** What makes such a summary trustworthy rather than only well formatted?

**A strong reply covers.** Five habits: separate observation from inference; give every time and ID a source such as a reflog entry, a tag or a log line; say "I do not know yet" early with the time of the next update; write "verified" only for checks run; send a short first version before the recovery.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.15


### Production incidents: working engineer level

#### Q378

**Question.** A pull request shows the same changed files as yesterday and three times as many commits. What happened, and which two comparisons explain why the views differ?

**Model answer.** The old and the rewritten version of the same commits both became reachable from the head branch. In Chapter 30 a teammate rebased the shared branch and force-pushed; a second person, with unpushed commits on the old version and a pull configured to merge, pulled and pushed the result. The two views answer different questions. The commit list is `git log <base>..<head>`: everything reachable from the head and not from the base, so it shows both series plus a merge commit nobody intended. The file view is `git diff <base>...<head>`, the diff from the merge base to the head, and two copies of one change are one change in a tree, so the files are unchanged. `git range-diff` between the old and the rebased series pairs every commit with an equals sign: the same changes under new IDs. It is not a display problem on GitHub: `git ls-remote` and a local `git log` show the commits are real. The layer is Git.

**Key terms.** two-dot commit list; three-dot diff from the merge base; old and rebased series both reachable; merge made by pull; git range-diff; same tree

**Common weak answer.** "GitHub has a display bug, the diff is fine so ignore it." Weak because the commits are really in the branch; merged as it is, duplicates and a pointless merge enter `main` and mislead `bisect` and `blame`.

**Follow-up.** How do you repair the branch without undoing the teammate's rebase, and how do you prove that no content changed?

**A strong reply covers.** Anchor the merged state and my own tip, `git reset --keep` to my tip before the pull, `git rebase --onto <rebased tip> <old shared tip>`, then push with an explicit lease. `git range-diff` pairs my commits with equals signs and `git diff --stat` against the anchored state prints nothing.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.9 and 30.16

#### Q379

**Question.** A job that runs `git describe` fails only on GitHub Actions. Name the default responsible and two remedies.

**Model answer.** The layer is GitHub Actions, and the default is in `actions/checkout`: it fetches a single commit and no tags, with `fetch-depth` at 1 and `fetch-tags` off, as of version 7.0.1. `git describe` needs a tagged ancestor and the commits between that tag and HEAD, so on the runner it stops with a message that no names were found and exit status 128, while every laptop has full history. Chapter 30 reproduces the runner with Git alone: a clone made with `--depth 1 --no-tags` has one commit, no tags and the same failure. The remedy the chapter applies is `fetch-depth: 0` on the checkout step, which fetches all history for all branches and tags, delivered on a branch as a pull request. The second remedy is to bring the missing history in another way; Chapter 14B, section 14B.12 shows that fetching the tag alone is not enough because the commits in between are still missing, and that `git fetch --unshallow` makes `git describe` work. Verification is a green run observed on GitHub.

**Key terms.** actions/checkout default; fetch-depth 1; no tags; shallow clone; fetch-depth: 0; tagged ancestor and commits between; GitHub Actions layer

**Common weak answer.** "The runner is flaky, re-run it." Weak because the failure repeats identically and began with a commit, which excludes flakiness; the failed step printed a Git message that points at the repository the runner had.

**Follow-up.** The checkout is corrected and the job still fails, and a colleague asks for an administrator merge because the change is trivial. What do you expect to find, and what do you answer?

**A strong reply covers.** A second defect behind the first: a template tracked under a name whose case differs from the name the code opens, visible in `git ls-files`. A red required check is not overridden; the status is cause removed in the files, confirmed when the run is green.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.11 and 30.18; [Chapter 14B](../textbook/ch14b-config-tags-signing.md), section 14B.12

#### Q380

**Question.** After a squash merge, with the head branch deleted on the server and pruned from your clone, `git branch -d` refuses to delete the merged branch. Why, and what do you check before `-D`?

**Model answer.** `git branch -d` deletes only a branch whose tip is reachable from its upstream, or from HEAD when it has no upstream or the upstream ref is gone, as it is here after the prune. A squash merge, done by GitHub, creates one new commit on `main` with a new ID and keeps none of the original commits, so the branch's commits are not ancestors of `main` and the refusal is correct. Before overriding it with `-D`, I compare trees, not commits: `git diff main <branch>` must be empty, and `git log main..<branch>` shows what the branch still names. `git cherry -v` is misleading here: patch IDs cannot see through a squash, because a squashed commit equals none of its parts, so every commit looks unmerged. In Chapter 30, section 30.12 the tree comparison showed that `main` matched the third commit and that a fourth commit, made after the merge and never pushed, added one file. `-D` destroys the branch reflog and the only name of unmerged commits; afterwards only the HEAD reflog holds them, by default for 30 days once unreachable. Whether work was pushed is read from `git status -sb`, not from memory.

**Key terms.** squash creates a new commit ID; not an ancestor; compare trees with git diff; git cherry cannot see through a squash; branch reflog is deleted; HEAD reflog

**Common weak answer.** "Git is wrong, the pull request was merged, so use `-D`." Weak because the refusal is correct about ancestry, and `-D` without a tree comparison is how a commit made after the merge loses its only name.

**Follow-up.** The branch was already removed with `-D` and held one commit that was never pushed. Where is that commit, and why do you not recreate and push the old branch?

**A strong reply covers.** In the HEAD reflog, which survives branch deletion: anchor it, create a new branch from current `main`, cherry-pick the one commit. Recreating the old branch would publish three commits whose content `main` already has. GitHub's "Restore branch" returns only what the server had.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.12; [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.11


### Production incidents: senior level

#### Q381

**Question.** `main` was force-pushed ten minutes ago. Before you restore it, which two things do you check, and what does the restoring command look like?

**Model answer.** The first message goes out before any command: nobody pulls or pushes `main`. Then I check two things. One, that the value I intend to restore is the newest good value. My `origin/main@{1}` from `git reflog show origin/main` is one witness; I collect the old tip from the other clones as well and compare with `git merge-base --is-ancestor`, because restoring from a stale clone loses commits pushed shortly before the incident. Two, what is being removed and whether anyone has built on it. In Chapter 30, section 30.6 the stray commits were unreviewed and nobody had built on them, and they were first given their own branch with an additive push; had someone built on the bad tip, the right move would be `git revert`. The restore is anchored in a rescue branch and pushed with an explicit lease: `git push --force-with-lease=main:<the bad ID I examined> origin rescue/main-before-force:main`. If anyone pushed to `main` meanwhile, it is refused. I verify with `git ls-remote origin`.

**Key terms.** newest good value; stale clone; git merge-base --is-ancestor; has anyone built on it; explicit lease; rescue branch; git ls-remote

**Common weak answer.** "I `git push --force` my local `main` back." Weak because a local `main` may be stale and lose recent commits, an unconditional force overwrites anything pushed during the recovery, and the stray commits are thrown away instead of being given a branch.

**Follow-up.** After the restore, what do teammates do with their clones, and what would have refused the original push?

**A strong reply covers.** `git fetch`, then `git status -sb`; a clone whose `main` shows `ahead` stops and asks. On GitHub, a ruleset with "Block force pushes" on the default branch rejects the push; on the Git side the default `push.default=simple` would have refused it.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.6 and 30.21

#### Q382

**Question.** A colleague says "I deleted the file with the key and pushed, so we are fine". Give the order of the response and say what the deletion did and did not do.

**Model answer.** The deletion added a snapshot without the file and removed none: the commit that added the key is still in history, `git show <commit>:<path>` still prints it, and `git branch -r --contains <commit>` may list more branches than the author knows, as it did in Chapter 30 when a teammate had based work on his. A private repository limits the audience; it does not end the exposure. The order is fixed, and its first step is not Git: contain by revoking or rotating the credential before any Git command, then assess which secret, since when, which refs, who could read it and whether it was used, then eradicate, recover, communicate and prevent. Revocation works against every copy, including those that cannot be reached, and GitHub's documentation says rotation may be sufficient and a rewrite may not be warranted. The verification that matters happens in the provider's console: the old credential is rejected. Whether it was used is answered only by the issuer's logs.

**Key terms.** deletion adds a snapshot; rotate first; contain assess eradicate recover communicate prevent; git branch -r --contains; private is not unexposed; issuer's logs

**Common weak answer.** "Rewrite history with a filter tool and force-push right away." Weak because every Git command typed before rotation is time in which the key still works, and a rewrite removes nothing from copies that were already taken.

**Follow-up.** After the rewrite and the forced push, no ref reaches the old commit. Is the secret gone from the server and from the clones?

**A strong reply covers.** No. The transcript in section 30.17 shows the server still returning the object by ID. In the sandbox `git gc --prune=now` on the server removes it; on GitHub that is a Support request, per its documentation. Each clone keeps it through reflogs until re-cloned or expired and pruned.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.7 and 30.17

#### Q383

**Question.** Why is `--force-with-lease` not a defense against the situation in which a teammate has unpublished commits on a branch you rebased?

**Model answer.** The lease protects commits on the server, and the teammate's commits are not on the server. A lease makes the push conditional on the server's ref still holding the expected value, so it refuses to overwrite something another person pushed. Unpublished commits exist only in the teammate's clone, built on the old series; the server has nothing to compare. The damage comes one step later and in their clone: their `git pull`, configured with `pull.rebase=false`, merges the old series they had with the rebased series they fetched, and the push of that merge makes both reachable. In section 30.16 the two reflogs show it: `pull: forced-update` on the remote-tracking branch and a merge made by pull on the local branch, and the pull request listed nine commits instead of five. The layer is Git. The controls are `pull.rebase true` or `pull.ff only`, and an agreement that whoever rewrites a shared branch announces it first with the old tip and the command teammates need.

**Key terms.** lease protects the server's commits; unpublished commits live in a clone; pull.rebase=false merges both series; duplicated commits; announce a rewrite; pull.ff only

**Common weak answer.** "With a lease a force push is safe for everyone." Weak because the lease checks one value on the server; it knows nothing of work that was never pushed, and the rewrite still invalidates what teammates built on.

**Follow-up.** Suppose the teammate had `pull.rebase=true`. Is a pull after a forced update then always safe for their work?

**A strong reply covers.** No. With no upstream named, the rebase takes the fork point from the remote-tracking reflog; a commit you had pushed and the force push removed counts as old upstream history and is not replayed, though the pull reports success. `ORIG_HEAD` and the reflog still name it.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.9 and 30.16

#### Q384

**Question.** When is `git revert -m 1` the wrong way to take a mistaken merge out of a topic branch?

**Model answer.** It is wrong whenever the merged branch will be merged again later, and whenever the goal is a pull request that lists only its own commits. A revert adds a commit that undoes the content; it does not remove the merge. The commits of the other branch stay ancestors of the topic branch, so the commit list stays long. Worse, once the topic branch is merged, `main` contains those commits together with a commit that undoes them, so the later real merge of that branch brings nothing: Git sees the commits as already present. A reverted merge is not a removed merge. The command is appropriate only when the merged branch will never be merged again as it is. For a topic branch with one author the merge is removed instead: anchor the tip, `git rebase --onto <merge>^1 <merge>`, then `git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes`. Verification is that `git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/develop <head>` exits 1. If the revert already happened, the repair is to revert the revert or rebuild.

**Key terms.** reverted merge is not a removed merge; commits stay ancestors; later merge brings nothing; rebase --onto the first parent; revert the revert; single-author topic branch

**Common weak answer.** "Revert is always the safe choice because it needs no force push." Weak because it is safe now and silently breaks later: the next merge of the same branch is empty, and the pull request still lists every foreign commit.

**Follow-up.** A different incident also had a faulty merge, on shared `main` with four commits on top of it, and there neither a revert of the merge nor a rebuild was used. Why?

**A strong reply covers.** `main` is shared, so nothing is rewritten, and reverting the merge would remove the feature it brought. One forward commit restored the two lost changes, adapted to the rename, with a message naming the merge and the lost commits.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.10 and 30.21

#### Q385

**Question.** A fix is in `git log main` and not in the file. Which command shows what happened, and why did `git log -- <file>` hide the commits?

**Model answer.** `git show --remerge-diff <merge>` shows it. It re-runs the merge and prints what the person who made it changed relative to Git's mechanical result. In Chapter 30, section 30.13 it showed one real conflict resolved for one side and, decisively, a hunk that Git had merged cleanly being removed. A resolution that changes a hunk Git had already merged is the signature of taking one side of the whole file, here with `git checkout --ours <path>`, where "ours" in a merge is the branch you are on and not the team's version. The commits were hidden because `git log` with a path simplifies history: at a merge whose result for that path equals one parent, it follows only that parent, and the lost fixes sit on the discarded side. `git log --full-history -- <path>` lists them. The preceding evidence is that `git merge-base --is-ancestor` exits 0 for the fix and no revert exists. The layer is Git; GitHub merged what it was given.

**Key terms.** git show --remerge-diff; history simplification; --full-history; ours is the current branch; whole-file resolution; cleanly merged hunk removed

**Common weak answer.** "Someone must have reverted it or the repository is corrupt." Weak because no revert exists and nothing supports corruption; the answer does not know that a merge commit can discard a change without any diff in the usual views.

**Follow-up.** Why could the pull request review not catch this loss, and which control would have?

**A strong reply covers.** After the bad merge the branch and the merge base agreed on those lines, so the pull request diff had nothing to show. A regression test for the lost behavior would have failed on the branch; reviewing a merge with `git show --remerge-diff` before pushing is the checklist control.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.13

#### Q386

**Question.** The server keeps no reflog. Where does the timeline of a server-side branch come from, on plain Git and on GitHub?

**Model answer.** A bare repository, which is what a server holds, keeps no reflog unless `core.logAllRefUpdates` is set. On plain Git the timeline is therefore the sum of what the clones remember. Each clone's `git reflog show origin/<branch>` records the server's value at every fetch or push from that clone, and `--date=iso` adds the times; local branch reflogs, the HEAD reflog and tags are further witnesses. In section 30.6 the timeline came from three clones' reflogs of `origin/main`. These records are per clone and expire: by default 90 days, 30 for unreachable entries, and they are gone when the ref is pruned. That is why preserving includes asking colleagues not to run `git fetch --prune`, `git gc` or a re-clone until their reflogs have been read. On GitHub, which is not Git, the platform adds its own records, described from its documentation: the Activity view, `PushEvent` records with the before value, and the audit log. Those also name the account, which no clone can.

**Key terms.** bare repository has no reflog; sum of what the clones remember; reflog of origin/branch; expiry and pruning; Activity view; PushEvent; audit log

**Common weak answer.** "Look at the server's reflog on GitHub." Weak because GitHub exposes no server-side reflog; the answer misses that the evidence is spread over clones, expires, and is destroyed by a prune, a `git gc` or a re-clone.

**Follow-up.** Outside a sandbox you cannot read a colleague's clone. How do you get that evidence, and what in the team's conduct decides whether it still exists?

**A strong reply covers.** Ask the colleague to run `git reflog show origin/main` and paste the output. People who expect blame run `git gc`, re-clone or stay silent, and the evidence is gone, which is why a blameless practice is a technical requirement.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.2 and 30.6

#### Q387

**Question.** What makes a postmortem blameless in practice, and why does that matter for the evidence?

**Model answer.** A blameless postmortem explains how the system allowed the incident and treats every person's action as reasonable given what they knew. In practice there is a test: replace every name by a role, and if the document still explains the incident, it is about the system. The useful question is never who ran the command but why running it looked right and why nothing stopped it; the template has a section for exactly that, the contributing conditions, and its list of what went badly carries no names. It matters for evidence because in a Git incident the evidence comes from people: one colleague's reflog, another's account of a reset, a developer who says a password was committed. People who expect blame run `git gc`, re-clone or stay silent, and the evidence is gone. That makes blamelessness a technical requirement, not a courtesy. For the same reason severity never depends on who caused the incident, the document is written within days while reflogs and memories exist, and the people involved review the timeline.

**Key terms.** reasonable given what they knew; replace names by roles; why did it look right; evidence comes from people; git gc and re-clone destroy it; contributing conditions

**Common weak answer.** "Blameless means we do not say who did it, to be kind." Weak because it treats the practice as courtesy; the point is that blame makes people destroy or withhold reflogs and accounts, and a name explains nothing that can be changed.

**Follow-up.** A postmortem arrives whose only action item reads "be more careful with force pushes". What is your verdict?

**A strong reply covers.** It has not found the cause. An action needs a control, an owner, a date and a way to know it works; here the strongest is the server refusing forced updates of the branch, not a habit that decays and does not reach new people.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.19

#### Q388

**Question.** The deploy job refuses to run from `production` and nobody knows why; three colleagues have clones and are still working. Run the incident: what are the stages in order, what is your first action, and what must be preserved before anything is touched?

**Model answer.** The loop has seven stages: stabilise, preserve, diagnose, recover, verify, communicate, prevent. My first action is not a Git command but one sentence in the channel: nobody pushes to or resets `production` until I say so. Communication therefore starts early, as soon as I know which branch people must leave alone and long before I know the cause. Preserving means giving every state I may need a name before anything moves, with `git branch rescue/<what> <id>`, and it means asking colleagues not to run `git fetch --prune`, `git gc` or a re-clone until their reflogs have been read. The reason is that the server keeps no reflog: the history of its branch exists only as the sum of what the clones remember, plus what GitHub records. Preserving and diagnosing use only commands that add refs or read state. Recovery takes the change that destroys least and is undone most readily; verification re-runs the commands that showed the problem and the check the affected system runs, here the release job's ancestry test.

**Key terms.** stabilise first; first message before the cause is known; rescue refs; no prune, gc or re-clone; server keeps no reflog; only commands that add refs or read state

**Common weak answer.** "First find out what happened, then tell people." Weak because colleagues keep pushing, resetting and cleaning up while you investigate, which spreads the damage and destroys the reflogs that are the only record of the server's branch.

**Follow-up.** A colleague sees "diverged" on that branch without having made commits and is advised to reset to the server. What is wrong with the advice, and what should the handbook say?

**A strong reply covers.** The reset makes a second clone adopt the rewritten history and build on it; in section 30.8 it turned one affected clone into two. The handbook line: "diverged, and I made no commits" means the server's history was replaced; stop and ask.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.2 and 30.8


### Production incidents: principal level

#### Q389

**Question.** Rank these controls by strength for "nobody force-pushes production": a handbook rule, a client alias, a ruleset, a review checklist. Justify the order.

**Model answer.** Strongest first: the ruleset, the client alias, the review checklist, the handbook rule. A control is something that still works when the person is new, tired or in a hurry, and the ranking follows from who has to cooperate. A ruleset is the server refusing: it applies to every client and tool whatever their configuration. That is GitHub, not Git. For the production branch, Chapter 30 names blocking force pushes, restricting deletions, requiring a pull request and an empty bypass list. A client alias is a safe default on the client: it works until someone has another configuration, which is how the force push to the wrong branch began. A review checklist depends on the reviewer doing the step. A handbook rule is training and habit: it decays and does not reach new people. Between the ruleset and the client sits automation, such as the release job's ancestry test, which runs every time but only on what it was written to see. I prefer one strong control to five weak ones.

**Key terms.** the server refuses; every client whatever its configuration; client default; checklist depends on the reviewer; habit decays; one strong control; empty bypass list

**Common weak answer.** "All four together, defense in depth." Weak because it does not rank: three of the four depend on each person's configuration, diligence or memory, and only the server-side rule holds when someone is new, tired or in a hurry.

**Follow-up.** You chose the ruleset. Which questions must still be answered before you call the control done?

**A strong reply covers.** What legitimate action it will block and the path for that case; whether the feature is available on the plan, since some ruleset features are plan-gated; and how I will know it works, through the ruleset's insights or an attempt in a sandbox.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.20 and 30.8

#### Q390

**Question.** A production branch was rewritten by a forced push, and a teammate has since shipped one legitimate commit on top of the rewritten history. You can keep the rewritten history and re-add what was lost, or restore the old history with another forced push. How do you decide, and how do you carry out the choice?

**Model answer.** The deciding question is whether commit IDs of that branch are recorded elsewhere. Keeping the rewritten history needs no further force, but the deployed tag is never an ancestor of the branch again and every recorded ID points off-branch; for a production branch that deployment records refer to by ID, I restore. Where adding suffices and nothing is recorded by ID, I do not rewrite, because a rewrite of shared history is a second incident for everyone with a clone. The restore in Chapter 30, section 30.8 has three steps: name the state about to be replaced with a rescue branch, `git cherry-pick` the teammate's commit onto the real history, then `git push --force-with-lease=production:<the ID I examined>`, conditional on the server's current value. Each clone that adopted the rewrite proves nothing of its own is lost with `git cherry -v origin/production production`, then moves with `git reset --keep origin/production`. Verification is the release job's own test: `git merge-base --is-ancestor <deploy tag> origin/production` exits 0.

**Key terms.** IDs recorded elsewhere; deployed tag as ancestor; restore and carry the newer commit over; explicit lease; git cherry -v before git reset --keep; second incident

**Common weak answer.** "Never force-push production, so keep the rewritten history and patch forward." Weak because it applies a rule without weighing the cost: the deployed commit is then never an ancestor of the branch and every recorded ID points off-branch.

**Follow-up.** The person who rewrote it says the result is "the same code, fewer commits". How do you test that claim, and what did the test reveal?

**A strong reply covers.** It is a claim about trees, so compare trees: `git diff --stat` between the old tip and the rewritten one. It showed a file that had lost a fix, because the interactive rebase dropped a commit when a todo line was deleted.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.8 and 30.22

#### Q391

**Question.** An incident on the production branch deployed nothing and no customer was affected. The CTO asks why you rated it SEV 2 and wants the root cause in two sentences that tell a non-specialist where the fix belongs. What do you say?

**Model answer.** Severity is assigned on what could have happened in the window, not only on what did. Nothing shipped, yet the only thing between the rewritten branch and production was one check, the release job's refusal to deploy when the running commit is not an ancestor of the branch; a shared release branch held wrong content, which is SEV 2 on the working scale of Chapter 30. The root cause in two sentences: a history clean-up on the production branch was force-pushed and dropped a fix; Git allows this, and our GitHub rules for that branch did not block force pushes. Naming the layer is what makes the sentence usable, because it tells the executive that the remedy is a rule on the platform, not more training. Then I add what was done and the check that proves it, what is not yet verified, and the control with its owner and date. I give no names: severity never depends on who caused the incident, and commands do not help the CTO decide anything.

**Key terms.** what could have happened in the window; one check stood between; mechanism and layer; missing GitHub rule; not yet verified; control with owner and date

**Common weak answer.** "It was a near miss with no impact, so SEV 3, and the cause was a developer's mistake." Weak because it rates only what happened, names a person where a missing rule is the cause, and gives the executive nothing to change.

**Follow-up.** Which rule about severity applies the moment a secret is involved, and why does following it cost little?

**A strong reply covers.** Raise the level at once: a live credential pushed anywhere is SEV 1 until rotation is confirmed, and the CTO and security are told immediately. Lowering the level later costs nothing.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.3 and 30.15

#### Q392

**Question.** A bare `git push --force` from a feature branch replaced `main`. Walk from that root cause to a control: which layers could have refused the action, which control do you choose, and what must you settle before it goes live?

**Model answer.** The root cause has two layers. In Git, one clone had `push.default=upstream` and a feature branch created from `origin/main`, so its upstream was `origin/main`; a bare push updates the upstream whatever its name, and `--force` removed the fast-forward check. On GitHub, no rule stopped a forced update of `main`. From there I ask four questions. Which layer could have refused: the platform, the pipeline, the client or a reviewer. What is the strongest control on that layer and on our plan: a ruleset that blocks force pushes on the default branch, which applies to every client. What legitimate action will it block, and what is the path for that case: the recovery in this very incident was a forced update of `main` with an explicit lease, so the route for a justified restore has to be agreed beforehand; that last point is my inference from section 30.20, not a step the chapter runs. And how will I know it works: the ruleset's insights or an attempt in a sandbox. I choose the server-side rule and still correct the clone.

**Key terms.** which layer could have refused; ruleset blocks force pushes; push.default=upstream; legitimate action blocked; how will we know it works; one strong control

**Common weak answer.** "Tell everyone to stop using `--force` and add it to the handbook." Weak because a habit decays and does not reach new people; the answer never asks which layer could have refused the push or how the control would be proven.

**Follow-up.** Git's default `push.default=simple` would have refused this push. Why is restoring that default in the affected clone not a sufficient control?

**A strong reply covers.** A safe default on the client works until someone has another configuration, and this incident began in a clone that had one. The server refusing applies to every client and tool whatever its configuration, so it ranks first.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.6 and 30.20

#### Q393

**Question.** A recovery on a shared branch can itself become the second incident. Name the ways the recovery fails under time pressure, how each is noticed, and the guard against each.

**Model answer.** Chapter 30 lists them, and each has a guard. A second "fix" such as `git reset --hard`, `git gc`, a re-clone or `git fetch --prune` destroys evidence, noticed when a reflog entry is missing; the guard is to stabilise first and ask for no clean-up before reflogs are read. The old value is restored from a stale clone, noticed when recently pushed commits are missing; collect the old tip from every clone and from tags and compare with `git merge-base --is-ancestor`. A bare `--force` overwrites a teammate's new push; always use `--force-with-lease=<ref>:<expect>` with the value examined. A revert is used where a merge had to be removed, noticed when a later merge brings nothing; decide by asking what will be merged later. Git clean-up starts before a credential is rotated; the order is fixed, rotation first. And the summary claims more than was checked; "verified" is written only for checks that were run. The common root is acting on one clone's belief about shared state.

**Key terms.** evidence destroyed by a second fix; stale clone; explicit lease; revert versus removing a merge; rotate before clean-up; verified only when checked

**Common weak answer.** "If the restore goes wrong we can always get it back from the reflog." Weak because the reflog is per clone, expires, and is the first thing a hasty clean-up destroys; the server has none.

**Follow-up.** A week after a history rewrite that removed commits, the old commits are back on the server. What happened, and which instruction prevents it?

**A strong reply covers.** A stale clone pushed the removed history back, through a merge or a plain pull that joined the old commits. Repeat the clean-up and find the clone; the guard is instructions per clone, and old branches are transplanted with `git rebase --onto <new> <old> <branch>`, never merged.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.21 and 30.22


## Area 16: Debugging

Q394 to Q420. History investigation and the diagnosis method: ranges, blame, bisect, pickaxe, interrupted operations.


### Debugging: foundational level

#### Q394

**Question.** What is the difference between `..` and `...`, in `git log` and in `git diff`?

**Model answer.** The dots mean different things in the two commands. In `git log` and `git rev-list` they select sets of commits by reachability. `A..B` is the commits reachable from B and not from A, the same set as `^A B` or `B --not A`. `A...B` is the symmetric difference: commits reachable from either tip but not from both, and `--left-right` marks which side each one is on. In `git diff` nothing is a range, because a diff always compares exactly two snapshots. `git diff A..B` is a synonym of `git diff A B`, the trees of the two tips. `git diff A...B` compares the tree of the merge base of A and B with the tree of B, the same as `git diff --merge-base A B`. So the meanings cross over: the diff that corresponds to the log range `A..B` is the three-dot diff. In a range an omitted side means HEAD.

**Key terms.** reachability; symmetric difference; merge base; two endpoints, not ranges; synonym of `A B`; `--left-right`

**Common weak answer.** "Two dots is a range and three dots is a wider range." Weak because that is true only for `git log`; in `git diff` two dots is not a range at all and three dots switches the left side to the merge base, and the answer never defines either form by reachability.

**Follow-up.** An engineer says "`A..B` is the commits between A and B". Where does the word "between" mislead, and what does an empty `A..B` prove?

**A strong reply covers.** A range is a reachability set, not an interval on a line: with merges in the graph it can contain commits made long before A. An empty `A..B` means B is an ancestor of A, which is the test `git merge-base --is-ancestor B A` performs.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14A](../textbook/ch14a-history-investigation.md), section 14A.2 and 14A.8

#### Q395

**Question.** What exactly does a row of `git blame` assert? Give three situations in which the named author did not write the logic on that line.

**Model answer.** A row asserts one thing: this line, as it exists in the revision being blamed, was last changed by that commit, according to the diffs Git computed between each commit and its parent. It prints that commit's author and author date. It says nothing about earlier versions of the line, about lines that were deleted, or about the reason. Three situations in which the named author did not write the logic. First, a formatter commit re-indented the line or changed its quotes, so the person who ran the formatter owns it; `-w` sees through whitespace and `--ignore-rev` through the whole commit. Second, the code was cut from one file and pasted into another: to plain blame a new file is new lines, and `-C` is needed to reach the commit that wrote them. Third, a squash merge: the person who performed the merge is the author of every line, and only the `Co-authored-by` trailers or the pull request name the writers. The next command after blame is `git show` on the commit.

**Key terms.** last changed, not written; depends on diff alignment; formatter commit; code moved between files, `-C`; squash merge; deleted lines have no row; `git show` next

**Common weak answer.** "Blame tells you who wrote the line." Weak because it reports the last change as a diff aligned it; the candidate will then name the person who ran a formatter or pressed the merge button, and cannot find a line that was removed.

**Follow-up.** The defect is a call that was removed from a line. Why can blame on the current file never name the commit that removed it, and what do you run instead?

**A strong reply covers.** Blame annotates lines that exist; a deleted or replaced line has no row, and the line standing there now may belong to a later commit. Use `git log -S` with the removed string, or `git log -L` on the function, which shows deleted lines; blaming the parent of a suspect commit steps behind it.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14A](../textbook/ch14a-history-investigation.md), section 14A.16, 14A.17 and 14A.18

#### Q396

**Question.** A developer says "my commits are gone". Which commands do you run before you touch anything, in which order, and what does each tell you?

**Model answer.** I run the fixed opening of ten read-only commands, in the same order every time. `git status` comes first, for its first line: a branch, a detached HEAD, or an operation in progress. `git branch -vv` shows where each branch points, its upstream, and ahead, behind or gone. `git remote -v` shows whether there is more than one remote or differing URLs. `git log --graph --decorate --oneline --all` shows where each name sits and which commits have no name. `git reflog`, read from the bottom up, is the sequence of events. `git rev-parse` turns names into exact IDs and says whether HEAD is a branch. `git show --stat HEAD` confirms which commit this is. `git diff` and `git diff --cached` find work that exists in no commit, which a wrong fix destroys without a trace. `git config list --show-origin --show-scope` shows upstream pairs and the push, pull and rebase settings with their scope. `git ls-files` shows whether the files in question are tracked. Nothing state-changing is typed until the root cause is written down.

**Key terms.** first line of git status; git branch -vv; reflog read bottom up; git diff and git diff --cached; read-only; fixed order; upstream; unnamed commits

**Common weak answer.** "I look at `git log`, find the commit in `git reflog` and reset to it." Weak because it skips the first line of `git status` and the two diffs, so a stopped operation or uncommitted work goes unnoticed, and it moves a ref before the cause is known.

**Follow-up.** Those commands describe one clone. Which of your conclusions remain unproven about the server, and which diagnostic that people treat as harmless does change something?

**A strong reply covers.** Remote-tracking branches show the server as of the last fetch; `git ls-remote origin` asks it directly. `git fetch` moves remote-tracking refs and, with pruning, deletes stale ones with their reflogs, so record `git rev-parse origin/main` first when the stale value is evidence.

**Reference.** [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.2 and 29.3

#### Q397

**Question.** Without running `git status`, how do you tell from the `.git` directory whether a merge, a rebase, a cherry-pick, a revert or a bisect is in progress? Name the files.

**Model answer.** An operation in progress is nothing but files in `.git`; Git has no process that is a rebase, and `git status` prints its first lines from those files. A merge leaves `MERGE_HEAD`, the commit being merged in, with `MERGE_MODE`, `MERGE_MSG` and `AUTO_MERGE`. A rebase leaves the directory `rebase-merge`, or `rebase-apply` with the older apply backend, plus `REBASE_HEAD`; inside the directory `head-name` is the branch that will be moved, `orig-head` its tip at the start, `onto` the new base and `git-rebase-todo` the remaining picks, and `.git/HEAD` holds a raw commit ID. A cherry-pick leaves `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD`, and a `sequencer` directory when several commits were requested. A revert leaves `REVERT_HEAD`. A bisect leaves `BISECT_LOG`, `BISECT_START` and `BISECT_TERMS`, with marks under `refs/bisect/`. `ORIG_HEAD` and `FETCH_HEAD` are records of past commands, not of an operation in progress. Because the state is files, a stopped operation survives a reboot and can be weeks old.

**Key terms.** MERGE_HEAD; rebase-merge or rebase-apply; CHERRY_PICK_HEAD; REVERT_HEAD; BISECT_LOG; sequencer; ORIG_HEAD is not an operation; state is files

**Common weak answer.** "I look for a lock file or for `ORIG_HEAD`." Weak because `ORIG_HEAD` is a record of a past command, not of an operation in progress; the answer names none of the real state files and misses bisect, which has no conflict and a clean working tree.

**Follow-up.** Git's own message for a leftover rebase proposes removing the `.git/rebase-merge` directory. What does deleting state files by hand do, and what do you use instead?

**A strong reply covers.** It ends the bookkeeping, not the operation: the record of where the branch was and what remains is gone, and a merge ended this way became an ordinary one-parent commit in Lab 35.2. Anchor HEAD first, then use `git rebase --quit` or `--abort`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.6


### Debugging: working engineer level

#### Q398

**Question.** `git diff main..feature` and `git log main..feature` use the same two dots. What does each do, and which diff form matches the log form?

**Model answer.** For `git log`, `main..feature` is a set defined by reachability: every commit reachable from `feature` and not from `main`, that is, what the branch has that `main` lacks. For `git diff` the two dots carry no range meaning: `git diff main..feature` is a synonym of `git diff main feature` and compares the trees of the two tips without reading the graph. If `main` gained commits after the fork, their changes are absent from the tree of `feature`, so that diff prints them as deletions the branch never made. The diff form that matches the log form is three dots, `git diff main...feature`, or the explicit `git diff --merge-base main feature`: it compares the merge base with the tip of `feature`, which is what the branch introduces. Chapter 14A, section 14A.2 shows the two forms disagreeing about two files, and the manual states that diff compares two endpoints, not ranges.

**Key terms.** reachable from `feature` and not from `main`; synonym of `git diff main feature`; trees of the two tips; three-dot diff; `--merge-base`; base progress shown as deletions

**Common weak answer.** "Both show what is on the feature branch and not on `main`." Weak because `git diff` has no ranges: two dots compares the two tips, so the candidate will read the base branch's own progress, reversed, as deletions made by the feature.

**Follow-up.** For one file, the three-dot diff of a branch shows a paragraph that `main` already contains, while the two-endpoint diff shows nothing. Which of the two is wrong, and how do you show why they differ?

**A strong reply covers.** Neither is wrong. The paragraph was written on the branch and cherry-picked to `main`: the tips agree, the merge base lacks it, so three dots reports it as a change of the branch. `git log --left-right --cherry-pick main...feature` drops both commits because they carry the same patch.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14A](../textbook/ch14a-history-investigation.md), section 14A.2 and 14A.8

#### Q399

**Question.** Git stores no renames. Name three commands whose output depends on rename detection, and describe a commit that defeats it.

**Model answer.** A commit records a snapshot and parent links; a rename is inferred when `git diff` sees one path disappear, another appear, and their contents similar enough. Identical blob IDs are an exact rename; otherwise Git computes a similarity index and pairs files at or above a threshold, 50% by default and adjustable with `-M`. Everything built on that pass inherits its limits: `git diff` and `git status` when they report a rename, `git log --follow` when it continues a file's history under the old name, `git blame` when it follows lines across a whole-file rename, and the rename handling of `git merge`. The commit that defeats it renames a file and rewrites about half of it in one step. In Chapter 14A, section 14A.4, such a pair is 43% similar, so `git status` prints a deletion and an addition and the trail ends there. Scale is a second limit: above `diff.renameLimit` candidates the inexact comparison is skipped. The prevention is to rename in one commit and edit in the next.

**Key terms.** renames are computed, not stored; similarity index; 50% default threshold; `git log --follow`; `git blame`; rename plus rewrite in one commit; rename first, edit in the next commit

**Common weak answer.** "Git records the rename in the commit when you rename the file through Git." Weak because nothing is recorded: detection runs at diff time on content similarity, which is why a rename combined with a rewrite breaks `--follow` and blame.

**Follow-up.** Two investigators run `git diff --name-status` on the same two commits and report different rename pairs. How is that possible, and what do you require in an incident report?

**A strong reply covers.** Rename pairs are the result of a heuristic, so a different threshold such as `-M90%`, `--no-renames`, the rename limit or a different Git version gives different pairs for identical commits. The report must quote the exact options used; only the two snapshots are facts.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14A](../textbook/ch14a-history-investigation.md), section 14A.4 and 14A.10

#### Q400

**Question.** Explain `-S` and `-G` to a colleague, with one commit that the first misses and the second reports, and one case where `-G` is noise.

**Model answer.** Both are filters of `git log`. `-S` with a string reports a commit when the number of occurrences of that string in a file changes: an inventory count. `-G` with a regular expression reports a commit when its patch has an added or removed line that matches: a ledger of movements. The argument of `-S` is literal unless `--pickaxe-regex` is given; the argument of `-G` is always a regular expression. The commit that `-S` misses edits a line and keeps the string. In Chapter 14A, section 14A.11, the commit that raised the pass mark changed the value on the `PASS_MARK` line, the count stayed the same, and only `-G` reported it. The noise case is the formatter commit that re-indented a line mentioning `PASS_MARK`: `-G` reports it although nothing of interest changed. Use `-S` for "when was this introduced or removed" and `-G` for "which commits touched lines that mention this", add `-p` to read the evidence, and remember that both search only the commits the walk visits.

**Key terms.** change in the number of occurrences; added or removed line matches; literal versus regular expression; line edited, string kept; formatter noise; counted per file; `--all` to widen the walk

**Common weak answer.** "`-S` searches for a string and `-G` does the same with a regular expression." Weak because it misses the real difference, a count per file against matching patch lines, so the candidate cannot explain why `-S` is silent when a value on the line changes.

**Follow-up.** `-S` named a commit as the removal of a statement, but that commit only edited the end of the line. What was wrong with the query, and in which other case does `-S` report a commit that neither added nor deleted the code?

**A strong reply covers.** The search string was longer than the stable part of the statement, so an edit of its tail changed the count; search the shortest string that is specific and read the patch. `-S` also counts per file, so code moved to another file is reported: one file lost an occurrence and another gained one.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14A](../textbook/ch14a-history-investigation.md), section 14A.11

#### Q401

**Question.** You found the commit that introduced a bug. Which commands tell you which releases and which open branches contain it?

**Model answer.** This is a reachability question: a release or a branch contains the commit when the commit is an ancestor of that tag or branch tip. `git tag --contains` with the commit lists every tag whose history includes it, which is the list of affected releases. `git branch --all --contains` lists the local and remote-tracking branches that include it, which covers work that was cut after the commit. `git describe --contains` names the commit relative to a tag that contains it. For one yes-or-no check in a script, `git merge-base --is-ancestor` with the commit and a release tag answers through its exit status. Then ask whether anything later touched the same code, with `git log` over the range from the commit to `main`, limited to the file. Chapter 14A, section 14A.19 runs these as step 8 of its method, after step 7 has confirmed the suspect with a test at the commit and at its parent, because every earlier tool produces a suspect and not a proof.

**Key terms.** `git tag --contains`; `git branch --all --contains`; reachability; `git describe --contains`; `git merge-base --is-ancestor`; ancestry, not content

**Common weak answer.** "Search `git log` on each release branch for the commit message." Weak because a message is not identity and the search is manual and incomplete; containment is a reachability fact that `--contains` reads from the graph.

**Follow-up.** A squash-merged copy of the faulty change also exists on another branch. Will those commands find it, and why?

**A strong reply covers.** No. `--contains` follows ancestry, and a squash merge or cherry-pick creates a new commit with a different commit ID and no parent link to the original. The graph knows ancestry, not content; search for the content instead, with `git log --all -S` and the faulty string.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14A](../textbook/ch14a-history-investigation.md), section 14A.19 and 14A.8

#### Q402

**Question.** `git push` prints "Everything up-to-date" and the commit is not on the server. Give three states that produce this and the command that separates them.

**Model answer.** The message is a statement about one ref: the local branch and the server's branch of that name point at the same commit. It says nothing about where the new commit is. Three states produce it. First, the commit is not on the branch that was pushed because HEAD is detached or a rebase stopped, and the commit extended the detached HEAD while the branch ref stayed put. Second, the commit is on another branch. Third, the push went to another remote or another branch than the one people are looking at. The first line of `git status` separates the detached or in-progress case. `git branch -a --contains <id>` says which branch, if any, holds the commit; in the case of Chapter 29, section 29.3, it listed only the detached HEAD. `git remote -v` and `git ls-remote origin` settle which server was addressed and what it holds now, which also rejects the theory of a stale pull request page. The layer is Git; GitHub displayed the branch it was given.

**Key terms.** statement about one ref; detached HEAD; stopped rebase; git branch -a --contains; git ls-remote; another remote or branch; first line of git status

**Common weak answer.** "The push worked, so GitHub must be showing a stale page." Weak because it blames the wrong layer without evidence: `git ls-remote origin` shows the server never received the commit, and the answer never asks which ref was pushed.

**Follow-up.** In the worked case the commits sat on a detached HEAD inside a stopped rebase. Why was finishing the rebase and force-pushing not the chosen fix?

**A strong reply covers.** Finishing gives the published branch new commit IDs on top of `main`, needs `git push --force-with-lease` on a branch with an open pull request, outdates review comments, and two more picks may conflict. Anchoring, aborting, cherry-picking the two commits and pushing a fast-forward only adds.

**Reference.** [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.3 and 29.11

#### Q403

**Question.** During a rebase, when does the branch ref move, and what follows from that for commits made while the rebase is stopped?

**Model answer.** The branch ref moves once, in one step, when the last pick succeeds. Until then HEAD is detached, the commits are replayed on the detached HEAD, and the directory `.git/rebase-merge` records in `head-name` which branch will be moved and in `orig-head` where it was. Git does this on purpose: leaving the original branch intact until the whole replay has succeeded is what makes `git rebase --abort` possible. The consequence is that any commit made while the rebase is stopped extends the detached HEAD and has no branch name. `git push origin <branch>` sends the ref, the ref has not moved, and the push reports that everything is up to date. In the case of section 29.3 a conflict was resolved with `git commit`, `git rebase --continue` was never run, and the developer worked inside the rebase for days. Those commits are reachable only from HEAD, so an abort leaves them with the reflog as their only anchor.

**Key terms.** ref moves at the end; detached HEAD; head-name and orig-head; abort stays possible; commits without a branch name; push sends the ref

**Common weak answer.** "Each replayed commit moves the branch forward, so the work is on the branch." Weak because the branch stays at its original tip until the rebase finishes; this belief is exactly why the developer pushed and saw nothing arrive.

**Follow-up.** How do you prove with commands that this is the state, rather than a stale pull request page, and how do you stop it from recurring?

**A strong reply covers.** `git log <branch>..HEAD` lists the commits only HEAD has, `.git/rebase-merge/head-name` names the branch, and `git ls-remote origin` shows the server equal to the local branch. Prevention: read the first line of `git status` before every commit and push, and show the state in the prompt with `__git_ps1`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.3 and 29.6

#### Q404

**Question.** What does `git rebase --abort` do to commits created during the stopped rebase and to uncommitted edits? How do you protect each before running it?

**Model answer.** `git rebase --abort` re-attaches HEAD to the branch named in `head-name`, leaves that branch at `orig-head`, removes `.git/rebase-merge` and resets the index and the working tree to the original tip. Commits made inside the stopped rebase leave the branch: they lose their only anchor and survive in the HEAD reflog alone. Uncommitted changes to tracked files, staged or unstaged, are discarded, and the command prints nothing; the transcript in section 29.7 shows both edits gone after a silent abort. The two kinds of work need different protection. For the commits, one backup ref before the abort: `git branch rescue/<what> HEAD`. For the uncommitted edits, which have no object and no reflog, write them out with `git diff` and `git diff --cached` redirected to patch files, or take a copy of the whole repository with `cp -Rp`, which also keeps the operation state. That is why the worked case ran the abort only after both diffs were empty.

**Key terms.** head-name and orig-head; commits survive only in the reflog; uncommitted edits discarded silently; rescue ref; patch files; copy of the repository

**Common weak answer.** "Abort is safe, it puts everything back the way it was." Weak because it restores the branch, not the work done since: commits made inside the rebase lose their name, and staged and unstaged edits are destroyed with no message and no recovery.

**Follow-up.** Why is a bundle made with `--all` not sufficient protection in this situation, and in which order do you create the rescue ref and the bundle?
