**Model answer.** Git has a per-transport policy, `protocol.<name>.allow`, with the values `always`, `never` and `user`. For `http`, `https`, `git` and `ssh` the default is `always`; for `file` it is `user`, which permits the transport only when `GIT_PROTOCOL_FROM_USER` is unset or 1, meaning a person typed the command. `git submodule` sets that variable to 0 before it does anything, because the URLs it uses come from `.gitmodules`, a file written by whoever authored the repository, and a recursive clone runs the same code. The `user` default dates from the fix for CVE-2022-39253 in Git 2.38.1. The wider point is that a recursive clone is the one common Git operation in which a repository you have not inspected decides what else is cloned and where it is written. CVE-2024-32002 and CVE-2025-48384 both allowed a recursive clone of a hostile repository to place content where a hook could run. So clone without recursion, read `.gitmodules`, then decide, and never set `protocol.file.allow` to `always` globally; use `-c` on single commands for repositories you created.

**Key terms.** `protocol.file.allow` defaults to `user`; `GIT_PROTOCOL_FROM_USER`; URLs come from `.gitmodules`; CVE-2022-39253; hooks run during a recursive clone; clone without recursion first

**Common weak answer.** "It is a bug in newer Git; fix it with `git config --global protocol.file.allow always`." Weak because the refusal is a deliberate security default, and the global setting switches it off for every repository you will ever clone.

**Follow-up.** How does the same reasoning apply to a GitHub Actions workflow that builds pull requests from forks of a repository with submodules?

**A strong reply covers.** A workflow that recursively checks out submodules of a fork's pull request lets the fork's `.gitmodules` choose what is cloned onto the runner. Do not enable recursion for untrusted code; `actions/checkout` leaves submodules off by default, per its definition file, which the textbook did not run.

**Reference.** [Chapter 23](../textbook/ch23-submodules.md), section 23.4 and 23.18

#### Q442

**Question.** Two branches moved the same gitlink and the merge conflicts. Why can Git not resolve it, when does it resolve it by itself, and what does a correct resolution look like?

**Model answer.** Each branch recorded a different library commit, and the two commits have diverged: neither is an ancestor of the other. The correct pointer is a library commit that contains both lines of development, and only the library's repository can create that; the superproject holds IDs, not content. The index gets three stages, each a gitlink, for the merge base, ours and theirs, and there are no conflict markers because there is no file to put them in. `git submodule status` shows `U`. Git resolves the pointer by itself when one commit is an ancestor of the other: it takes the descendant and prints a note that it is fast-forwarding the submodule. That needs both commits in the submodule's local repository; where the submodule is not checked out, Git reports a conflict instead, and `-X theirs` does not help. A correct resolution checks out, inside the submodule, a library commit that contains both sides, for example the library's own merge after a `git -C <path> fetch`, then runs `git add <path>` and `git commit` in the superproject.

**Key terms.** diverged library commits; three stages, no conflict markers; the answer exists only in the library; ancestor case resolves to the descendant; both commits must be local; `git add <path>` stages the checked-out commit

**Common weak answer.** "Pick ours or theirs, the newer one wins." Weak because with diverged commits neither side contains the other, so choosing one drops the other branch's library changes, and `-X theirs` does not resolve a submodule conflict anyway.

**Follow-up.** You resolve the conflict by merging inside the submodule yourself. What has to be pushed, in which order, and what happens to a teammate if the order is wrong?

**A strong reply covers.** The merge commit made inside the submodule exists only in your clone, so it must be pushed to the library's remote first and the superproject merge second. In the wrong order a teammate's pull fails with `not our ref`; `push.recurseSubmodules=check` guards against it.

**Reference.** [Chapter 23](../textbook/ch23-submodules.md), section 23.10

#### Q443

**Question.** Explain how `git subtree split` can reproduce the original upstream commit IDs. What would break that?

**Model answer.** A subtree has no special structure in Git: the vendored directory is an ordinary tree of mode 040000 and its files are blobs in your own object database, with no `.gitmodules` and no configuration. The whole mechanism is two trailer lines in the message of the squash commit that `git subtree add` or `git subtree pull` creates: `git-subtree-dir`, the prefix, and `git-subtree-split`, the ID of the upstream commit that the content corresponds to. `git subtree split` walks your history and synthesizes a history that contains only what happened under the prefix, with the prefix removed from the paths. Through the trailers it finds the upstream commits, so the synthetic branch consists of the upstream commits themselves, with their original IDs and authors, and on top of them your commits reduced to their library part. Upstream can merge that branch as a normal contribution. What breaks it is anything that discards or rewrites those trailers: squash-merging or rebasing the commits that `git subtree` created, or editing their messages. Mixed use of `--squash` breaks the update path too.

**Key terms.** `git-subtree-split` trailer; `git-subtree-dir`; ordinary tree, mode 040000; synthesized history under the prefix; original upstream IDs; squash-merge or rebase destroys the trailers

**Common weak answer.** "Git remembers where the subtree came from, like a submodule does." Weak because there is no stored link at all: the only record is text in commit messages, and any history rewrite of those commits removes it.

**Follow-up.** A teammate squash-merged the pull request that carried a subtree update. What was lost, how do you check, and what rule do you set?

**A strong reply covers.** The commits that `git subtree` created were replaced, so the `git-subtree-split` trailer that the next pull depends on is discarded or rewritten. Search with `git log --grep` for the trailer. The rule: never squash-merge or rebase subtree commits, and update only through one script that always passes `--squash`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 23](../textbook/ch23-submodules.md), section 23.13 and 23.16

#### Q444

**Question.** What does the sparse index change, why only in cone mode, and what makes a command slower with it?

**Model answer.** A sparse checkout alone leaves the index at full size: every command still reads, and often rewrites, an index proportional to the whole repository. With `index.sparse=true`, written by `git sparse-checkout set --sparse-index`, all entries of a directory outside the cone are replaced by one sparse directory entry: mode 040000, a tree ID, the skip-worktree bit and a path ending in a slash. In the chapter's example 33 entries become 14, and the counts of entries read and of file-system checks both follow the cone. The tree IDs are those of HEAD, so Git can compare such an entry with a commit without opening it. It needs cone mode because cone mode defines the checkout by whole directories, which the chapter names as the precondition. The cost: a command that needs paths inside a collapsed directory first expands the index to a full one in memory, which Git itself calls a slow operation; `git ls-files` without `--sparse` does that. A tool that runs such a command on every prompt or save cancels the benefit. The feature is marked experimental.

**Key terms.** sparse directory entry, mode 040000; one tree ID per directory outside the cone; index shrinks with the cone; cone mode is the precondition; expansion to a full index in memory; external tools may not cope

**Common weak answer.** "The sparse index makes sparse checkouts faster, so always enable it." Weak because it helps only when the index itself is the bottleneck, and any tool that asks for every path forces an expansion that is slower than an ordinary index.

**Follow-up.** Git prints a hint that the sparse index is expanding and suggests that your working tree has content outside the cone. Do you accept that diagnosis?

**A strong reply covers.** Not without checking. In the chapter's run the hint's guess was wrong: the cause was a command that asks for every path, while the working tree matched the cone. Find the tool that runs such commands; if it cannot be changed, go back with `git sparse-checkout set --no-sparse-index`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 24](../textbook/ch24-monorepos.md), section 24.6

#### Q445

**Question.** What does `scalar clone` set up, which parts live outside the repository, and how do you remove each?

**Model answer.** According to `git help scalar` it sets up four things: a partial clone in which only commit and tree objects are cloned, with the working tree in `<enlistment>/src`; a cone-mode sparse checkout with only the top-level files unless `--full-clone` is given; configuration for large repositories, for example `commitGraph.changedPaths=true`, `core.untrackedCache=true` and `status.aheadBehind=false`; and background maintenance through the scheduler of `git maintenance start`, unless `--no-maintenance` is given. Three things end up outside the repository: a registration in the global configuration as `scalar.repo`, scheduler entries, on macOS under `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, and one file-system monitor process per enlistment. The textbook has no transcript of the command; its contained test on Git 2.55.0 found that the repository received `core.fsmonitor=true` and a daemon was left running, that `--no-maintenance` does not prevent this, and that the manual page does not list the setting although the source does. To remove them: `scalar unregister` undoes the registration and the scheduler entries, `scalar delete <enlistment>` also removes the directory, and `git fsmonitor--daemon stop` inside the working tree stops the daemon.

**Key terms.** partial clone plus cone-mode sparse checkout; large-repository settings; scheduled maintenance; global `scalar.repo` registration; file-system monitor daemon; `scalar unregister` and `git fsmonitor--daemon stop`

**Common weak answer.** "It is a faster `git clone`." Weak because it leaves out the parts that outlive the clone: a global registration, scheduler entries and a daemon that `--no-maintenance` does not prevent.

**Follow-up.** An engineer reports a background process and scheduler entries that they cannot explain. How do you establish that Scalar is the cause?

**A strong reply covers.** `scalar list` shows the registered enlistments, and `git fsmonitor--daemon status` inside a working tree shows whether its monitor is running. Then `scalar unregister` and `git fsmonitor--daemon stop` remove them.

**Reference.** [Chapter 24](../textbook/ch24-monorepos.md), section 24.7 and 24.12

#### Q446

**Question.** Our CI computes affected projects with `git diff main..HEAD`. What is wrong, and why does the fix fail in a shallow clone?

**Model answer.** Two dots compare the two tips, so the diff also contains everything `main` did since the branch forked. The pipeline then runs, and blames, jobs for projects the pull request never touched; in the chapter's example the two-dot diff lists four projects and the correct one lists one. The fix is three dots, `git diff --name-only main...HEAD`, which means from the merge base to the second commit: what the branch did since it forked. A build system then extends that list by dependency, which Git cannot know. The fix fails in a shallow clone because the merge base is a commit in the past, and a job that fetched one commit per branch with `--depth 1` does not have it: the diff stops with a no-merge-base error and `git merge-base` exits with status 1. Worse, a script that swallows the error concludes that nothing changed and skips every test. Use a full-depth fetch, or a blobless clone made with `--filter=blob:none`, which has every commit and tree; that is enough, because `git diff --name-only` compares trees.

**Key terms.** two dots compare tips; three dots diff from the merge base; shallow clone has no merge base; swallowed error skips every test; blobless clone has all commits and trees; build system adds dependencies

**Common weak answer.** "Two dots and three dots are the same for `git diff`; add `--depth 1` to make the job fast." Weak because the two forms answer different questions, and the correct one needs history that a depth-1 clone was told not to have.

**Follow-up.** State the rule for which CI jobs may be shallow, and name another kind of job that breaks for the same reason.

**A strong reply covers.** Jobs that build one snapshot may be shallow; jobs that compare, describe or compute versions may not. Version stamping with `git describe` breaks too, because a shallow clone has no tags behind its boundary. `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` confirms the state.

**Reference.** [Chapter 24](../textbook/ch24-monorepos.md), section 24.9

#### Q447

**Question.** `git status` is slow in one repository and `git log -- path` in another. How do you find out what each command is doing, without a stopwatch?

**Model answer.** I count work instead of timing it. A Git command is slow when the amount of data it must touch is large, and the dimensions are independent: tracked files, commits and trees, blob content, loose objects and packs, refs. First I measure them with `git ls-files | wc -l`, `git rev-list --count --all`, `git count-objects -v` and `git for-each-ref | wc -l`. Then I ask Git what one command did: `GIT_TRACE2_PERF=1` prints a table whose data rows carry counters, and counters are reproducible where times are not. For `git status` the counters are the index entries read, the `lstat` calls, and the directories and paths visited in the search for untracked files; when those are in the hundreds of thousands, the remedies are sparse-checkout, the untracked cache and the file-system monitor. For `git log -- path` I read the statistics line of the changed-path filters: with no line, or with filters reported as not present, every commit's tree is compared with its parent's, and the fix is `git commit-graph write --reachable --changed-paths`. Neither remedy changes history.

**Key terms.** count work, not time; `GIT_TRACE2_PERF=1`; `lstat` calls and directories visited; changed-path filter statistics; independent dimensions of size; the remedy follows the counter

**Common weak answer.** "The repository is too big; run `git gc` or split it." Weak because it measures nothing: the two commands touch different data, and the chapter maps each to its own remedy, none of which is a blanket cleanup or a history rewrite.

**Follow-up.** The changed-path statistics line appears in one clone and not in another clone of the same repository. Name the conditions under which Git does not use the commit-graph.

**A strong reply covers.** Replace objects or commit grafts turn off reading and writing of the commit-graph, and so does a shallow repository, where `git commit-graph write` writes nothing and says nothing. `core.commitGraph=false` bypasses it on purpose. The file may also have been written without `--changed-paths`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 26](../textbook/ch26-performance.md), section 26.2, 26.6 and 26.9

#### Q448

**Question.** Compare shallow, blobless and treeless clones: what each holds, what each answers correctly, and what each costs later.

**Model answer.** A shallow clone, `--depth 1`, holds the commits within the given distance of the tip with their complete trees and blobs: one commit of 96 in the chapter's repository. History questions come back wrong or failing, silently; the later cost is expensive fetches for the server and an unshallow when someone needs history. A blobless clone, `--filter=blob:none`, holds every commit and tree and only the blobs of the checkout. History questions are right; commands that read only commits and trees fetch nothing, and commands that need content fetch it on demand from the promisor remote. Its cost is one request per commit for `git log -p` and `git blame`, many small packs, and dependence on the server; `git backfill` and maintenance repair the first two. A treeless clone, `--filter=tree:0`, holds every commit and only the trees and blobs of the checkout, so a path-limited log fetches trees one commit at a time: 93 requests in the chapter. Shallow suits throwaway snapshot builds, blobless suits developers and history-reading CI, treeless suits builds that need commit history and nothing else.

**Key terms.** boundary commits; all commits and trees, blobs on demand; promisor remote; silently wrong history answers; one request per commit; `git backfill`; a treeless clone fetches trees per commit

**Common weak answer.** "They are three levels of the same optimisation; pick the smallest." Weak because a shallow clone cuts history and gives wrong answers with exit status 0, while partial clones keep the structure of history and pay with on-demand fetches and dependence on the server.

**Follow-up.** You asked for a blobless clone and the result is as large as a full one. What are the two causes, and what misleading state is left behind?

**A strong reply covers.** A clone from a local path copies files and ignores the filter, so use a `file://` URL; and a server without `uploadpack.allowFilter` ignores it too. Each prints a warning and produces a complete clone that is still configured as partial, with `remote.origin.partialclonefilter` set.

**Reference.** [Chapter 26](../textbook/ch26-performance.md), section 26.11, 26.12 and 26.13

#### Q449

**Question.** A partial clone fails with `could not fetch ... from promisor remote`. What are the two possible causes, and how do you make a laptop independent of the server for a week?

**Model answer.** A partial clone leaves out objects that a designated remote has promised to deliver, and the message means a command needed one and the promise could not be kept. The two causes are that the server is unreachable, or that the object no longer exists there, for example after a history rewrite. Everything local keeps working: in Chapter 26, section 26.12 `git log` and `git status` succeed offline, while `git show` of an old version and `git switch` to another branch fail, and the switch fails before it touches the working tree. To prepare the laptop, run `git backfill` while online: it fetches the missing blobs reachable from `HEAD` in batches, and `git maintenance run` then merges the resulting packs. Two limits: `git backfill` is experimental and needs Git 2.49 or later, and it covers the current branch, so in the chapter two objects of another branch stay missing. Check what is still absent with `git rev-list --objects --all --missing=print`. If the laptop must be fully independent, the right shape is a full clone or a bundle.

**Key terms.** promisor remote; server unreachable; object deleted on the server; `git backfill`; blobs reachable from `HEAD`; `git rev-list --objects --all --missing=print`; a partial clone is not a backup

**Common weak answer.** "The repository is corrupt; clone it again." Weak because missing promised objects are by design and `git fsck` exits 0; cloning again does not help while the server is unreachable, and the answer prepares nothing for offline work.

**Follow-up.** Why is a partial clone not a backup, and what does `git fsck` say about the objects it lacks?

**A strong reply covers.** It cannot be completed without its promisor remote: if the server loses the repository, or a history rewrite removes an object there, the promised objects are gone. `git fsck` exits 0, because a missing object referenced from a promisor pack counts as promised, not as corruption.

**Reference.** [Chapter 26](../textbook/ch26-performance.md), section 26.12, 26.16 and 26.17

#### Q450

**Question.** How do you ship weekly updates to a site with no network route to the server? What goes wrong if one shipment is lost?

**Model answer.** As bundles. A bundle is a file that holds a pack and the refs that go with it. I send one full bundle first, made with `git bundle create` and `--all`, and the site clones from it. Each week I send an incremental bundle made from a range, from a tag that records what was sent last up to the new tip. It contains only the objects the range adds and records the old end of the range as a prerequisite: a commit the receiver must already have. The site runs `git bundle verify`, fetches from the file with a refspec and fast-forwards. If one shipment is lost, the prerequisite of the next bundle is missing at the site, and both `git bundle verify` and the fetch refuse it, naming the missing commit. An incremental bundle is thin on purpose, and its deltas may be based on objects it does not contain. The fix is to apply the missing bundle, or to cut a new one from what the site has. Prevention: number the bundles and tag each basis.

**Key terms.** one full bundle, then incremental bundles; a range with a tag as its basis; prerequisite commit; `git bundle verify`; the refusal names the missing commit; thin on purpose; number the bundles

**Common weak answer.** "Copy the repository directory, or send patches each week." Weak because it has no notion of what the receiver must already have: an incremental bundle is refused without its prerequisite commit, and the answer has no plan for a lost shipment.

**Follow-up.** Besides objects and refs, what does a bundle not carry, and how can a bundle also reduce the load of ordinary clones for sites that do have a network?

**A strong reply covers.** A bundle carries no reflogs, hooks or configuration. `git clone --bundle-uri` takes the bulk of a clone from a bundle, for example on a CDN, then offers what it brought and fetches only the remainder from the server; it is incompatible with `--depth`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 26](../textbook/ch26-performance.md), section 26.14 and 26.16


### Architecture: principal level

#### Q451

**Question.** Why are hooks not cloned? Describe three ways to share them and the security cost of each.

**Model answer.** `git clone` transfers objects and refs. `.git/hooks` and `.git/config` are not transferred, by design: otherwise cloning a repository would mean agreeing to run its author's programs. The first way to share is a tracked directory such as `.githooks` plus `core.hooksPath`. The directory travels, the setting is configuration that each clone must make once, and from then on every pull can change what runs on the next commit, so changes there need review as careful as changes to CI. The second way, since Git 2.54, is a hook declared in configuration with `hook.<name>.command` and `hook.<name>.event`; a hook in the global file runs in every repository of that user, which suits a personal scanner and equally an attacker who can write that file. The third is an installer: a setup script, `init.templateDir`, or a hook manager such as the pre-commit framework, where each pinned hook repository is third-party code that runs on your machine and, in CI, next to your credentials. All three turn a pull into an update of the programs on your machine, and none of them is enforcement.

**Key terms.** clone transfers objects and refs only; `core.hooksPath`; configuration-defined hooks since Git 2.54; hook manager; pull becomes code update; third-party code; not enforcement

**Common weak answer.** "Put the hooks in the repository and everyone gets them." Weak because the files travel and the setting that activates them does not, and the answer ignores that a shared hook is code other people can change and that runs with your permissions.

**Follow-up.** A repository reaches you as a tar archive that includes its `.git` directory. What is the risk, and what is the safe way to inspect it?

**A strong reply covers.** Its `.git` came from an untrusted source, so its configuration and hooks run with your permissions: in the chapter's demo `git status` executed a command set in `core.fsmonitor` and a branch switch ran a `post-checkout` hook. The manual's remedy is `git clone --no-local`, which transfers objects and refs only.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14C](../textbook/ch14c-stash-rerere-attributes-hooks.md), section 14C.11 and 14C.12

#### Q452

**Question.** The CTO asks for a guarantee that no commit with a private key reaches `main`. Which layers do you propose, and what does each one fail to catch?

**Model answer.** No client-side layer can carry a guarantee, so I propose three layers. Layer one is a `pre-commit` hook that inspects the index for a key pattern. It gives fast feedback and fails open in four ways: it is not installed by cloning, `--no-verify` skips it, it does not run for commits made in the web interface, through an API or by a tool with its own Git implementation, and several commands that create commits do not run the commit hooks. Layer two is the place every push must pass and its author does not control. On a Git server you run, that is a `pre-receive` hook, which no client option skips. On github.com you cannot install server-side hooks; the equivalents are rulesets and push protection, which rejects a push containing a recognized secret, so it misses what it does not recognize. This is described from GitHub's documentation. Layer three is the same check in CI, required by a ruleset before a merge; it guards the merge, not the push. If a key still gets through, rotate it.

**Key terms.** client hooks fail open; `--no-verify`; `pre-receive` on a server you run; rulesets and push protection on GitHub; required CI check; recognized patterns only; rotate the key

**Common weak answer.** "We install a pre-commit hook that blocks secrets." Weak because that hook is a file in one clone that one option skips; it is feedback, not enforcement, and the answer names no place that every change must pass.

**Follow-up.** The team answers that the pre-commit framework already solves this, because its configuration is versioned and its tools are pinned. Is that a control?

**A strong reply covers.** No. It is better than hand-copied scripts, but `pre-commit install` is still a step each clone must take, `git commit --no-verify` and the framework's `SKIP` variable skip it, and each hook repository is third-party code. What enforces is the CI run, required by a ruleset. The course describes the framework from its documentation only.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14C](../textbook/ch14c-stash-rerere-attributes-hooks.md), section 14C.13 and 14C.10

#### Q453

**Question.** A team wants SHA-256 for a new service that is hosted on GitHub. What do you tell them, and how would an existing repository be converted later?

**Model answer.** I tell them to create it with SHA-1. SHA-256 repositories work locally, but GitHub had no publicly available support for them on 1 October 2026; a private preview is reported only by secondary sources and is unverified. Repositories with different object formats cannot exchange objects, so the failure would appear at the first push, after the work is done. Waiting matches the project's own plan: SHA-1 is not being deprecated, and Git 3.0 changes only the default for new repositories, on the condition that forges are ready. A later conversion is possible, but it is a migration project with a cut-over date, not a setting. History crosses the format boundary only as a stream: `git fast-export --all` piped into `git fast-import` in a repository made with `git init --object-format=sha256`. Every object gets a new ID, so signatures do not survive, and commit IDs quoted in messages, issue trackers and CI configuration point at nothing. Code that expects forty hexadecimal digits must be repaired first.

**Key terms.** no public GitHub support on 1 October 2026; formats cannot exchange objects; `git fast-export` into `git fast-import`; every object ID changes; signatures do not survive; cut-over date

**Common weak answer.** "Start on SHA-256, it is the future, and GitHub will accept it" or "switch later with a setting". Weak because github.com had no public support on the course's baseline date, the two formats cannot exchange objects, and a conversion renames every object: it is a migration, not a configuration change.

**Follow-up.** One of the two new formats can be adopted and reverted in place and the other cannot. Which is which, and why is that difference fundamental and not a gap in the tooling?

**A strong reply covers.** The ref format: `git refs migrate --ref-format=reftable` converts in place and back, within limits (no linked worktrees, no concurrent writers), because ref storage is local and the protocol never sees it. The object format decides every object ID, so changing it renames all of history.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14D](../textbook/ch14d-frontier.md), section 14D.5 and 14D.3 and 14D.13

#### Q454

**Question.** Submodule, subtree, package manager: decide for (a) an internal protocol-definition repository used by eight services, (b) a 300-line utility copied from an open-source project, (c) a tokenizer library published on a package index.

**Model answer.** For (c), use the package manager. A library that is published as a package gets versioning, transitive dependencies and security advisories from the package tooling, which neither Git mechanism attempts; a submodule there rebuilds a worse package manager. For (b), use a subtree: a small dependency that changes rarely and must be present in every clone. A plain clone is complete, with no init, no update and no second set of credentials. The price is that every vendored version stays in your history, the link to upstream lives in commit-message trailers, and everyone must update with the same options. For (a), a submodule is defensible if the definitions must remain a separate repository with their own access rules and release cadence: each of the eight services gets an exact, reviewable pin, and a release is reproducible from one superproject commit ID. I would accept it only if the team adopts the recursion and push-check configuration in every clone and CI job. If the definitions can be published with versions, a package is the better answer.

**Key terms.** published package means package manager; subtree for small, rarely changing, present after a plain clone; submodule keeps a separate repository and access rules; exact reviewable pin; local configuration in every clone; access separation lost with a subtree

**Common weak answer.** "Submodules for all three, because they are Git's built-in dependency mechanism." Weak because it ignores what each option records and what a plain clone contains, and it takes on the stale, unpushed and uninitialized failure states where a package or a copy would have none.

**Follow-up.** For case (a), the service teams keep asking for one change that updates the definitions and their service together. What does that request tell you about the design?

**A strong reply covers.** With a submodule that change is two repositories in order: commit and push in the library, then a pointer commit. If one atomic commit across both is the real wish, the projects may belong in one repository, which Chapter 24 weighs against its costs.

**Reference.** [Chapter 23](../textbook/ch23-submodules.md), section 23.14 and 23.16

#### Q455

**Question.** You are asked to introduce submodules for a team of thirty. Which four configuration settings and which CI check do you require, and why?

**Model answer.** I require four settings. `submodule.recurse true` makes switch, pull, checkout and reset follow the gitlink, which removes the stale submodule after a pull and the silent rollback that `git commit -a` makes of it. `push.recurseSubmodules check` refuses to push a pointer to a library commit that is on no remote, which prevents the `not our ref` failure for teammates. `diff.submodule log` makes diffs list the library commits between two pointers, so a reviewer can see a rewind. `status.submoduleSummary true` shows the same in `git status`. All four are local configuration and cannot be shipped with the repository, so each clone and each CI job has to set them, which in practice means a setup script. The CI check runs on a fresh clone with submodules and has an explicit step, `git submodule status`, that fails if any line starts with `-` or `+`. It is needed because an empty submodule directory is not an error to Git, so a job without it fails later and elsewhere, or silently skips tests.

**Key terms.** `submodule.recurse`; `push.recurseSubmodules check`; `diff.submodule log`; `status.submoduleSummary`; local configuration, set in every clone and CI job; `git submodule status` fails on `-` or `+`

**Common weak answer.** "Tell everyone to run `git submodule update --init` after cloning and add it to the README." Weak because it covers only the uninitialized state, relies on memory, and leaves the stale pointer, the unpushed commit and the unreadable one-line diff in place.

**Follow-up.** Assume all thirty engineers have those four settings. Which submodule failures can still happen?

**A strong reply covers.** A pointer to a commit on a library branch that is later rebased or deleted still passes `check` and becomes unobtainable, so record only commits on a protected branch or a tag. A commit made on a detached HEAD inside the submodule is still left behind by the next update.

**Reference.** [Chapter 23](../textbook/ch23-submodules.md), section 23.16, 23.12 and 23.7

#### Q456

**Question.** A shared schema library is consumed by five services. One architect wants each service to pin the library as a submodule; another wants the library and the five services in one repository. Both positions are defensible. Compare what each records and what each costs, and say which facts would decide it.

**Model answer.** With submodules each service records a gitlink, an exact commit ID, plus a URL in `.gitmodules`. The pin is reviewable as a one-line diff, a release is reproducible from one superproject commit ID, and the library keeps its own repository, permissions and release cadence. The cost: a change spanning library and service is two repositories in order, consumers pin and drift apart, and the stale, unpushed, uninitialized and detached states appear unless every clone and CI job carries the local configuration. With one repository a single commit and a single review change the schema and its consumers together, and there is one version of the library: what is in the tree. The cost: anyone who can clone reads everything, ownership needs path-based rules, CI must compute what a change affects, Git needs tuning as size grows, and a broken `main` blocks everyone. Three facts decide: whether the code changes together, whether the readers differ, and whether someone will own the tooling. If all three favour it, I choose one repository; otherwise submodules with that configuration enforced.

**Key terms.** gitlink pin versus one tree version; two repositories in order versus one atomic commit; access separation kept or lost; submodule failure states; affected-project CI and ownership rules; coupling, readers and tooling ownership decide

**Common weak answer.** "Monorepo, because submodules are painful", or the reverse. Weak because it argues from taste: it does not state what each option records, which costs move from coordination to tooling, or that a difference in readers settles the question for separate repositories.

**Follow-up.** The decision is one repository. What does the migration itself cost in Git terms, and what must exist before the first team moves in?

**A strong reply covers.** Merging repositories creates new commit IDs, so it is planned as a migration with a freeze. Path-based ownership rules and affected-project CI must exist first; without them the result is a slow repository with a red `main`.

**Reference.** [Chapter 23](../textbook/ch23-submodules.md), section 23.14 and [Chapter 24](../textbook/ch24-monorepos.md), section 24.2 and 24.13

#### Q457

**Question.** We are considering one repository for all services. Name three costs we would stop paying and three we would start paying. Which are Git's and which are tooling's?

**Model answer.** A monorepo exchanges coordination across repositories for tooling inside one. You stop paying three things. A change to a library and its users is one commit and one review, not one pull request per repository merged in order with a published version between them. There is one version of each internal dependency, what is in the tree, so consumers no longer pin and drift. And integration is no longer tested late, with release and dependency-update automation holding the repositories together. You start paying three things. Git performance degrades with total size unless tuned, and Git has no per-directory read permission, so whoever can clone reads everything: both are Git's. Ownership and review need path-based rules, which on GitHub is the CODEOWNERS file: that is the platform's. CI must compute what a change affects, which takes a dependency-aware build system and people to maintain it: that is tooling's, with Git contributing only the diff against the merge base. The failure radius also grows: a broken `main` blocks everyone. Neither layout wins outright.

**Key terms.** atomic cross-project commit; one internal version; no per-directory read permission; path-based ownership; affected-project CI and a build system; failure radius of `main`; performance degrades with size

**Common weak answer.** "A monorepo is simpler because everything is in one place, and Git scales since large companies use it." Weak because it names no cost, does not separate what Git provides from what a build system and GitHub must provide, and rests on companies whose largest repositories are not Git.

**Follow-up.** Under which conditions would you advise against the move however much is spent on tooling?

**A strong reply covers.** When some people may read some projects and not others, since Git cannot restrict reading within a repository. When projects never change together, so atomic commits buy nothing. When the content is large binaries, and when nobody will own affected-target CI and ownership rules.

**Reference.** [Chapter 24](../textbook/ch24-monorepos.md), section 24.2 and 24.13

#### Q458

**Question.** A required check has been pending for two days on a documentation pull request. Cause, and the design that avoids it?

**Model answer.** Nothing is broken in Git; this is GitHub and GitHub Actions. The workflow that produces the required check has a `paths` filter, the documentation pull request touches no matching path, and so the workflow never starts. Per GitHub's documentation, a workflow that a path filter, a branch filter or `[skip ci]` keeps from starting never reports, so its required check stays pending and the pull request cannot merge. The contrast that matters: a job that starts and is skipped by a condition reports success. Saving CI time with a path filter and protecting `main` by requiring that workflow's check therefore do not combine. The design the textbook proposes, and labels as its own inference and not a GitHub recipe, is to start one workflow on every pull request, compute the affected projects inside it, skip jobs by condition, and require one final job that fails if any job that ran has failed. The required check then always reports, and the saving comes from skipped jobs, not from a workflow that never starts.

**Key terms.** path filter means the workflow never starts; a check that never reports stays pending; a skipped job reports success; one workflow on every pull request; affected projects computed inside; one aggregate required job

**Common weak answer.** "GitHub is stuck; re-run the checks or have an administrator bypass the requirement." Weak because there is nothing to re-run: the workflow was never triggered, and bypassing the rule removes the protection without fixing the design.

**Follow-up.** In your design the single workflow computes the affected projects itself. Which failure inside that step would let a pull request merge untested, and how do you close it?

**A strong reply covers.** A shallow checkout has no merge base, and a script that swallows that error concludes nothing changed, skips every job, and the aggregate passes. Fetch full depth or use a blobless clone, and make the compute step fail on any Git error.

**Reference.** [Chapter 24](../textbook/ch24-monorepos.md), section 24.9 and 24.12

#### Q459

**Question.** A team asks for a directory that only they can read. What do you answer?

**Model answer.** That Git cannot provide it. Git has no per-directory read permission: a repository is one object database, and whoever can clone it reads everything. A sparse checkout is not access control, because it narrows one working tree while the index, the history and the objects stay complete, and `git show HEAD:<path>` prints a file outside the cone. On the GitHub layer, CODEOWNERS only requests reviews, and a ruleset or branch protection that requires them protects writes, not reads. So if some people may see some projects and not others, those projects are separate repositories. That is one of the textbook's stated cases where a monorepo is the wrong tool, and it is why its advice for an AI/ML platform is to split by coupling and keep components with other owners or other access rules in their own repositories. I would also ask what the restriction is for: if it is about who approves changes, path-based ownership inside the monorepo answers it; if it is about who may see the content, only a repository boundary does.

**Key terms.** no per-directory read permission; one object database; sparse checkout is not access control; CODEOWNERS protects writes, not reads; separate repository; split by coupling and access rules

**Common weak answer.** "Use CODEOWNERS or a sparse checkout to hide the directory." Weak because CODEOWNERS governs review of changes and a sparse checkout governs one working tree; neither stops anyone who can clone from reading every file in history.

**Follow-up.** They accept a separate repository, but its code must still be built together with the monorepo. Which ways of bringing it in keep the read restriction, and what do they cost in CI?

**A strong reply covers.** A submodule or a package registry keeps the dependency's own permissions; a subtree does not, since whoever reads the repository reads the copy. In GitHub Actions the job's token is scoped to the triggering repository, so a private submodule needs a separate token or SSH key, per the documentation.

**Reference.** [Chapter 24](../textbook/ch24-monorepos.md), section 24.2, 24.8 and 24.13

#### Q460

**Question.** To onboard engineers to a large monorepo you can standardize on `scalar clone`, or on a scripted blobless and sparse clone that the team builds by hand. Both are defensible. Compare them and say how you would decide.

**Model answer.** Both produce the same data layout: a partial clone that holds commits and trees and fetches a blob when a command first needs it, with a cone-mode sparse checkout limiting which blobs the checkout needs. `scalar clone` is one command that has shipped with Git since 2.38 and is not labelled experimental. It writes a list of large-repository settings that is maintained with Git and changes between releases, and it schedules background maintenance. What it leaves behind is outside the repository: a registration in global configuration, scheduler entries, and one file-system monitor daemon per enlistment, which in the textbook's contained test started even with `--no-maintenance`. The hand-built route is `git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse`, a `git sparse-checkout set` line in the onboarding script, settings written with `git config set`, and `git maintenance run` in the foreground. It has none of those side effects, and the team owns the script and the choice of settings. I would use Scalar on developer machines, with its removal documented, and the scripted clone where schedulers and daemons are not allowed, such as CI.

**Key terms.** same data layout; partial clone plus cone-mode sparse checkout; global registration, scheduler entries, monitor daemon; settings list changes between releases; hand-built clone has no side effects; `git maintenance run` in the foreground

**Common weak answer.** "Use Scalar, it is the official tool", or "avoid it, it is Microsoft's". Weak because neither names what the command writes outside the repository, what the scripted alternative obliges the team to maintain, or that the two fit different machines.

**Follow-up.** Whichever you choose, the clone is partial. What new failure do engineers meet when the server is unreachable, and how do you prepare for it?

**A strong reply covers.** A command that needs a blob that is not local fails with a message that it could not fetch the object from the promisor remote. Before going offline, run `git backfill --sparse`, experimental and in Git 2.49 or later, to download the history of the cone; otherwise reconnect and repeat.

**Reference.** [Chapter 24](../textbook/ch24-monorepos.md), section 24.7 and 24.14

#### Q461

**Question.** A consultant recommends `git gc --aggressive` every night. What do you answer?

**Model answer.** No, on three grounds. First, it targets a problem Git already handles: since Git 2.54 automatic maintenance uses the geometric strategy, which merges only small packs, so the cost of a run is proportional to new data, while `git gc` rewrites everything every time. Second, `--aggressive` discards all existing deltas and recomputes them, and the manual's own verdict is that it is probably not worth it without benchmarks for your repository. Third, a cron job that runs `git gc` beside automatic maintenance is unsafe housekeeping: the manual says `git gc` modifies the object database without taking the lock the way `git maintenance run` does, and recommends `git maintenance run --task=gc`. What I ask the consultant for is the measurement: which dimension is large, and which counter shows it. A slow `git status` or a slow path-limited log has other remedies. If objects really are badly packed, as in the Dropbox report where delta candidates were chosen poorly, the answer is one deliberate, benchmarked repack on the server, not a nightly habit. Leave `maintenance.auto` on.

**Key terms.** geometric strategy since 2.54; `--aggressive` recomputes every delta; benchmarks first; `git gc` does not take the maintenance lock; `git maintenance run --task=gc`; measure the dimension that is large

**Common weak answer.** "More garbage collection cannot hurt, so schedule it." Weak because it rewrites every pack each night for no measured gain, runs without the maintenance lock, and duplicates what automatic maintenance already does incrementally.

**Follow-up.** Suppose measurement does show that the packs are far larger than the content explains. What would justify a one-off full repack with non-default settings, and how would you run it?

**A strong reply covers.** Evidence that delta selection went wrong, as in Dropbox's 2026 report, where a server-side repack with a larger window and depth took a monorepo from 87 GB to 20 GB by its own figures. Run it once, with benchmarks for our repository, and not beside automatic maintenance.

**Reference.** [Chapter 26](../textbook/ch26-performance.md), section 26.3, 26.15 and 26.17


## Area 18: CTO interview

Q462 to Q482. Cross-cutting questions on judgment, trade-offs and communication. They assume every other area.


### CTO interview: foundational level

#### Q462

**Question.** "The merge is blocked." Give one root cause in each of the three layers (Git, GitHub, GitHub Actions) and say why the layer matters for the fix.

**Model answer.** Git stops a merge when both sides changed the same lines: that is a conflict, and the fix is a resolution in the working tree and the index. GitHub stops a merge when a ruleset requires a review that has not been given: the fix is a review, or a change to the rule by someone allowed to make it. GitHub Actions stops a merge when a required check has not reported success: the fix is in the workflow, in the code under test or in the check configuration. In a chat message the three look alike, and the fixes have nothing in common. So the first step is evidence that names the layer, and every explanation says which layer acted. A pull request, a review and a ruleset are GitHub objects; Git itself has commits, branches and merges only.

**Key terms.** layer; conflict; ruleset; required check; GitHub object; evidence before fix

**Common weak answer.** "There must be a conflict." Weak because it assumes the Git layer from a symptom that names no layer, and two of the three causes involve no conflict at all.

**Follow-up.** Someone reports "CI is red". Give one possible cause in each layer, and say what decides between them.

**A strong reply covers.** A Git fact: the commit lacks a file. A GitHub fact: the check ran on the merge ref and not on the branch tip. A GitHub Actions fact: the runner image changed. The wording of the complaint decides nothing; evidence does.

**Reference.** [Chapter 1](../textbook/ch01-fundamentals.md), section 1.5; [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.1

#### Q463

**Question.** What is the difference between a symptom and a hypothesis? Restate "the commit is broken" as a symptom.

**Model answer.** A symptom is what was observed, without interpretation: the exact text on the screen, the failing check, the missing line. A hypothesis is a mechanism plus a prediction, for example "if the branch was reset, the branch reflog has a `reset: moving to` entry". "The commit is broken" is already a guess, because it names a cause. As a symptom it becomes, for example, "CI fails with a timeout after 60 seconds on `main`, and the same test passes on the author's laptop". The distinction matters because a guess stated as a symptom removes every other mechanism from consideration before any evidence exists. I ask the reporter for the exact text, for the last three commands they remember, and whether anything was done since. The scrollback often contains the commit ID that the recovery will need.

**Key terms.** symptom; hypothesis; mechanism plus prediction; exact text; no interpretation

**Common weak answer.** Treating the reporter's sentence, such as "my commits are gone", as the diagnosis. Weak because the sentence names no state and no layer.

**Follow-up.** Why does the method want the symptom recorded before any command is run?

**A strong reply covers.** Verification repeats the commands that showed the problem, and the evidence must have changed for the predicted reason. Without a recorded symptom there is nothing to compare the result with.

**Reference.** [Chapter 1](../textbook/ch01-fundamentals.md), section 1.10; [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.2

#### Q464

**Question.** A CTO does not ask "which command fixes this". Which four questions does a CTO ask about a repository problem, and which of them can a command answer?

**Model answer.** The four questions are: what happened, how do you know, what will the fix change, and how do we stop it from happening again. No repair command answers any of them. "What happened" is a statement about state: what the working tree, the index, HEAD, the refs and the server held. "How do you know" is evidence: the output of read-only commands, kept. "What will the fix change" is a risk statement: which refs move, whether uncommitted work or published history is touched, and how the change is undone. "How do we stop it" is a control: a setting, a rule or a check, not a promise to be careful. Commands serve the second question only. That is why I diagnose with read-only commands first and choose the fix after I can name the root cause and its layer: Git, GitHub or GitHub Actions.

**Key terms.** state; evidence; root cause; layer; lowest-risk fix; control

**Common weak answer.** "I would find the command that fixes it and run it." Weak because it answers none of the four questions and acts before the state is understood, which is when most of the damage is done.

**Follow-up.** Give the four answers, one sentence each, for the case "the fix was committed and did not ship".

**A strong reply covers.** CI checked out the commit, and the commit lacked one of the two edited files; `git status` showed that file modified and not staged; the fix is one new commit and rewrites nothing; prevention is reading `git status` and `git diff --cached` before each commit.

**Reference.** [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.1; [Chapter 1](../textbook/ch01-fundamentals.md), section 1.10 and 1.12


### CTO interview: working engineer level

#### Q465

**Question.** In the root-cause framework every step up to and including naming the root cause is read-only. Why is that rule there, and what is the one kind of change that is allowed before the fix?

**Model answer.** Because most damage in a Git incident is done after the incident, by the first repair attempt. The original problem is rarely destructive: Git keeps unreachable commits for weeks. The second command, typed before the state was understood, is what removes an uncommitted change or rewrites a published branch. Read-only diagnosis cannot make the situation worse, and it can be repeated. The method therefore has three phases with different permissions. The first is read-only and ends when the root cause and its layer are named. The second preserves: it adds a backup ref, a copy of the repository or a bundle, and removes nothing. The third is the first moment at which a ref moves or a file is overwritten. Preservation is the one kind of change allowed before the fix, because it only adds.

**Key terms.** read-only; first repair attempt; preserve; backup ref; three phases; uncommitted work

**Common weak answer.** "Looking first is slower; I fix it and check afterwards." Weak because a fix chosen before the diagnosis is the usual source of the loss that cannot be recovered.

**Follow-up.** What does the "preserve" phase add, and why does time pressure never justify skipping it?

**A strong reply covers.** A name for every state that may be needed: a backup ref, a copy of the repository, or a bundle. A backup ref takes about a second and keeps one commit and everything it reaches from garbage collection for as long as the ref exists.

**Reference.** [Chapter 1](../textbook/ch01-fundamentals.md), section 1.10; [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.1 and 29.2

#### Q466

**Question.** Why is one hypothesis "a belief, not an analysis"? How many do you write before testing, and what makes a test a good one?

**Model answer.** With one hypothesis I look for confirmation, and almost any output can be read as confirming it. With three I look for the command whose output separates them. So I write at least three before testing any, each as a mechanism plus a prediction. A good test is one read-only command whose output would differ if the hypothesis were true. I run it, keep the output and discard what it rules out. The mechanism that survives is the root cause, and I name its layer. The step before this is being able to state what the working tree, the index, HEAD, the refs, the reflogs and the server hold, because hypotheses are generated from the state and not from the wording of the report.

**Key terms.** mechanism plus prediction; at least three; distinguishing command; confirmation; read-only test

**Common weak answer.** "I usually know what it is from experience." Weak because experience supplies the first hypothesis only, and the procedure exists for the cases in which that one is wrong.

**Follow-up.** A developer says "my commits are gone". Give three hypotheses, each with the command whose output would separate it from the others.

**A strong reply covers.** The branch was reset: `git reflog show <branch>` has a reset entry. The commits were made on a detached HEAD, for example inside a stopped rebase: the first lines of `git status` say so. The commits are on another branch: `git branch -a --contains <id>` names it.

**Reference.** [Chapter 1](../textbook/ch01-fundamentals.md), section 1.10; [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.2

#### Q467

**Question.** Every explanation in this course ends in the same seven-line form. What are the seven lines, and how does "root cause" differ from "mechanism"?

**Model answer.** The lines are: observed behavior, Git state, mechanism, root cause, why Git does this, correct fix, and prevention. The mechanism is what Git does with a given state. It is general and it is not a fault. The root cause is the one fact that, had it been different, would have prevented the symptom. It is specific to the case. In the example of the fix that was committed and did not ship, the mechanism is that `git commit` records the index and CI checks out the commit, while the local test reads the working tree. The root cause is that the second edited file was never added to the index. The line "why Git does this" gives the design reason, here that the index exists so that you choose what a commit contains. Prevention then changes a habit, a setting or a rule, so that the problem cannot recur silently.

**Key terms.** observed behavior; state; mechanism; root cause; design reason; prevention

**Common weak answer.** Giving the mechanism as the root cause, for example "Git only commits staged files". Weak because it describes normal behavior and names nothing that could have been different.

**Follow-up.** Why does the fix line ask for the lowest-risk fix and not for "the correct fix"?

**A strong reply covers.** Several fixes usually repair the state. They are ranked by what each can destroy and how each is undone: adding a ref or a commit comes before moving a ref, overwriting the working tree, rewriting the server or removing the safety net.

**Reference.** [Chapter 1](../textbook/ch01-fundamentals.md), section 1.10 and 1.12

#### Q468

**Question.** What does it mean to "understand the state" of a repository before forming a hypothesis? Name the places you must be able to describe and a command for each.

**Model answer.** It means being able to say, for the repository in front of me, what seven places hold, each with the command that shows it. The working tree: which files differ from the index and which are untracked or ignored, from `git status` and `git diff`. The index: what the next commit would record and whether conflict stages exist, from `git diff --cached` and `git ls-files -s`. HEAD: a branch or a raw commit ID, and whether an operation is in progress. The refs: where each branch, tag and remote-tracking branch points and what each upstream is, from `git branch -vv` and `git for-each-ref`. The history of the refs, from `git reflog`. The server as it is now, from `git ls-remote origin`, as opposed to its state at the last fetch. And what GitHub recorded: pushes, rule evaluations and checks. Hypotheses come after that.

**Key terms.** working tree; index; HEAD; refs and upstreams; reflog; `git ls-remote`; platform records

**Common weak answer.** "I look at `git log`." Weak because the log shows the history reachable from HEAD and none of the other six places.

**Follow-up.** Which of these places does a colleague's clone not share with yours, and why does that matter in an investigation?

**A strong reply covers.** The working tree, the index, HEAD, local branches, reflogs, stashes and configuration belong to one clone. Evidence must therefore be collected in the clone where the event happened, and a statement such as "it is gone" is a statement about that clone.

**Reference.** [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.2

#### Q469

**Question.** Ten minutes into an incident the CTO asks for a status, and you have no root cause yet. What do you say?

**Model answer.** I give the same four parts as a final summary, with what I have. What happened: what is affected, since when, and the impact in business terms, without names. Root cause: not known yet, and I say when the next update comes. What was done: the things that are already true, for example that the affected branch is frozen and its current state is preserved under a backup ref. Prevention: nothing yet. I separate what I observed from what I infer, and I give every time and every ID a source. I do not say that something is verified unless I ran the check. The first message goes out as soon as I know which branch people must leave alone, long before I know the cause, because silence during an incident is read as "it is worse than they say".

**Key terms.** observed versus inferred; time of next update; frozen branch; backup ref; not yet verified; business impact

**Common weak answer.** "I will report when I have found the cause." Weak because silence is read as bad news, and the team keeps pushing to the affected branch in the meantime.

**Follow-up.** What is the first instruction to the team in an incident on a shared branch, and why is it not a Git command?

**A strong reply covers.** One sentence that stops the spread: nobody pushes to or resets the affected branch until told otherwise. Stabilising usually means stopping people and not a process, because Git almost never destroys committed work by itself.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.2 and 30.15


### CTO interview: senior level

#### Q470

**Question.** A colleague's answer to every Git problem is "delete the folder and clone again". What does a fresh clone restore, and what does it destroy?

**Model answer.** A clone brings what the server has: commits, trees, file contents, annotated tags, and the server's branches as remote-tracking branches. So it repairs a damaged local repository as far as the work was pushed. It destroys everything that exists only in that `.git` directory and working tree: uncommitted and untracked files, the index, local branches and commits that were never pushed, stashes, reflogs, hooks and local configuration. None of those arrive with a clone, because each clone has its own. In an incident it is the worst trade, since the reflogs are evidence: the history of a server-side branch exists only as the sum of what the clones remember, plus what the platform records. So before anyone clones again I copy the directory or read its reflogs, and I ask colleagues not to run `git fetch --prune`, `git gc` or a new clone until that is done.

**Key terms.** local only; reflog; stash; unpushed commits; evidence; copy first

**Common weak answer.** "Cloning again gives you a clean, correct repository." Weak because "clean" means that the unpushed work and the local evidence are gone, and the cause was never identified.

**Follow-up.** When is a fresh clone the correct step, and what must come before it?

**A strong reply covers.** After a deliberate history rewrite, for example the removal of a secret: a stale clone that merges old and new history brings the secret back. First preserve unpushed work; then clone again, or rebase onto the new history and never merge.

**Reference.** [Chapter 1](../textbook/ch01-fundamentals.md), section 1.5; [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.2; [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.7

#### Q471

**Question.** A branch and a tag are both names. Why does this course tell you to gate a deployment on a commit ID or an image digest, and not on either name?

**Model answer.** Because a name is a ref, and a ref can be moved; a commit ID cannot refer to anything else. A branch moves with every push, and after an amend, a rebase or a cherry-pick it can point at a new commit object with the same tree as the reviewed one: the diff is empty and the ID differs, because the committer line is part of the commit object. A tag is meant as a promise about content, but `git tag -f` followed by a forced push replaces it on the server, while clones that already have the tag keep the old value: fetch refuses to overwrite an existing tag, and a plain fetch does not report the difference. Then two builds labelled with one version contain different code. So the deploy gate compares the approved commit ID, and a server-side rule forbids updating or deleting release tags.

**Key terms.** ref versus ID; committer line; same tree; moved tag; fetch does not overwrite tags; approved ID

**Common weak answer.** "Tags are immutable, so deploying a tag is safe." Weak because a tag is a movable ref unless the server forbids it, and clones disagree silently after a move.

**Follow-up.** Two commits have different IDs and an empty diff between them. How do you prove that they hold the same content, and what happens to the approval?

**A strong reply covers.** Compare the trees: `git rev-parse X^{tree} Y^{tree}` prints the same ID twice. Then either move the branch back to the reviewed commit or have the new commit approved; they are not the same commit.

**Reference.** [Chapter 6](../textbook/ch06-commits.md), section 6.4; [Chapter 14B](../textbook/ch14b-config-tags-signing.md), section 14B.11

#### Q472

**Question.** After a squash merge, `git branch -d` refuses to delete the branch, a second pull request from the same branch lists the old commits again and conflicts, and "is my branch merged?" gets different answers. State the single mechanism behind all three.

**Model answer.** Content was merged without ancestry. A squash merge puts one commit with a single parent on the base branch. It copies the changes of the branch and records no link to the commits of the branch. In Git, "merged" means reachable, and the merge base is computed from parent links only. So the branch tip is not an ancestor of `main`: `git branch -d` (which compares with HEAD once the branch has no upstream left to compare with), `git branch --merged` and `git merge-base --is-ancestor` all answer "not merged". The merge base stays at the original fork point, so a second pull request from the same branch lists the old commits again, and the three-way merge sees both sides adding the same file with different content. Git never compares patches to guess that a change is already there. The prevention is one squash per branch: delete the head branch after the merge and start new work from `main`.

**Key terms.** content without ancestry; reachable; merge base; single-parent commit; fork point; one squash per branch

**Common weak answer.** "GitHub has not updated the branch status yet." Weak because nothing is out of date: Git's answer is correct for its definition of merged, and the cause is the merge method.

**Follow-up.** The branch was reused and now carries new commits on top of the squashed ones. What is the lowest-risk repair, and how do you test "merged" correctly from now on?

**A strong reply covers.** Transplant only the new commits with `git rebase --onto origin/main <last squashed commit>`. Test content and not ancestry: an empty `git diff main <branch>`, or a merge-tree comparison once `main` has moved further.

**Reference.** [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.12; [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.9 and 17.12; [Chapter 27](../textbook/ch27-open-source-team-workflows.md), section 27.3

#### Q473

**Question.** "A remote-tracking branch is a record of your last fetch, not a view of the server." Describe two failures that follow from forgetting this: one in which the record is too old, and one in which it is newer than what you have looked at.

**Model answer.** Too old: `git status` says that the branch is up to date with `origin/main` while the server has newer commits. Status compares two local refs and opens no connection, so the statement is only as fresh as the last fetch. Before a decision that depends on the server, such as tagging or cutting a hotfix branch, I fetch, or I ask with `git ls-remote origin main`, which changes nothing. Newer than I looked: `git push --force-with-lease` overwrites a teammate's commit that I never saw. The lease compares the server's ref with my remote-tracking ref, and a fetch had already moved that ref to the teammate's commit, so "nothing changed since I looked" was true for Git and false for me. A remote-tracking ref records what my clone fetched, not what I have seen or integrated. The defence is `--force-if-includes` together with the lease, or an explicit expected value.

**Key terms.** remote-tracking ref; last fetch; `git ls-remote`; lease; any fetch renews it; `--force-if-includes`

**Common weak answer.** "`origin/main` is the branch on GitHub." Weak because it is a local ref, and both failures come from treating it as live.

**Follow-up.** Why does Git not contact the server for `git status`, and what should a release script compare against instead?

**A strong reply covers.** Every command except the transfer commands works offline and at once; a status that needed the network would be slow, and useless without a connection. Scripts compare against `git ls-remote`, never against a remote-tracking ref of unknown age.

**Reference.** [Chapter 12](../textbook/ch12-remote-operations.md), section 12.4 and 12.8

#### Q474

**Question.** During an investigation, where can the real clock change what Git shows you? Give two cases and say what you do about each.

**Model answer.** Two cases that the textbook demonstrates. First, date arguments: `--since=2026-09-10` is read as that date at the present time of day, so commits made earlier that morning are omitted, and an `--until` boundary shifts in the same way. In incident notes and scripts I write the full timestamp, for example `--since='2026-09-10 00:00'`, and I state the time zone. Second, retention: reflog entries are trimmed against the real clock, by default after 90 days, and after 30 days for entries that the current tip no longer reaches. So evidence that exists today may not exist next month, and I anchor what I may need with a branch or a tag at once. A related detail: since Git 2.53.0, `git fsck` ignores reflog entries dated later than the moment it starts, so a commit with a future committer date can be reported as dangling while `git reflog` still lists it.

**Key terms.** date parsing; time of day; retention; reflog expiry; anchor with a ref; time zone

**Common weak answer.** "Git history is immutable, so time does not matter." Weak because commits are immutable, while reflogs are subject to expiry in real time and date filters are parsed relative to now.

**Follow-up.** A postmortem timeline gives a time for each event. What must each time carry?

**A strong reply covers.** A time zone and a source: the reflog entry, the tag, the log line or the message it was taken from. Observed facts and inferences are marked as what they are.

**Reference.** [Chapter 14A](../textbook/ch14a-history-investigation.md), section 14A.9; [Chapter 13](../textbook/ch13-recovery.md), section 13.4; [Chapter 3](../textbook/ch03-git-internals.md), section 3.8

#### Q475

**Question.** A wrong version string, a "no merge base" error in a changed-files step, and an empty changelog, each of them only in CI. What is the common root cause, and what rule do you give the teams?

**Model answer.** Each job asked a history question of a clone that was told to have no history. The `actions/checkout` action defaults to `fetch-depth: 1` and `fetch-tags: false`, so the runner has one commit, a `.git/shallow` file that marks it as a boundary, and no tags. That is a GitHub Actions default and not Git misbehaving: a shallow repository is complete up to its boundary, and Git cannot know that the question reaches further. `git describe` needs a tagged ancestor and the commits in between; a comparison needs a merge base; a changelog needs the walk. The rule: a job that builds one snapshot and is thrown away may be shallow; a job that compares, describes or computes a version may not. Those jobs set `fetch-depth: 0` or use a blobless clone, which has every commit and tree. Nobody silences the error with `--always` or a fallback value, because that ships a wrong version.

**Key terms.** shallow clone; `fetch-depth`; boundary commit; `git describe`; merge base; blobless clone

**Common weak answer.** "CI has a different Git version." Weak because the layer is wrong: the cause is a checkout default, and a depth-1 clone made on a laptop fails the same way.

**Follow-up.** How do you confirm from inside a job that the clone is shallow, and how do you make a release job fail instead of shipping a fallback version?

**A strong reply covers.** `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` prints true and `.git/shallow` exists. Make the release job fail when `git describe --exact-match` fails, and never append a fallback to the version command.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20A](../textbook/ch20a-actions-fundamentals.md), section 20A.8; [Chapter 24](../textbook/ch24-monorepos.md), section 24.9; [Chapter 26](../textbook/ch26-performance.md), section 26.11; [Chapter 14B](../textbook/ch14b-config-tags-signing.md), section 14B.12

#### Q476

**Question.** A senior engineer with ten years of Git says that a fixed diagnosis ritual is for juniors. Respond.

**Model answer.** The ritual exists because people under pressure skip the one command that would have shown the cause, and seniority does not change that. The textbook cites a study of Stack Exchange data: in 2020, 40.0% of the people asking Git-command questions had been registered for more than five years, against 21.2% of all askers. Long experience does not remove the need to ask. A fixed procedure replaces confidence: the same commands, in the same order, including when I think I already know the answer. The evidence is then collected before anything changes, has the same shape in every incident, and can be handed to a colleague. In the worked case of the push that had nothing to push, the decisive fact, a rebase still in progress with HEAD detached, was visible in `git status`, and the developer had worked inside that rebase for days.

**Key terms.** fixed procedure; pressure; same order every time; evidence before change; confidence is not evidence

**Common weak answer.** "Experts can go straight to the cause." Weak because it is the belief the cited data contradicts, and it is how an unfinished rebase went unnoticed for days.

**Follow-up.** Which parts of the picture can the fixed set of local commands never show, and where do you get them?

**A strong reply covers.** What the server holds now, from `git ls-remote origin` and not from a remote-tracking ref; and what GitHub recorded: which authenticated account moved a ref and whether a rule allowed it. A clone cannot know who pushed, and the author field of a commit does not say.

**Reference.** [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.1 and 29.3; [Chapter 1](../textbook/ch01-fundamentals.md), section 1.11


### CTO interview: principal level

#### Q477

**Question.** "Never force-push" and "force-push your own branch with a lease" are both defensible team rules. Where do you draw the line, and on which layer do you enforce each side of it?

**Model answer.** I draw the line at who else has the commits. A forced push replaces the server's ref, and every clone that held the old commits must be repaired by its owner, so on a branch that others pull or push it turns one person's problem into every clone's problem. On default, release and production branches the rule is no forced update at all, enforced where the server refuses: a ruleset that blocks force pushes and deletions. A client alias or a handbook line is weaker, because it works only until someone has another configuration. On those branches the undo is `git revert`. On a personal topic branch a rewrite is acceptable with `--force-with-lease` plus `--force-if-includes`, or with an explicit expected value, because the bare lease is defeated by anything that fetches in the background. The exception is an incident in which the forced push is itself the repair: then the expected old value is stated and the team is told first.

**Key terms.** who else has the commits; ruleset; the server refuses; `--force-if-includes`; expected value; revert on shared branches

**Common weak answer.** "`--force-with-lease` is always safe." Weak because a background fetch renews the lease, and no client-side flag protects a branch in the way a server rule does.

**Follow-up.** A pull request branch is personal, but it carries a reviewer's comments and an approval. What does a forced push do there?

**A strong reply covers.** This is platform behavior, not Git: a forced push marks review comments as outdated, and a push to the head branch reruns workflows and can dismiss approvals. Verification therefore includes reading the pull request page again.

**Reference.** [Chapter 12](../textbook/ch12-remote-operations.md), section 12.8; [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.9 and 29.10; [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.20

#### Q478

**Question.** Git's safety nets have limits. For the reflog, `ORIG_HEAD` and `--force-with-lease`, state what each protects and one situation in which it fails.

**Model answer.** The reflog records past values of HEAD and of each branch in one clone, so a commit that a ref no longer names can be found again. It fails for work that was never committed or staged, because no object exists. It is trimmed by a retention policy, by default 90 days, and 30 days for entries that are no longer reachable. A branch's own reflog goes when the branch is deleted. And it is local: the server's history is not in it. `ORIG_HEAD` holds the position before the last reset, merge, rebase or am. It is one file with no notion of a branch or a command, and cherry-pick does not write it, so using it as "undo the last command" can move a branch to a value left by another operation. `--force-with-lease` refuses when the server's ref differs from my remote-tracking ref, and any fetch renews that lease. So I anchor with a ref, undo by reflog entry, and state the expected value.

**Key terms.** retention; local only; no object for uncommitted work; one file; any fetch renews the lease; backup ref

**Common weak answer.** "The reflog means nothing is ever lost." Weak because it ignores uncommitted work, expiry, the log of a deleted branch and everything that happened on the server.

**Follow-up.** Which single habit covers the weaknesses of all three, and what does that habit not preserve?

**A strong reply covers.** Give the state a name before changing anything: `git branch rescue/<what> <id>` or a ref under `refs/backup/`. It keeps the commit and everything it reaches. It does not hold reflogs, the index, uncommitted files or operation state.

**Reference.** [Chapter 13](../textbook/ch13-recovery.md), section 13.4 and 13.8; [Chapter 12](../textbook/ch12-remote-operations.md), section 12.8; [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.5

#### Q479

**Question.** One team wants a linear history through squash merges; another wants merge commits. State what each choice costs in terms of mechanisms, so that the decision is an informed one.
