**Model answer.** A squash merge puts one single-parent commit on `main`. The cost is ancestry. The commits of the branch are not reachable from `main`, so `git branch -d` refuses once the remote-tracking branch is gone, tests for "merged" fail, and any reuse of the branch, or a branch stacked on it, shows the old commits again and can conflict, because the merge base never moved. The remedy is procedural: delete the head branch after merging, start new work from `main`, and transplant stacked work with `git rebase --onto`. A merge commit keeps ancestry, so those problems do not arise, and `git log --first-parent main` lists the integrations one line each. Its cost appears when a merge is reverted: the revert removes the content and leaves the merge in the graph, so merging the repaired branch later brings only the new commits, unless the revert is reverted first. Neither choice is wrong. I choose per repository and write the consequence into the team's procedure.

**Key terms.** ancestry; single-parent commit; merge base; first-parent history; revert of a merge; delete the head branch

**Common weak answer.** "Squash is cleaner and merge commits are messy." Weak because it argues about appearance and names none of the mechanisms that produce the later incidents.

**Follow-up.** After a merge was reverted, what is the correct sequence to bring the repaired feature back, and where do you write that down?

**A strong reply covers.** Revert the revert and then merge the branch, or recreate the branch as new commits. Write the procedure into the message of the revert commit, where the next person will read it.

**Reference.** [Chapter 17](../textbook/ch17-pull-requests.md), section 17.9 and 17.12; [Chapter 11](../textbook/ch11-reset-revert-restore.md), section 11.9; [Chapter 8](../textbook/ch08-merge.md), section 8.13

#### Q480

**Question.** Several incidents in this course trace back to a default. Name three, give the layer of each, and say whether you would change the default or add a control around it.

**Model answer.** First, a GitHub Actions default: `actions/checkout` fetches one commit and no tags, so a job that runs `git describe` gets a wrong version or fails. I keep the default, because most jobs need only the snapshot, and set `fetch-depth: 0` in the jobs that ask history a question. Second, a Git default: creating a branch from a remote-tracking branch records that branch as the upstream, so after `git switch -c feature origin/main` a plain `git pull` integrates `main` while the push targets another branch. I create feature branches with `--no-track` or from local `main`, and read the brackets in `git branch -vv` before the first push. Third, a GitHub default: naming an environment that does not exist creates it without protection rules, so a production gate that was assumed from the YAML never existed. There I add a control: create environments first, keep their configuration in a reviewed script, and read the rules back.

**Key terms.** default; layer; `fetch-depth`; upstream; environment protection rules; verify the gate

**Common weak answer.** "Git and GitHub have bad defaults." Weak because each default is right for its common case; the failure was not knowing which question the job, the branch or the gate depended on.

**Follow-up.** What is the general test for whether to change a default for everyone or to add a check at the place where it bites?

**A strong reply covers.** Ask why the default exists and what a change would block that is legitimate. A client default works until someone has another configuration; a server rule or a pipeline check applies to everyone, so prefer the strongest layer that can refuse the action.

**Reference.** [Chapter 20A](../textbook/ch20a-actions-fundamentals.md), section 20A.8; [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.4; [Chapter 20B](../textbook/ch20b-actions-delivery-debugging.md), section 20B.4

#### Q481

**Question.** You enabled a control after an incident. How do you know that it works, and what else do you check about it?

**Model answer.** A control that was never exercised is an assumption. The last of the four questions that lead from a root cause to a control is exactly this: how will you know it works. For a ruleset the evidence is Rule Insights, which records every ref update that the ruleset evaluated as passed, failed or bypassed. For a fix in code it is a regression test that fails when the fix is removed. For a gate such as environment reviewers it is a harmless run that must wait, plus reading the configuration back from the API, because the YAML only names the environment. I check three more things. Which layer the control sits on: a refusal by the server outranks a client default or a checklist line. What legitimate action it will block, and what the path for that case is. And who is exempt, because an exempt actor skips enforcement without the signals that a bypass generates.

**Key terms.** verify the control; Rule Insights; regression test; legitimate exception; bypass and exemption; strongest layer

**Common weak answer.** "We turned on branch protection, so it cannot happen again." Weak because nothing was tested: the rule may not match the branch, may be bypassed, or may depend on a feature the current plan does not include.

**Follow-up.** The postmortem lists ten actions. How do you decide which of them matter?

**A strong reply covers.** Prefer one strong control to five weak ones. Rank by strength: the server refuses, automation checks, a safe client default, a checklist or review step, training. An action without an owner and a date is a wish.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.20; [Chapter 20B](../textbook/ch20b-actions-delivery-debugging.md), section 20B.4; [Chapter 29](../textbook/ch29-production-troubleshooting.md), section 29.8

#### Q482

**Question.** A postmortem draft names the engineer who ran the command and ends with one action: "engineers will take more care with force pushes". What do you send back, and why?

**Model answer.** Two corrections. First, the names. Replace every name by a role and read the document again: if it still explains the incident, it is about the system; if it does not, the cause has not been found. "An engineer force-pushed production" explains nothing. "The production branch accepted a forced update from any member with write access" names something that can be changed. Blameless is also a practical requirement: the evidence comes from people's reflogs and accounts, and people who expect blame clone again, run `git gc` or stay silent. Second, the action. A promise to be careful is the weakest kind of control: it decays and does not reach new people. I ask which layer could have refused the action and what the strongest control on that layer is, here a ruleset that blocks force pushes on the branch, with an owner, a date and a way to know that it works.

**Key terms.** roles instead of names; system not person; control; strongest layer; owner and date; evidence comes from people

**Common weak answer.** "Add a line to the handbook and remind everyone." Weak because it is the lowest-ranked control and leaves the branch accepting the same push tomorrow.

**Follow-up.** The team objects that a ruleset on the production branch will block a legitimate emergency fix. How do you answer?

**A strong reply covers.** That is one of the four questions for every control: what will it block that is legitimate, and what is the path for that case. Define the path in advance instead of leaving the branch open to everyone, and check afterwards that the control works.

**Reference.** [Chapter 30](../textbook/ch30-incident-response.md), section 30.19 and 30.20
